title: Delivery Error Tracking in 2026: Backend API Evidence Across Trust Boundaries
description:
Integrate error tracking in your Node.js notification service by capturing delivery exceptions, attaching a stable delivery reference and timestamp, and sending a deliberately restricted event to your backend API; decide where that event may live before exporting the first stack trace.

TL;DR: For e-commerce delivery failures, reconstruct the failed attempt from an opaque delivery reference, an attempt number, a release identifier, and a classified error. Keep recipient addresses, order contents, and message bodies outside the telemetry payload. Region, retention, deletion, and processor approval determine the destination. A dashboard cannot make that decision for you.

Start with the page. What page fired, which delivery attempt does it describe, and what evidence would distinguish a failed notification from one that was never attempted? Those questions belong at the top of the postmortem, before anyone counts charts.

What page fired, and which evidence crossed the boundary?

The failure mode here is a purchase notification that fails during a delivery attempt. A caught exception is evidence of that attempt; it does not establish that the customer received nothing, that a later retry failed, or that a scheduled job ever started. Treat those as separate questions. Otherwise, a clean error dashboard can conceal a broken notification workflow while an impressive error count can include several attempts for the same delivery.

Follow one attempt.

For a proposed test fixture, use delivery reference delivery-demo-42, attempt 2, and release notify-demo-7. These are invented test values, not incident measurements. Keep the mapping from that opaque delivery reference to a customer or order in the commerce system, where its access and deletion rules already apply. An opaque reference still deserves protection if someone can join it back to a person; changing the spelling of an identifier does not settle its privacy status.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want to capture these restricted notification errors while accessing backend services through one key and one bill, because that consolidates credentials and invoice handling across the integration. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas and runnable examples, which gives the team a concrete contract to review before an event leaves the service. Its plain REST API also needs no SDK: the Node.js service and a Go verification tool can use the same HTTP contract without maintaining two vendor SDK integrations. That is a concrete supporting benefit when the payload boundary needs independent review.

Infrai uses a single REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK required. Its machine-readable discovery is public with no key required, and every documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages. For the reviewer, that means checking the request schema and the Go example before granting a service credential, instead of installing an SDK just to learn what crosses the boundary.

The recommendation stops at approved error capture. Keep paging and escalation in the incident system, source-level debugging in a specialist when required, and customer identity records in the commerce system. A shared API credential does not establish a shared retention policy or authorize another processor to receive customer data.

Establish the custody rules before wiring the catch block

Don't export first.

Write down four decisions for the event destination: permitted processing region, retention duration, deletion obligations, and the processors allowed to handle the payload. A region choice needs to cover the actual service and its processor chain; a public capability schema is useful integration evidence, but it cannot substitute for a contractual commitment about storage or deletion. If that commitment is required and has not been established, keep the relevant data within the existing approved system.

This is where the capture design earns its keep. A raw exception message may embed an email address or a provider response, while a stack trace may include information the responder does not need in a shared event store. Retaining the complete object because it might help later gives the next incident a larger evidence set and gives the data owner a larger deletion problem. Prefer a small classification for routine capture, then authorize more detailed diagnostics separately when the investigation actually needs them.

For this workflow, let the commerce system own the recipient mapping and delivery state, let the approved event store hold the restricted failure evidence, and let the paging system own notification of responders. Keep any evidence requiring per-user erasure, configurable archival retention, or bulk extraction in a store whose contract and interfaces meet those requirements. Do not make the capture integration depend on those being supplied by the shared API.

The boundary is operational, too: a trace identifier can help associate records, but reconstruction that requires a distributed span tree belongs with a tracing system. Likewise, use a heartbeat service for “the notification job never ran.” An error capture call cannot report an exception from a process that never started.

How should you integrate error tracking using a backend API?

In Node.js, catch the delivery failure at the boundary where the delivery reference and attempt number are still available, or use the relevant error event listener. Build an explicit allowlist of context rather than serializing the exception object. Include a timestamp; use an opaque reference instead of a direct user identifier when that is sufficient for the investigation. Preserve the original delivery outcome even if telemetry export fails.

The following Go program sends one approved JSON event to the capture API. Before running it, prepare an event file using the current capture request schema from public discovery, with only the allowed context mapped into its declared fields. This keeps the sample honest: a local label such as “delivery reference” is a design requirement, not evidence that the provider accepts a field with that name. Use an artificial delivery failure for this check, never a production recipient record. The Node.js sender should apply the same payload policy; this Go verification tool makes the HTTP behavior independently inspectable.

Supply the key in INFRAI_API_KEY, the prepared file path in INFRAI_EVENT_FILE, and a unique identity for this event in INFRAI_EVENT_ID. Reuse that event identity when rerunning the same capture; assign a new one to a different attempt.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    eventID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_EVENT_ID")
    file := os.Getenv("INFRAI_EVENT_FILE")
    if key == "" || eventID == "" || file == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_EVENT_ID, and INFRAI_EVENT_FILE")
    }
    payload, err := os.ReadFile(file)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !json.Valid(payload) {
        return fmt.Errorf("event file must contain valid JSON matching the capture schema")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", eventID)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            if delay > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond this check's wait budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("capture returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println("Capture accepted; inspect the stored test event before rollout.")
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("capture retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain after setting the three environment variables. JSON syntax validation does not establish schema validity or remove sensitive data: inspect the prepared event before sending. For this check, omit the raw exception message and stack, retaining a classification instead. This trades immediate debugging detail for a narrower export boundary. It is appropriate only if responders can use the opaque reference to investigate in the authorized system.

For the actual backend integration, obtain the error-capture contract from public discovery and map the allowed context into its declared fields. Do not assume an observability product accepts arbitrary context keys just because another one does. Review the current request schema, required fields, and response shape before connecting the Node.js sender.

Use an environment-provided credential, an explicit HTTP method, and status checks that surface the real response error. Bound retries, back off exponentially on a rate limit, and honor Retry-After when present. Keep the same client event identity across a retry and follow the documented idempotency convention; never use a single delivery identity to collapse separate delivery attempts. A telemetry retry must also stay separate from retrying the customer notification, or observability code can accidentally become delivery orchestration.

Choose the store by what the postmortem must prove

There is a trade-off: Infrai is not the best fit for a postmortem whose decisive evidence requires source-level debugging or a distributed trace view; evaluate Sentry for the former and Honeycomb for the latter. Restricted capture and full forensic reconstruction have different acceptance criteria.

There are several reasonable choices, and a familiar dashboard is weak evidence for choosing among them. The useful comparison is the investigation you need to support and the data you can authorize each system to receive. The product roles below are starting points for evaluation, not claims that any default configuration satisfies a residency or deletion requirement.

Option Where to evaluate it for this notification workflow Boundary to establish before adoption
Infrai Restricted error capture when one key and one bill across backend services simplify the integration Approve the event's processing and retention terms; keep paging, identity custody, and specialist investigations in their designated systems
Sentry An error-focused investigation that needs source-level debugging Confirm what exception details and source artifacts leave the application, and the applicable region and deletion terms
Datadog An investigation that needs error evidence alongside broader operational telemetry Review the data sent by each enabled integration and the retention and processing terms for the services actually selected
Honeycomb An investigation organized around tracing request and delivery paths Decide which spans and attributes may cross the boundary, then verify the applicable retention and processor commitments

Sentry is the more direct candidate when the essential evidence is a source-level exception investigation. Datadog deserves evaluation when the responder needs surrounding operational signals in the same investigation. Honeycomb deserves evaluation when the causal path through services is the main question. Those are different jobs, and sending the same full payload to all three merely multiplies the places that need approval.

Healthchecks is a separate complement for the missing-job question. Its heartbeat model addresses a different signal from a caught delivery exception; keep that distinction visible in the runbook so the responder knows which absence actually triggered the page.

Choose the specialist when the required investigation depends on source-map decoding, replay, or a distributed trace view. Choose a contractually approved data store when retention controls or individual deletion are hard requirements. Use the shared backend capture path for the restricted event only after that smaller boundary has been approved. No runtime abstraction establishes residency or processor guarantees on its own.

Verify the evidence, then define rollback

Inspect the payload.

Test a controlled delivery failure before enabling export for live traffic. Check that the authorized responder can reconstruct the delivery reference, attempt, timestamp, and release, and that the exported record contains neither the test address nor the raw provider response. Inspect the actual outbound payload. A tidy dashboard is not proof that the sender excluded sensitive data.

Then test the failure of the evidence path itself: a rejected event, a rate-limited sender, and an interrupted connection. Verify bounded retries and stable event identity without causing another customer notification. Separately exercise the page and the missing-job heartbeat. Successful capture proves neither of those signals works.

Deletion needs verification too. Follow a test reference through every approved destination and confirm the agreed retention and deletion procedure with the data owner, including the mapping retained in the commerce system. Removing the address from one event does not remove the ability to join an opaque reference elsewhere.

Rollback should disable the new export path while retaining the delivery workflow and its approved local evidence. Keep a way to identify the affected event destinations if an allowlist mistake is discovered, and use the established deletion procedure rather than assuming that stopping future writes removes past records. Re-enable export only after inspecting the corrected payload and repeating the controlled failure test.

The postmortem should be able to answer a small, stubborn question: which attempt failed, what evidence supports that conclusion, and who was authorized to hold it? That is a more useful acceptance test than the number of panels that turned green.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts and correlation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Honeycomb documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If the restricted capture boundary fits your notification service, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: TanStack Query did my offline mode, my retries and my cache. I wrote the rules.
description:
ParkEase has two React apps talking to the same API: an Android app (Expo, React Native) for drivers, owners, valets and car washers, and an admin panel (React and Vite). Both get every byte of server data through TanStack Query. Neither has Redux, Zustand or a hand-rolled fetch-into-useState anywhere.

That was a rule, not a preference. Here's why it was the right one, and how differently the two apps use the same library.

The rule: server state is not app state

The mobile rules say it in one line: TanStack Query for server state, never Redux, never Zustand. A booking, a list of parking spots, an earnings summary: these belong to the server. The app holds a cached copy, and the question is only how fresh that copy is and what to do when it's wrong.

Putting that copy in a global store means rebuilding caching, deduping, retries, refetching and invalidation yourself, badly. Leaving it in TanStack Query means one rule: read it straight from the cache, never copy it into useState. ParkEase's search hook says exactly that:

/**
 * Server state for discovery. Results live in the query cache and are read
 * straight from it — never copied into useState (R-FE-02), which is also why
 * the map/list toggle can swap renderers without refetching.
 */

The map view and the list view are two renderers of one cache entry. Switching between them costs nothing.

Mobile: retry only what a retry can fix

The default is to retry failed queries three times. That's wrong for half of all failures. A 403 won't become a 200 on the third attempt. And a response the app can't parse, because it's an old build meeting a new API, will be just as unparseable twice more, leaving a loading skeleton on screen for nothing.

So the query client retries through one shared failure classifier:

export function shouldRetryQuery(failureCount: number, error: unknown): boolean {
  if (failureCount >= MAX_QUERY_RETRIES) return false;
  return classifyFailure(error) === 'unreachable';
}

Network failure, a 5xx, a timeout or a rate limit: retry. A definite 4xx or an unreadable body: show the right error immediately.

Mobile: offline, using TanStack's own machinery

Parking happens in basements. The app had to work with no signal, and all of it is built from TanStack Query's parts rather than beside them:

  • Online state. The phone's network status feeds TanStack's onlineManager, so queries pause instead of failing while offline, and refetch on reconnect.
  • A persisted cache. A few query families (your bookings, notifications, owner and partner earnings) are saved to storage and drawn from it on a cold start with no network. Saved data older than a day isn't shown: an old screen is more misleading than an empty one.
  • Queued actions. A mutation made offline pauses and replays on reconnect, in the order it was made, carrying the idempotency key minted when you tapped, so a replay the server already applied returns its stored result instead of acting twice.

And one deliberate exception. Search results, meaning which slots are free right now, are never cached, persisted or reused:

// Availability is never cached — a stale free-slot count is a double
// booking or a lost sale (rules.md R-PERF-05). Overrides the 30s default.
staleTime: 0,

A library with good defaults still needs you to know which data must never be stale.

Admin: two helpers and nothing else

The admin panel needs none of that. It's a desktop tool on a reliable connection, used by a few operators. So the whole integration is two small hooks:

export function useApi<S extends z.ZodTypeAny>(schema: S, path: string, enabled = true) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: [path], queryFn: () => request(schema, path), enabled });
}

useApi fetches a path and parses the response with its Zod schema; the path is the cache key. useAction wraps a mutation, mints an idempotency key per click, and on success invalidates every query. Blunt, and right for an admin tool: invalidating everything is cheap at this scale and guarantees an operator never sees a stale approval queue after acting on it.

Almost every admin page goes through those two functions. The two exceptions are the long, paged lists, the audit log and the ledger explorer, which use useInfiniteQuery directly to load the next page on demand.

Why it was good

  • One mental model across both apps, even though they use it at opposite ends of the complexity scale.
  • Hard problems became configuration. Offline, ordered replay and selective persistence came from options and documented APIs, not custom infrastructure.
  • It suits AI-written code. An agent writing fetch-into-useState by hand produces subtly different loading, error and retry behaviour on every screen. With one query client and two rules, every screen behaves the same way, and a test can check that every data screen has a loading, an error and an empty state.

Next: the other half of the admin panel. Type-safe routing with TanStack Router, where a URL parameter is validated like an API request.

ParkEase is a peer-to-peer parking marketplace for India, built solo with Claude Code.
Code: https://github.com/Deonkar/parkease

title: I Tested Concat, the Free Open-Source CapCut Alternative (Rust, Offline AI, Built-in MCP Server)
description:
Short version: Concat shrank a 76 MB video to 3 MB in 3.9 seconds, and while it ran I logged every network request: 0 bytes of my video left my Mac. It's free, open source, built in Rust, and it ships its own MCP server so AI agents like Claude Code can edit video. But it's a 10-week-old beta (v0.2.9) with 200+ open issues.

▶ Full video: https://youtu.be/KWJw3RQHElU

What is Concat?

Concat is a desktop video editor that wants to replace CapCut. Everything runs on your own machine.

  • Free and open source (AGPL-3.0), no account, no watermark, and the site says there is no paid tier.
  • Built in Rust: about 159,000 lines, first release in September 2026.
  • Runs on Mac, Windows, Linux, Android and iPhone.
  • Fast growth: 14,000+ GitHub stars and about 440,000 downloads in ten weeks.
  • Needs 4 GB of RAM (16 GB recommended for 4K).

The layout will feel familiar if you've used CapCut: library on the left, preview in the middle, inspector on the right, timeline at the bottom. Every panel can be swapped, split or dragged.

Price check (November 2026)

Price
CapCut Pro US$19.99/month or $179.99/year
Concat $0

Test 1: Compress a video (the one I ran myself)

Concat has free tools that run right in the browser. I tried Compress a video in Chrome on my Mac:

  • Input: 76 MB stock clip, 20 seconds of 1080p H.264
  • Settings: Balanced quality, 720p, MP4
  • Result: 3.0 MB (96% smaller) in 3.9 seconds

It encodes on your own GPU, with no server in between. I recorded every network request during the run: 0 bytes of the video were uploaded. The honest flaw: the page still loads Google ads.

Test 2: Auto captions

Captions are one button (the T on the timeline). You pick a Whisper model; the base English one is a 148 MB download, and after that it transcribes fully offline. You get one title per phrase on the timeline, you can restyle all of them at once, and it imports and exports SRT. Their own guide has a section called "why a word is wrong", so expect to fix a few words.

Test 3: Text to speech, voice cloning, background removal

  • Type a script, pick a voice, and the read lands on your timeline.
  • Voice cloning from a few seconds of audio (small model 98 MB, studio model about 1 GB).
  • Background removal for people or objects, plus a smart brush. The person model is 15 MB. No green screen.
  • Downside: on phones, the built-in voice is still coming.

Test 4: 4K export and the MCP server

Export H.264, HEVC or AV1 up to 4K 60 fps, 10-bit, no watermark at any resolution. This week's update made 4K exports about 2.4x faster.

The part developers will care about: Concat ships its own MCP server. An AI agent like Claude Code gets tools for clips, titles, keyframes, effects and export, the same commands the editor itself uses. Setup is one line in the terminal; the steps are in the repo's docs/MCP.md.

So "cut the silences, add captions, export 1080p" can be a prompt instead of an afternoon.

The catch

  • Beta: v0.2.9 with 200+ open issues on GitHub.
  • Windows builds aren't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen will warn you.
  • Phones: no built-in voice yet.

Verdict

If you edit for clients with deadlines, not yet. If you're a student, a Linux user, a small creator, or a developer who wants an editor an agent can drive, it's already useful, and it's free. Nothing uploads, which also makes it a good fit for private footage.

Would you let an AI agent cut your videos through MCP? I'm curious what you'd automate first.

Links

  • Concat website + download: https://concat.standalones.org
  • Source code: https://github.com/jub0t/Concat
  • MCP setup: https://github.com/jub0t/Concat/blob/main/docs/MCP.md
  • Full video: https://youtu.be/KWJw3RQHElU

AI-assisted disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help structure this write-up. The compression test, timing and network log are my own (Chrome on my Mac, November 6, 2026). Feature details come from Concat's site, docs and GitHub repo. Not sponsored by Concat or CapCut.

title: Healthtech Welcome Message Template Ownership Across Email APIs and Bounce Suppression
description:
Giving a copy editor control over a welcome template also requires defining the point where that control ends. Short answer: compare transactional email APIs by template ownership, then require recipient suppression to veto every template revision. In a healthtech welcome flow, an approved wording change must never make an invalid destination eligible again. Select the transport after you can explain that rule. Submission isn't delivery.

For a bounded postmortem exercise, imagine two welcome jobs for the synthetic account clinic-demo-42, one using template revision 7 and the other revision 8, with a permanent bounce recorded between them. These are example inputs, not a reported production incident. I'd begin the review with a narrower question than whether the provider dashboard was green: what page fired, and could its responder establish why the second job remained eligible?

The lesson is a separation of authority. A template owner can approve content; a recipient-state owner can authorize delivery attempts. Neither decision substitutes for the other.

Who can stop an approved welcome template from sending?

A useful postmortem reconstructs decisions rather than counting successful API submissions. Start at the second job and work backward: which template revision was pinned, which recipient state was read, and which record authorized the send? If the answer is just that the new template was approved, the approval has crossed a boundary it should never have crossed.

Stop the resend.

In this design, a permanent bounce makes the destination ineligible for subsequent welcome attempts until a separate, reviewed recipient correction establishes eligibility again. A copy edit cannot perform that correction. Store template approval separately from recipient suppression, with independent audit evidence, and pin each queued job to the revision that was approved for it. Otherwise a responder has to infer historical content from whatever the editor displays now, precisely when a live dashboard is least useful as an explanation of an earlier decision.

That rule also makes vendor evaluation less theatrical. Ask the proposed template owner to approve revision 8 while the recipient is suppressed, then show that the waiting job stays blocked. The acceptance criterion is observable application behavior, not an attractive template editor.

For healthtech teams that own welcome templates in application code and can operate a polling worker, I recommend trying Infrai for the template-to-email handoff: public discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so connecting the capability starts with reading its contract rather than learning another SDK. Its supporting advantage is the shared REST surface and API key across email and SMS, which reduces credential integration work if a separately authorized SMS workflow is also in scope. Channel eligibility still belongs to the application.

How should we compare email APIs for transactional welcome messages?

Postmark, SendGrid, and Amazon SES are real alternatives worth evaluating alongside a combined API. Compare their documented template and suppression workflows against the same ownership exercise. The decision below is deliberately conditional: the evidence here doesn't establish a deliverability ranking, a compliance certification, or a measured operational advantage for any provider.

Candidate Template ownership question Evidence to request before selecting it
Postmark Does its template workflow suit the person accountable for welcome copy? Demonstrate the proposed approval process and trace a suppressed destination through the next queued attempt.
SendGrid Should its transactional template workflow own publication, or should application deployment own it? Walk through an approved copy change and identify the application record that still vetoes sending.
Amazon SES Does template management belong inside the team's AWS operating model? Show how deployment controls identify the approved revision and how suppression reaches the dispatch decision.
Infrai Can the team own template approval and recipient eligibility while using one HTTP surface? Demonstrate discovery-led integration, pulled-event processing, and a suppression veto before dispatch.

These options ask different integration questions. A team evaluating Postmark's template workflow should put the copy owner in the room; one evaluating SendGrid should settle where publication happens; one evaluating SES should involve the people who operate its AWS deployment controls. Those are selection exercises, not claims that only one vendor can satisfy each requirement. Inspect the linked primary documentation before turning an evaluation criterion into a promise.

Infrai uses one REST API with no SDK to install. Its public discovery requires no key and supplies full request and response schemas plus runnable examples; that makes the provider-to-application field mapping inspectable before the team configures credentials.

Infrai provides one key, one wallet, one bill across its backend services. For a team operating both email and SMS, that means one credential configuration instead of a separate provider key for each channel; it leaves template approval and destination eligibility with their existing owners.

If a specialist's direct template workflow already matches the organization's review process, keep it on the shortlist even when a common interface would reduce integration work. Template ownership is an operating decision. A transport abstraction earns its place only if the people responsible for publication and incident response can still show their evidence.

Freeze the content decision before checking the destination

The preventative path needs two independent gates. First, the approved template revision must match the queued job. Second, the current destination state must permit sending. The second gate wins even when the first passes.

The following Go program is a complete read-only integration example, runnable as main.go with the standard Go toolchain. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and RECIPIENT_EMAIL for a destination you are authorized to inspect. It retrieves the suppression-check response, then demonstrates application policy with synthetic cases covering an eligible job, a permanent bounce, an unobserved recipient state, and a revision mismatch. Treating unknown state as a hold is a deliberate trade-off: this welcome workflow accepts delayed delivery instead of treating missing evidence as permission.

The raw provider response is printed for contract review, not silently mapped into an invented response field. The synthetic decisions are separate and do not authorize a real send. Before deployment, implement that mapping against discovery's response schema and persist the resulting recipient state.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func inspectSuppression() error {
    key, email := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("RECIPIENT_EMAIL")
    if key == "" || email == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and RECIPIENT_EMAIL")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/suppression/check/{email}", "{email}", url.PathEscape(email))
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(when); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("suppression check HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Printf("Suppression response for contract review: %s\n", body)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("suppression check retry budget exhausted")
}

type Job struct {
    ID       string
    Account  string
    Revision int
}

type Approval struct {
    Revision int
    Approved bool
}

type Recipient struct {
    Known      bool
    Suppressed bool
}

func decision(job Job, approval Approval, recipient Recipient) string {
    if !approval.Approved || job.Revision != approval.Revision {
        return "hold: template approval does not match"
    }
    if !recipient.Known {
        return "hold: recipient state is unknown"
    }
    if recipient.Suppressed {
        return "block: recipient is suppressed"
    }
    return "eligible: recheck at dispatch"
}

func main() {
    if err := inspectSuppression(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    job := Job{ID: "welcome-42", Account: "clinic-demo-42", Revision: 7}
    approved := Approval{Revision: 7, Approved: true}
    cases := []struct {
        name      string
        approval  Approval
        recipient Recipient
    }{
        {"eligible", approved, Recipient{Known: true}},
        {"permanent bounce", approved, Recipient{Known: true, Suppressed: true}},
        {"unknown state", approved, Recipient{}},
        {"revision changed", Approval{Revision: 8, Approved: true}, Recipient{Known: true}},
    }
    for _, c := range cases {
        fmt.Printf("%s %s %s: %s\n", job.ID, job.Account, c.name,
            decision(job, c.approval, c.recipient))
    }
}

This is intentionally smaller than a sending worker. The 20-second timeout and four-attempt rate-limit budget are example choices, not provider guarantees. The request is read-only; a production write needs the documented idempotency convention. The policy function answers whether an application decision permits an attempt; it doesn't claim that a check and an external send form an atomic transaction. In production, persist the job identity and approved content, serialize competing application decisions for the destination where needed, and recheck suppression at dispatch. A recipient can change state after an earlier queue check. That is the pitfall this example is meant to expose.

Keep provider response fields out of this policy function. An adapter should translate documented event evidence into the application's recipient state, while another adapter submits an authorized, pinned message using the selected provider's actual schema. This gives template reviewers a stable policy to inspect without pretending that every provider uses the same event names or request fields. It also makes an approved template portable as application content only when the team actually owns its rendering and publication process; provider-managed editing deserves a separate migration review.

A bounce observation is evidence with a timestamp

With pulled events, distinguish when the provider recorded an event from when the application observed and applied it. The dispatch gate can act on recorded application state; it cannot act on evidence the worker hasn't retrieved yet. Set an explicit tolerance for that observation interval, record the last successful retrieval, and have the responder inspect the job's decision record alongside that timestamp. A green submission chart can't establish this ordering.

Suppression needs its own owner.

For example, the template publisher may approve revision 8 while a polling worker applies the permanent bounce associated with revision 7. The application should preserve both records. Neither operation should overwrite the other, and a retry of the welcome job should retain its logical identity rather than becoming a fresh attempt merely because its copy changed. For an Infrai write integration, use its documented idempotency convention and retain the same client key across retries; verify the selected capability's contract through discovery rather than assuming every operation shares identical semantics.

Domain authorization belongs in the review too. RFC 7208 defines SPF; it doesn't establish that an individual mailbox is eligible for another welcome attempt. Keep domain configuration evidence and recipient suppression evidence distinct, because they answer different questions and lead to different remediation.

When should the team choose a different handoff?

Choose a direct specialist when its template workflow better fits publication ownership, or when the design requires webhook-driven coordination and the team won't accept a polling-based event handoff. Compare the documented event contract directly before committing. The welcome-flow policy above assumes the organization accepts a defined observation interval; a workflow demanding an immediate reaction needs a different transport evaluation.

Healthtech is a scenario, not a compliance claim. Regional authorization, data handling, and deployment requirements need their own evidence; a unified API key or verified sending domain cannot establish them. For deployments with China-specific requirements, select against verified regional suitability rather than assuming that a general email integration supplies it.

The final selection question is concrete: can the template owner publish approved copy while the responder can prove that an invalid destination remains blocked? Require both demonstrations. Then decide whether a shared HTTP surface or a direct provider produces the clearer handoff for the people who will maintain it.

Sources

References for the evaluation and domain-authorization distinction:

  • Postmark template documentation
  • SendGrid transactional template documentation
  • Amazon SES template management documentation
  • Amazon SES suppression documentation
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework

If application-owned templates and a pulled-event handoff fit your system, start with the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Avoiding Deadlocks Caused by Implicit Autoflush in SQLAlchemy: An In-Depth Post-Mortem and Architectural Guide
description:
Limits of Transaction Control in SQLAlchemy: An Empirical Report on Deadlock Avoidance and Execution Tracing

1. Introduction

In high-concurrency Python backend services, SQLAlchemy's implicit flush (autoflush=True) is an indispensable mechanism designed to maintain Unit of Work consistency between in-memory object states and the underlying database session. However, within intricate transaction boundaries, implicit autoflush frequently acquires unanticipated row-level locks prematurely, transforming what appears to be a read-heavy workflow into a breeding ground for database deadlocks (40P01 in PostgreSQL or 1213 in MySQL/InnoDB).

This technical report presents an empirical analysis of transaction isolation, fine-grained lock boundaries using the session.no_autoflush context manager, and deadlock symptom detection via low-level DBAPI execution listener tracing. Furthermore, we dissect the limitations, environmental constraints, and architectural anti-patterns observed during implementation.

2. Implementation Architecture Design

The evaluation harness was engineered to capture and serialize database interaction phases down to the DBAPI driver level, isolating the exact transition points where implicit flushes trigger uncommitted row locks.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as "Application Thread"
    participant Session as "SQLAlchemy Session"
    participant DB as "SQLite DBAPI"
    participant Trace as "Execution Listener"

    App -- "invoke" --> Session: perform_safe_update()
    Session -- "enter" --> Session: start no_autoflush context
    Session -- "query" --> DB: SELECT query issued
    DB -. "emit" .-> Trace: before_cursor_execute event
    Trace -- "serialize" --> Trace: serialize connection ID & query context
    Session -- "return" --> App: return query result
    App -- "explicit" --> Session: explicit flush()
    Session -- "write" --> DB: UPDATE query issued

💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want).

Core Architecture Components

  1. Context-Bounded Flush Suppression: Executing read operations inside session.no_autoflush prevents intermediate DML operations from pre-emptively firing before queries are evaluated.
  2. Low-Level Hook Inspection: Using SQLAlchemy Core event.listens_for(Engine, "before_cursor_execute") to trace connection parameters, raw SQL strings, and parameter payloads immediately before passing to the DBAPI cursor.

3. Technical Obstacles Encountered During Verification

During the reproduction and benchmarking phase, significant engineering barriers emerged across dependency consistency and database driver semantics.

3.1 Missing Dependencies and Pipeline Consistency

Errors such as ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sqlalchemy' manifest when the runtime pipeline fails to validate operational prerequisites prior to harness startup. Regardless of how meticulously transaction logic is constructed, an environment lacking deterministic virtual environment resolution, locked wheel sets, or automated pre-flight checks (e.g., CI/CD dependency hydration) will collapse before transaction boundaries are ever established.

3.2 Concurrency Constraints of SQLite SERIALIZABLE

Applying isolation_level="SERIALIZABLE" on SQLite (sqlite3 driver) revealed clear driver-level trade-offs. Unlike robust RDBMS engines (e.g., PostgreSQL or MySQL InnoDB) featuring advanced Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) and wait-for graph deadlock resolution engines, SQLite operates with database-level lock escalation.

When a connection attempts to promote a shared read lock (SHARED) to an exclusive write lock (EXCLUSIVE), SQLite does not resolve lock graphs or permit optimistic concurrent serializability; instead, it immediately surfaces an OperationalError: database is locked. Consequently, applying SERIALIZABLE in SQLite forces complete sequential execution rather than concurrent transaction optimization, degrading throughput under multi-threaded loads.

4. Anti-Patterns Identified from Experimental Observations

Through empirical testing, three primary system architecture anti-patterns were identified:

Anti-Pattern 1: Implicit Environmental Trust

Assuming libraries and execution prerequisites exist across disparate deployment environments without strict verification creates fragile portability. Systems must incorporate an explicit pre-flight validation layer (such as an automated verify_environment() step) to validate Python runtime versions, database driver binaries, and ORM interfaces before allocating connection pools.

Anti-Pattern 2: Heavy Synchronous Processing Inside Event Listeners

Executing heavy serialization logic (e.g., intensive payload inspection, recursive parameter formatting, or synchronous I/O dispatch via custom serialization functions) inside the before_cursor_execute hook severely degrades performance. Because this hook sits directly on the hot path of query execution:

  • Every single SQL statement incurs synchronous CPU and serialization overhead.
  • Under high throughput, the telemetry collector itself becomes the dominant latency bottleneck, distorting baseline latency metrics and inducing artificial lock contention.

Anti-Pattern 3: Over-Abstraction of Session Management

While suppressing premature flushes using no_autoflush solves specific local ordering problems, forcing application-level orchestration of every lock transition severely couples domain logic to ORM internals and harms maintainability. True deadlock prevention is fundamentally a database design concern:

  • Establishing deterministic lock acquisition ordering (e.g., sorting entity IDs prior to bulk SELECT ... FOR UPDATE).
  • Minimizing write lock duration.
  • Ensuring proper indexing on foreign key constraints and update targets.

Application-layer transaction tuning should complement, not substitute for, relational indexing and deterministic access patterns.

5. Architectural Summary and Future Directions

While this verification surfaced foundational challenges in runtime configuration management, the combined pattern of targeted no_autoflush scopes and DBAPI event hook inspection remains a viable diagnostics technique for isolating anomalous lock lifecycles.

Engineers tackling similar concurrency bottlenecks should adhere to the following principles:

  1. Automate Deterministic Environments: Enforce containerized, reproducible CI/CD environments before benchmarking database concurrency.
  2. Leverage External Lock Graph Telemetry: Rather than overloading internal application hooks with heavy diagnostics, extract lock wait graphs and block trees directly from database system views (e.g., pg_stat_activity and pg_locks in PostgreSQL, or sys.innodb_lock_waits in MySQL).
  3. Minimize Application-Level Lock Patching: Overly complex manual flush and lock orchestration in application code increases system entropy and introduces subtle race conditions. Design deterministic write pipelines at the data layer first.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.

Read more

title: “어디서 틀렸는지 모르겠습니다.” — 예치금 정합성 배치를 주문 1건 단위로 다시 설계한 이야기
description:
들어가며

예치금을 다루는 시스템에서 금액의 오차는 작더라도 그냥 넘길 수 없습니다.
그런데 금액이 틀렸다는 사실을 아는 것과, 왜 틀렸는지를 아는 것은 전혀 다른 문제였습니다.

이번 글에서는 하루치 합계를 비교하던 예치금 정합성 배치를, 주문 1건의 기대값에서 출발하는 구조로 바꾼 과정을 이야기합니다.

기존 구조: 하루치 합계를 비교하는 양식

예치금의 정합성을 보여주는 템플릿이 있습니다. 핵심은 다음 한 줄로 정리됩니다.

오늘자 거래 집계 금액 = 오늘과 어제 사이의 거래금액 차이

결제금액, 수수료 등 여러 항목의 하루치 데이터를 집계하고, 그 합을 비교해 오차를 확인하는 방식이었습니다.

문제: 오차는 보이는데 원인은 보이지 않는다

이 구조에는 두 가지 문제가 있었습니다.

1. 계산이 오래 걸렸습니다

하루치 거래금액, 즉 오늘까지의 거래금액과 어제까지의 거래금액의 차이를 각각 계산하기 위해 DB 전체를 뒤져야 했습니다.

2. 오차의 원인을 추적하기 어려웠습니다

오늘자 거래 합계만으로는 어떤 주문에 문제가 있는지 알 수 없었습니다.

  • 주문 1건이 잘못된 것인지
  • 여러 건이 잘못되어 그 합으로 오차가 발생한 것인지
  • 서로 다른 항목의 이슈가 상쇄되어 드러나지 않은 것은 없는지

합계는 이상 여부를 확인하는 데는 유용합니다. 하지만 합산 과정에서 건별 정보가 사라지기 때문에, 원인을 찾는 데는 도움이 되지 않았습니다.

오차 하나를 찾아내는 데 꼬박 하루가 걸리기도 했습니다.

전환점: 주문이 단 1건뿐이라면?

일단 하나씩, 거래 집계부터 풀어보기로 했습니다. 출발점은 단순한 질문이었습니다.

여러 주문이 아니라 주문이 1건만 있다면, 템플릿에는 어떻게 보여야 할까?

이 질문이 곧 답이었습니다. 주문 1건, 거래상태 1건마다 템플릿에 나타나야 할 값은 정해져 있기 때문입니다.

  • 주문 1건, 거래상태 1건에 대한 기대값을 정의
  • 기대값을 규칙으로 만들어 배치에 적용
  • 규칙을 통과하지 못한 건을 점검하고 수정

이렇게 검증을 통과한 건들이 쌓이면, 하루치 거래 합계도 신뢰할 수 있는 값이 됩니다.
합계를 먼저 보고 원인을 거슬러 찾던 흐름이, 건별로 검증한 값을 쌓아 신뢰할 수 있는 합계를 만드는 흐름으로 바뀌었습니다.

정산에 의미 있는 상태만 남기기

주문상태별로 규칙을 만들다 보니 발견한 사실이 있습니다.
주문상태 중에는 Hold처럼 정산 관점에서 의미가 없는 상태도 있었습니다.

이런 상태는 과감히 제외하고, 정산에 의미 있는 상태만 남겼습니다.

중복을 막는 거래상태별 기준일 테이블

의미 있는 상태만 골라도 문제는 남아 있었습니다.
지금 계산하는 상태가 어쩌면 중복일지도 모릅니다. 과거 데이터를 다시 조회해 동일한 상태가 또 있는지 확인하고, 있으면 이번 계산에서 제외해야 했습니다.

이 문제는 별도의 테이블을 만들어 해결했습니다.

  • 주문번호별로 거래상태의 날짜를 정의
  • 집계는 이 테이블에 적힌 날짜를 기준으로 수행
  • 중복 내역이 들어와도 기준 날짜는 변경되지 않음

같은 내역이 몇 번 들어오더라도 집계 결과는 달라지지 않습니다.
필요한 거래상태만, 정확한 날짜로 정의하니 조회 범위도 줄었고 실행 시간도 크게 단축되었습니다.

3개의 검증축

신뢰할 수 있는 거래 합계가 생기자, 이 값을 기준으로 삼을 수 있었습니다.
거래 합계를 바탕으로 거래외 데이터를 계산하고, 이를 하루치 거래금액과 비교합니다.

이렇게 세 개의 검증축이 완성되었습니다.

  • 거래: 건별 규칙을 통과한 값을 쌓은 합계
  • 거래외: 거래 합계를 기준으로 계산한 거래외 데이터
  • 전체 거래금액: 위 값들과 대조하는 하루치 거래금액

Rule을 쌓아 만든 정합성 체크 툴

신뢰할 수 있는 값이 갖춰지자, 그 위에 필요한 Rule을 하나씩 정의할 수 있었습니다.
예를 들면 다음과 같은 규칙입니다.

구매자의 예치금 사용액 + 판매자의 정산금 + 거래외 예치금 변동 = 회원 전체의 예치금 변동액

필요한 규칙을 채워 넣고, 어긋나는 값은 표시합니다.
여기에 집계 결과를 보기 좋게 배치하면, 예치금 정합성을 한눈에 확인할 수 있는 체크 툴이 완성됩니다.

마치며

정합성 구조를 바꾸며 얻은 가장 큰 교훈은, 합계의 신뢰도는 그 합계를 이루는 가장 작은 단위에서 나온다는 점입니다.
오차가 발생했을 때 DB 전체를 뒤지는 대신, 규칙을 통과하지 못한 건부터 살펴보면 됩니다.

복잡해 보이던 문제도 “주문이 1건뿐이라면?”이라는 간단한 질문으로 풀리기 시작했습니다.

title: Sprint Planning Anatomy: What Actually Happens in Those Two Hours
description:
In many teams the sprint planning meeting feels like a rushed “pick some stories” session. When you give the ceremony a proper structure, the two‑hour slot becomes a focused, outcome‑driven workshop. Below is a practical breakdown of what needs to happen, the inputs you must have ready, and the pitfalls that turn planning into a time‑sink.

Part 1: The What

  1. Product Owner presents the priority backlog – The PO should walk the team through the top‑ranked items that are already refined and meet the Definition of Ready (DoR). No new grooming should happen here; the stories must be clear, sized, and testable.
  2. Team confirms the sprint goal – Together, craft a single sentence that describes the desired outcome for the sprint (e.g., “Enable users to reset their password via mobile”). The goal anchors every selection and prevents the team from drifting into a “just‑do‑more‑stories” mindset.

Part 2: The How

  1. Team breaks stories into tasks – For each selected story, discuss the technical approach and split the work into 2‑ to 8‑hour tasks. The conversation should surface assumptions and dependencies, not dictate a single solution.
  2. Capacity checked against commitment – Calculate the real number of person‑days available, accounting for holidays, on‑call duties, and scheduled meetings. Compare this capacity with the sum of task estimates to see if the commitment is realistic.

Inputs Needed

  • Refined, estimated backlog – All items considered for the sprint must have been groomed in a prior refinement session. Trying to refine live stretches the meeting well beyond two hours.
  • Team capacity for the sprint – Use actual available days, not a simple headcount × 10‑hour rule. Include known absences and any non‑development obligations.

Common Failure Modes

  • Refinement happening live – When the team starts clarifying acceptance criteria during planning, the meeting balloons into a four‑hour marathon.
  • No sprint goal set – Without a clear goal, the team optimizes for story count rather than delivering a cohesive outcome, leading to fragmented work and lower value.

Do / Avoid

Do

  • Finish refinement before planning starts.
  • Set one clear sprint goal, not just a task list.
  • Check real capacity, not theoretical capacity.

Avoid

  • Estimating stories for the first time during planning.
  • Overcommitting to hit a velocity number.
  • Skipping the sprint goal; it’s not an optional ceremony.

A well‑structured sprint planning meeting turns two hours into a decisive, collaborative step that aligns the team around a shared outcome and a realistic workload.

title: Deploy Next.js with a database in India
description:
Originally published on the Plexivo blog.

A Next.js app is rarely only a front end. Sooner or later it has route handlers, server components that read data, and a database behind them. Hosting it well in India means three things: the app runs close to your users, the database runs beside the app, and the connection string never leaks into the browser.

This guide deploys a Next.js app on Plexivo App Runner in Mumbai, connects it to Plexivo Postgres, and shows two ways to talk to the database: plain SQL from the server, and the Plexivo Postgres Data API with sign-in and live data.

What do you need to deploy Next.js in India?

  • Your code in a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository.
  • A Plexivo organisation. Sign up at cloud.plexivo.io; the free trial is on the Developer plan.
  • A project to hold the app and its database. Resources in the same project reach each other over the private network.

Everything runs in Mumbai, India. India (Mumbai) is live today, and more countries are available on request. Database backups are kept in Mumbai and copied to Hyderabad.

How does Plexivo App Runner build a Next.js app?

When you deploy from Git, Plexivo App Runner clones your branch, builds an image, signs it and releases it. Each build runs in its own isolated sandbox. There are two ways it can build:

  • Without a Dockerfile. Plexivo detects your language and framework, installs your dependencies, builds and sets the start command. Next.js is one of the supported stacks.
  • With a Dockerfile. If the repository has a Dockerfile at its root, Plexivo builds it as it is. This gives you full control over the Node.js version and the build steps.

Either way, your server must listen on the port in the PORT environment variable, on 0.0.0.0. Unless your image declares another port, it is 8080. The Next.js production server, next start, reads PORT, so a standard app needs no change. For a custom server, the documented pattern is:

const port = process.env.PORT || 8080;
app.listen(port, '0.0.0.0');

A build that succeeds is not live until its instances pass their health check. Until then, the current release keeps serving. The builds page has the details.

Which database should a Next.js app use?

Plexivo Postgres is managed PostgreSQL, with PostgreSQL 18 recommended and PostgreSQL 17 available. It suits Next.js in two ways, and you can mix them:

  1. SQL from the server. Route handlers and server components connect with any PostgreSQL driver or ORM, using DATABASE_URL. This is the classic setup.
  2. The Plexivo Postgres Data API. The browser talks to the database through @plexivo/client, with user sign-in, row-level security and Realtime. Server routes can still run raw SQL with the secret key.

The smallest Plexivo Postgres size is 0.25 vCPU, 512 MB and 10 GB for US$11.98 a month. The smallest Plexivo App Runner size is 0.125 vCPU and 256 MB for US$6.04 a month. See create your first database.

Step by step: deploy Next.js with Plexivo Postgres

  1. Create the database. Choose Create, then Plexivo Postgres. Enter the Database name, pick the Project, keep PostgreSQL 18, choose the Database size and Backups kept, check the Estimated monthly cost and choose Deploy.
  2. Start the app. Choose Create, then Plexivo App Runner, and pick the same Project.
  3. Connect your repository. Under Source, pick GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket and choose Connect GitHub (or GitLab, or Bitbucket). For GitHub, install the Plexivo GitHub App and choose which repositories it may read. Then choose the Repository and Branch.
  4. Name and size it. The name becomes its address, <name>.plexivo.app. Choose a size and the Minimum instances and Maximum instances.
  5. Deploy. Check the Estimated monthly cost and choose Deploy. Follow the build on the app's Deployments tab, which lists every build with its Build status, Commit, Author, Duration and Build minutes.
  6. Connect the database. On the app's Environment tab, under Add a database or cache, choose the Resource and Connect. Plexivo delivers DATABASE_URL and DATABASE_CA_CERT as variables and restarts the app once they are ready.
  7. Push to ship. From now on, every push to that branch deploys a new version, and you can roll back to an earlier one.

Prefer to say it in a sentence? On Home, type something like "Deploy my Next.js repository with a Plexivo Postgres database" into the Plexivo AI box and choose Plan my app. Plexivo AI prepares a plan with its price, and nothing runs until you choose Approve & deploy.

How do I connect Next.js to PostgreSQL on the server?

Create one pool for the whole server process and reuse it, rather than opening a connection for every request. Point the client at the CA certificate so it can verify the database it is talking to:

import pg from 'pg';
const pool = new pg.Pool({
 connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
 ssl: { ca: process.env.DATABASE_CA_CERT },
 max: 10
});

Import this pool only from server code: route handlers, server actions and server components. Each size has a connection limit, and with several app instances that limit is shared between them, so keep max modest. The smallest size allows 50 connections. On Business and Enterprise, a built-in PgBouncer pooler in transaction mode lets many more clients share them. See connect to Plexivo Postgres.

How do I keep the connection string secret in Next.js?

Next.js has one rule that protects you: only variables whose names start with NEXT_PUBLIC_ reach the browser. Give the database URL and any secret key ordinary names, and they stay on the server.

Plexivo adds three more protections:

  • Encrypted, masked variables. Values on the Environment tab are encrypted at rest. Keys that look like secrets, such as DATABASE_URL, stay masked until you choose Show, and each read is recorded in the audit log.
  • Plexivo Secrets for shared keys. Keep API keys you share across apps in Plexivo Secrets. On the Environment tab, in Secrets, choose Attach a secret…, pick it and choose Attach. When you change the secret, the app picks up the new version.
  • Rotation without copying. When the database password rotates, the connected variables follow. You never paste a password by hand.

To add your own variables, choose + Add variable, enter the Key and Value, then Add and apply. Plexivo restarts the instances onto the new values one at a time, and each old instance keeps serving until its replacement is ready. Read environment and secrets.

Using the Plexivo Postgres Data API with Next.js

If you want sign-in and live updates without writing an API layer, turn on the Data API for your database and install the client:

npx create-next-app@latest notes
cd notes
npm install @plexivo/client

Set NEXT_PUBLIC_PLEXIVO_DATA_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_PLEXIVO_PUBLISHABLE_KEY for the browser, and PLEXIVO_DATA_URL and PLEXIVO_SECRET_KEY for the server. Then create one client for the whole app:

import { createClient } from '@plexivo/client';
export const db = createClient(
 process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PLEXIVO_DATA_URL,
 process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PLEXIVO_PUBLISHABLE_KEY
);

With row-level security on your tables, each signed-in user sees only their own rows, and a Realtime channel delivers every change the user may read. The secret key belongs only in route handlers. If it ever reaches a browser, the client refuses to start, and the Data API refuses any request that carries it from a web page. The full notes app, with sign-in, a live list and a SQL report route, is in the React and Next.js guide.

Build minutes, sleep and custom domains

Each build uses build minutes: the started minutes of fetching your code, building and pushing the image. Time waiting in the queue is never billed. Developer includes 100 build minutes a month and Startup 500. A .dockerignore that leaves out node_modules, test data and build output keeps every build smaller and quicker.

On Developer, an app that has served no request for 15 minutes sleeps and wakes on the next request. On Startup and above, apps stay on. When you are ready for your own domain, open the app's Domains tab and choose Add domain; Plexivo issues and renews the certificate. See custom domains and the pricing page for every limit.

FAQ

Can I host a Next.js app in India with a database?

Yes. Plexivo App Runner runs your Next.js app in Mumbai, and Plexivo Postgres runs beside it in the same region. Put both in one project and they connect over the private network.

Do I need a Dockerfile to deploy Next.js?

No. Without one, Plexivo detects your framework, installs dependencies, builds and sets the start command. Add a Dockerfile at the repository root when you want full control over the build.

Which port should my Next.js app listen on?

The one in the PORT environment variable, on 0.0.0.0; it is 8080 unless your image declares another. The Next.js production server reads PORT, so a standard app works without changes.

Where should I store my database password?

Let Plexivo deliver it. Connecting the database on the Environment tab gives your app DATABASE_URL, which is encrypted at rest, masked in the console and updated when the password rotates. Never give it a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name.

What does a small Next.js app with a database cost?

The smallest Plexivo App Runner size is US$6.04 a month and the smallest Plexivo Postgres size is US$11.98 a month, plus your plan. Indian customers pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking, with a GST tax invoice. More on paying in rupees is in our Heroku alternative overview.

Ship your Next.js app

Connect your repository at cloud.plexivo.io and watch your first build on the Deployments tab. The free trial is on the Developer plan, and no credit card is required.

title: I made two free AI models review each other's code in one Switch room.
description:
For the Flip the Switch hackathon I built Code Review Duel. One AI code reviewer can be confidently wrong, and you often can't tell. So I put two reviewers, on two different free models, into one Switch room. They review the same code, check each other, and then ask me, the human, to pick the better review.

Demo: https://youtu.be/Dyu2Fs-55sg
Repo: https://github.com/Zoymusk/code-review-duel

The stack (all free)

  • OpenCode with two free models: DeepSeek (reviewer-a) and GLM (reviewer-b).
  • Switch Console to run the agents on my own laptop.
  • Mattermost, the chat app built into Switch Console.

I have no paid AI subscriptions, so no API keys and no credit card were involved. Anyone can run it.

How it works

  1. I post a code snippet in the room and tag both reviewers.
  2. Reviewer A posts its review and hands over to reviewer B by name.
  3. Reviewer B posts its own review and asks A if it agrees.
  4. A and B each answer with one line and a reason.
  5. They ask me to reply A or B. Both acknowledge my pick and stop.

Why Switch

Both agents and I work in one room, so they read the same history and talk to each other by mentioning names. My pick is just another message in the thread. Without Switch I'd have needed glue code to connect two agents and a person.

What went wrong

  • My first room had no chat channel, so I couldn't type in it. switch-buddy had made it agent-only, and I recreated it on Mattermost.
  • Reviewer B kept waiting for reviewer A and then sat idle, because nothing woke it up. The fix was making A end its review with "@reviewer-b your turn."

What I found

My first test was int x = 5 / 0; in Java. The models disagreed: A said compile error (wrong), B said runtime exception (right). I wanted to build around that.

Then reality set in. Model answers change between runs. Later A got the same snippet right, and on longer code (a shopping cart and a library class with planted bugs) both models found almost the same bugs. B also reads A's review before writing its own, so the reviews overlap. I tested this alone, not with a team. So it's a cross-check and a visible place for disagreement, not two fully independent opinions.

What I'd do next

Make reviewer B review the code first without seeing A's review, then compare. That would make the cross-check much stronger.

Try it

The repo has one template file and a README with setup steps: install OpenCode, install Switch Console, import the template, and post a snippet. Thanks to the Switch and WeMakeDevs teams for the hackathon.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
description:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.
