title: Container Queries and Focus Management: Building Resilient Components with TailwindCSS v4
description:
Container Queries and Focus Management: Building Resilient Components with TailwindCSS v4

When integrating meta/astryx into a production TypeScript stack last quarter, we hit a painful wall: our card components looked pristine in desktop viewports but collapsed into unusable layouts when nested inside sidebars or widget containers. The root cause wasn't the design system itself—it was our reliance on viewport-based media queries instead of container queries. Combined with improperly managed focus trapping in modal overlays, our accessibility score tanked.

Let's walk through the hard-won fixes.

The Container Query Problem

Viewport-based breakpoints assume a global coordinate system. When meta/astryx components lived inside a max-w-xs sidebar, our md: and lg: classes fired anyway, rendering a responsive grid that had no space to breathe.

TailwindCSS v4 gives us container queries out of the box:

// Mark a container context
<div className="@container">
  {/* Children respond to container width, not viewport */}
  <div className="@sm:grid @sm:grid-cols-2 @lg:grid-cols-4">
    {/* Card components resize based on container, not screen size */}
  </div>
</div>

In your Tailwind config, container queries are enabled by default in v4. The @sm, @md, @lg prefixes correspond to container widths (640px, 768px, 1024px).

Practical Component Example

Here's a reusable card component that adapts to its container context:

export function ResponsiveCard({
  title,
  children,
  variant = 'default'
}: {
  title: string
  children: React.ReactNode
  variant?: 'default' | 'elevated'
}) {
  return (
    <article
      className={`
        @container rounded-lg border border-slate-200
        ${variant === 'elevated' ? 'shadow-lg' : 'shadow-sm'}
        p-4 @sm:p-6 @lg:p-8
      `}
    >
      <h2 className="@sm:text-lg @lg:text-xl font-semibold text-slate-900">
        {title}
      </h2>
      <div className="mt-4 @sm:mt-6 @lg:grid @lg:grid-cols-2 @lg:gap-4">
        {children}
      </div>
    </article>
  )
}

The beauty: drop this component anywhere—sidebar, modal, main content—and it responds intelligently to available space.

Focus Trapping and Modal Accessibility

Our second catastrophe: screen readers navigated straight through our modal overlay into the background DOM. Users with keyboard-only input couldn't escape modals without tabbing through 200 hidden elements.

Using Radix primitives (which meta/astryx often builds on), focus management becomes declarative:

import * as Dialog from '@radix-ui/react-dialog'

export function AccessibleModal({
  isOpen,
  onOpenChange,
  title,
  children
}: {
  isOpen: boolean
  onOpenChange: (open: boolean) => void
  title: string
  children: React.ReactNode
}) {
  return (
    <Dialog.Root open={isOpen} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>
      <Dialog.Portal>
        {/* Backdrop with inert attribute prevents focus escape */}
        <Dialog.Overlay
          className="fixed inset-0 bg-black/50 data-[state=open]:animate-fadeIn"
          aria-hidden="true"
        />
        <Dialog.Content
          className="fixed left-1/2 top-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2 w-96 max-w-screen rounded-lg bg-white p-6 shadow-xl focus:outline-none"
          role="dialog"
          aria-labelledby="modal-title"
          aria-modal="true"
        >
          <Dialog.Title id="modal-title" className="text-lg font-semibold">
            {title}
          </Dialog.Title>
          <div className="mt-4">{children}</div>
          <Dialog.Close
            className="absolute right-4 top-4 p-2 text-slate-500 hover:text-slate-900 focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500"
            aria-label="Close dialog"
          >
            ✕
          </Dialog.Close>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  )
}

Radix handles focus trap internally: Tab cycles only within the modal, Escape closes it, and screen readers announce role and title on entry.

Micro-Interaction: Smooth Dismissal

Combine container queries with a discrete fade animation:

@keyframes fadeIn {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: scale(0.95);
  }
  to {
    opacity: 1;
    transform: scale(1);
  }
}

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  .modal-enter {
    animation: fadeIn 200ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
  }
}

Tailwind's data-* selectors make this trivial:

className="data-[state=open]:animate-fadeIn"

Integration with meta/astryx

When testing meta/astryx's component library, ensure your container context is set at the layout boundary—typically your main content wrapper. This prevents collision between the design system's internal breakpoints and your application's responsive strategy.

// pages/dashboard.tsx
export default function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <div className="@container flex gap-6">
      <aside className="w-64">
        {/* Sidebar + cards inside 256px container */}
      </aside>
      <main className="flex-1">
        {/* Main area responds to its own container width */}
      </main>
    </div>
  )
}

The Real Tension

Container queries solve isolation beautifully, but they carry a performance cost on older browsers and complex nesting scenarios. Radix's focus management is bulletproof for accessibility compliance, yet it adds another dependency to your bundle. The trade-off: pick your battles. For component libraries like meta/astryx that ship into varied contexts, container queries are non-negotiable. For highly controlled admin dashboards, viewport breakpoints might suffice.

The question isn't which is objectively better—it's whether your integration pattern demands resilience in unknown containers or predictable, controlled layouts.

title: Comment recadrer automatiquement une vidéo en 9:16 avec ffmpeg et la différence d'images
description:
Le recadrage automatique des logiciels de montage est souvent vendu comme du suivi de sujet par IA. Pour le cas le plus courant, une personne qui bouge devant un fond immobile, une méthode bien plus simple trouve le même cadrage : comparer chaque image à la précédente et regarder où l'image a changé. L'outil de recadrage de l'application de bureau osFoundry fonctionne ainsi, en Rust et ffmpeg. Voici la même méthode en une soixantaine de lignes de Python, appliquée à un clip de 7.5 secondes en 1920×1080 composé de trois plans. Elle donne les mêmes recadrages que l'application, au pixel près.

1. Réduire la vidéo en images grises de 64×36

Inutile d'examiner les images en taille réelle pour trouver ce qui a bougé. ffmpeg peut fournir la vidéo en octets bruts, à quatre images par seconde, réduite à 64×36 et convertie en un octet de gris par pixel :

import math, re, subprocess, sys

FFMPEG, SRC = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
W, H, FPS = 64, 36, 4

raw = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-loglevel", "error", "-i", SRC,
     "-vf", f"fps={FPS},scale={W}:{H}", "-pix_fmt", "gray", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"],
    capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
frames = [raw[i:i + W * H] for i in range(0, len(raw) - W * H + 1, W * H)]

Chaque image fait 2304 octets. Le clip de 7.5 secondes donne 30 images, donc 29 paires à comparer. La réduction moyenne aussi la plus grande partie du grain, ce qui compte pour l'étape suivante.

2. Trouver le centre de ce qui a changé

Pour chaque paire d'images, on calcule la différence de chaque cellule, on ignore les petites différences et on calcule le centre de masse du reste, pondéré par l'ampleur du changement de chaque cellule :

def centroid(prev, curr, floor=12):
    total = sx = sy = 0
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(prev, curr)):
        d = abs(b - a)
        if d < floor:
            continue
        total += d
        sx += d * (i % W)
        sy += d * (i // W)
    if total < W * H * 0.5:
        return None
    return sx / total / W, sy / total / H

samples = [centroid(a, b) for a, b in zip(frames, frames[1:])]

Ces deux constantes rendent la méthode utilisable. Le seuil de bruit de 12 (sur 255) écarte les changements dus au capteur et à la compression. Sur ce clip, avec le seuil à 12, 381 cellules sur 2304 en moyenne comptent comme modifiées. Avec le seuil à 1, il y en a 1855, soit presque toute l'image, et le centre est attiré vers le milieu : le premier échantillon tombe à 0.44 de la largeur au lieu de 0.40.

La seconde vérification renvoie None quand le changement total est minuscule. Si rien n'a bougé, le « centre du changement » est le centre du bruit, et le suivre fait dériver le cadre sans raison. None veut dire « garde la position précédente ».

3. Limiter la vitesse du cadre

Un centroïde brut saute dès qu'une deuxième personne entre dans le plan. Plafonner le pas à 5% de l'image par échantillon l'empêche de traverser l'écran d'un coup :

def smooth(samples, step=0.05):
    cur = next((s for s in samples if s), (0.5, 0.5))
    out = []
    for s in samples:
        if s:
            cur = tuple(min(1, max(0, c + max(-step, min(step, t - c))))
                        for c, t in zip(cur, s))
        out.append(cur)
    return out

track = smooth(samples)

Elle part de la première vraie observation, si bien qu'un clip qui s'ouvre sur une image fixe ne fait pas de panoramique depuis le centre.

4. Trouver les coupes avec le score de scène de ffmpeg

Le filtre select de ffmpeg attribue à chaque image un score de scène entre 0 et 1, et showinfo affiche les images qui passent le seuil. Les horodatages vont sur stderr, pas sur stdout :

log = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-hide_banner", "-i", SRC,
     "-filter_complex", "select='gt(scene,0.35)',showinfo", "-f", "null", "-"],
    capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
cuts = [round(float(t) * 1000) for t in re.findall(r"pts_time:([\d.]+)", log)]

Sur ce clip, cela trouve des coupes à 1767 ms et 4733 ms. Afficher le score de chaque image (select='gte(scene,0)',metadata=print) montre la marge : les deux coupes obtiennent 0.616 et 0.432, et aucune autre des 225 images ne dépasse 0.068.

5. Un recadrage par plan

Enfin, on fait la moyenne de la trajectoire à l'intérieur de chaque plan et on place une fenêtre 9:16 autour de ce point. 1080 × 9/16 donne 607.5 ; la largeur est arrondie à 606, un nombre pair, car H.264 exige des dimensions paires.

duration = len(frames) * 1000 // FPS
per = duration / len(track)
bounds = [0] + [c for c in cuts if 0 < c < duration] + [duration]
cw = int(1080 * 9 / 16) // 2 * 2
for start, end in zip(bounds, bounds[1:]):
    a = int(start // per)
    part = track[a:max(a + 1, math.ceil(end / per))]
    bx = sum(p[0] for p in part) / len(part)
    x = min(max(round(1920 * bx - cw / 2), 0), 1920 - cw)
    print(f"{start / 1000:.2f}-{end / 1000:.2f}s  crop={cw}:1080:{x}:0")

0.00-1.77s  crop=606:1080:369:0
1.77-4.73s  crop=606:1080:668:0
4.73-7.50s  crop=606:1080:932:0

Ce sont les trois mêmes recadrages que ceux de l'application pour ce clip. Le script entier a pris 3.5 secondes sur ce Mac, presque tout dans la boucle en Python pur.

Les coupes comptent plus qu'il n'y paraît. Moyenné sur tout le clip, le sujet se trouve à x = 707, à seulement 50 pixels d'un recadrage centré simple (657), parce que la femme marche à gauche dans un plan et à droite dans un autre. Ce n'est qu'à l'échelle du plan que la moyenne a un sens.

Remettre les plans bout à bout

Les recadrages deviennent un seul filter_complex : on découpe chaque plan, on le recadre et on assemble les morceaux. C'est la forme que construit l'application :

[0:v]trim=start=0.000:end=1.767,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:369:0[v0];
[0:v]trim=start=1.767:end=4.733,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:668:0[v1];
[0:v]trim=start=4.733:end=7.500,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:932:0[v2];
[v0][v1][v2]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0[out]

(Supprimez les retours à la ligne en le passant à -filter_complex.) La sortie fait 606×1080 et dure autant que l'entrée.

Le Rust de l'application explique pourquoi elle n'anime pas le recadrage à l'intérieur d'un plan, alors que ffmpeg le pourrait :

/// 🔴 Per scene, not per frame. ffmpeg can animate a crop, but a crop that moves continuously is
/// a pan the editor never asked for; cutting between fixed framings is what an editor would
/// actually do, and it is also what stays honest when the tracking is wrong — a bad framing
/// lasts one scene rather than smearing across the whole clip.
pub fn reframe_segments(
    cuts: &[i64],
    duration_ms: i64,
    track: &[(f64, f64)],
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    target: f64,
) -> Vec<ReframeSegment> {

Où la différence d'images échoue

La méthode trouve ce qui bouge, pas qui compte. Elle marche quand le sujet est l'élément principal qui bouge et que la caméra reste fixe. Elle échoue quand :

  • la caméra fait un panoramique : toutes les cellules changent et le centre tombe près du milieu ;
  • le fond est chargé, comme la circulation ou une foule ;
  • deux personnes bougent de part et d'autre et la moyenne se retrouve entre elles.

Les reflets sont un cas plus léger. Dans le premier plan de ce clip, le reflet de la femme dans une vitre bouge aussi, mais il reste proche d'elle, donc le cadre la trouve quand même. Un détecteur de visages ou de personnes gère mieux les cas difficiles, au prix d'un modèle. La réponse de l'application à ces cas est un réglage manuel : l'utilisateur glisse un point sur le sujet et l'analyse est ignorée.

L'application de bureau utilisée ici est gratuite sur la page de téléchargement d'osFoundry.

title: 🎃 The Real Nightmare Isn't a Bug. It's a Bug Nobody Notices. 🎃
description:
Imagine deploying a new feature.

All tests pass. CI is green. No errors in the logs. Everything looks fine.

Then a user reports that their payment was processed twice.

Here's a simplified example of what can go wrong:

async function processPayment(order) {
  try {
    return await paymentAPI.charge({
      amount: order.total,
      customerId: order.customerId
    });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === "TIMEOUT") {
      return await paymentAPI.charge({
        amount: order.total,
        customerId: order.customerId
      });
    }

    throw error;
  }
}

Looks reasonable, but there's a problem.

The first request might have reached the payment service and completed successfully. Only the response got lost.

The retry sends another charge request.

Now imagine this happening with a real customer.

One way to prevent this is to use an idempotency key:

async function processPayment(order) {
  return await paymentAPI.charge({
    amount: order.total,
    customerId: order.customerId,
    idempotencyKey: `payment-${order.id}`
  });
}

Now the payment service can recognize repeated requests for the same operation and return the original result instead of charging the customer again.

Of course, this depends on the payment provider correctly supporting and implementing idempotency.

That's what makes production bugs interesting. Sometimes the code works exactly as written. The problem is that nobody considered what would happen under real-world conditions.

A green test suite is good news, but it doesn't mean you've tested every possible failure.

Sometimes the scariest bugs are the ones that never show up in your test results. 👻

Happy Halloween! 🎃

title: I ran 33 LLM models behind one endpoint for a month. Here is what broke.
description:
I built a small gateway that pools free LLM tiers — NVIDIA NIM, Kilo, OpenRouter, a couple of
community endpoints — behind a single OpenAI-compatible URL. Thirty-three models, one API key,
no monthly bill. It ran real daily work for a month.

It also broke in six different ways, and every single break was something I would have avoided
if someone had written it down first. So I did.

The numbers first

What Measured
Free tier rate limit 40 requests/min, sliding window
Burst probe result 45 requests → 24 success, 20 rate-limited, 1 upstream 503, in 12.8s
Fast model, 95K context 18.6s
Slow model, same context 83s
Requests that hung and then failed every one, at 178–194s

That last row is the one that cost me the most sleep.

Break 1: the 180-second hang that was not my bug

Every request through one particular relay hung for exactly 178 to 194 seconds and then failed
with a connection error. My code was fine. The relay had a hard 180-second timeout of its own,
and it sat on the socket without sending a single byte until the deadline expired.

The fix is not a longer timeout. It is an inter-chunk idle deadline: if no SSE chunk arrives
within N seconds, abort and retry on a fresh connection. A total-duration timeout will not save
you, because a stalled connection still counts as in-flight.

Break 2: one 429 froze every model on the provider

Free tiers rate-limit at the channel level, not the model level. A single greedy request tripped
a 429 and the cooldown I wrote disabled every model behind that provider for two minutes —
including ones I was not even calling.

Two fixes: pace client-side at ~85% of the measured entitlement instead of bursting, and scope
any cooldown to the exact model that was limited.

Break 3: the retry stampede

Fifteen parallel workers hit the same failure and retried on the same second. One upstream
hiccup became an outage. Exponential backoff without full jitter is the bug — the workers
stay synchronized.

Break 4: a byte-order mark broke my config

A scheduled job started throwing Unexpected token '﻿'. The JSON config was written by
PowerShell's Set-Content -Encoding UTF8, which emits a BOM. JSON.parse does not tolerate it.
The fix is one line, but finding it was not.

Break 5: the stream that connected and said nothing

Some proxies accept the connection and send zero bytes. No error, no data — the request just
sits there. This looks identical to a slow model until you instrument the difference between
connect-fail, idle-fail, and slow-success.

Break 6: I lost a batch at item 700

No checkpoints. A crash at item 700 of 1000 meant reprocessing everything, and the bill doubled.
An append-only checkpoint journal with content-hash dedupe keys makes any job resumable in
seconds.

What I actually built

The gateway is about 600 lines: a candidate selector that respects per-model cooldowns, a pacer
that keeps under the sliding window, a failover ladder (primary → fallback → local Ollama), and
one JSONL line per request so that a 3am question has an answer in the morning.

Three of the recipes — the pacer, the 15-second messaging window, and the postmortem template —
are MIT licensed in this repository: llm-ops-recipes.

The other 27 (JSON repair loops, provider failover ladders, model tiering, golden-set regression
gates, cost accounting, and two full postmortems) are in the
LLM Ops Cookbook.

The one thing I would tell myself a month ago

Measure the limit before you design around it. I spent two days building a cooldown system
before running a 45-request burst probe that told me, in 13 seconds, exactly what the real
constraint was.

If you'd rather not rebuild this from scratch, I packaged the exact scripts I use: LLM Ops Cookbook — 30 one-page recipes for running LLM workloads that don't fall over. There is also a free sample if you want to see the format first.

title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: How Small Models + Skillware Beat Frontier LLMs
description:
Stop forcing LLMs to write disposable Python scripts on the fly. Here is how deterministic capability bundles slash token burn by 84.8%, cut costs by 97.3%, and let 8B local models outperform GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 5.

Right now, the AI engineering world is trapped in a very expensive delusion: the prompt-driven execution paradigm.

We give an auto-regressive language model a massive markdown dump of API docs, tell it to dynamically synthesize Python or bash scripts on the fly, and pray that it respects security boundaries because we wrote "IMPORTANT: DO NOT DELETE PROD" in all caps in the system prompt.

When it works, it feels like magic. When it hits production, it's a disaster. You get Prompt Rot (switching models breaks all your tool shims), Quadratic Attention Tax (paying frontier rates to re-read static OpenAPI schemas on every turn), and the dreaded Context Poisoning Cliff—where an agent fails a script attempt, dumps a massive stack trace into its own context window, and spirals into terminal hallucination by attempt #8.

In a new paper from ARPA Hellenic Logical Systems ("Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems", arXiv:2611.07652v1, we formalize the antidote: Capability Engineering.

The RPG Hotkey Analogy

Think about how skills work in an RPG like Morrowind or Diablo. When your character casts a spell or triggers an ability, you don't open a chat box and negotiate with the game engine to invent the physics of a fireball at runtime.

You press a hotkey. If the preconditions hold (you have the mana, you're outside a sanctuary town, targeting a valid hostile), the engine executes pre-compiled, deterministic logic and produces the exact same state transition every time.

Skillware brings this exact discipline to AI agents:

The Principle of Separation of Cognition and Capability: The model decides when to act and selects the parameters; the capability bundle governs how the action is executed. The assistant is a guest in this case, while the hard function does the work.

What is a Skillware Bundle?

Instead of loose SKILL.md files or brittle prompt wrappers, Skillware packages capabilities into self-contained, versioned, 5-role software bundles:

  1. Contract (manifest.yaml): Typed JSON Schema inputs/outputs, required env vars, cryptographic publisher identity, and an immutable Constitution (e.g., confirmed: true gates for destructive actions).
  2. Effect (skill.py): Pre-compiled, deterministic Python logic subclassing BaseSkill. Zero runtime code synthesis.
  3. Directive (instructions.md): Progressive disclosure guidance loaded Just-In-Time (JIT) only when needed.
  4. Assurance (test_skill.py): Hermetic offline pytest suites that verify the Effect honors the Contract in <100ms without calling a single LLM API.
  5. Corpus & Presentation (data/, card.json): Static offline datasets (like OFAC sanctions lists or statutory lexicons) bundled right next to the code for 100% air-gapped execution.

Universal In-Process Adapters (Zero IPC Latency)

Unlike MCP (which requires spinning up and supervising out-of-process client-server daemons over stdio/HTTP sockets), Skillware executes in-process in CPython in <1.2ms. Its universal interface morphisms (to_gemini_tool(), to_claude_tool(), to_openai_tool(), to_ollama_prompt()) automatically translate your manifest.yaml into any provider's native tool dialect on the fly.

from skillware.core import SkillLoader

# 1. Load a verified, offline-tested capability bundle
bundle = SkillLoader.load_skill("finance/wallet_screening")
skill = bundle["class"]()

# 2. Auto-transmute contract to host dialect (Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, Ollama)
tools = [SkillLoader.to_gemini_tool(bundle)]

# 3. Pre-flight AST schema validation + deterministic local execution
try:
    result = skill.execute(dict(call.args))
except SkillwareParamValidationError as exc:
    result = {"error": f"Invalid arguments: {exc}"}

The SLM Parameter Paradox: 8B Local > Frontier Cloud

We evaluated 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions (SKILLWARE-BENCH), testing multi-step email handling, UK corporate registry resolution, on-chain sanctions screening, and adversarial prompt injection.

The headline finding? The SLM Parameter Paradox.

When you stop forcing models to write disposable code and restrict them strictly to semantic routing and schema parameter selection, 3B–8B local models equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier giants (including GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 5):

  • 97.3% Cost Reduction: Dropping from $15.58 (Frontier LLM dynamically writing code) to $0.42 per 1,000 turns using a local 8B SLM + Skillware.
  • 84.0% Context Excision: Progressive JIT disclosure (mode="brief") compresses tool signatures to ~30 tokens, slashing total token burn by up to 84.8%.
  • Zero Parameter Corruption: Pre-flight JSON Schema validation drops parameter errors from 18.5% down to 0.0% and eliminates all 464 runtime script debugging loops.
  • 56.2% Lift for Open-Weight Models: Meta Llama 4 Maverick jumps from a 37.5% pass rate (vanilla) to 93.8% when equipped, while Qwen 3.8 Flash and Gemma 4 (31B) hit 100.0%.
  • 1.2ms Zero-Token Firewall: Instead of using a second LLM to audit incoming text for prompt injection (which doubles your cost and still gets jailbroken), Skillware uses a 3-stage deterministic normalization pipeline (stripping zero-width Unicode smuggling, Cyrillic/Greek homoglyphs, and hidden DOM spans) in 1.2ms with 0 tokens burned.

From Python Loops to Drones and Neural Interfaces

Why does sub-millisecond, in-process determinism matter beyond saving API budget? Because software agents are only Scale I.

Under ISO 13849 SIL-3 safety standards, physical fault mitigation in robotics and industrial Digital Twins must execute within 10ms, and high-frequency robotic/UAV control loops run at 500Hz (1–2ms). You cannot run a drone or a surgical neuroprosthetic over a 2.5-second cloud LLM loop or an out-of-process JSON-RPC socket.

By establishing a formal Clock-Domain Crossing (CDC) between slow cognitive deliberation (~1s) and sub-millisecond deterministic motor schemas (<1.2ms), Skillware lays the foundation for installing verified capabilities across autonomous IoT, embodied robotics, and eventually Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs).

Try It Out

The era of prompt engineering is closing; the era of Capability Engineering has begun. Stop renting disposable logic by the token.

  • Install via PyPI: pip install skillware
  • GitHub Repository: github.com/arpahls/skillware
  • Documentation & Registry: skillware.site
  • Read the Full Paper: arXiv:2611.07652v1 | DOI: `10.5281/zenodo.21552745

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
description:
Vercel CLI now includes vercel doctor, which checks your setup and shows the command that fixes each problem it finds.

It checks the CLI version and install, your login and current team, the project link, and your project configuration in vercel.json. It also reports active incidents from the Vercel status page.

Each check reports OK, Warning, Failed, or Skipped. When vercel upgrade can't update the installed CLI, the install check shows where the CLI runs from and how to reinstall it.

Doctor runs without a login or a linked project, and it never prompts, logs in, or links a project, so coding agents can run it before guessing at a fix. Add --json to get each check's status and suggested commands as structured output.

Update to the latest CLI version and run vercel doctor to check your setup, or read the doctor command reference.

title: Why Naive Text Extraction Destroys RAG on Multi-Column PDFs (and How to Fix Reading Order)
description:
When an AI retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline hallucinates on a question sourced from a scientific paper or financial report, the debugging process almost invariably looks at the wrong layer. Engineers test alternative embedding models, tweak chunk token budgets, or introduce expensive cross-encoder rerankers.

Yet in a surprising fraction of failure cases, the corruption happens before embedding: in the text extraction layer where the parser attempts to reconstruct human reading order from a format that was never designed to store it.

What a PDF File Actually Stores

A PDF is essentially a set of rendering commands designed to place ink or pixels consistently across any screen or printer. Under the hood, text lives inside stream operators bracketed by BT (Begin Text) and ET (End Text):

BT
  /F1 11 Tf
  72 700 Td
  [(Retrieval) -250 (augmented) -250 (generation)] TJ
  0 -14 Td
  (depends on document layout.) Tj
ET

Here, Td moves the coordinate cursor, Tj outputs raw glyph codes, and TJ outputs strings separated by numerical kerning shifts. Crucially:

  1. There is no concept of a "sentence" or "paragraph" in an untagged PDF stream.
  2. The order of rendering commands in the file reflects the sequence in which the generator tool drew elements—not necessarily how a human reads them.
  3. Kerning offsets (like the -250 in the example above) are horizontal spacing nudges, leaving the parser to guess where word spaces belong.

When you pass this document to an automated parser, the tool must guess which glyphs form words, which words form lines, and in what order those lines should be concatenated.

The Multi-Column Braiding Problem

The most damaging extraction error occurs in two-column or multi-column layouts—the standard format for arXiv papers, IEEE publications, and corporate annual reports.

When an extraction library attempts to "fix" raw stream order by sorting text visually by vertical position ($y$-coordinate), it reads across both columns simultaneously. Line 1 of column A is followed immediately by line 1 of column B, then line 2 of column A, then line 2 of column B:

Column A:                          Column B:
Rats were fed a                    All authors declare
standard chow diet                 no competing
for fourteen days.                 financial interests.

Result of naive Y-coordinate sorting:
"Rats were fed a All authors declare standard chow diet no competing for fourteen days. financial interests."

This resulting text is insidious because it never throws a Python exception, passes character-count heuristics, and retains plausible English vocabulary. But when this chunk is sliced into a 512-token window and passed to an embedding model, the vector represents a semantic blend of laboratory protocol and financial disclosures. The vector sits in embedding space near neither topic, making accurate retrieval mathematically impossible.

Three Practical Tiers to Recover Reading Order

Depending on your pipeline constraints and throughput requirements, here are three practical engineering approaches for handling multi-column documents:

Tier 1: Geometric Block Partitioning with Vertical Banding

If you run lightweight CPU-only ingestion using libraries like PyMuPDF (fitz), you can operate on layout bounding boxes (blocks) rather than flat character dumps.

A common naive heuristic splits the page at the horizontal midpoint, but that fails when full-width titles, abstracts, or wide tables appear in the middle of a page. A more robust approach groups blocks into vertical bands separated by spanning elements:

# Practical 2-column reading order parser with vertical band guards
def extract_two_column_page(page, span_threshold=0.75):
    """
    Extracts text from a two-column page while preserving reading sequence.
    Groups text into vertical bands whenever a full-width block appears
    (e.g., page title, abstract, or full-width table/figure), preventing
    mid-page spanning elements from corrupting the sequence.
    """
    # PyMuPDF block format: (x0, y0, x1, y1, text, block_no, block_type)
    # block_type == 0 represents text blocks
    text_blocks = [b for b in page.get_text("blocks") if b[6] == 0]
    if not text_blocks:
        return ""

    page_width = page.rect.width
    midpoint = page_width / 2.0

    # Sort blocks by top coordinate to process page bands top-to-bottom
    text_blocks.sort(key=lambda b: b[1])

    ordered_blocks = []
    current_left = []
    current_right = []

    def flush_columns():
        nonlocal current_left, current_right, ordered_blocks
        if current_left:
            ordered_blocks.extend(sorted(current_left, key=lambda b: b[1]))
            current_left = []
        if current_right:
            ordered_blocks.extend(sorted(current_right, key=lambda b: b[1]))
            current_right = []

    for b in text_blocks:
        x0, y0, x1, y1 = b[0], b[1], b[2], b[3]
        box_width = x1 - x0

        # Spanning elements act as horizontal barriers between column bands
        if box_width >= page_width * span_threshold:
            flush_columns()
            ordered_blocks.append(b)
        elif x0 < midpoint:
            current_left.append(b)
        else:
            current_right.append(b)

    flush_columns()

    return "\n\n".join(b[4].strip() for b in ordered_blocks if b[4].strip())

Note: In production environments with varying margins or 3-column formats, dynamic gutter detection via horizontal projection profiles replaces the static midpoint.

Tier 2: Layout-Aware Vision and Segmentation Models

When documents include irregular multi-column grids, floating callout boxes, and complex multi-row tables, geometric heuristics begin to accumulate edge-case failures.

Layout-aware vision models (such as Docling, Marker, or layout segmentation vision transformers) treat the rendered page as a visual artifact. These architectures predict semantic regions (headings, captions, body paragraphs, tables) and explicitly infer the reading order graph between bounding boxes before converting elements into structured Markdown.

This approach requires significantly higher compute (typically GPU acceleration), but it prevents table rows from collapsing into unstructured text strings.

Tier 3: Producer-Side Tagged PDFs

If your team produces the documents entering the RAG corpus (e.g., internal research memos or documentation exports), the cleanest long-term solution is emitting Tagged PDF (PDF/UA or ISO 32000 tagged structures).

Tagged PDFs embed a structural logical tree directly into the file container, explicitly specifying reading sequence regardless of visual layout positioning. This eliminates heuristic guesswork for both screen readers and downstream AI extractors.

Audit Checklist Before Benchmarking Embedding Models

Before spending budget on new embedding endpoints or vector database re-indexing, run this quick quality audit on your raw text chunks:

  1. Spot-check multi-column transitions: Extract 20 random pages from multi-column documents and check whether sentences jump horizontally across columns.
  2. Inspect table headers: Confirm whether numbers in parsed output remain linked to their column and row descriptors or have flattened into meaningless lists of floats.
  3. Verify formula integrity: Check whether mathematical symbols and sub/superscripts maintain syntactic continuity or fragment across line breaks.
  4. Compare coordinate-sorted vs. raw output: A substantial divergence in text sequence often highlights where layout heuristics are struggling.

Clean document structure upstream is the most reliable foundation for downstream retrieval accuracy.

title: Ming-3.0-tts on a 16 GB card: the GPU sat mostly idle, and why a bigger one barely helps
description:
When a speech model runs slower than real time, the reflex is to rent a bigger GPU. With Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B that buys very little. An RTX 2000 Ada sat idle more than two thirds of the time. An RTX 4090 worked at most one moment in five, and the speedup was about 17%.

The model comes from the inclusionAI team at Ant Group. They released weights and code under MIT, with their own benchmarks and a frank list of limitations. It copies a voice from a few seconds of sample audio, builds one from a text prompt describing it, and turns inline tags like [Laughter] or [Sigh] into sounds. Their model page only mentions H800-80GB and H20-96G cards, with no memory figure. We ran their unmodified code on a small card to get one. Every number is in our Ming-3.0-tts memory and speed test on an RTX 2000 Ada.

Low GPU utilisation is the first thing to check

"Real time" is a ratio: seconds of audio produced per second of compute. A 20.7-second English paragraph cost 31 to 32 seconds on the RTX 2000 Ada. On the 4090, a 20.9-second paragraph cost 27 seconds. Its faster host processor may explain part of that gain.

The culprit is the decode loop, which builds the audio step by step, 80 milliseconds per step. Between steps, Python code on the CPU prepares and launches the next one. Keeping up with playback takes 12.5 steps per second. We measured about 8.3 to 8.9. The GPU is a fast bus stuck behind a slow ticket check at every stop.

Before sizing hardware for a text-to-speech (TTS) model, run nvidia-smi while it speaks and read utilisation, the share of time the GPU is working. If it stays low, a faster card will not buy you speed. One possible way out, untested by us: vLLM-Omni, an engine built for fast serving, which Ming's roadmap marks as supported.

Emulate the small card before you rent it

No real card below 16 GB ran. Two 12 GB RTX 3080 Ti machines booted without the SSH access our installer needs, and no 8 GB card was available to rent. So we faked one. PyTorch, the library Ming runs on, has a call, torch.cuda.set_per_process_memory_fraction, that limits how much GPU memory the process may take. We lowered it on the 16 GB card until loading broke.

With caps of 8, 4 and 3 GiB, the output WAVs had the same md5 checksum as the uncapped run, and speed did not change. At 2.75 GiB, setup died with "CUDA out of memory". Add roughly 0.4 GB for the driver and the article's estimate lands at a 4 GB card. Nobody ran that on real hardware, and a smaller chip may also be slower.

Copy the hashing habit: loading under a cap proves little, matching bytes prove the cap changed nothing.

Log the timings with every request

Our custom backend, a short Python file that wraps the authors' code behind an HTTP API, returns its own measurements next to the audio. This came back for a cloned line with three tags on the RTX 2000 Ada:

"timings": { "gpu_s": 11.02, "realtime_factor": 0.63, "peak_vram_mib": 2922 }

That request spent 11.02 seconds of GPU time on 7.0 seconds of audio. Strip the tags and the same line took 8.05 seconds for 5.3 seconds of audio. Tags are extra sound, and sound costs time. Log these fields from day one.

Three traps you will hit

  • Numbers. Before speaking, English text goes through normalisation, a step that spells numbers and symbols out as words. It read 4521 as "four thousand five hundred twenty, one", pause included, and turned the phone number 555-0142 into a subtraction. Spanish text bypasses that step, and "1.249,99 euros, un 12,5 %" turned into nonsense. Spelling English numbers as words did not help. Check every price by ear.
  • Tags by language. The authors document tags for English and Chinese. We only tried them in English, so tags in Spanish text remain untested.
  • The OpenAI speech route. OpenAI-style apps request speech from a dedicated endpoint, which on InferenceKey cannot yet carry a custom backend's audio (open, IK-531). The example goes through the chat route and decodes the WAV out of the message text.

What the test does and does not show

We ran each clip through Whisper, OpenAI's speech-to-text model: 17 of 19 lines matched word for word across English, Spanish and Chinese, and both misses were numbers. A speaker-recognition model rated the clones 0.87 in English and 0.84 in Spanish, both cloned from an English reference. Keep in mind that Ming relies on that same model to capture a voice, which tilts the score towards Ming. No human listened, each line ran once, and the reference was a clean synthetic clip from Kyutai's Pocket TTS. The backend handles a single request at once, so concurrent load is untested.

My read: good for recorded narration, wrong for a live voice agent. If you need Spanish speed more than cloning or tags, our Spanish Pocket TTS voice on CPU reached 1.05x real time on a desktop CPU. Nobody has compared the two for quality.

From empty caches, the backend was ready to serve after 60.3 seconds, about half of it installing Python libraries. The article's appendix has the setup, per-request tables and VRAM ladder for Ming-3.0-tts.

Credit for the model goes to inclusionAI at Ant Group, to OpenAI for Whisper, to Kyutai, who made Pocket TTS, and to the AI Search channel, whose news video pointed us to Ming. The SDK example, the audio samples and every measurement are in the Ming-3.0-tts research article on inferencekey.com.

title: Modelling a Year-End Inventory Snapshot: Cut-Off Events, Lot Status, Variance Audit Trails and Opening Balances
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

If you model a food factory's year-end inventory snapshot as a set of events, five objects matter more than the trial balance:

  1. Cut-off / freeze events — a timestamp (and production stop rules) after which receipts, issues, outputs and dispatches belong to the next year.
  2. Lot-status inventory snapshots — counts of raw materials, WIP and finished goods by lot, location and status (including QA hold / quarantine / rework), plus third-party and in-transit lines.
  3. Variance audit trail — every difference with reason code, value and named approver, linked back to a count and an observer note.
  4. eTIMS stock alignment — invoice and credit-note quantities that reconcile to the same year-boundary movements, supporting opening and closing stock by item.
  5. Opening-balance lock — January's opening stock loaded only from the signed closing pack, not from a parallel spreadsheet.

Kenya Revenue Authority's stock management functionality notice cites section 23A(2)(b) of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 and expects records of stock received, purchased, sold, transferred, returned, adjusted or otherwise disposed of, aligned with TIMS/eTIMS invoices. The Star (2 Oct 2026) reported manufacturers preparing for a January 2027 rollout; People Daily framed the operational test as reconciling transactions with goods actually held and moved.

Below is the 12-point year-end stocktake I recommend for Kenyan food and agro processors — different from a routine count or a full month-end close — with a year-end file template and FAQ. Full references on the canonical post.

What the guidance and the law actually say

KRA stock management for electronic invoicing. On its stock management functionality page, KRA informs taxpayers that they must maintain accurate and up-to-date stock records while invoicing through TIMS/eTIMS, in accordance with section 23A(2)(b) of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015. The records should cover stock that is received, purchased, sold, transferred, returned, adjusted or otherwise disposed of, and they should align with the transactions invoiced through TIMS/eTIMS. KRA links this to correct tax reporting, accurate business records and compliance, and has been running consultative forums with businesses.

Manufacturers and the January 2027 prep window. The Star (2 October 2026) reported that KRA issued a public notice on 7 September 2026 requiring accurate stock records through TIMS/eTIMS, and that preparations point toward a January 2027 rollout. The Kenya Association of Manufacturers has asked for clarity on how the functionality will sit beside existing ERP systems, how conversion of raw materials into finished goods (including wastage, by-products, damaged goods and samples) will be captured, how imports and inter-warehouse transfers will be treated, and what happens during system downtime. KRA's George Obell was quoted saying the initiative targets missing-trader fraud and unfair competition. The same piece notes that eTIMS architecture already includes stock inventory, stock by item, imported items, stock-in and stock-out histories, movements and opening and closing stock — exactly the ledger your year-end snapshot should be able to support.

Accounting for every unit. People Daily (10 October 2026) walks through the basic equation: opening stock plus what came in, minus what went out, should equal what remains. A physical shortfall needs investigation with supporting documents — purchase invoices, sales records, transfer notes, adjustment records and physical counts — not a silent journal. Multi-branch businesses need consistent product codes and transfer records. Electronic invoicing improves visibility; it does not replace physical controls for damage, theft, returns, internal use or transfers.

Five-year retention. Section 23 of Kenya's Tax Procedures Act, 2015 requires a person to keep documents required under a tax law so that tax liability can be readily ascertained, and to retain them for five years from the end of the reporting period they relate to (subject to the exceptions in the Act). Your year-end stocktake pack belongs in that set. East African Standard EAS 39 (Hygiene in the food and drink manufacturing industry — Code of practice) clause 14 also expects records of actions taken to assure food safety to be indexed, filed and maintained for a suitable period — so confirm with your quality lead whether food-safety retention for the same year-end evidence runs longer than the tax minimum. Our eTIMS guide for food and agro manufacturers and food safety records checklist cover those two sides of the same filing cabinet.

Why year-end stocktakes go wrong in food plants

Factories rarely fail the annual count because nobody showed up. They fail because year-end is treated as a finance deadline instead of an operations freeze.

The patterns are familiar. Planning starts in the last week of December. Production is still issuing material while stores are counting. WIP has no status on the sheet. Held finished goods are mixed into free stock. Stock at a co-packer or third-party warehouse is guessed from last month's email. In-transit trucks are invisible to both sites. Nobody from outside the counting team observes. Variances are posted as "year-end adj" without a named approver. Opening balances for January are loaded from a spreadsheet that does not match the signed count. And when eTIMS or an auditor later asks for the year-boundary story, the pack cannot be found in under five minutes.

None of that survives a world in which stock movements and electronic invoices are expected to tell one story — and in which January's opening stock is simply last year's closing stock with a signature.

The 12-point year-end stock take checklist for food processors

Plan and freeze (start in November)

1. Publish the year-end stocktake plan in November.

Write the freeze window, count dates by warehouse and cold room, team leads, observer or auditor attendance, cut-off rules for receipts and dispatches, and the date opening balances will be locked. Brief stores, production, QA, dispatch and finance. A plan that only exists in someone's head is how the 31st becomes a scramble.

2. Announce a production and movement freeze for the count window.

Decide which lines stop, which can finish work-in-progress already in process, and which receipts or dispatches are blocked until after the count. Tell suppliers and logistics partners where needed. A year-end count against a moving warehouse invents variances that January will inherit.

3. Post every open slip before anyone counts.

GRNs, production issues and outputs, transfers, delivery notes, credit notes and returns that belong to the closing year must be in the system before the count starts. Use the same discipline as in our stock count reconciliation checklist and supplier intake checklist. Incomplete ledgers invent year-end "losses".

Count everything that is yours — and everything that affects yours

4. Count raw materials and packaging by lot and location.

Blind counts where practical. Partial bags, open drums, returned packaging and near-expiry lots get their own lines. Confirm units of measure before you chase a variance. FEFO and expiry write-offs at year-end belong here: see FEFO and batch expiry tracking.

5. Count work-in-progress with a status, not a guess.

List every open tank, silo, line, vat or pallet of WIP at the freeze: product, batch or order, quantity, stage and owner. Decide whether each line is finished into the closing year, carried as WIP into January, or written off with approval. WIP with no status becomes opening stock nobody can defend.

6. Count finished goods separately from blocked stock.

Sellable FG is one figure. Stock on hold, in quarantine, in rework, in the returns bay or awaiting disposal is another. Record status on the sheet, as in our QA hold checklist. Held pallets counted as free stock are how January's available-to-promise lies.

7. Include third-party, consignment and co-packer stock.

Stock at a co-packer, bonded store, distributor warehouse or customer site that is still yours needs a count confirmation — preferably with the third party's signed sheet or a joint count. Guessing from last month's email is not a year-end figure.

8. Include in-transit stock with named sender and receiver.

Trucks, containers and inter-branch transfers that left before the freeze and have not yet been received need a line: document number, contents, quantity, sender, receiver and expected arrival. People Daily's multi-branch point applies at year-end too: goods that left one store must not vanish from both sites' closing and opening balances. Tie dispatch evidence to the same discipline as our finished goods dispatch checklist.

Observe, reconcile, align and lock

9. Have an auditor, external observer or independent internal observer present.

Year-end counts that only the usual store team sees are harder to defend. Note who observed, which locations they covered and any exceptions they recorded. If your statutory auditor attends, treat their presence as part of the pack, not a courtesy visit.

10. Reconcile variances only with named approval — then lock the year-end adjustment list.

Every difference carries item, lot, location, system quantity, counted quantity, difference, value, reason code and approver. The counter does not approve their own write-off. "Year-end adj" is not a reason. KRA's stock-management notice expects returns, adjustments and disposals to be recorded. Run the recount and investigation steps from the stock count reconciliation checklist before anyone posts.

11. Align year-end stock with eTIMS invoices and stock records.

Confirm that invoices and credit notes for the closing year were transmitted as required, that quantities match what left the warehouse, and that your inventory ledger can support opening and closing stock by item — the same objects The Star noted already exist in eTIMS architecture. Document any legitimate year-end variances (wastage, by-products, samples, damage) with the same reason codes KAM has been asking KRA to clarify. See our eTIMS guide.

12. Assemble the year-end pack, lock opening balances for the new year, and retain the file.

File the November plan, freeze notice, posted-transaction list, count and recount sheets, WIP and hold registers, third-party confirmations, in-transit register, observer notes, approved adjustment list, eTIMS/invoice match summary, and a sign-off page from operations and finance. Load January opening balances only from that signed closing stock — not from a parallel spreadsheet. Plan to keep the pack at least five years under section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act, and confirm longer food-safety retention with your quality lead (EAS 39 clause 14: records of actions to assure safety kept for a suitable period).

A simple year-end stocktake file

Section What to record
November plan Freeze window, count dates, teams, observer, lock date for opening balances
Freeze notice Lines stopped / WIP finish rules; receipt and dispatch cut-off
Posting completeness Open GRNs, issues, outputs, transfers, dispatches posted before count
RM & packaging Blind sheets, lots, locations, UoM, near-expiry, recounts
WIP register Order/batch, stage, quantity, owner; finish / carry / write-off decision
FG & blocked stock Sellable vs hold / quarantine / rework / returns / disposal
Third-party / co-packer Location, confirmation or joint count, signed sheet
In-transit Document no., qty, sender, receiver, expected arrival
Observer Name, locations covered, exceptions
Adjustments Variance, reason code, value, named approver
eTIMS / invoice alignment Invoice & credit-note match; opening/closing by item support
Opening balances Loaded from signed closing stock only
Retention Pack filed; tax min. five years; food-safety period confirmed
Sign-off Operations + finance names, dates

If you cannot point to last year's year-end pack in under five minutes, January's opening stock is not under control.

An illustration

This is an illustrative example, not a real case. A mid-sized dairy plans its year-end count for 30 December. Production runs until midday. Three silos of WIP have no stage written on the sheet. Twelve pallets of flavoured yoghurt on QA hold are counted into free stock. Stock at a co-packer is taken from a November email. Two trucks that left for Mombasa on the 29th appear on neither the dairy's nor the depot's count. Finance posts a balancing adjustment labelled "year-end" so the trial balance closes, then loads January opening balances from a spreadsheet that was edited after the count.

By mid-January the co-packer returns a lower figure, the held yoghurt is released and sold, the trucks arrive with shortages, and the WIP is finished with scrap that was never recorded. Opening stock nobody trusts is now the base for every variance report of the new year. Under KRA's stock-management expectation — records of what was received, sold, adjusted and disposed of, aligned with eTIMS invoices — that tidy December close is exactly the kind of story that does not hold. The fix is not a better journal in January. It is checks 1–3, 5–8 and 10–12 done before anyone signs in December.

How FactoraERP helps

FactoraERP keeps stock by item, lot, location and status, and records receipts, production issues, output and dispatch as they happen, so a year-end freeze starts from a live ledger rather than a pile of slips. Blind count sheets, recounts, variance reason codes and approved adjustments link each write-off to a count and a named approver. QC results and holds sit on the same stock: a batch on hold is not available for picking until QA releases it. Recipes can declare primary product, co-product, by-product or waste, which supports the conversion and wastage explanations manufacturers need when stock records and invoices must align. See factoraerp.com.

Free download: eTIMS readiness checklist for factories

Kenyan manufacturers increasingly need their operational records, stock records and invoices to tell one consistent story — especially at the year boundary. If you want a free eTIMS readiness checklist for factories, sign up for the FactoraERP Insights newsletter at https://isaacmuthui.substack.com. You will get practical operations notes for food and agro manufacturers. No spam; unsubscribe anytime. For background, see our guide to eTIMS for food and agro manufacturers.

FAQ

What is a year-end stocktake in a food factory?

It is the annual physical and documentary count that locks closing stock for the year and opening stock for the next: freeze, counts of raw materials, WIP and finished goods, third-party and in-transit stock, observer presence, approved variances, eTIMS/invoice alignment and a signed pack.

How is this different from a routine stock count or month-end close?

A routine stock count compares physical quantities with the system and posts approved variances. Month-end close covers the full period (cut-off, production, yields, purchases, sales, accruals). Year-end stocktake focuses on the annual freeze, complete coverage (including third-party and in-transit), observer presence and locking opening balances you will defend for the next year.

When should we start planning the year-end stocktake?

In November. Publish the freeze window, count dates, teams and observer arrangements early enough that production, stores and logistics can prepare — not in the last days of December.

What does KRA expect on stock records for eTIMS?

KRA's stock-management notice, citing section 23A(2)(b) of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015, expects accurate records of stock received, purchased, sold, transferred, returned, adjusted or otherwise disposed of, aligned with TIMS/eTIMS invoices. Consult your tax adviser for how that applies to your registration and timeline.

When is the eTIMS stock-tracking rollout expected?

Reporting in The Star on 2 October 2026 described preparations for a January 2027 rollout, following a 7 September 2026 public notice and ongoing consultations with manufacturers. Treat dates as reported and confirm current guidance with KRA.

How long should we keep the year-end stocktake pack?

Section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 sets a general five-year retention period for documents required under a tax law, with exceptions. EAS 39 clause 14 expects food-safety records to be kept for a suitable period. Confirm both with your accountant and quality lead.

Can a small plant run year-end stocktake on paper?

Yes, if the November plan and freeze are written, slips are posted before counting, WIP and holds have registers, third-party and in-transit lines exist, adjustments have reason codes and named approvers, opening balances come only from the signed close, and the pack is filed together. Software helps when lots, locations, holds and third-party sites outgrow paper.

Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd

title: The best workflow engine is a programming language
description:
The idea of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on top of unreliable, stateless infrastructure isn't new. We've had message queues, job runners, microservice choreographies, and full-blown workflow engines for a long time. What we never had was a version of it that felt good to write.

I'd spent about six months working on a fork of Temporal, mostly on weekends, trying to turn it into a serverless answer with DX that felt more Vercel-native. Eventually it dawned on me that to ship that experience, I'd need to own the execution environment too. So I dropped the fork, joined Vercel, and started hacking on a new framework from scratch alongside Nathan Rajlich.

Code is already a DAG

A workflow is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Before Temporal (and Cadence before it), nearly every workflow framework made you draw that DAG by hand. Apache Airflow is the canonical example. You describe your pipeline as an explicit graph of tasks and dependencies, and your actual logic gets buried inside the nodes."

That always felt backwards to me. We already have a tool for expressing "do this, then that, and these in parallel, and branch here." It's called a programming language. An abstract syntax tree is a DAG. Software itself is a DAG.

I knew that in the abstract, but it didn't truly hit me until I saw Temporal, where you write what looks like normal sequential code and the engine makes it durable underneath. It was the dream all along.

What running Temporal taught me

Temporal is great once your infrastructure exists. I was starting from scratch, and setting it up meant:

  • Standing up Temporal Cloud (or self-hosting the server: Frontend, History, Matching, and Worker services, plus a Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL backend and sharding).

  • Running your own worker fleet: Temporal never executes your code. Your workers poll the server and run your workflows and activities. In practice that's a Kubernetes cluster you own.

  • Wiring it all together: task queues, activity registration, client config.

  • Managing the workers yourself: scaling, uptime, restarts, and the build-and-deploy pipeline for the worker processes.

  • Setting up encryption: workers talk to the control plane over the internet, so you're configuring mutual TLS and a data converter to encrypt payloads before they leave your environment.

Once all of that was in place, the workflow dream mostly became real. But I wanted something easy to start that could still scale as my project grew into production.

Versioning in-flight workflows

Beyond owning the worker build-and-deploy process myself, there was a harder problem. If I changed my workflow code while runs were still in flight, I was kind of stuck. There were no longer any workers running the old, correct version of that code. Replay would hit my new code with an old event history and break on a non-determinism error.

The official answer is the patching API (patched() / GetVersion). You branch your code on a change ID and march it through a multi-stage deprecate-then-remove lifecycle as old runs age out of retention. It works, but it means evolving workflow code very carefully. Over enough changes, the workflow code rots into a thicket of version flags.

I couldn't explain Temporal signals

Whenever I tried to show running Temporal demos to friends, signals / queries / updates turned into the single most confusing part. They're three separate primitives for getting data in and out of a running workflow, each with its own rules. Queries can't block, signals are fire-and-forget and get buffered, and you have to know when to reach for which. The concepts did land but it wasn't very intuitive. To me, that was a DX smell. If I can't explain the human-in-the-loop primitive without a whiteboard, it's too complicated. That's why Workflow SDK replaces all three with a single primitive, the hook.

What Workflow SDK looks like today

With Workflow SDK, you write one file of normal code. "use workflow" marks an orchestrator; "use step" marks a unit of side-effecting work. In between it's just await, try/catch, Promise.all, loops, and conditionals.

A few things fall out of that one file:

  • No DAG file: The compiler reads the directives and splits the code into workflow and client/step bundles. The graph is your control flow.

  • Retries: Uncaught errors retry by default. Throw new FatalError(...) to stop. Throw new RetryableError(..., { retryAfter }) for custom backoff. Set fn.maxRetries = n to tune.

  • Ad-hoc webhooks: const webhook = createWebhook() creates a real, callable URL inside a running workflow, in a single line. The run parks until someone hits it, with no route or handler.

  • Hooks: Webhooks are sugar over a more general primitive. Create a hook with createHook<T>(), await it, and the data someone sends is what comes back. This one concept replaces signals, queries and updates

Here's an ad-hoc webhook end to end. An approval that can pause for seconds or for weeks, with nothing extra to deploy.

A library, not a platform

Traditional engines make you bring infrastructure to the framework. Workflow SDK brings the framework to infrastructure you already have.

DBOS had the right idea

While I was working out how to actually build this, I studied every workflow engine I could find. The one that stood out was DBOS, an open-source durable execution library that runs almost entirely client-side. The only thing its server needs is Postgres.

Workflow SDK adopts that shape. There's no bespoke orchestrator to self-host or pay for, and no new stateful system to operate. The only infrastructure it needs is infrastructure you already run: your app, a database, a queue. All the heavy lifting happens in the library.

The backend is swappable

Workflow SDK pushes the idea past one database. The whole thing is a spec, a way of writing workflows, steps, and hooks that any infrastructure can back. You mix and match the substrate to fit your stack:

  • Redis / Kafka / etc. for your streams

  • Postgres / Cassandra / the file system / Turso / Durable Objects / etc. for durability

  • Vercel Queues / SQS / Cloudflare Queues / etc. for your queue

The runtime only ever talks to a single interface, the World, which covers storage, queuing, auth, and streaming. Swapping any layer never touches your workflow code.

In fact, we maintain a first-party Postgres world inspired by DBOS, using Postgres for durability, queueing, and streaming. And in every world, there's no worker fleet and no control plane. A framework integration exposes two plain HTTP endpoints that deploy like the rest of your app.

Even the Vercel backend is "just" a CRUD API

The Vercel Workflow Server, the thing that backs workflows on Vercel, is stateless and does no compute or orchestration at all. It's just like the Postgres world, but extended with Vercel's authentication and multi-tenancy. A CRUD API, nothing more. It even runs as a regular Vercel deployment. All the heavy lifting, all the actual workflow logic, lives in the open-source, Apache-licensed client-side library, which can be extended freely.

So the "managed" offering isn't a black box you're locked into. It's just another World, one implementation of a spec you can read, fork, and extend. The data format isn't bespoke either. You can swap out any piece of the stack.

Some patterns lean on the platform

I should be upfront. A few of Workflow SDK's design choices are shaped by how Vercel executes code. The clearest example is versioning, the same code-evolution problem that makes traditional engines so painful.

Our answer is to pin each run to the specific deployment that started it. The run keeps executing against the exact copy of the code it began on, so changing your workflow never breaks in-flight runs. It's a clean solution, but it was only easy to build because Vercel already keeps immutable deployments around for long periods. The official Postgres world doesn't track and route versions this way yet. Encouragingly, community worlds have already implemented the spec as intended. Platformatic's version-safe durable workflows on Kubernetes is a great example.

And I think that's exactly the right trade. Pinning moves the complexity of versioning off the developer writing workflows and onto the infrastructure. That burden lands on the world author, the infra provider, and us as the framework authors. If everyone using a framework hits the same hard problem and has to solve it themselves in the same painful ways, the framework has failed them. A good framework moves that complexity upstream.

Steps should be free

Performance is the next big problem for us to solve. Invoking a step isn't cheap. Each step involves networking and a trip over a queue to durably commit its result correctly. For correctness, that's the right thing to do. But it works against the pitch that distributed computing should feel like function calls.

When you write ordinary code, you don't think twice about the overhead of a function call. It's so fast it's effectively free. But if every step carried a heavy overhead, the abstraction leaks. You start rationing steps, reasoning about granularity, declining to turn a small function into a checkpoint because it's "not worth a step."

So the goal is blunt: steps should be free.

In the ideal version of this, you could take any function in an existing codebase, add "use step", and everything would just work, with no serialization constraints and no performance penalty.

That dream drives us.

What if any developer could turn a plain function into something with the performance, networking, observability, and availability of a standalone microservice, but using just two words: "use step"? That would change how we write code.

Workflow v5 (in beta at the time of writing) already delivers up to a 5x performance improvement with no change to the user-facing API, and v6 will push it further while making third-party worlds just as fast. We're sharing details as we go in this GitHub discussion, and you can start testing today with npm install workflow@beta.

I set out to build a durable framework that feels like writing ordinary code, runs on the infrastructure you already have, and is fast enough that you never think twice about reaching for a step. It's real today, and we're building the rest of it in the open.

Come build Workflow SDK with us

If designing durable systems under real-world constraints sounds like fun, the Workflow team at Vercel is hiring.

See open roles.

title: Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available
description:
The Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available on all plans, giving you one place to see your security posture across every account and project.

You can access the Security Dashboard in the UI or run vercel security check in the Vercel CLI.

As teams grow and coding agents make it faster to spin up projects, small misconfigurations add up quietly. The Security Dashboard automatically flags issues like:

  • Team members without 2FA

  • Long-lived credentials that can be replaced with OIDC

  • Public preview deployments

  • Non-sensitive and stale environment variables

The Security Dashboard UI

Misconfigurations are ordered by risk with the most severe first, and each finding links to the settings that fix them.

Findings that are just noise for your team can also be muted, and all results can be exported to a CSV file for triage or reporting.

The Security Dashboard CLI

You can also run the same checks in your terminal through the new Vercel CLI vercel security check command, allowing your agents to work through the findings for you.

An agent using vercel security check --findings can read what failed, apply the fix and re-check to confirm. Fixes an agent can apply include:

  • Turning on Git fork protection

  • Marking an environment variable as sensitive

  • Replacing a static credential with OIDC federation

You can also scope the check to one project with --project when you want a narrow change set.

In CI or any other non-interactive environment, the command writes the report to stdout as JSON automatically, giving agents structured output without extra flags.

Get started by running your first scan from the Security Dashboard, and learn more in the Security Dashboard documentation.
