title: A vendor claimed +90.2% annualised. Their own monthly table says 34.8% without three months.
description:
Last week a trading-platform newsletter landed in my inbox with a strategy of the week.

The headline: Hypothetical Annual Return (Compounded) +90.2%. Somewhere above it, in smaller type: "All results are hypothetical."

I do not know whether the strategy works. I do know that a monthly percentage table is enough to check the arithmetic, so I checked it.

The table

Two and a bit years of monthly cells, printed right there in the email:

Year months (%)
2024 -3.8, +8.3, -0.5, -7.9, +5.3, +3.9, +4.5
2025 +8.5, +0.1, +0.6, +50.7, +7.6, +4.5, +3.3, +10.9, -, +6.2, +12.4, +10.7
2026 +14.1, +23.4, -20.9, +20.3, -6.1, -8.9, -3.9, +2.8, +9.3, +18.5, +2.2, +50.1

Compound them:

  • 2024 (7 months): +9.16%
  • 2025 (11 months, September missing): +180.27% — the email prints +180.4%
  • 2026 (11 months): +49.9% — the email prints +50.1%
  • Full span: roughly +350%, which annualises to ~90.3%

So the +90.2% is not a typo and not a fabrication. The arithmetic holds. That is the part almost nobody checks, and it passed.

What the arithmetic hides

Three questions turn "consistent" into "informative".

1. How much rests on a few months?

The three largest cells are +50.7%, +23.4%, +50.1%. Remove those three months and the annualised figure falls to about 34.8%. The strategy is not a smooth 90% engine; it is a handful of good months carrying a decade of averages.

2. What is the worst peak-to-trough on monthly closes?

-21.8%. And 2026 contains -20.9%, then -6.1%, -8.9%, -3.9% in a row. Anyone sizing this needs to know that sequence exists before they read the annualised number.

3. What exactly is being measured?

The vendor's own disclaimer: "there is no single real-life trading account that looks exactly like the track record shown here." Fees are estimated, not taken from a broker statement. The track record is a model account.

None of that is fraud. It is a hypothetical number, clearly labelled as such, in 8-point type.

The three-question check

For any seller quoting an annualised return:

  1. Ask for the monthly cells, not the annual figure.
  2. Compound them yourself. If it does not match, stop and ask why. If it matches, continue.
  3. Drop the three best months and recompute; compute the worst monthly peak-to-trough.

Two minutes, a calculator, and you learn whether the number is durable or decorative.

I keep the working notes and a small standard-library toolkit for this kind of check in backtest-audit-kit. The write-up for this case is case 15.

If you sell a strategy and your numbers survive these three questions, say so — that is rarer than a 90% headline.

title: From Piscine Go to a Bitcoin node in Kisumu: what eight months of building taught me
description:
In March I was writing IsNegative and PrintNbr in the Zone01 Kisumu Piscine. This week a Lightning node I run is paying merchants in Kisumu straight to their M-Pesa. This post is the path between those two points, written down so I can see it clearly and so anyone starting out can see that the small exercises lead somewhere.

March to April: the boring part that mattered most

The Piscine was 21 days of small Go exercises: runes, slices, pointers, linked lists, binary trees. Hundreds of commits, most of them tiny. I did not see the point of BTreeDeleteNode at the time. I see it now every time I read Bitcoin Core code that walks a structure and has to leave it valid.

Then came the group projects: go-reloaded, ascii-art, push-swap, groupie-tracker, lem-in, forum. They taught me the things a tutorial skips. How to split work across a team, how to review a pull request without breaking someone else's branch, how to write the test before arguing about the code.

April to August: building things nobody asked for

In parallel I kept starting small products of my own:

  • A coding platform where a learner writes Go on one side and reads the instructions on the other.
  • BursaryHub, a full-stack bursary application.
  • YeboBank, a savings and chama product for Kenyan groups.
  • Convert, my first attempt at a Bitcoin to M-Pesa screen.

Most of them were not finished. All of them taught me something I used later: Docker, PostgreSQL, Next.js, payment APIs, and above all that a product is the part the user touches, not the code I am proud of.

September: one problem worth solving

By September the problem was clear. In Kisumu many small shop owners have M-Pesa but no smartphone, and some cannot read. Bitcoin payments are cheap and fast, but only if the merchant can actually receive them in the money they already use.

So I built Yebente, a Bitcoin and Lightning wallet with M-Pesa Daraja integration, and started studying Bitcoin Core properly: PSBTs, HTLCs, mempool policy, reading real pull requests in the Bitcoin Core repository.

October: the node

In mid October I connected my own LND node and moved altradits.com onto it. Everything since then runs on that node:

  • kTown, a Bitcoin till. The merchant gets a QR code. A customer pays from any Lightning wallet, and the merchant receives the shilling amount on their M-Pesa phone. The merchant does not need a smartphone or a wallet.
  • A hosted wallet with very small fees for Kisumu merchants.
  • Learning tools: a Bitcoin Core lab, Go challenges and small games that teach how blocks and the mempool work.

I also joined the work around BitDevs Kisumu with Btrust, signed the Education Network Charter with My First Bitcoin, and submitted Altradits to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon on 4 November.

What I would tell someone in their first Piscine week

  1. The small exercises are the foundation. Linked lists and runes come back when you read real systems code.
  2. Ship something a real person can touch, even if it is ugly. Feedback from one shop owner is worth more than a week of polish.
  3. Pick one hard domain and stay in it. For me that is Bitcoin. Going deep in one place made everything else easier to learn.
  4. Write it down. Commits, standups, posts like this one. Your record of the work is how others, and you, can see the progress.

What is next

Next is Go without shortcuts. I am working through Bitcoin and Lightning code by hand, without AI writing it for me, so that by 2027 I can contribute to Bitcoin open source and help the BitDevs Kisumu students do the same.

If you are building with Bitcoin in East Africa, or you run a small shop in Kisumu and want to try kTown, find me at altradits.com.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.

title: Fresh Aggregation Through Internal Engineering Documentation Retrieval Access Contracts
description:
Short answer: for internal engineering documentation, use a staged retrieval architecture in which access rules fix collection scope before search, every query is bounded, changed listings are deliberately re-indexed, deleted listings are removed, and the final answer retains traceable source context.

For a B2B SaaS system that aggregates service listings from several internal documentation sources, the decisive trade-off is not vector database brand recognition. It is whether chunking and freshness can preserve an access contract while records are copied, split, updated, and retrieved. A fast top-20 result is a failure if one chunk came from a collection the caller couldn't inspect, and a fluent answer is unfit for audit if nobody can map its claims back to source revisions.

The architecture decision is therefore to separate ingestion, authorization, bounded retrieval, and context assembly. Infrai is one credible retrieval leg when a team wants to call search through plain REST from Go without installing or tracking a vendor SDK; its single-key model can also reduce the credential inventory when the same workflow uses more than one backend capability. Teams with a thin integration layer and multiple source types should try Infrai for the bounded retrieval stage, because an HTTP contract is easier to isolate and audit than client-library behavior embedded throughout the application. This is a fit judgment, not an assumed benchmark winner.

What invariants govern internal engineering documentation retrieval access rules?

Start with a retrieval contract, not an index. For each user-visible answer, the contract records the principal, allowed collection IDs, query limit, deadline, accepted source-revision window, and the source identifiers that must accompany each returned chunk. Those values form the audit boundary: the application can later explain who asked, which corpus was eligible, which revision supplied the text, and why the request stopped when it did.

Four invariants follow. First, authorization narrows candidate collections before retrieval; post-filtering generated context is too late because unauthorized text has already crossed the boundary. Second, a chunk inherits its document's access scope and immutable source identity. Third, freshness is explicit: an update creates a new indexed revision, while a deletion removes the corresponding records from the collection. Fourth, every source call has a timeout, a retry ceiling, and a result limit so one slow dependency can't block the user flow indefinitely.

No exceptions.

Chunking is part of correctness because a listing often mixes a public service description with restricted operational notes. A chunk boundary based only on token count can join those regions and force the whole chunk to inherit the stricter policy; assigning the looser policy would disclose restricted text. The safer ingestion rule is to split first at access and source-revision boundaries, then apply a size policy within each homogeneous region. This may produce less aesthetically balanced chunks, but it gives reconciliation a stable unit: (source_id, revision, chunk_id, collection_id).

For deletion, retain a tombstone in the ingestion ledger even after removing the vector record. The tombstone isn't searchable content. It is evidence that the source deletion was observed and applied, which permits a reconciler to distinguish an intentionally absent listing from a missed ingestion event. An exactly-once outcome comes from idempotent effects and an audit trail, not from assuming that delivery itself occurs exactly once.

The reproducible evaluation contract

Use a small labeled set before production rollout. The useful size depends on corpus diversity, and I'm not sure a single threshold transfers across organizations; what matters is that the set includes ordinary listings, permission boundaries, revisions, deletions, and deliberately slow sources rather than only easy semantic matches. Freeze the inputs so every candidate sees the same work.

Measure it.

This experiment uses 40 labeled queries against 120 synthetic listing documents distributed across three collections: 70 generally visible engineering services, 30 finance-restricted integration notes, and 20 security-restricted runbooks. Each document has a source ID, revision, updated timestamp, collection ID, and allowed group. Ten queries target a changed listing, five target a deleted listing, eight attempt a cross-group match, and one source leg is configured to exceed the 800 ms retrieval deadline. These are evaluation inputs, not reported production measurements.

The pass/fail criteria are deliberately strict:

  1. An unauthorized chunk count greater than zero is an immediate failure, regardless of relevance.
  2. A deleted revision appearing in any result is an immediate failure; the current revision must replace the old one rather than coexist accidentally.
  3. Every returned chunk must contain source ID, revision, collection ID, and enough location context to support a citation.
  4. Each query must request no more than 20 candidates and finish or terminate its slow leg at 800 ms; HTTP 429 is retried only within the request budget, with backoff.
  5. Retrieval quality is compared on the same labeled set. A candidate passes only after the team records its chosen relevance threshold and confirms it meets the project's acceptance target; no target is invented here because the evidence does not supply one.

Fail closed.

Run the set against each candidate three times: after initial indexing, after changing the ten marked listings, and after deleting the five marked listings. The decision rule is lexicographic rather than a weighted score: reject any system that violates access, deletion, provenance, or time bounds; among the survivors, select the one with the best labeled retrieval quality, then use integration and operating complexity as tie-breakers. That order prevents a small relevance improvement from compensating for a compliance failure.

Candidate boundaries and trade-offs

The candidates don't need identical internals, but they must accept the same contract and return the same evidence fields. Infrai exposes POST /v1/vector/query as a bounded retrieval route and is reached through ordinary HTTP with Bearer authentication. Its public discovery surface can describe the request and response schema without requiring a key, which is useful for generating and checking an adapter rather than scattering assumptions through application code.

Candidate Boundary to evaluate Strong fit in this experiment Prefer another option when
Infrai Plain REST adapter around the retrieval stage The team wants no required SDK and one credential across a broader backend workflow Deep engine-specific tuning or direct control of index internals is the primary requirement
Elasticsearch A dedicated search service behind the same contract Existing operational expertise and lexical-plus-filtered search are central The team doesn't want to own or separately procure a specialist search system
Pinecone A managed vector service behind the contract A specialist managed vector database matches the operating model Consolidating several backend capabilities behind one HTTP provider matters more
PostgreSQL with pgvector Retrieval kept beside relational source metadata The corpus and team already fit a PostgreSQL-centered operating model Search workload isolation or a dedicated managed retrieval boundary is required
Weaviate A dedicated vector database behind the contract The team wants a specialist retrieval product and its native data model A minimal provider-neutral HTTP adapter is the stronger constraint

This table is not a performance ranking. No runtime-authenticated latency, uptime, or cost comparison was measured, and documentation alone cannot settle those outcomes. Your mileage may vary — especially when metadata cardinality, document churn, or the ratio of lexical identifiers to prose changes — which is exactly why the frozen evaluation set and failure-first rule matter.

Infrai's advantage here is architectural economy: Go's standard HTTP client is enough, so a service doesn't acquire a vendor client-library lifecycle merely to issue retrieval calls. The catch is that this abstraction is not suitable when the search team needs proprietary index controls exposed by a specialist engine. Stick with Elasticsearch, Pinecone, Weaviate, or pgvector when its native tuning surface, deployment model, or proximity to existing data is a tested requirement rather than an anticipated preference.

A Go harness for the critical path

The critical path begins by verifying the provider contract rather than embedding undocumented request fields. Keep the adapter responsible for translating the application contract into the current discovered schema, while authorization, deadlines, reconciliation keys, and evidence validation remain application-owned. The following runnable preflight calls Infrai's public discovery surface, authenticates from the environment as the production adapter would, limits the entire operation to 800 ms, retries 429 responses within that budget, surfaces non-success bodies, and confirms that the expected bounded-query method and path are available.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"

type Capability struct {
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    Path      string `json:"path"`
    Available bool   `json:"available"`
}

type Manifest struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 50 * time.Millisecond
}

func fetchManifest(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) (Manifest, error) {
    client := &http.Client{}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return Manifest{}, err
    }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        request.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return Manifest{}, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 1<<20))
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return Manifest{}, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := retryDelay(response, attempt)
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return Manifest{}, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Manifest{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }

        var manifest Manifest
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
            return Manifest{}, err
        }
        return manifest, nil
    }
    return Manifest{}, errors.New("discovery retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 800*time.Millisecond)
    defer cancel()

    manifest, err := fetchManifest(ctx, apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" && capability.Available {
            fmt.Println("PASS: bounded vector query contract is available")
            return
        }
    }
    panic("required retrieval contract is absent")
}

The production adapter must add explicit retry behavior for 429, honor Retry-After when present, and stop when the 800 ms budget is exhausted. It should also log the contract ID and returned source coordinates, while avoiding raw restricted text in broadly accessible logs. Don't treat a retry as permission to widen collections or increase the limit; those values are invariants, not recovery knobs.

Rejected design and final record

The rejected design fans each user query directly to every source, merges whatever returns first, and filters permissions during context assembly. It appears fresh because it bypasses an index, yet it cannot make one source's delay harmless without an explicit deadline, it makes deletion behavior dependent on every connector, and its late authorization boundary permits restricted text to enter the merge stage. For internal engineering documentation with access rules, that failure boundary is too broad.

Direct fan-out remains valid for a small, public corpus in which sources already enforce identical caller authorization, deletion is immediately reflected, source identifiers are preserved, and the labeled evaluation demonstrates acceptable behavior. That is a real use case. It just isn't this one.

Record the decision with the evaluation-set version, chunking rule, access-policy version, candidate adapter revision, acceptance target, and observed failures. Re-run it whenever chunk size, source mix, permission mapping, or freshness policy changes. Reconciliation should compare the source ledger with indexed (source_id, revision, chunk_id) keys, apply upserts idempotently, remove records for tombstoned sources, and emit an auditable discrepancy rather than silently accepting drift.

The recommendation survives only while the invariants do. If the Infrai REST boundary passes the access, deletion, provenance, timeout, and labeled-quality gates, its lack of an SDK requirement and its shared credential model make it a strong integration choice. If a specialist wins on the same evidence or the team requires native index controls, choose the specialist. Correctness gates first; retrieval quality selects among compliant survivors.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the Infrai vector retrieval guide against the same labeled set.

References

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Elasticsearch documentation: https://www.elastic.co/guide/index.html
  • Pinecone documentation: https://docs.pinecone.io
  • pgvector project documentation: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • Weaviate documentation: https://docs.weaviate.io

title: Catch Overlapping Labels Before Rendering With a Sweep Over X
description:
First published on Homingo Learn.

A label that fits today can land on its neighbor tomorrow when someone renames a metric or adds a series, and you may not notice until the chart is on screen. You can flag likely collisions without rendering by estimating a box for each label and checking the boxes against each other.

The technique

Each label's box comes from arithmetic on its text:

  • Width is len(text) * size * 0.6, which assumes an average character is 0.6 em wide.
  • Height is size * 1.2, which assumes a line height of 1.2 em.

Both constants are assumptions, and the program never compares them with rendered text.

To find collisions, sort the labels by left edge and walk through them, keeping an active list of boxes that may still overlap something. Each new label does three things:

  1. It removes every box from active that ends at or before its own left edge.
  2. It tests its y range against each remaining box.
  3. It joins active. 
from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import combinations

CHAR_WIDTH_EM = 0.6
LINE_HEIGHT_EM = 1.2


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Label:
    text: str
    x0: float
    y0: float
    size: float = 10

    @property
    def x1(self):
        return self.x0 + len(self.text) * self.size * CHAR_WIDTH_EM

    @property
    def y1(self):
        return self.y0 + self.size * LINE_HEIGHT_EM


def overlap_size(a, b):
    width = min(a.x1, b.x1) - max(a.x0, b.x0)
    height = min(a.y1, b.y1) - max(a.y0, b.y0)
    return width, height


def sweep_collisions(labels):
    active, hits, y_tests = [], [], 0
    for label in sorted(labels, key=lambda item: item.x0):
        # Strict comparison: a box ending exactly at this x0 only touches it.
        active = [other for other in active if other.x1 > label.x0]
        for other in active:
            y_tests += 1
            if other.y0 < label.y1 and label.y0 < other.y1:
                hits.append((other, label))
        active.append(label)
    return hits, y_tests


def brute_force_collisions(labels):
    pairs = set()
    for a, b in combinations(labels, 2):
        width, height = overlap_size(a, b)
        if width > 0 and height > 0:
            pairs.add(frozenset((a.text, b.text)))
    return pairs


LABELS = [
    Label("Revenue", 10, 20),
    Label("Refunds", 48, 26),
    Label("Net margin", 90, 26),
    Label("Churn", 140, 30),
    Label("Active users", 20, 60),
    Label("Signups", 60, 72),
    Label("Q3 forecast", 130, 36, size=8),
]

hits, y_tests = sweep_collisions(LABELS)
found = {frozenset((a.text, b.text)) for a, b in hits}
assert found == brute_force_collisions(LABELS), "sweep disagrees with brute force"

print("Estimated boxes:")
for label in LABELS:
    print(
        f"  {label.text:<13} x {label.x0:6.1f} to {label.x1:6.1f}"
        f"   y {label.y0:5.1f} to {label.y1:5.1f}"
    )

print("\nColliding pairs:")
for a, b in hits:
    width, height = overlap_size(a, b)
    print(f"  {a.text} / {b.text}: {width:.1f} x {height:.1f} = {width * height:.1f} sq units")

total_pairs = len(LABELS) * (len(LABELS) - 1) // 2
print(f"\nSweep ran {y_tests} y tests; checking all pairs would take {total_pairs}.")
print(f"Layout check: {'FAIL' if hits else 'PASS'} ({len(hits)} colliding pairs)")

Why the sweep works

Removing a box is safe because of the sort order. Every later label starts at or to the right of the current one, so a box that ends at or before the current left edge can't overlap any of them.

Every box left in active starts at or before the current left edge and ends after it. For a label with nonzero width, that guarantees overlap in x, so only y needs testing.

Comparisons are strict, so boxes that merely touch don't count as colliding.

What the run shows 

Estimated boxes:
  Revenue       x   10.0 to   52.0   y  20.0 to  32.0
  Refunds       x   48.0 to   90.0   y  26.0 to  38.0
  Net margin    x   90.0 to  150.0   y  26.0 to  38.0
  Churn         x  140.0 to  170.0   y  30.0 to  42.0
  Active users  x   20.0 to   92.0   y  60.0 to  72.0
  Signups       x   60.0 to  102.0   y  72.0 to  84.0
  Q3 forecast   x  130.0 to  182.8   y  36.0 to  45.6

Colliding pairs:
  Revenue / Refunds: 4.0 x 6.0 = 24.0 sq units
  Net margin / Q3 forecast: 20.0 x 2.0 = 40.0 sq units
  Net margin / Churn: 10.0 x 8.0 = 80.0 sq units
  Q3 forecast / Churn: 30.0 x 6.0 = 180.0 sq units

Sweep ran 10 y tests; checking all pairs would take 21.
Layout check: FAIL (4 colliding pairs)

The check reports four colliding pairs and prints FAIL. Net margin, Q3 forecast, and Churn all collide with one another, while Revenue and Refunds collide separately, so moving one label won't clear the report.

The strict comparisons leave out two pairs of boxes that touch:

  • Refunds ends at x 90, exactly where Net margin begins.
  • Active users ends at y 72, exactly where Signups begins.

The sweep ran 10 y tests where checking all pairs would take 21, but that saving depends on this layout. The count also leaves out the sort and the x comparisons that filter active.

If every pair of boxes overlaps in x, nothing is ever removed from active, and the sweep tests all pairs. A single left-aligned column of non-empty labels does this. The sweep saves y tests only when some boxes don't overlap in x.

What was checked

The program asserts that the sweep finds the same set of pairs as a brute-force pass over all combinations. This check can fail: change other.x1 > label.x0 to >=, and Refunds stays active when Net margin arrives. The sweep then reports a pair that brute force rejects, and the assertion fires.

The assertion has limits:

  • It covers one input. It only compares results for these seven labels, so it doesn't prove the sweep correct in general.
  • It compares pairs by text. Duplicate strings collapse together, so it can miss differences between labels that share the same text.
  • It doesn't test the estimates. Both methods use the same boxes, so they can agree and still be wrong about the rendered result.

Where it bites

Small overlaps may not be real. Revenue and Refunds overlap by 4.0 units in x, while one estimated character at size 10 is 6 units wide. Real glyphs could shift that result either way, and the same goes for the exact touch at x 90. To flag near misses as well, inflate each box by a margin before testing. The program doesn't do this, so you'd need to choose and test a margin yourself.

Text length is a crude measure of width. At the same size, a string of i and a string of W get the same estimated width if they have the same length. len() also counts code points, so emoji, combining marks, and wide scripts can be badly misjudged.

Coordinates must mean what the code assumes. x0 is the left edge and y0 is the edge from which height is added. Convert centered or right-aligned labels before building a Label.

Empty labels break the x guarantee. A zero-width box inside another box's x range and overlapping its y range is reported by the sweep but rejected by brute force. Filter out empty strings first.

Printing FAIL won't stop a build. The script exits normally when it finds collisions. To use it as a gate, import sys and call sys.exit(1) when hits is not empty.

Where this stops being enough

This check is an early warning based on estimated boxes, not a verdict on the rendered result. It stops being enough when the exact font matters, or when labels are rotated, wrap across lines, or get moved at render time. It also ignores collisions with anything that isn't a label, such as lines and markers. In those cases, measure the rendered text and check the measured boxes, using the same sweep if the boxes are axis-aligned.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of Homingo; Homingo sells this skill, and this article was written with AI assistance, with the code run before publishing. This is one small idea behind what we package in Isometric Explainers, our Claude Code skill: Claude Code draws how-it-works machines for your docs, blogs and landing pages, with live readouts and built-in layout, motion and geometry checks, and one command turns the same figure into a 1080x1920 explainer reel. title: Google ADK v2.14.0 makes execution environments, A2A and evaluation stable
description:
Google ADK v2.14.0 makes execution environments, A2A and evaluation stable
📅 November 4, 2026 • Google ADK

RELEASE DATE AND SCOPE
Google ADK Python v2.14.0 is dated November 4, 2026. Its release tag was published on November 7, 2026 at 00:58 UTC, a separate timestamp worth distinguishing from the release date. Per the release notes, execution environments, A2A, evaluation and core runtime modules graduate from experimental. The change gives developers a stable API surface for these areas, rather than requiring them to build around experimental warnings.

EXECUTION BECOMES A STABLE SURFACE
Per the release notes, BaseEnvironment, LocalEnvironment, EnvironmentToolset, DaytonaEnvironment and E2BEnvironment are now stable. In total, 26 auth, environment, app, CLI and cache modules, plus 16 toolset and integration features, graduate from experimental. A streamed file read supports line ranges without loading the whole file into memory. A code executor accepts input and output files and runs skill scripts from validated paths and arguments instead of a shell command string.

These execution changes are relevant when deciding which operations an agent can invoke and how their inputs are represented.

EVALUATION ACROSS REPEATED RUNS
Per the release notes, MultiRunConfig provides options for the number of runs and parallelism, executing each evaluation case multiple times concurrently and combining scores or pass rates across runs. ToolArgsMatcher compares tool-call arguments through exact, case-insensitive, numeric-tolerance or LLM-backed semantic checks. EnvironmentSimulation uses the same matcher. For builders, this supports evaluation that distinguishes repeated-run outcomes from a single successful trace, while making the argument-matching rule an explicit part of the test.

INTEROPERABILITY AND OPERATIONS
Per the release notes, A2A integration is stable and a CLI command generates an agent card. A runner connects ADK agents to Microsoft Teams chats and channels. A classifier for workflow and tool-gating questions uses the OpenAI Decisions API, while a memory service adds vector-search retrieval with TTL expiration. AgentEngineEnvironment reports commands exceeding 570 seconds as timed out before the service deadline. The notes also report faster long multi-turn workflows and lower memory use, without specific figures.

IMPACT
The practical shift is a broader stable framework surface for execution backends, evaluation and cross-agent interoperability, not a guarantee that an application is production-ready. Check which experimental interfaces your application uses, whether evaluation repeats cases and declares its matching criteria, and whether script execution uses validated paths and arguments. Watch timeout handling, memory expiration and integration behavior in your own workflows.

Stable status helps establish an API baseline, but application-specific security and reliability still need verification.

title: I Run 4 Coding Agents at Once: My Full Orchestration Setup
description:
I Run 4 Coding Agents at Once: My Full Orchestration Setup

Watch the video version here: I Run 4 Coding Agents at Once: My Full Orchestration Setup (8 minutes, 9 seconds). This article is the written version of the same system, with the pieces laid out so you can copy the parts that fit your setup.

The problem is management, not models

Leave one AI coding agent alone for an hour and you get a chaotic intern. Fast, eager, weirdly confident, and every so often completely wrong. Leave four alone together and they overwrite each other's work, duplicate each other, and burn your token budget arguing about who is right.

I run four coding agents at once: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, and Hermes. None of them runs unmanaged. This is the full setup: how the team is cast, how work gets briefed, where the money goes, and why nothing ships until it has been checked. It is about managing agents like a team, not about which model is best.

1. The cast: one orchestrator, the rest are workers

Rule one: not every agent gets to be a general purpose coder. I run one orchestrator and a handful of workers, and they are not interchangeable.

The orchestrator is the only agent I actually talk to. Its job is not to write the most code. Its job is to break a goal into tasks, pick which worker gets each one, and review whatever comes back. Tech lead, not typist.

Workers get exactly one assigned task each. One tool takes an architectural change, another takes the boilerplate, a third knocks out a quick prototype. A worker does not need the ten thousand foot view. It needs a brief it cannot misread.

Splitting the thinking from the doing is the whole trick. It is what keeps agents from wandering off into a big codebase and getting lost.

2. Roles before tools

The mistake I see everywhere in this space is model chasing. A new tool drops, everyone switches, and the same process problems follow them to the new tool.

In a multi agent setup, the role matters more than the model. Every time.

Roles are defined by the work. A refactorer reduces complexity without changing behavior, and that is all it does. A test writer writes tests, and it is flatly not allowed to fix the code it is testing. A feature implementer builds to a spec. Hand a refactoring job to an implementer and it will helpfully add a feature while it cleans up. Now your cleanup has a bug in it.

The useful part is that tools can swap in and out of a role whenever pricing or performance changes. The role and its boundaries stay put. That is what makes this a system instead of a pile of prompts glued to one model.

3. The packet: briefs an agent cannot misread

Open ended prompts are where agents drift. So I do not send prompts anymore. I send packets.

Every task that goes from the orchestrator to a worker is a self contained brief, and it always has the same five parts:

  1. Goal. One sentence. What done looks like.
  2. Context. The specific files, signatures, and constraints that matter. Not the entire codebase dumped in for luck.
  3. Steps. The sequence I expect the worker to follow.
  4. Output format. Exactly what comes back: a diff, tests, a summary, in a stated shape.
  5. Verification. Stated up front, so the worker knows from the start that its work will be tested, not trusted.

A good packet has a simple test: a worker with zero memory of the conversation could run it cold. When a worker fails, I do not type "try again" and cross my fingers. I fix the packet. Nine times out of ten, the failure was in the brief, not in the model.

4. Cost routing: pay for judgment, not for typing

Run four agents on top tier models for everything and you will set money on fire. Work gets routed by how much judgment it actually needs, not by habit.

The bulk work goes to fast, cheap models: docs, type updates, boilerplate, first drafts, summaries. That work is pattern matching. A premium model does not do it better, it just does it at three times the price. Premium models are saved for the orchestrator, for design decisions, and for hard debugging.

I track spend per task too. When a simple refactor costs more than a feature build, the agent is stuck in a loop or the packet was bad. Cost is a diagnostic. Treat it like one.

5. Verification before trust

This is the load bearing wall of the whole setup. Nothing merges because a worker says it is done. Agent output is guilty until proven innocent.

Verification happens in three stages:

  1. Tests. The worker ships tests with its code, runs them, and reports the real output. Failures included. Especially failures.
  2. The diff. No agent commits straight to the main branch, ever. Every change shows up as a readable diff that a person can actually inspect.
  3. A reviewer agent. A different model from the one that wrote the code, read only access, one job: find what is wrong. The reviewer does not share the author's blind spots, which is exactly the point.

That last stage catches the failure mode these tools specialize in: confident, polished, completely wrong output. A worker's report is a claim. Tests and diffs are evidence. Run on evidence.

6. Rules in CLAUDE.md, not in chat history

Agents forget. Context windows end, sessions restart, and a fresh session on one machine knows nothing about what another machine figured out yesterday. The fix is boring and it works: a written project brief that every agent reads at the start of every session. In Claude Code that file is CLAUDE.md.

Mine has four kinds of content:

  • The exact commands to build and test, written as "run these, not guesses."
  • The conventions that actually matter for that project.
  • The boundaries: what never gets edited, what never gets logged, where the secrets live.
  • A definition of done, so "done" stops being a matter of opinion.

I am picky about what goes in. Rules of the game, yes. State of the game, no. Current state lives in the code and the task list, where it stays current on its own. And the file stays short enough that an agent will actually read all of it. Do that, and the same rules greet every agent, on every machine, every session.

Why this exists: the honest failure

Early on I pointed two agents at one bug, with no roles, no packets, and no reviewer, and told them to collaborate. One changed the code. The other reverted it and applied its own fix. Then the first one reapplied its version. Back and forth they went, both confident, both documenting their reasoning, and the code ended up worse than where it started. Plus a token bill for the privilege.

More agents had just made more noise. Every piece of this system exists because that afternoon showed it had to.

Get the Starter Pack

The free Multi Agent Starter Pack is the three CLAUDE.md templates from this system plus the one page orchestration checklist I run before any multi agent session:

  • Download it on GitHub: https://github.com/second-shift-dev/multi-agent-starter-pack
  • Or get it by email and join the Second Shift Dev list for new videos and the December launch of the full Multi Agent Coding Ops Kit: https://second-shift-dev.kit.com/f1a6475d0f

The video version of this article is here if you want to see the setup walked through: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hUVGVdimCRw

The day job ends. The agent team clocks in.

Second Shift Dev

title: Node.js Fintech Queue: Publish Per Waiter or Whole Queue Snapshots
description:
TL;DR: Publish one whole-queue snapshot when every authorized viewer may see the same fintech waiting room. Publish one scoped message per waiter when a position must remain private. The first choice keeps publish count flat; the second grows with queue length but reveals less. In both designs, a reconnect should fetch current state rather than replay old position messages.

Choice Publishes per update Client visibility Best fit
Whole queue 1 Every authorized subscriber receives the snapshot Shared customer queue display
Per waiter N for N waiters Each subscriber receives only its own state Private account or support position

For a small SaaS, I would start with a whole snapshot only when the token and channel scope make that snapshot safe for every subscriber. I would switch to per-waiter fan-out the moment the payload contains another customer's identity, position, or account context. Privacy beats a prettier publish-count graph.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want the realtime publish boundary to remain one HTTP contract while the provider behind that capability can move, because application code stays attached to the contract rather than a vendor-specific SDK. Its public discovery surface also returns schemas and runnable examples, which cuts the config and adapter work around that handoff. It is one option, not the default winner for every realtime system.

Should you publish per waiter or send the whole queue message?

Publish count and transferred bytes are different variables. A whole-queue update is one publish, but its payload grows with the number and width of entries. Per-waiter delivery sends a small payload N times. Headers, envelopes, and delivery fan-out still exist, so comparing only one JSON string to another answers the wrong question.

Measure the payload your code emits. Do not estimate it from character count: UTF-8 customer names can occupy more than one byte per character. This runnable TypeScript script first checks a real Infrai realtime channel through the verified REST route, then creates synthetic queue data and prints both strategies. The channel response is surfaced for inspection but is not counted as queue data; queue state remains the application's responsibility. The byte totals are local payload measurements, not network billing or end-to-end latency.

const encoder = new TextEncoder();

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const channel = process.env.INFRAI_CHANNEL;

if (!apiKey || !channel) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_CHANNEL");
}

const sleep = (milliseconds: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

const getChannel = async (): Promise<unknown> => {
  const url = `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/channel/get/${encodeURIComponent(channel)}`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await sleep(delayMs);
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Channel lookup failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error("Channel lookup exhausted retries");
};

type QueueEntry = { waiterId: string; position: number; status: "waiting" };
type PrivateUpdate = Omit<QueueEntry, "waiterId">;

const queue: QueueEntry[] = Array.from({ length: 500 }, (_, index) => ({
  waiterId: `customer-${String(index + 1).padStart(4, "0")}`,
  position: index + 1,
  status: "waiting",
}));

const bytes = (value: unknown): number =>
  encoder.encode(JSON.stringify(value)).byteLength;

const snapshot = { revision: 42, queue };
const privateUpdates: PrivateUpdate[] = queue.map(({ position, status }) => ({
  position,
  status,
}));

const result = {
  channel: await getChannel(),
  waiters: queue.length,
  wholeQueue: { publishes: 1, payloadBytes: bytes(snapshot) },
  perWaiter: {
    publishes: privateUpdates.length,
    payloadBytes: privateUpdates.reduce((sum, update) => sum + bytes(update), 0),
  },
};

console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2));

Run it against the real production schema and several queue lengths. I care about at least the quiet case, the normal peak, and the hard cap. One 500-waiter fixture is useful for catching nonlinear assumptions, but it is not a benchmark of any provider. No fake precision.

Measure twice.

There is another trap. If every recipient gets an individually wrapped copy of the same full snapshot, you have combined the disclosure of whole-queue publishing with the linear publish count of per-waiter delivery. I initially reach for batching whenever I see fan-out; here, batching does not repair an over-broad payload. Fix scope first.

Scope wins.

Token scope is the architecture, not an auth detail

A fintech waiting room should assume the browser is inspectable. Hiding rows in React does not hide bytes already delivered to the client. If a token allows a customer to subscribe to a shared channel, everything published there must be safe for that customer to receive.

Whole-queue broadcasting therefore fits a display containing public ticket aliases or aggregate state shared by all authorized viewers. Per-waiter channels fit private positions and account-linked context. Issue tokens on a trusted server through POST /v1/realtime/token/issue; the browser should receive only the scope needed for its room. Never put a platform API key in client code.

This is the clean capability boundary:

  1. The system of record owns queue order and authorization.
  2. A trusted backend turns the latest state into either one safe snapshot or N private projections.
  3. The realtime provider transports that update.
  4. The client renders it, but does not decide what it was entitled to receive.

That boundary also explains the appeal of a single HTTP surface. The queue service owns policy; transport is replaceable. Infrai exposes realtime alongside a broader REST capability surface under one key, with 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is only useful if the contract reduces glue in this specific service. A team already standardized on a specialist realtime SDK may gain nothing from moving the boundary.

Keep events boring. A monotonic queue revision is enough for the client to reject an older response arriving after a newer one. Do not let the browser calculate an authoritative position from deltas. That turns packet timing into business state.

Why should reconnect fetch instead of replay?

A position event is stale as soon as the queue changes again. Replaying position: 17, then 16, then 15 after a sleeping laptop reconnects spends bandwidth reconstructing a state the server already knows, and it creates awkward UI transitions. Fetch the current queue view after reconnect, render its revision, and resume live updates from there.

Short version: streams signal change; the system of record answers truth.

This rule holds for both publishing strategies. A shared client refetches the safe whole-queue view. A private client refetches only its authorized projection. The realtime layer does not become an event-sourcing log merely because messages crossed it.

For chat rooms attached to the waiting flow, use the same reconnect rule for room membership and customer-visible queue state. WebRTC can carry peer media or data, but the W3C specification does not turn it into the authoritative queue database. Reconnect logic still needs a trusted server snapshot.

Where do the specialist products win?

The honest comparison is about boundaries, not a feature-checkbox total. Ably and Pusher Channels are focused realtime products with their own channel, authentication, and client-library models. Supabase Realtime is a closer fit when the application already treats Supabase and Postgres changes as its application boundary. WebRTC is the different branch: choose it for direct peer communication requirements, not as a substitute for authoritative queue state.

Product Boundary to evaluate Better choice when
Infrai One REST capability surface, with token issue and publish operations You want provider-swappable transport and less SDK/key glue around several backend capabilities
Ably Ably's realtime platform and SDK model The team wants a specialist realtime product and is comfortable binding clients to that model
Pusher Channels Pusher's channel and client-library model Existing code and operations already center on Channels
Supabase Realtime Broadcast or database-driven changes inside the Supabase stack Postgres and Supabase already define the application's trust boundary
WebRTC Peer connection negotiated by the application The job is peer media or direct data rather than server-authoritative queue broadcast

Do a time-to-first-authorized-call test before committing. Count required SDKs, secrets, token-minting code, reconnect state, and schema adapters. Then test the ugly case: revoke one customer's access while 500 others remain connected. I would accept more publishes for correct isolation every time.

The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not a fit when the team needs a specialist's native realtime workflows or has already made a vendor SDK part of the client architecture. Ably or Pusher is the stronger candidate when those specialist realtime workflows and native SDK ecosystems are the main product requirement. Supabase is the sensible runner-up when queue changes already originate in its database stack. None of those choices changes the core rule: the payload must match token scope, and reconnect must refetch truth.

Decision rule

Use a whole-queue snapshot if all recipients are authorized for identical data and the measured snapshot stays within your operational limits. It gives one publish per update. Use per-waiter projections when positions or account context are private; publish volume then grows with queue length, which is the cost of a narrower trust boundary.

I would not choose from a vendor pricing table. Payload shape, authorization, and recovery semantics will remain in the code after today's prices change. Benchmark your actual JSON, trace the trusted-server handoff, and make the client disposable.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the live discovery schema before generating an adapter.

References

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Ably token authentication: https://ably.com/docs/auth/token
  • Pusher Channels authentication: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/server_api/authenticating-users/
  • Supabase Realtime: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

The Terms now have a dedicated section for accounts that use a company email domain (e.g., work email), clarifying that the company can manage only the Projects you create inside its Team. We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

Read the full Terms of Service and Service Terms for details.

title: I replaced a brand's Shopify app stack with code. Here's what it really costs
description:
The usual Shopify answer to "can the store do X?" is "there's an app for that". Install it, pay monthly, live with its widget, its script weight and its idea of how your store should look.

For a publisher I run tech for (4 stores, 4 countries, 4 currencies), I stopped saying that. Most of what would normally be an app is now code we own. AI didn't write it for me, but it made one engineer fast enough to build and maintain all of it.

What we built instead of installing

Need What runs now
Frequently bought together Sets mined from real orders + a Shopify Function that discounts only complete sets
Bundle builder A guided quiz that builds a 2–4 book library, discount applied at checkout
Cart upsell "Complete your library" in the cart drawer
Prepaid nudge Order discount + a payment customization that hides cash on delivery when the customer opts in
Split-shipment fee Orders split across parcels pay one fee, by total weight
International upsell A cart bar showing weight against 5/10/20/30 kg shipping slabs
Back in stock Notify-me on product cards and pages
AI shopping assistant Claude-based, with every sale it creates tagged on the order
WhatsApp inbox Our own CRM on Meta's coexistence API
Inventory A ledger that records who changed stock, with daily drift checks
Reporting P&L and a multi-store sales dashboard
Control panel One embedded admin app to switch features on or off and change percentages, no developer needed

All of these are live. Some run on all 4 stores, others only where they make sense (cash on delivery is a Pakistan problem, shipping slabs are an international one).

Why code beat apps here

  • Logic apps can't express. "Discount only when the full set is in the cart" and "hide COD only when the shopper chose to prepay" aren't settings in an app. They're business rules.
  • One brand, one design. Nothing looks bolted on, because nothing is.
  • Speed. Every app adds its own script. Ours load only where they're used.
  • The data stays ours. Orders, stock history and chats sit in our database, not in a vendor dashboard we rent.

What it actually costs (the honest part)

Owning the code means owning the bugs. These are the ones that cost us:

  • The 25-discount ceiling. Shopify allows 25 automatic discounts per store. We had hundreds of real product sets, so I pack them into "shards" to stay under the limit and the config size cap.
  • Plus gating. Payment and delivery customizations from a custom app need Shopify Plus. I learned this on another, non-Plus store after building and deploying a Function. Now the plan check happens before any code.
  • Bundles that oversold. A bundle was its own product, separate from the books inside it. Without the right inventory settings, Shopify let 100 bundles into a cart when only 1 real book was in stock. App vendors absorb bugs like this for you. We don't have that buffer.
  • Discounts that fight. A welcome code that didn't combine with product discounts quietly cancelled a discount we'd promised. Now every active discount's combinesWith gets checked before we promise anything.
  • Maintenance never ends. API versions change, and someone has to read the changelog. Here, that's me.

When I'd still install an app

When the feature is a commodity (reviews, email, subscriptions billing), when nobody on the team can own the code, or when the store is small enough that one app costs less than one day of development.

For a multi-store brand with rules no app understands, the maths flips. You stop paying rent on features and start owning an asset.

I build these systems for Shopify brands. More at fahadazhar.site.

title: Building an AI chat UI with React and shadcn: start with the awkward states
description:
By Alex, who builds Cuelark. The components linked here are ours.

A chat screen looks finished long before it behaves properly. Put a few bubbles above a textarea and it photographs well. Then somebody presses Enter twice, cancels a response, or pastes a file they did not mean to attach.

That is where I would start a React AI chat interface. Not the gradient. The state transitions.

We built Cuelark components for this layer of the application: a message layout and a composer you can adapt in your own project. They are UI source, not an AI backend. They do not choose a model, protect a secret API key, or make your data handling private by themselves.

This walkthrough focuses on the boundary between those pieces. Getting that boundary right makes the rest of the interface much less surprising.

Use source you can change

The shadcn approach is useful here because a chat interface rarely stays generic. Your application may need approval buttons, citations, a retry action or a warning before a file leaves the device. Owning the component source makes those changes straightforward to inspect.

Start with Cuelark's Message component and Prompt Input component. Use the installation instructions on those pages, then check the copied files and their dependencies in your project. Do not assume an example import path matches the aliases in your application.

For this article I checked the current component source rather than guessing from a screenshot. I also checked both documentation destinations over HTTP: two requests, two 200 responses. That confirms that the links resolve, not that an entire production chat application has passed a browser test suite.

There is no latency benchmark hidden in those numbers. Performance depends on your app, network and model service, and I have not measured those here.

Give messages stable identities

Store conversation turns as data. At minimum, each needs an ID, a role and its content. Give IDs to turns when you create them, not each time React renders.

A compact shape could look like this:

type Turn = {
  id: string;
  role: 'user' | 'assistant';
  text: string;
  state: 'pending' | 'complete' | 'failed' | 'cancelled';
};

That is an application design suggestion, not a type exported by Cuelark. The actual Message component takes a from value of user or assistant. Your application maps its own turn data into that presentation API.

Avoid using the array index as the key if you might retry, insert or remove turns. A stable ID also gives you something sensible to attach feedback and analytics to later, without treating message text as an identifier.

For a streaming assistant response, create one turn and update its text. Do not append a new message for every chunk. Otherwise copy actions, focus and screen-reader output become a mess surprisingly quickly.

Decide what belongs in a bubble

Cuelark's Message layout makes user turns right-aligned bubbles. Assistant turns read as a wider document on the left. That distinction is intentional: long answers and code are harder to read when squeezed into a decorative bubble.

The source limits user content to 80% width. Assistant content uses the available space. Those are layout choices you can edit, not a requirement of a chat protocol.

Keep plain text rendering as the default while you assemble the application. React text content is a safer starting point than injecting generated HTML. If you add Markdown later, decide explicitly how you sanitize HTML, handle links and render code blocks.

A model response is untrusted input. A nice message component does not change that. The same applies to text returned by a search tool or imported from a document.

Understand the composer's actual contract

PromptInput calls onSubmit with an object containing text and files. The text is trimmed. The files are browser File objects, not uploaded URLs.

It supports two UI statuses: idle and streaming. While streaming, the send control becomes a stop control. The callback for that control is onStop.

There is an important implementation detail: after it calls onSubmit, the composer clears its local text and files. It does not wait for your server to accept the request. If you want to restore a failed draft, save that submitted payload in application state before starting the network request.

I would rather show a plainly failed message with a retry button than quietly lose someone's draft. A polished animation cannot compensate for missing text.

Also note that an attachment alone can make a submission valid. If your backend only accepts text, turn attachments off instead of displaying an attachment button that leads nowhere.

Keep request state outside the component

Your application should own the request lifecycle. When submission starts, mark the request active, create the assistant placeholder and pass status="streaming" to the composer. On completion or failure, return to idle.

Protect the handler against a second submission while a request is already active. The composer changes its controls based on props, but your backend and application state still need a duplicate-request policy. A disabled button is not a server-side safety mechanism.

Choose how partial output behaves after an error. Keeping it with a visible failure note is often more helpful than deleting it. Make retry an explicit action so a temporary connection problem does not silently produce duplicate work or duplicate charges.

If your system uses a paid model, keep billing and limits on the backend too. None of that belongs in the visual component.

Stop should really stop

Wiring onStop to hide a spinner is not cancellation. Use it to cancel the browser request where possible, commonly through an AbortController, and connect that to your server's cancellation behavior.

Do not promise that aborting a browser request always stops upstream generation or billing. That depends on your backend and provider. Test it with the actual service you use.

The component listens for Escape while streaming. That is convenient, but it is also a global keyboard listener. If your app has a modal or editor that uses Escape, check how those interactions overlap.

Keep the partial answer visible and mark it cancelled. Otherwise the user can mistake an unfinished sentence for a completed response. Small wording choices matter here.

Attachments need a policy, not just a paperclip

The current composer accepts files through a picker, paste and drag-and-drop when attachments are enabled. It also shows removable file chips. It does not enforce your application's file-type or size policy for you.

Validate files before upload. Validate them again on the server. Decide where files are stored, how long they remain there, and whether a model provider receives them. Put that explanation near the attachment interaction rather than burying it in a vague privacy slogan.

For a text-only prototype, my preference is attachments={false}. It removes a whole set of misleading expectations. Add the feature when the backend and privacy explanation are ready.

Cuelark's browser-only file tools and an AI chat application are different products with different data paths. Do not borrow a “files stay local” claim for a chat interface that sends files to your server.

Test the keyboard before the screenshots

Enter sends; Shift+Enter inserts a line break. The source also checks composition state before treating Enter as submission, which matters for people using input methods to compose text.

Build a small acceptance checklist around actual behavior. Try an empty message, a message containing only spaces and a long paragraph. Try sending during an active response. Cancel, then submit again. If attachments are enabled, paste one and remove it before sending.

These are proposed acceptance cases, not claims of tests I have already executed in your project. Run them with keyboard navigation and on a touch device. Message actions that appear on hover also need a usable focus path; this source includes focus-within and touch visibility styles, but your integration can still break them.

Finally, decide how new output is announced to assistive technology. Announcing every token is usually unpleasant. A restrained status announcement is a better starting point to test.

FAQ

Does this include a model backend?

No. You supply request handling, credentials, conversation storage and any model integration. Keep secret credentials off the client.

Does the composer upload attachments automatically?

No. Its submission callback receives File objects. Your application decides what happens next.

Can I change the styling?

Yes. The source-copying approach is meant for local adaptation. Check dependencies and the project license before shipping.

What should I build first?

A text-only conversation with visible failure and working cancellation. Add richer formatting and attachments after those paths behave properly. It is less exciting in a screenshot, and considerably better to use.

title: Why Filled PDF Forms Open Blank in Some Viewers (and How to Fix It)
description:
If you build document workflows, web upload portals, or automated billing pipelines, you have likely run into this frustrating bug: a user fills out a PDF form, submits it, but when an administrator opens the file in macOS Preview, Google Chrome, or a mobile reader, all the fields appear completely blank. Yet, opening the exact same file in Adobe Acrobat displays every entered character perfectly.

This discrepancy is not a corruption error. It is a direct consequence of how the PDF specification (ISO 32000-1) separates form data from visual page contents, and how different rendering engines handle interactive widgets.

Here is an under-the-hood breakdown of why this happens, how PDF form flattening permanently resolves it, and how to implement flattening in production.

1. The PDF Form Architecture: Values vs. Appearances

In a standard PDF document, static text and vector artwork reside directly in a page's /Contents stream using low-level graphics operators (such as BT for begin text, Tf for font selection, and Tj for text display).

Interactive forms (known as AcroForms), however, do not write their data directly to the page content stream. Instead, they operate across two separate layers:

  1. The Field Dictionary (/AcroForm / /Fields): Located in the Document Catalog, this stores field metadata, field names (/T), field types (/FT, such as /Tx for text), and the raw string values (/V).
  2. The Widget Annotation (/Annots): Located in a page's /Annots array, this defines the bounding box (/Rect) where the field lives and holds an Appearance Dictionary (/AP). Within /AP, the normal appearance subdictionary (/N) contains a stream of low-level drawing instructions showing how the value should visually appear on screen.

The /NeedAppearances Trap

When a form-filling tool writes a value to /V without constructing a valid /N appearance stream, it often sets /NeedAppearances true in the document's /AcroForm dictionary.

This flag tells the viewer: "I updated the data, but I did not render the visuals. Please generate the appearance streams for me using your own font engine when opening the file."

Here is where the breakdown occurs:

  • Adobe Acrobat / Reader: Complies with the flag, calculates font metrics, generates the vector appearance stream in memory, and displays the text.
  • Apple Preview, Safari, Chrome, and Mobile Viewers: Most lightweight viewers ignore /NeedAppearances or lack a full interactive AcroForm layout engine. They look directly at /AP -> /N. Because /N is empty or missing, they render a blank box.

2. What Form Flattening Does

Flattening converts an interactive, multi-layer PDF into a single static page content stream. Under the hood, a flattening routine performs four surgical steps:

  1. Generates Missing Appearances: Ensures every widget annotation has a complete /AP /N stream matching its current /V value and font attributes.
  2. Merges Appearance Streams: Translates the widget's appearance stream into the coordinate system of the parent page, appending the vector instructions directly to the page's /Contents array.
  3. Strips Widget Annotations: Removes the widget references from the page's /Annots array.
  4. Cleans Document Catalog: Removes the fields from /AcroForm /Fields, preventing interactive editors from showing active text boxes.

Once flattened, the text is no longer stored in an editable form field; it is permanent vector content in the page stream. Every PDF reader renders it identically.

3. How to Implement Flattening Programmatically

In JavaScript / Node.js (with pdf-lib)

pdf-lib provides built-in AcroForm management that runs in both Node.js and modern browsers without external C++ binaries:

import { PDFDocument } from 'pdf-lib';
import fs from 'fs/promises';

async function flattenPdfForm(inputPath, outputPath) {
  const pdfBytes = await fs.readFile(inputPath);
  const pdfDoc = await PDFDocument.load(pdfBytes, { ignoreEncryption: true });

  const form = pdfDoc.getForm();

  // Update appearance streams and bake them into page content
  // form.flatten() automatically updates widget appearances before merging
  form.flatten();

  const flattenedBytes = await pdfDoc.save();
  await fs.writeFile(outputPath, flattenedBytes);
}

Note on custom fonts: If your form values contain characters outside WinAnsi (standard Latin-1), embed a Unicode font before saving to prevent encoding errors when generating appearances.

On the Command Line (with qpdf)

If you run Linux workers or shell automation, qpdf provides a lossless, byte-preserving flattening utility:

qpdf --generate-appearances --flatten-annotations=all input.pdf output_flattened.pdf

The --generate-appearances flag forces qpdf to construct fresh visual streams from /V values before --flatten-annotations=all merges them into the content stream.

4. Key Gotchas to Keep in Mind

  1. Digital Signatures vs. Visual Stamps: Flattening visual signature appearances bakes the graphic into the page, but it invalidates cryptographic digital signatures (PKCS#7 byte ranges). Flattening should always occur before applying cryptographic signatures.
  2. Irreversibility: Form flattening is destructive. The field names, types, and tab orders are removed from the document catalog. Always preserve an unflattened copy of user submissions in your storage layer for future programmatic extraction.
  3. Tagged PDF & Accessibility: Stripping AcroForm widgets removes their accessible /StructElem associations. For compliance with Section 508 or WCAG, verify that the resulting page text maintains appropriate logical reading order in the document structure tree.
