title: Run Less, Prove More: Diff-Scoped Test Gating for Agent Patches
description:
An agent patch rarely needs your whole suite. It needs a scope you can defend line by line, and a safety net over everything the scope excludes. Most review pipelines get this backwards: they run everything, watch it go red at random, and then learn nothing about which failure the patch actually caused.

This is a selection strategy, not a speed trick. The gate runs a narrow set of tests, emits a receipt explaining why each test was included, and escalates to the full suite whenever a widening trigger fires. Flaky tests are frozen separately — and a freeze is only granted once a property check covers the same behavior.

The cost is a product, not a number

Write the cost down before optimizing it. For a patch p:

cost(p) = |selected(p)| * t_avg + |frozen| * t_skip  + widen(p) * |full| * t_avg

widen(p) is binary here on purpose. Either a trigger fired or it did not. If you make widening a judgment call, reviewers will quietly skip it under deadline, and your escape rate becomes invisible until production finds it.

Measure t_avg on your own repo. Do not reuse numbers from a blog post — including this one.

Why "only run tests that import the changed file" fails

Naive diff selection is a well-known footgun. Four failure modes matter for agent patches specifically:

  1. Shared fixtures. A conftest.py change alters fixtures used by tests that never import the modified module.
  2. Runtime wiring. Entry points, plugin registries, DI containers, and string-based imports create edges no static parser sees.
  3. Contract drift. An agent changes a serializer or CLI flag; every consumer test still passes locally because none of them are in the import closure.
  4. Editable surfaces. Settings modules, migrations, and schema files are imported indirectly by nearly everything.

Each of those becomes a widening trigger in step 3. That is the whole design: be aggressive about narrow selection, be mechanical about widening.

Step 1 — Build a reverse import map

The map is the only expensive part, and it is cacheable per commit.

# scope.py — diff-scoped test selection for a Python repo
import ast, json, pathlib, subprocess

ROOT = pathlib.Path(".").resolve()
SKIP = {".venv", "build", "dist", "node_modules", ".git"}

def changed_files(base: str) -> list[str]:
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "diff", "--name-only", f"{base}...HEAD"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    ).stdout
    return [f for f in out.splitlines() if f.endswith(".py")]

def module_name(rel: str) -> str:
    parts = list(pathlib.Path(rel).with_suffix("").parts)
    if parts and parts[-1] == "__init__":
        parts.pop()
    return ".".join(parts)

def imports_of(path: pathlib.Path) -> set[str]:
    try:
        tree = ast.parse(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    except SyntaxError:
        return set()
    names: set[str] = set()
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, ast.Import):
            names.update(a.name for a in node.names)
        elif isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom) and node.module and node.level == 0:
            names.add(node.module)
    return names

def build_reverse_map() -> dict[str, set[str]]:
    reverse: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
    for path in ROOT.rglob("*.py"):
        if SKIP & set(path.parts):
            continue
        rel = str(path.relative_to(ROOT))
        reverse.setdefault(module_name(rel), set()).add(rel)
        for imp in imports_of(path):
            reverse.setdefault(imp, set()).add(rel)
    return reverse

Store the map keyed by commit SHA. Rebuilding it on every patch is the mistake that makes people abandon the idea.

Step 2 — Compute the importer closure

Walk importer edges upward from the changed modules. Include ancestor packages so pkg.sub also matches pkg.

def importer_closure(seeds: set[str], reverse: dict[str, set[str]]) -> set[str]:
    seen: set[str] = set()
    stack = list(seeds)
    while stack:
        mod = stack.pop()
        for candidate in (mod, *mod.split(".")):
            for f in reverse.get(candidate, ()):
                if f not in seen:
                    seen.add(f)
                    stack.append(module_name(f))
    return seen

def select(base: str = "origin/main") -> dict:
    reverse = build_reverse_map()
    changed = changed_files(base)
    seeds = {module_name(f) for f in changed}
    closure = importer_closure(seeds, reverse)
    tests = sorted(f for f in closure if f.startswith("tests/"))
    return {"base": base, "changed": changed, "selected": tests,
            "widened": None, "reason": []}

A test file is selected because something it imports changed. Nothing else. That is a claim you can audit, which is the point.

Step 3 — Fire widening triggers

Triggers are checked before selection, and any hit short-circuits to the full suite. Keep the list short enough that people actually read it.

Trigger Why narrow scope is unsafe Action
conftest.py, tests/fixtures/**, pytest.ini changed Shared fixtures leak across the whole suite Full suite
settings/**, migrations/**, schema.* changed Imported indirectly by nearly everything Full suite
Changed file uses importlib, entry_points, or a plugin registry Static edges are incomplete Full suite
Changed file is imported by more than your configured fan-out threshold Blast radius is structural, not local Full suite
Public CLI, HTTP route, or serialized payload changed Contract consumers live outside the closure Full suite + contract tests
A frozen test's file is in the closure The freeze suppressed a relevant signal Unfreeze and rerun

Set the fan-out threshold from your own map: print the top 20 modules by importer count and pick a cutoff below the monoliths. On most repos it is embarrassingly obvious.

Step 4 — Cover the excluded surface with properties

Narrow selection is only honest if something else checks the code you did not run. That is what the property layer is for — not coverage theater, but invariants that hold across inputs the suite never generates.

# tests/properties/test_ledger_props.py — illustrative; assert properties your
# module actually promises before adding this file.
from hypothesis import given, settings, strategies as st
from app.ledger import reconcile

rows = st.lists(
    st.fixed_dictionaries({"amount": st.integers(-10**6, 10**6),
                           "ref": st.text(max_size=8)}),
    max_size=50,
)

@settings(max_examples=200, deadline=None)
@given(entries=rows)
def test_reconcile_is_order_insensitive(entries):
    assert reconcile(entries) == reconcile(list(reversed(entries)))

@settings(max_examples=200, deadline=None)
@given(entries=rows)
def test_reconcile_is_total(entries):
    total = sum(e["amount"] for e in entries)
    assert sum(reconcile(entries).values()) == total

These two properties survive refactors that would break every example-based test. They also fail loudly when an agent "optimizes" a fold into a loop that drops the tail.

Step 5 — Freeze flaky tests behind a substitute

A freeze without a substitute is a coverage withdrawal with better branding. Gate it:

freeze(test) is legal only if
  (a) it has an owner and an expiry date, and
  (b) at least one property check covers the behavior the test asserts.

Record both in the receipt. If (b) is unmet, the correct output is a red gate — not a freeze. This is the single rule that keeps quarantine from becoming silent debt.

Step 6 — Emit a scope receipt

Everything above is worthless if the reviewer cannot see it. Write the selection, the triggers checked, the freezes applied, and the property files run into one JSON artifact attached to the patch.

python scope.py --base origin/main --out scope.json
jq -r '.selected[]' scope.json | xargs pytest -q --timeout=300
jq -r '.properties[]' scope.json | xargs pytest -q

A reviewer reading scope.json should be able to answer "what did this gate not run, and why is that acceptable" in under a minute.

Step 7 — Measure the escape rate

Track one number weekly: full-suite failures that the narrow gate did not catch. Run the full suite on a schedule against the same commits and diff the results. If the escape rate is zero for a month, your triggers are probably too conservative — widen less. If it is nonzero, every escape names the missing trigger. Add it.

This is where a free execution lane helps. The narrow gate belongs on the developer's machine because it must be fast; the scheduled full-suite baseline is throughput work that does not need interactivity. MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option fit that second lane: the server runs the scheduled baseline, and the model handles the boring parts — classifying diff hunks into widening triggers and drafting property candidates for human review.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Do not let a model approve a trigger decision. Classification is a draft; the trigger list is code, and the trigger list is what the gate obeys.

Limitations, and who should skip this

  • Static edges only. Dynamic dispatch, getattr chains, and subprocess CLIs are invisible. That is what the trigger table is compensating for, imperfectly.
  • Python-shaped. The recipe ports to other languages only if you can build a reliable import graph; dynamic languages and macro-heavy code make it fragile.
  • Needs a stable baseline. Without a trustworthy full-suite run to compare against, the escape rate is unmeasurable and the narrow gate is unfalsifiable.
  • Skip it for schema migrations, auth and crypto changes, shared integration suites against live external services, and any repo where most tests are end-to-end. Those belong on the full suite every time, and no selection heuristic will save you.
  • Skip it if your team will not maintain the trigger list. An unmaintained trigger list is worse than no gate, because it looks like coverage.

The takeaway

Scope is a claim, not an optimization. Write the claim down, make widening mechanical, put properties behind every freeze, and measure how often the claim is wrong. Your agent patches will merge faster for the same reason good tests do: the reviewer stops guessing.

If you try one piece, try the receipt. It is thirty lines of JSON and it changes how the whole gate is argued about.

title: Hacking Your Own Keyboard: Building a Custom Screenshot Tool in Python When Windows Won't Let You Own Win+Shift+S
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Windows has a built-in screenshot tool (Snip & Sketch / Snipping Tool) that owns the Win+Shift+S shortcut, and it's notoriously difficult to override. But what if you want your own custom screenshot utility—one that captures to clipboard, saves with custom filenames, or even runs OCR? This tutorial shows you how to build a Python-based screenshot tool that can intercept global hotkeys, including the elusive Win+Shift+S, by using low-level keyboard hooks and a little Windows API trickery. By the end, you'll have a working, extensible tool that you can bind to your own hotkey or even attempt to hijack the system shortcut (with caveats).

Table of Contents

  • 1. Why Windows Won't Let You Own Win+Shift+S
  • 2. Prerequisites and Setup
  • 3. Building the Screenshot Capture Module
  • 4. Global Hotkey Interception with keyboard Library
  • 5. Attempting to Override Win+Shift+S
  • 6. Adding OCR and Clipboard Integration
  • 7. Packaging as a Background App
  • 8. Full Code Example
  • 9. Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why Windows Won't Let You Own Win+Shift+S

On Windows 10 and 11, Win+Shift+S is a system-level shortcut registered by the built-in screen snipping tool. The Windows shell (explorer.exe) registers this hotkey globally, and it takes precedence over most user-level hotkeys. This is because the hotkey is registered with the MOD_WIN modifier and is handled at a higher privilege level. When you try to register a hotkey with the same combination using standard APIs (like RegisterHotKey), you'll get a conflict error.

However, there are workarounds:

  • Low-level keyboard hooks: Using SetWindowsHookEx with WH_KEYBOARD_LL, you can intercept keystrokes before the system processes them. This allows you to "swallow" the key combination and execute your own code instead.
  • Modifying the system shortcut: You can disable the built-in shortcut via registry settings or Group Policy, but that's invasive and not always reliable.
  • Using a different hotkey: The simplest and most robust approach is to use your own hotkey (e.g., Ctrl+Alt+S). This tutorial covers both: building a custom tool with your own hotkey, and an attempt to override Win+Shift+S using low-level hooks.

2. Prerequisites and Setup

You'll need Python 3.8+ and the following libraries:

  • Pillow – for image capture and processing
  • keyboard – for global hotkey registration (works on Windows, Linux, and macOS)
  • pytesseract – for OCR (optional)
  • pyperclip – for clipboard operations
  • pywin32 (optional) – for low-level Windows API access if you want to try the hook approach

Install them with pip:

pip install Pillow keyboard pytesseract pyperclip pywin32

Note: keyboard requires administrator privileges on Windows to register global hooks. Run your script as administrator.

3. Building the Screenshot Capture Module

First, let's create a simple module that captures the entire screen or a region. We'll use Pillow's ImageGrab which works cross-platform on Windows.

Create a file screenshotter.py:

import time
import tkinter as tk
from PIL import ImageGrab

class Screenshotter:
    @staticmethod
    def capture_fullscreen():
        """Capture the entire screen."""
        return ImageGrab.grab()

    @staticmethod
    def capture_region(bbox):
        """Capture a specific region given a bounding box (x1, y1, x2, y2)."""
        return ImageGrab.grab(bbox=bbox)

    @staticmethod
    def select_region():
        """Let the user select a region with a crosshair overlay."""
        # Create a fullscreen overlay window
        root = tk.Tk()
        root.attributes('-fullscreen', True)
        root.attributes('-alpha', 0.3)
        root.configure(bg='gray')

        # Canvas for drawing selection rectangle
        canvas = tk.Canvas(root, cursor='cross', bg='gray')
        canvas.pack(fill=tk.BOTH, expand=True)

        start_x = start_y = 0
        rect = None

        def on_press(event):
            nonlocal start_x, start_y, rect
            start_x, start_y = event.x, event.y
            rect = canvas.create_rectangle(start_x, start_y, start_x, start_y, outline='red', width=2)

        def on_drag(event):
            nonlocal rect
            canvas.coords(rect, start_x, start_y, event.x, event.y)

        def on_release(event):
            nonlocal root
            # Get final coordinates
            x1 = min(start_x, event.x)
            y1 = min(start_y, event.y)
            x2 = max(start_x, event.x)
            y2 = max(start_y, event.y)
            root.destroy()
            # Capture the region
            img = ImageGrab.grab(bbox=(x1, y1, x2, y2))
            return img

        canvas.bind('<ButtonPress-1>', on_press)
        canvas.bind('<B1-Motion>', on_drag)
        canvas.bind('<ButtonRelease-1>', on_release)

        root.mainloop()
        # The function will return after mainloop ends, but we need to get the image
        # This is a simplified version; for a full implementation, use a callback.
        # We'll improve this later.
        return None

This is a basic version. For a robust region selection, we'll use a more advanced approach later.

4. Global Hotkey Interception with keyboard Library

The keyboard library makes it easy to register global hotkeys. It uses low-level hooks on Windows, so it can detect keys even when your app is not focused. However, it cannot intercept Win+Shift+S directly because the system handles it first. But you can register your own hotkey like Ctrl+Alt+S.

Let's create a script that listens for a hotkey and triggers a screenshot action:

import keyboard
from screenshotter import Screenshotter
from PIL import Image
import time

def on_hotkey():
    print("Hotkey pressed! Taking screenshot...")
    img = Screenshotter.capture_fullscreen()
    timestamp = time.strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    filename = f"screenshot_{timestamp}.png"
    img.save(filename)
    print(f"Saved {filename}")

keyboard.add_hotkey('ctrl+alt+s', on_hotkey)
print("Listening for Ctrl+Alt+S...")
keyboard.wait()

This works, but it's not very interesting. Let's make it more feature-rich: capture region, copy to clipboard, and run OCR.

5. Attempting to Override Win+Shift+S

Now, the fun part: trying to intercept Win+Shift+S. The keyboard library allows you to register a hotkey with the Windows key, but it won't work because the system captures it first. However, we can use keyboard.hook to listen for all key events and suppress them if they match our combination.

Here's an attempt:

import keyboard
import time

def on_key_event(event):
    # Check if the combination Win+Shift+S is pressed
    # event.name gives the key name, event.is_keypad, etc.
    # We need to track state of modifiers
    if event.event_type == 'down':
        if event.name == 's' and keyboard.is_pressed('win') and keyboard.is_pressed('shift'):
            # Suppress the event to prevent system action
            # But this might not work because the system may have already handled it
            print("Intercepted Win+Shift+S")
            return False  # Suppress the key event
    return True

keyboard.hook(on_key_event)
keyboard.wait()

Why this fails: On Windows, the Win+Shift+S shortcut is processed by the shell at a very low level, likely before the keyboard library's hook can see it. The keyboard library uses WH_KEYBOARD_LL, which is a low-level hook, but the shell may have a higher priority or handle it in a different thread. In practice, the hook may receive the event but returning False might not prevent the system from opening the snipping overlay.

Alternative approach: Use SetWindowsHookEx directly with WH_KEYBOARD_LL and set the LLKHF_INJECTED flag to detect injected events? Not helpful. Actually, the only reliable way is to disable the system shortcut via registry or use a utility like AutoHotkey that uses a different hooking mechanism.

Let's try a more aggressive approach: use keyboard.block_key for the Windows key and then listen for Shift+S? That would break the Windows key entirely. Not ideal.

Practical solution: Accept that you can't easily override Win+Shift+S and instead use Ctrl+Alt+S or Ctrl+Shift+S. This is what most custom screenshot tools do. If you really want to hijack Win+Shift+S, you can disable the built-in shortcut by modifying the registry:

  • Navigate to HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced
  • Create a DWORD value DisabledHotkeys with a string value containing the hotkey, e.g., "S"? That's for disabling Win+S, not Win+Shift+S. Actually, you can use DisabledHotkeys to disable specific hotkeys that include the Windows key. Setting it to "S" disables Win+S, but Win+Shift+S may still work.

A more reliable method is to disable the Snipping Tool via Group Policy or remove the shortcut from the Start Menu. But that's beyond the scope of this tutorial.

For the sake of this tutorial, we'll focus on building a robust tool with your own hotkey. If you still want to attempt Win+Shift+S, you can try the hook approach and see if it works on your system—sometimes it does if you run as administrator and use a lower-level hook like WH_KEYBOARD_LL with SetWindowsHookEx from pywin32. Here's a more advanced implementation:

import ctypes
from ctypes import wintypes

# Define necessary structures
user32 = ctypes.WinDLL('user32', use_last_error=True)

# SetWindowsHookExW function
WH_KEYBOARD_LL = 13
WM_KEYDOWN = 0x0100
WM_KEYUP = 0x0101

# Define callback type
HOOKPROC = ctypes.WINFUNCTYPE(ctypes.c_long, ctypes.c_int, wintypes.WPARAM, wintypes.LPARAM)

# Define KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT
class KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [
        ("vkCode", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("scanCode", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("flags", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("time", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("dwExtraInfo", wintypes.ULONG_PTR),
    ]

# Global hook handle
hook_handle = None

def hook_proc(nCode, wParam, lParam):
    global hook_handle
    if nCode >= 0:
        kb = ctypes.cast(lParam, ctypes.POINTER(KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT)).contents
        # VK codes: VK_LWIN=0x5B, VK_RSHIFT=0xA1, VK_S=0x53
        if wParam == WM_KEYDOWN and kb.vkCode == 0x53:  # S key
            # Check if Win and Shift are pressed
            if (user32.GetAsyncKeyState(0x5B) & 0x8000) and (user32.GetAsyncKeyState(0xA1) & 0x8000):
                print("Intercepted Win+Shift+S")
                # Return 1 to suppress the event
                return 1
    return user32.CallNextHookEx(hook_handle, nCode, wParam, lParam)

# Set the hook
CALLBACK = HOOKPROC(hook_proc)
hook_handle = user32.SetWindowsHookExW(WH_KEYBOARD_LL, CALLBACK, None, 0)
if not hook_handle:
    raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())

# Message loop
import threading
import time

def message_loop():
    msg = wintypes.MSG()
    while user32.GetMessageW(ctypes.byref(msg), None, 0, 0) != 0:
        user32.TranslateMessage(ctypes.byref(msg))
        user32.DispatchMessageW(ctypes.byref(msg))

thread = threading.Thread(target=message_loop)
thread.start()
print("Listening for Win+Shift+S...")

try:
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    user32.UnhookWindowsHookEx(hook_handle)

This code sets a low-level keyboard hook and checks for the specific key combination. It might work on some systems, but it's not guaranteed. In practice, the Windows shell may still open the snipping bar before the hook runs, because the shell has its own hook that runs earlier. The only way to guarantee it is to disable the system shortcut.

6. Adding OCR and Clipboard Integration

Let's make our tool genuinely useful. We'll add a region selector that lets the user draw a rectangle, then capture, copy to clipboard, and optionally run OCR.

For region selection, we'll use tkinter with a fullscreen transparent overlay. Here's a more complete implementation:

# region_selector.py
import tkinter as tk
from PIL import ImageGrab

class RegionSelector:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = tk.Tk()
        self.root.attributes('-fullscreen', True)
        self.root.attributes('-alpha', 0.3)
        self.root.configure(bg='gray')
        self.canvas = tk.Canvas(self.root, cursor='cross', bg='gray')
        self.canvas.pack(fill=tk.BOTH, expand=True)
        self.start_x = 0
        self.start_y = 0
        self.rect = None
        self.image = None

        self.canvas.bind('<ButtonPress-1>', self.on_press)
        self.canvas.bind('<B1-Motion>', self.on_drag)
        self.canvas.bind('<ButtonRelease-1>', self.on_release)

    def on_press(self, event):
        self.start_x = event.x
        self.start_y = event.y
        self.rect = self.canvas.create_rectangle(self.start_x, self.start_y, self.start_x, self.start_y, outline='red', width=2)

    def on_drag(self, event):
        self.canvas.coords(self.rect, self.start_x, self.start_y, event.x, event.y)

    def on_release(self, event):
        x1 = min(self.start_x, event.x)
        y1 = min(self.start_y, event.y)
        x2 = max(self.start_x, event.x)
        y2 = max(self.start_y, event.y)
        self.root.destroy()
        # Capture after destroying overlay
        self.image = ImageGrab.grab(bbox=(x1, y1, x2, y2))

    def select(self):
        self.root.mainloop()
        return self.image

Now, integrate it into the main tool. We'll also add OCR with pytesseract and clipboard copy with pyperclip.

7. Packaging as a Background App

To run the tool in the background, you can either run the script directly (with pythonw.exe on Windows to avoid a console window) or package it with PyInstaller into a standalone executable. We'll cover both.

  • To run without console: use pythonw.exe your_script.py
  • To package: pyinstaller --onefile --noconsole screenshot_tool.py

Make sure to include the required libraries. PyInstaller will bundle them.

8. Full Code Example

Let's put it all together into a single script screenshot_tool.py:

import sys
import time
import tkinter as tk
import keyboard
import pyperclip
import pytesseract
from PIL import ImageGrab, Image

# Configuration
SAVE_DIR = "screenshots"
USE_OCR = True

class RegionSelector:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = tk.Tk()
        self.root.attributes('-fullscreen', True)
        self.root.attributes('-alpha', 0.3)
        self.root.configure(bg='gray')
        self.canvas = tk.Canvas(self.root, cursor='cross', bg='gray')
        self.canvas.pack(fill=tk.BOTH, expand=True)
        self.start_x = 0
        self.start_y = 0
        self.rect = None
        self.image = None

        self.canvas.bind('<ButtonPress-1>', self.on_press)
        self.canvas.bind('<B1-Motion>', self.on_drag)
        self.canvas.bind('<ButtonRelease-1>', self.on_release)

    def on_press(self, event):
        self.start_x = event.x
        self.start_y = event.y
        self.rect = self.canvas.create_rectangle(self.start_x, self.start_y, self.start_x, self.start_y, outline='red', width=2)

    def on_drag(self, event):
        self.canvas.coords(self.rect, self.start_x, self.start_y, event.x, event.y)

    def on_release(self, event):
        x1 = min(self.start_x, event.x)
        y1 = min(self.start_y, event.y)
        x2 = max(self.start_x, event.x)
        y2 = max(self.start_y, event.y)
        self.root.destroy()
        self.image = ImageGrab.grab(bbox=(x1, y1, x2, y2))

    def select(self):
        self.root.mainloop()
        return self.image

def take_screenshot():
    # Choose mode: 1=fullscreen, 2=region
    print("Choose mode: 1=fullscreen, 2=region")
    # For demo, we'll just do fullscreen if no input
    # In real app, you can bind different hotkeys for different modes
    # Here we'll use the hotkey to trigger a region capture
    selector = RegionSelector()
    img = selector.select()
    if img is None:
        return

    # Save to file
    import os
    os.makedirs(SAVE_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    timestamp = time.strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    filename = os.path.join(SAVE_DIR, f"screenshot_{timestamp}.png")
    img.save(filename)
    print(f"Saved {filename}")

    # Copy to clipboard
    img.save_to_clipboard()
    print("Copied to clipboard")

    # OCR if enabled
    if USE_OCR:
        try:
            text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img)
            if text.strip():
                pyperclip.copy(text)
                print("OCR text copied to clipboard")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"OCR failed: {e}")

def main():
    # Register hotkey: Ctrl+Alt+S
    keyboard.add_hotkey('ctrl+alt+s', take_screenshot)
    print("Screenshot tool running. Press Ctrl+Alt+S to capture a region.")
    print("Press Ctrl+C to exit.")
    keyboard.wait()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

To run this, you need to have pytesseract installed and the Tesseract OCR engine separately. You can download it from GitHub or use a package manager. Also, img.save_to_clipboard() is a method in Pillow that works on Windows to put the image on the clipboard.

9. Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why can't I override Win+Shift+S?

A: Windows registers this hotkey at the system level, and it takes precedence over user-level hooks. Even low-level keyboard hooks may not be able to suppress it because the shell processes it early. The most reliable way is to disable the built-in shortcut via registry or Group Policy, or use a different hotkey.

Q: Do I need administrator privileges to run the global hotkey?

A: Yes, the keyboard library requires admin rights on Windows to set global hooks. Run your script as administrator, or use a task scheduler with highest privileges.

Q: Can I make the region selector work without Tkinter?

A: Yes, you can use pygame or PyQt, but Tkinter is built-in and sufficient for this purpose. For a more polished overlay, you could use PyQt5 with a transparent window.

This tool is a starting point. You can extend it with features like delayed screenshots, multi-monitor support, or uploading to cloud services. The key takeaway is that while you can't easily own Win+Shift+S, you can build a powerful custom screenshot tool that fits your workflow.

For more developer insights and tools, check out Tamiz's Insights.

title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY Failed. The INVALID Index It Left Can Still Tax Every Write
description:
• Book: Database Playbook
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You ask your coding agent for a unique index on users.email. It writes CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which is the right call on a live table. The deploy fails. The agent reruns the migration, gets told the index already exists, adds IF NOT EXISTS, and CI goes green. Weeks later someone runs \d users and sees the word INVALID at the end of the index line.

None of this is a bug. The Postgres CREATE INDEX docs say that if a concurrent build hits "a deadlock or a uniqueness violation in a unique index", the command fails "but leave[s] behind an 'invalid' index. This index will be ignored for querying purposes because it might be incomplete; however it will still consume update overhead."

Queries get nothing from it. Depending on where the build died, your writes may still be paying for it. Both kinds of leftover are easy to reproduce in a throwaway Docker container, and so is the other error agent-written migrations hit with CONCURRENTLY: cannot run inside a transaction block.

What "failed halfway" leaves behind

A concurrent build is not one transaction. Per the same docs, the index "is actually entered as an 'invalid' index into the system catalogs in one transaction, then two table scans occur in two more transactions." The catalog row commits first. Anything that kills the command after that point leaves the row in place: a duplicate key, a deadlock, a statement_timeout, a cancelled deploy.

Two flags in pg_index tell you which kind of leftover you have. indisvalid = false means the index "cannot safely be used for queries." indisready = false means "the index must be ignored by INSERT/UPDATE operations."

The order in which those flags flip decides the cost. In the Postgres source, index_concurrently_build() runs the first table scan and only afterwards marks the index ready, with a comment saying that once this commits, new transactions "must insert new entries into the index for insertions and non-HOT updates." That gives two outcomes:

Where the build died indisvalid indisready Writes maintain it
First scan (a duplicate already in the table) false false No
Second scan or final wait (late duplicate, deadlock, timeout, cancel) false true Yes

The second row is the expensive one. A January 2026 postgres.ai write-up showed an invalid-but-ready index gaining leaf entries on INSERT and UPDATE, blocking HOT updates on its column (0% HOT when updating the indexed column in their test), and adding WAL and VACUUM work. Their test marked the index invalid by hand rather than by a real failed build, but the write path is the same. For unique indexes the docs add one more cost: "if a failure does occur in the second scan, the 'invalid' index continues to enforce its uniqueness constraint afterwards." You can get unique-violation errors from an index the planner will never use.

The first row is cheaper, but it still blocks a retry under the same name and shows up in \d looking like a real index.


An invalid index answers no queries, but a ready one still takes every new entry.

Reproduce the cheap kind: a duplicate in a unique build

Start a throwaway Postgres 18 from the official Docker image and open psql:

docker run --name pg-cic -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=demo -d postgres:18
docker exec -it pg-cic psql -U postgres

Build a table with a duplicate nobody knows about, then ask for a unique index:

CREATE TABLE users (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

INSERT INTO users (email)
SELECT 'user' || g || '@example.com'
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) AS g;

-- the duplicate the migration does not know about
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('user42@example.com');

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_key
  ON users (email);

The last statement fails with could not create unique index "users_email_key" and a DETAIL line naming the duplicated key, the same shape as this 2019 pgsql-bugs report. Run \d users and the index is still listed, with INVALID at the end of its line, as in the docs' own example. This is not a lab-only case: GitLab's tracker has an issue about a unique index found invalid in production, where the rebuild failed on duplicated values.

Now do what a retry loop does. Run the same statement again and it fails because a relation named users_email_key already exists. Add IF NOT EXISTS and it passes. The docs for that clause say Postgres only issues a notice when "a relation with the same name already exists", and that "there is no guarantee that the existing index is anything like the one that would have been created." Nothing in that check looks at validity. The migration is recorded as applied and the index is still invalid.

Reproduce the expensive kind: a timeout in the final wait

After the second scan, the build "must wait for any transactions that have a snapshot ... predating the second scan to terminate." A long report or a transaction someone left open is enough to hold that wait. Add a statement_timeout (golang-migrate exposes one as x-statement-timeout) and the build gets cancelled after it already marked the index ready.

Open a second terminal with docker exec -it pg-cic psql -U postgres and hold a snapshot there:

-- session B
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT count(*) FROM users;
-- leave this transaction open

Back in the first session:

-- session A
SET statement_timeout = '5s';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_created_at_idx
  ON users (created_at);

On 200,000 rows the two scans should finish well inside five seconds. The build then sits waiting for session B. If you query pg_stat_progress_create_index from a third session while it waits, the phase column reads waiting for old snapshots. When the timeout fires, run COMMIT; in session B. You now have one leftover of each kind.

Find every leftover in pg_index

This query lists every invalid index, whether writes maintain it, and its size:

SELECT n.nspname AS schema,
       c.relname AS index_name,
       t.relname AS table_name,
       i.indisready AS maintained_on_write,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(c.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_index i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
JOIN pg_class t ON t.oid = i.indrelid
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE NOT i.indisvalid
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(c.oid) DESC;

Expect users_email_key with maintained_on_write = false and users_created_at_idx with true. To see the difference, insert another batch of rows and run the query again:

INSERT INTO users (email)
SELECT 'late' || g || '@example.com'
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS g;

The ready index grows with the table. The other one is ignored by inserts, so it does not.

One caution before you drop anything: an index that another session is building right now is also invalid. Check pg_stat_progress_create_index first. If it has a row for that table, leave the index alone.


Query pg_index for invalid entries before any retry.

Clean up without locking the table

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY removes an index "without locking out concurrent selects, inserts, updates, and deletes." It takes one index name per command and cannot run in a transaction block, so send each one on its own:

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS users_email_key;
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS users_created_at_idx;

A unique build that failed on real duplicates will fail the same way next time, so fix the data before you retry. Deleting the newer row is the quick demo fix. In a real table, decide which row wins (or merge them) before you delete anything:

DELETE FROM users a
USING users b
WHERE a.email = b.email
  AND a.id > b.id;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_key
  ON users (email);

The docs name a second recovery path: rebuild in place with REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY. The REINDEX page says "only REINDEX INDEX is able to perform a concurrent build on an invalid index." If that rebuild fails too, it leaves its own invalid index suffixed _ccnew (drop it and retry) or _ccold (drop it, the rebuild itself succeeded).

Then make the deploy refuse to finish with a leftover in place. Run this as the last step, after every migration has completed:

DO $$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid) THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'invalid index left behind';
  END IF;
END $$;

"cannot run inside a transaction block": the opt-out per tool

The docs are blunt: "a regular CREATE INDEX command can be performed within a transaction block, but CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot." The error reads CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, as in this Prisma discussion. You hit it two ways. Either the migration tool wraps each file in BEGIN/COMMIT, or the file holds several statements sent as one query, which the Postgres protocol docs say run "as a single transaction" in an implicit transaction block.

Agents walk into this honestly. golang-migrate's getting-started guide tells you to wrap multi-command migrations in a transaction, so an agent that read the docs will do exactly that.

Rails. Active Record wraps every migration in a transaction when the adapter supports DDL transactions. disable_ddl_transaction! turns that off for one migration, and the add_index docs add: "Concurrently adding an index is not supported in a transaction."

class AddUniqueIndexToUsersEmail < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.0]
  disable_ddl_transaction!

  def change
    add_index :users, :email, unique: true,
              algorithm: :concurrently
  end
end

Knex. "By default, each migration is run inside a transaction." Export config.transaction = false from the file (or set disableTransactions globally):

exports.config = { transaction: false };

exports.up = (knex) =>
  knex.raw(
    'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_key ' +
      'ON users (email)'
  );

exports.down = (knex) =>
  knex.raw('DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS users_email_key');

golang-migrate. It does not add a transaction itself, but its Postgres driver README warns that "running multiple SQL statements in one Exec executes them inside a transaction." Put the statement alone in its own file, with no BEGIN/COMMIT, or enable x-multi-statement so statements run one by one:

-- 000042_users_email_key.up.sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_key
  ON users (email);

-- 000042_users_email_key.down.sql
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS users_email_key;

If a run fails anyway, the guide says the database is marked dirty and you must check whether the migration partly applied before migrate force VERSION. For this migration, "partly applied" means an invalid index: drop it first.

Prisma. There is no per-migration opt-out. The closest open issue, #9154 ("Run a migration by hand and update the migration table manually"), has users asking for CONCURRENTLY support, and no fix has shipped. One user in the discussion linked above reports it works when each CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY sits alone in its own migration. The other route: prisma migrate dev --create-only, run the statement by hand, then prisma migrate resolve --applied <migration_name>. Verify either route on your Prisma version before you rely on it.

Whichever tool you use, paste rules like these into the file your coding agent reads:

- One CONCURRENTLY statement per migration file.
- Turn the tool's transaction wrapper off for that file.
- After a failed run, query pg_index for invalid indexes.
- Drop leftovers with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then retry.
- Never answer "already exists" with IF NOT EXISTS.
- End every deploy with the invalid-index check.

If this was useful

Index builds, migration tooling and the locks behind them are the part of Postgres that bites hardest once a table is big and live. The Database Playbook covers how to choose a store and how to change its schema without taking writes down, which is the job an agent-written migration has to get right.

title: Zod vs Valibot vs ArkType for MCP Tool Schemas
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

When I built the NestJS MCP server earlier this week, I used Zod for the tool schemas without thinking about it, because every SDK example does. Then I noticed the v2 TypeScript SDK types inputSchema as "any Standard Schema that can also emit JSON Schema", and the docstring names Zod 4, Valibot and ArkType. So today I wrote the same tool schema in all three, registered them on one MCP server, and measured what actually changes.

Short version: all three work. The differences that mattered were in the JSON Schema the model sees, how each one treats a datetime with a +05:00 offset, cold start, bundle size, and one ArkType setting that made the same schema about 18x slower.

What I ran

Everything is on one shared 8 vCPU Xeon VM with 16 GB, on November 7, 2026:

  • Node.js 24.22.1
  • zod 4.6.7, valibot 1.5.0 with @valibot/to-json-schema 1.8.0, arktype 2.2.9
  • @modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.4.0, connected with InMemoryTransport
  • tinybench 6.2.3 for the parse numbers, esbuild 0.28.2 for bundle sizes

Load average sat around 0.7 to 1.7 during the runs. It's a shared box, so treat the numbers as relative, not absolute.

One tool, three schemas

The tool is a create_task with a title, optional body, a priority enum with a default, a tag list with a default, an optional due date and an optional assignee email. That's roughly what my real tools look like: a few strings with limits, an enum, an array, and two formats.

import * as z from "zod";

export const zodTask = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1).max(120),
  body: z.string().max(5000).optional(),
  priority: z.enum(["low", "normal", "high"]).default("normal"),
  tags: z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(10).default([]),
  dueAt: z.iso.datetime().optional(),
  assigneeEmail: z.email().optional(),
});

import * as v from "valibot";
import { toStandardJsonSchema } from "@valibot/to-json-schema";

const valibotTaskRaw = v.object({
  title: v.pipe(v.string(), v.minLength(1), v.maxLength(120)),
  body: v.optional(v.pipe(v.string(), v.maxLength(5000))),
  priority: v.optional(v.picklist(["low", "normal", "high"]), "normal"),
  tags: v.optional(v.pipe(v.array(v.pipe(v.string(), v.maxLength(30))), v.maxLength(10)), []),
  dueAt: v.optional(v.pipe(v.string(), v.isoTimestamp())),
  assigneeEmail: v.optional(v.pipe(v.string(), v.email())),
});

// Plain Valibot schemas don't carry ~standard.jsonSchema, so wrap them.
export const valibotTask = toStandardJsonSchema(valibotTaskRaw);

import { type } from "arktype";

export const arkTask = type({
  title: "1 <= string <= 120",
  "body?": "string <= 5000",
  priority: type("'low' | 'normal' | 'high'").default("normal"),
  tags: type("(string <= 30)[] <= 10").default(() => []),
  "dueAt?": "string.date.iso",
  "assigneeEmail?": "string.email",
});

Registering them is the same call for all three:

import { McpServer, InMemoryTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server";
import { Client } from "@modelcontextprotocol/client";

const server = new McpServer({ name: "tasks", version: "1.0.0" });
for (const [name, schema] of [["zod", zodTask], ["valibot", valibotTask], ["arktype", arkTask]] as const) {
  server.registerTool(
    `create_task_${name}`,
    { description: `Create a task (${name})`, inputSchema: schema },
    async (args) => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(args) }] }),
  );
}

const [clientSide, serverSide] = InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair();
await server.connect(serverSide);
const client = new Client({ name: "test", version: "1.0.0" });
await client.connect(clientSide);
console.log((await client.listTools()).tools);

The one Valibot gotcha: if you pass valibotTaskRaw directly, registerTool accepts it without complaint. The error only shows up later, when a client calls tools/list:

Schema library "valibot" does not implement StandardJSONSchemaV1 (`~standard.jsonSchema`). Upgrade to a version that does, or wrap your JSON Schema with fromJsonSchema().

So a server that boots fine can still be broken for every client. The fix is the toStandardJsonSchema() wrap above. Zod 4.2+ and ArkType 2.2 have ~standard.jsonSchema built in. I'd add a test that calls listTools() once, so this fails in CI instead of in front of a user.

What the model sees in tools/list

This is the part I care about most for MCP, because the JSON Schema is what the LLM reads when it decides how to call your tool. The SDK asks every library for draft 2020-12 and stamps type: "object" on the root.

Same fields, three different outputs:

Field Zod 4.6.7 Valibot 1.5.0 ArkType 2.2.9
priority enum + type: "string" + default: "normal" enum + type: "string" + default: "normal" enum only, sorted alphabetically, no default
tags maxItems, items, default: [] maxItems, items, default: [] maxItems, items, no default
dueAt format: "date-time" + a long regex pattern format: "date-time" ISO 8601 regex pattern, no format
assigneeEmail format: "email" + regex format: "email" format: "email" + regex

Valibot gave the cleanest schema. Zod's is correct but the datetime regex is about 400 characters of noise in every tools/list response. ArkType dropping the defaults surprised me. The model has no way to know priority falls back to "normal", so it'll either guess or always send it. If your tool descriptions rely on defaults, put them in .describe() text as well.

Validation errors the model gets back

When a call fails validation, the SDK returns isError: true with the issues joined into one string. I sent title: "", priority: "urgent", 11 tags and assigneeEmail: "nope":

zod:     title: Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters, priority: Invalid option: expected one of "low"|"normal"|"high", tags: Too big: expected array to have <=10 items, assigneeEmail: Invalid email address
valibot: title: Invalid length: Expected >=1 but received 0, priority: Invalid type: Expected ("low" | "normal" | "high") but received "urgent", tags: Invalid length: Expected <=10 but received 11, assigneeEmail: Invalid email: Received "nope"
arktype: title: title must be non-empty, tags: tags must be at most length 10 (was 11), priority: priority must be "high", "low" or "normal" (was "urgent"), assigneeEmail: assigneeEmail must be an email address (was "nope")

All three are good enough for a model to fix its own call. ArkType's read most like English. Valibot and ArkType echo the bad value back, which helps when the model sent something weird.

The datetime trap

I'm in Pakistan (UTC+5), so the first thing I tried was local time with an offset, which is what I'd expect an assistant to send for someone here. Five strings in total:

Input Zod z.iso.datetime() Valibot isoTimestamp() ArkType string.date.iso
2026-11-07T11:00:00Z pass pass pass
2026-11-07T11:00:00+05:00 fail pass pass
2026-11-07 fail fail pass
2026-11-07T11:00Z fail fail pass
next friday fail fail fail

Zod's datetime only accepts Z unless you opt in. I'd have shipped that bug without this test:

dueAt: z.iso.datetime({ offset: true }).optional(),

ArkType goes the other way. string.date.iso is any ISO 8601 date, so a bare date passes. If the tool needs a full timestamp, that's the wrong keyword and you need your own pattern.

Parse speed, and the ArkType clone setting

First run, the full task schema with a valid input, then an invalid one, calling each library's normal parse (safeParse, v.safeParse, arkTask(x)):

valid input, mean invalid input, mean
Zod 679 ns 1,612 ns
Valibot 710 ns 1,149 ns
ArkType 4,914 ns 11,634 ns

That's the opposite of ArkType's reputation, so I split the schema apart. With no defaults and no formats, ArkType was the fastest by far: 71 ns against Zod's 295 ns and Valibot's 453 ns. Adding the email check took it to 123 ns. Adding .default() on any single field took it to about 4,900 ns.

The cause is cloning. When a schema has morphs (and defaults count), ArkType clones the input before applying them so your original object isn't mutated. You can turn that off:

// arktype.config.ts, imported before anything that imports "arktype"
import { configure } from "arktype/config";
configure({ clone: false });

With clone: false the default-only schema ran at 55 ns, and the full task schema at 270 ns, which includes about 47 ns for the { ...good } spread I added so each call got a fresh object. The trade-off is real: with cloning off, ArkType writes priority: "normal" into the object you passed in. I checked, and the returned value is the same object as the input. For MCP tool args I'm fine with that, since the args object comes straight from the parsed request. I ran the ArkType tool through the MCP client again with clone: false and the handler still got {"title":"x","tags":[],"priority":"normal"}. For shared config objects I'd leave cloning on.

To be fair, even 5 µs per tool call doesn't matter next to an LLM round trip. I only went looking because the number looked wrong.

Cold start and bundle size

Cold start matters more to me than parse speed, because my MCP servers on Vercel are stateless and build a fresh server per request. I timed import plus first parse in a fresh Node process, 21 runs each, median:

import + first parse
Valibot 5.8 ms
Zod 43.7 ms
ArkType 159.6 ms

Bundle size, esbuild --bundle --minify --format=esm --platform=browser, entry imports one schema and calls parse once:

minified gzip
Valibot 5.3 KB 2.0 KB
Valibot + @valibot/to-json-schema 19.2 KB 5.3 KB
Zod Mini (zod/mini) 20.9 KB 7.1 KB
Zod 85.4 KB 25.1 KB
ArkType 156.4 KB 47.6 KB

Zod and ArkType include JSON Schema output already, so adding the conversion call barely changed their size. Valibot needs the extra package, and it's still the smallest. On a server none of these sizes matter much, but the cold start difference follows the same order.

What I'm doing in my own MCP servers

I'm keeping Zod in the NestJS server. It's what the MCP and AI SDK examples use, its JSON Schema output was accurate here, and I already know its quirks. Any datetime field I add there gets { offset: true } from now on.

For the next serverless MCP endpoint I build, I'll try Valibot. It had the cleanest tools/list output and the fastest cold start, and the only extra step is one toStandardJsonSchema() wrap.

ArkType I'd pick for hot validation paths outside MCP, where the defaults-clone cost is easy to turn off and I don't care what JSON Schema it emits. For MCP tools specifically, the missing defaults in tools/list put me off.

I only tested one schema shape on one VM. If your schemas are mostly nested unions or recursive types, the order could change, and I'd like to hear what you see. The scripts are small enough to rerun in a few minutes. If you're testing your own server end to end, my notes on testing an MCP server and MCP security cover the rest of what I check before shipping.

FAQ

Can I use Valibot or ArkType instead of Zod for MCP tool schemas?

Yes. The MCP TypeScript SDK v2 (I tested @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.4.0) accepts any Standard Schema that also implements ~standard.jsonSchema. Zod 4.2+ and ArkType 2.2 do this out of the box. Valibot needs toStandardJsonSchema() from @valibot/to-json-schema.

Why does my Valibot MCP tool fail at tools/list?

A plain Valibot schema has no ~standard.jsonSchema, so the SDK can't turn it into JSON Schema. registerTool accepts it, but tools/list throws 'Schema library "valibot" does not implement StandardJSONSchemaV1'. Wrap the schema with toStandardJsonSchema().

Why is ArkType slower than Zod in my benchmark?

In my test ArkType was the fastest on a schema without defaults (71 ns vs Zod 295 ns), but any .default() made it clone the input first, which pushed a parse to about 4.9 microseconds. configure({ clone: false }) from arktype/config brought the full schema to 270 ns, at the cost of mutating the input object.

Does Zod accept ISO datetimes with a timezone offset?

Not by default. In Zod 4.6.7, z.iso.datetime() accepted 2026-11-07T11:00:00Z but rejected 2026-11-07T11:00:00+05:00. Use z.iso.datetime({ offset: true }) if clients or LLMs may send local times.

Which validation library has the smallest bundle?

Valibot. In my esbuild test the task schema bundled to 2.0 KB gzip with Valibot (5.3 KB with JSON Schema conversion), 7.1 KB with zod/mini, 25.1 KB with Zod and 47.6 KB with ArkType.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Aspose.PDF 26.10 HTML to PDF: Blank Charts and Small Fonts
description:
Aspose.PDF for Java turns HTML into a PDF through HtmlLoadOptions, and version 26.10 came out on 31 October 2026. Before real templates go through it, a few behaviors are worth checking, from how it treats page scripts and canvas charts to what evaluation mode does and which advisory records carry the product's name. Each section below reports what a run on Java 17 against 26.10, or a query to the advisory databases, produced.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Page Scripts Do Not Run, So Canvas Charts Come Out Blank

CSS grid columns lay out correctly in 26.10, where 26.9 stacked them in one column, but scripts moved the opposite way. Text set with textContent and list items added with createElement each altered the page in separate 26.9 probes and did nothing in 26.10. No license was loaded for these probes, which leaves the licensed behavior untested. This bar chart shows what that means for a canvas.

import com.aspose.pdf.Document;
import com.aspose.pdf.HtmlLoadOptions;

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class CanvasChartCheck {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // A bar chart drawn on a canvas, with a caption the same script fills in afterwards.
        String html = "<html><body style='font-family:Arial'><h1>Monthly orders</h1>"
                + "<canvas id='bars' width='320' height='140'></canvas><p id='caption'>Chart: not drawn</p>"
                + "<script>var ctx = document.getElementById('bars').getContext('2d');"
                + "[40, 90, 65].forEach(function (v, i) { ctx.fillStyle = '#1f3c78'; ctx.fillRect(20 + i * 90, 140 - v, 60, v); });"
                + "document.getElementById('caption').textContent = 'Chart: drawn';</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        try (Document document = new Document(
                new ByteArrayInputStream(html.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)), new HtmlLoadOptions())) {
            document.save("canvas-chart.pdf");
        }
    }
}

The page kept an empty space where the 320 by 140 canvas should be, with no bars in it, and the caption still read Chart: not drawn. The canvas calls are not the cause, because a probe with one textContent line and no canvas also left its paragraph as written. HtmlLoadOptions has no script setting, Aspose's HTML conversion guide lists none, and the 26.10 release notes, with 11 bug fixes and no added APIs, never mention scripts. Reports that embed JavaScript charts drawn on canvas lose them on this route, along with anything else a script fills in.

Fixed-Width Tables Widen the Page or Shrink the Text

HtmlPageLayoutOption.ScaleToPageWidth is documented as the option that scales wide content to the page instead of clipping it. This check applies it to an eight-column table fixed at 1200px.

import com.aspose.pdf.Document;
import com.aspose.pdf.HtmlLoadOptions;
import com.aspose.pdf.HtmlPageLayoutOption;

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class WideTableCheck {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Eight fixed 150px columns make a 1200px table, about one and a half times the width of A4.
        StringBuilder row = new StringBuilder("<tr>");
        for (int m = 1; m <= 8; m++) {
            row.append("<td style='width:150px;border:1px solid #999'>Month ").append(m).append("</td>");
        }
        String html = "<html><body style='font-family:Arial'><h1>Usage by month</h1>"
                + "<table style='border-collapse:collapse;width:1200px'>" + row + "</tr></table></body></html>";

        // The documented option for wide content, applied before the import.
        HtmlLoadOptions options = new HtmlLoadOptions();
        options.setPageLayoutOption(HtmlPageLayoutOption.ScaleToPageWidth);

        try (Document document = new Document(
                new ByteArrayInputStream(html.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)), options)) {
            System.out.println("Pages: " + document.getPages().size());
            document.save("wide-table.pdf");
        }
    }
}

It printed Pages: 1, and that one page was 595 by 842 points, with Month 8 ending at x = 474 and the table's right border at x = 505. The table was scaled down as documented, which 26.9 did not do, and the option applied to the whole page. Cell text, 12 pt by default, came out at 5.5 pt, and the default 24 pt heading at 11 pt. Without the option the text stayed at 12 pt and the page grew to 1,086 points to hold the table. A fixed-width block followed the same pattern, widening the page to 1,236 points by default and dropping to 4.7 pt text with the option.

Both cases cleared once the template stopped fixing pixel widths. Setting the table to width:100% with table-layout:fixed, with no pixel widths left on its cells, kept the page at 595 points and the text at 12 pt, and max-width:100% held the block inside the margins. Holding a template to a standard paper size took that edit in these runs.

Font Data, Installation and Evaluation Mode

A one-page account statement saved with default settings measured 211,791 bytes, and the same statement with setEmbedFonts(false) on the load options measured 34,101 bytes. isEmbedFonts() returns true on a new HtmlLoadOptions, and in the larger file the two embedded Arial font programs account for 177,231 bytes, while the statement's text uses only 39 distinct characters. Both files are evaluation output, and each also holds the embedded font behind the evaluation notice.

Turning embedding off is the library's own switch, and it leaves the fonts to the machine that opens the file. PDF/A requires embedded fonts, and the PDF/A conversion log Aspose writes lists every unembedded one as an error, so archived output has to keep its fonts. For services that store or mail statements in volume, every file carries that font data.

The library is not on Maven Central, where com.aspose:aspose-pdf returns 404. It comes from Aspose's own repository, which every build and any internal proxy has to list next to the Maven dependency.

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>aspose</id>
        <url>https://releases.aspose.com/java/repo/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.aspose</groupId>
        <artifactId>aspose-pdf</artifactId>
        <version>26.10</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Version 26.10 ships as one JAR whose POM lists no dependencies, and Aspose's install docs set JDK 1.8 as the floor. Aspose.PDF for Java is commercial, and a .lic file loaded with com.aspose.pdf.License lifts evaluation mode. Until then, the licensing documentation says each page carries a watermark and only four elements of any collection are processed, pages and form fields included.

Every PDF from these runs had the evaluation notice across its top edge, and building a document page by page in code threw IndexOutOfRangeException when the fifth page was added, citing the four-element evaluation limit. An HTML import with seven page breaks did produce seven pages. Aspose's 30-day temporary license removes both limits, and it is issued only to business email addresses.

Advisory Records Under the Aspose.PDF Name

Neither OSV nor GHSA held an entry for com.aspose:aspose-pdf on Maven when queried on 4 November 2026. NVD has four records that name Aspose.PDF or the Aspose PDF Exporter plugin, out of 11 for the keyword aspose.

  • CVE-2019-5042, CVSS 3.1 score 8.8 (NIST), CVSS 3.0 score 8.8 (Cisco Talos, the CNA): Aspose.PDF 19.2 for C++, a use-after-free when a crafted PDF's FunctionType 0 elements are parsed
  • CVE-2019-5066, score 9.8 (NIST and Talos): The same C++ release, a use-after-free while decoding LZW-compressed streams
  • CVE-2019-5067, score 9.8 (NIST and Talos): The same C++ release, uninitialized memory access from invalid parent object pointers
  • CVE-2015-20125, CVSS 3.1 score 7.5, CVSS 4.0 score 8.7 (VulnCheck, the CNA): A WordPress plugin called Aspose PDF Exporter, versions before 2.0, a path traversal published on 20 October 2026, with NVD analysis deferred

NVD scopes the three 2019 records to the C++ edition at 19.2 without a fixed release, and none of the four covers the Java library.

Aspose.PDF Behaviors and a Chromium-Based Option

Across these unlicensed checks, Aspose.PDF for Java 26.10 skipped page scripts, left canvas charts blank, widened the page for fixed-width tables or scaled their text to 5.5 pt, embedded about 177 KB of font data in a one-page file, capped code-built documents at four pages in evaluation mode and installed from a repository outside Maven Central.

For HTML that depends on page scripts or canvas charts, IronPDF for Java is another commercial option, since it renders HTML through Chromium. On 2026.11.3, a page with the canvas markup above plus a grid section drew the bars and changed the caption to Chart: drawn. Scripts run by default, and setEnableJavaScript on ChromePdfRenderOptions is the switch. Fixed-width content still has to change in the template there as well, because with UseFitToPageRendering(1400) the wide banner in that run printed at 5.2 pt. It installs from Maven Central as com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, where 2026.11.3 came out on 3 November 2026 as the 23rd monthly-numbered release since 2025.1.1.

To run your own scripted and chart templates through it, IronPDF has a free trial with a 30-day key.

Aspose.PDF is a trademark of its respective owner, we have no affiliation with Aspose, and the versions, advisory records and run results above come from Aspose's public documentation, NVD, OSV, the GitHub Advisory Database and our own test runs in November 2026.

Drafted with AI. Code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against com.aspose:aspose-pdf 26.10 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 on 4 November 2026.

title: Muse Image now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Image from Meta Superintelligence Labs is now available on AI Gateway. It is their first image model and a separate family from Muse Spark, returning images rather than text. Send a prompt and get an image back, or send an image with an instruction and get it changed. One model does both, so you don't switch models to move from generating to editing.

To use Muse Image, set model to meta/muse-image-1.0 and call generateImage from the AI SDK:

To steer the result toward art you already have, pass reference images in prompt.images alongside the text, and the model blends them into what it draws.

Editing

Pass the image you want changed in prompt.images with an instruction, and the model changes what you asked for and leaves the rest:

title: GLM 5.3 Flash now available on AI Gateway
description:
GLM 5.3 Flash from Z.ai is now available on AI Gateway as zai/glm-5.3-flash.

GLM 5.3 Flash is a multimodal coding model with a 1M-token context window. It accepts both text and image inputs and supports function calling, structured output, and streaming.

To include images, pass them with text in a message. A request can include multiple images using URLs, Base64 data URLs, or binary data:

title: Vitest Explained: Tests That Finish Before You Blink
description:
You change one line in the checkout code, a discount that should only apply above fifty dollars, and now you need to know whether anything else broke. The honest answer is that you do not know, and guessing costs more than checking. Running the shop by hand means adding items to the cart, applying the code, and doing the maths yourself, every single time you change anything. A test runner takes that job over. Vitest watches your files, reruns the checks the moment you save, and tells you in under a second whether the totals still add up. This post sets it up on a small shop cart, breaks one test on purpose, and fixes it.

What I would check before using it

My judgement is that Vitest is the right default when the project already runs on Vite, and a good choice for most new JavaScript and TypeScript projects besides. If your front end builds with Vite, Vitest reuses the same config, the same plugins, and the same module handling, so setup is quick. Its test API will also feel familiar if you have used Jest: describe, test, and expect work the way you would guess, so the team learns the runner, not a new dialect. The watch mode is the part that changes daily work. It reruns only the tests touched by your last save, so the feedback arrives while the change is still fresh in your head, instead of at the end of a long run.

Before adopting it, I would check three things. First, the Node version. Vitest 5 needs Node 22.12 or newer, or Node 24, so an older Node on a shared server or a team laptop will refuse to install it, and that is a real blocker, not a warning. Second, whether the project is still CommonJS. Vitest is built for ESM, and a codebase full of require calls and __dirname tricks will fight it. Third, what the existing tests already use. A large Jest suite with heavy custom mocks and module name mapping is not worth migrating for speed alone; the migration cost will eat the benefit for months.

The verdict, in short: choose Vitest for Vite projects and new ESM codebases, where it is fast to set up and fast to run. That recommendation flips if the project runs on old Node, leans on CommonJS, or already has a big Jest suite that works. In those cases, keep what works and revisit the question when the project moves to ESM.

A worked example that is not a toy

The shop in this example sells stationery. Three order rows are enough to show the problem: a notebook at 19.99, two pen sets at 4.99 each, and sticky notes at 7.50. The subtotal is 37.47, and with 17 percent tax the total should be 43.84. Two functions do the work, one that adds up price times quantity and one that adds tax, and the test file checks both numbers.

// cart.js
export const ORDER_ITEMS = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 19.99, qty: 1 },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 4.99, qty: 2 },
  { name: "Sticky notes", price: 7.5, qty: 1 },
];

export function cartTotal(items) {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0);
}

export function totalWithTax(items, rate) {
  return cartTotal(items) * (1 + rate);
}

// cart.test.js
import { describe, expect, test } from "vitest";
import { ORDER_ITEMS, cartTotal, totalWithTax } from "./cart.js";

describe("cart totals", () => {
  test("adds up the three order rows", () => {
    expect(cartTotal(ORDER_ITEMS)).toBe(37.47);
  });

  test("adds 17 percent tax to the total", () => {
    expect(totalWithTax(ORDER_ITEMS, 0.17)).toBe(43.84);
  });
});

The project was set up with npm install --save-dev vitest, and the tests were run with npx vitest run. The subtotal test passed, and the tax test failed:

AssertionError: expected 43.83989999999999 to be 43.84 // Object.is equality

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 1 passed (2)
   Start at  04:03:07
   Duration  307ms (transform 51%, import 23%, tests 18%, worker 8%)

The problem is floating point arithmetic, not Vitest. In binary, 37.47 times 1.17 is not exactly 43.84, it is 43.83989999999999, and toBe checks exact equality, so the test fails even though the shop maths is right. Money should never be compared exactly in floating point. The fix belongs in the function, not in the test: round the result to cents before returning it, so the shop always charges a whole number of cents.

export function totalWithTax(items, rate) {
  const total = cartTotal(items) * (1 + rate);
  return Math.round(total * 100) / 100;
}

Running the tests again gave a clean pass, and the whole run took 256 milliseconds:

 RUN  v5.1.0 /home/hatch/workspace/.toolchains/verify/vitest-demo

 ✓ cart.test.js (2 tests) 5ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  04:03:18
   Duration  256ms (transform 52%, import 28%, worker 11%, tests 9%)

That timing is the point of the tool. The feedback arrives before you have time to switch to another tab, which is what makes running the tests after every save feel cheap instead of dutiful. The same failure would have been caught just as well by a slower runner, but a slow runner gets run less often, and a test suite that is run less often catches the bug later, when the cause is harder to find.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

1. Comparing money with toBe. Floating point totals almost never land exactly, so expect(totalWithTax(items, 0.17)).toBe(43.84) fails with AssertionError: expected 43.83989999999999 to be 43.84. The fix is to round money to cents in the code, as the worked example does, or use toBeCloseTo(43.84).

2. Forgetting to await a promise in a test. A test that calls fetchOrderTotal(items, 0.17).then((total) => expect(total).toBe(999.99)) without awaiting or returning the promise passes, even though the expected value is plainly wrong. Vitest finishes the test before the promise resolves, so the check inside never runs. The fix is to mark the test async and await the call, or return the promise.

3. Naming the test file cart.tests.js. Vitest only picks up files ending in .test.js or .spec.js, so the file is ignored and the run ends with No test files found, exiting with code 1. The fix is to rename it to cart.test.js.

4. Importing from the wrong path. A test that imports from ./missing-module.js fails before any test runs, with Error: Cannot find module './missing-module.js'. The fix is to check the relative path from the test file, not from the project root, and to remember that Vitest needs the file extension in ESM imports.

Where this leaves you

Vitest earns its place the first time a save triggers a run that finishes before you reach for the mouse. It is a fast runner with a familiar API, and its real value is that testing becomes cheap enough to do after every change. The habits that matter are small: round money before comparing it, await every promise, and name test files so the runner finds them. The next step is to add one test file to a project you already work on, run npx vitest, and change one line of the code under test. When the failing test names the line you just touched, the loop will make sense.

Further reading

  • Vitest, Getting Started
  • Vitest, Why Vitest
  • Vitest API, expect
