title: How to Manage Kubernetes Across Multiple Clouds Without Vendor Lock-In: A Layer-by-Layer Guide
description:
Kubernetes itself is portable, so lock-in comes from the services around it: cloud-specific networking, load balancers, storage, identity, secrets, observability, managed databases, and management consoles. Keep each layer portable with Git and infrastructure as code, the same open-source components on every cloud, Gateway API, external secrets, OpenTelemetry, and databases you can run anywhere, and manage the fleet with tools that work on every cloud. Control Plane runs the same workload definition across AWS, GCP, Azure, and clusters you already run, with networking, identity, and observability built in.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Where lock-in hides: cloud-specific CNIs, load balancer controllers, IAM bindings, secret managers, monitoring agents, managed databases, and cloud consoles.
  • The portable stack: Terraform or OpenTofu for provisioning, Argo CD or Flux for GitOps, Cilium where you can run it, Gateway API for ingress, Rook-Ceph, Longhorn, or application-layer replication for data, External Secrets Operator or HashiCorp Vault for secrets, workload identity federation for cloud access, OpenTelemetry and Prometheus for observability, and PostgreSQL or MySQL you can run anywhere.
  • The cost of portability: more clusters and components to operate, cross-cloud egress, and sometimes lowest-common-denominator features. A managed service is worth its lock-in when you document an exit plan.
  • How Control Plane fits: Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds where each workload runs, deploys one workload definition active-active across AWS, GCP, Azure, your own Kubernetes clusters, and on-premises servers, with networking, identity, and observability built in.

Which parts of Kubernetes cause cloud lock-in?

Each layer has a cloud-specific default, a portable alternative, and a trade-off.

Layer Cloud-specific default Portable option Trade-off
Provisioning Cloud console, CloudFormation, ARM or Bicep templates Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, or Crossplane Extra tooling to maintain; new cloud features can arrive later
Deployment AWS CodePipeline, Azure Pipelines, Cloud Build Argo CD or Flux (GitOps) You operate the GitOps controller
Networking (CNI) AWS VPC CNI, Azure CNI, GKE Dataplane V2 Cilium where supported, with rules written as standard NetworkPolicy GKE Dataplane V2 and Azure CNI Powered by Cilium are already Cilium-based; on EKS, replacing the VPC CNI changes pod IP addressing and some AWS integrations
Ingress and load balancing AWS Load Balancer Controller, GKE Ingress, Application Gateway Ingress Controller Gateway API implementations such as Envoy Gateway, Cilium, Istio, or NGINX Gateway Fabric The Gateway still provisions a cloud load balancer, and Gateway classes and annotations differ per provider
Service-to-service security Cloud-specific options or none Istio, Linkerd, or Cilium Cluster Mesh Operational overhead of a mesh, plus proxy latency and resource use
Storage and data Provider block storage classes (EBS, Persistent Disk, Azure Disk) Rook-Ceph or Longhorn, or application-layer replication, with StorageClass names set per overlay Different performance and durability; self-managed storage to operate
Identity IAM roles for service accounts, Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Microsoft Entra Workload ID One pattern on every cloud: Kubernetes service account tokens federated to each provider, with bindings kept in per-cloud overlays A separate binding per provider
Secrets AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault External Secrets Operator or HashiCorp Vault You run and secure the secrets layer
Observability CloudWatch, Cloud Monitoring, Azure Monitor Prometheus, Grafana, and OpenTelemetry Self-managed collection and storage
Databases Amazon Aurora, Spanner, Azure Cosmos DB PostgreSQL or MySQL run portably, or a managed service with a documented migration path You handle backups, replication, and upgrades
Cluster management EKS, GKE, and AKS consoles Rancher, Karmada, or Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management Another management plane to operate and secure

Each cloud-specific default lowers setup effort and raises switching cost. Decide and document where you accept lock-in, and keep an exit plan for each case.

How do I manage Kubernetes across multiple clouds without vendor lock-in?

Manage every cluster from Git and infrastructure as code, run the same open-source component at each layer on every cloud, route traffic globally, and test moves to a second cloud on a schedule. The ten steps below build that setup.

  1. Git and a GitOps controller for every cluster. Keep manifests, Helm charts, and Kustomize overlays in Git, with one base per application and an overlay per cloud for StorageClass names, load balancer annotations, and identity bindings. Run Argo CD or Flux so each cluster reconciles from Git. See Argo CD vs Flux.
  2. Infrastructure as code for clusters and cloud resources. Define clusters, networks, IAM roles, and DNS zones in Terraform, OpenTofu, or Pulumi, with shared modules and provider-specific parameters. Crossplane manages cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources.
  3. The same networking on every cluster where you can. Run Cilium where the provider allows it: GKE Dataplane V2 and Azure CNI Powered by Cilium are Cilium-based, and EKS supports Cilium in chaining or replacement mode. Write network rules as standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy so they apply whichever CNI enforces them. For ingress, adopt Gateway API so routing definitions are the same on every cloud; the community ingress-nginx project was retired in March 2026.
  4. Secrets from one source. Run External Secrets Operator on every cluster against one backend, such as HashiCorp Vault, so every workload fetches secrets the same way.
  5. Workload identity per cloud. Configure workload identity federation so pods get cloud credentials without long-lived keys. Each cloud wires it differently: IRSA uses a service account annotation, EKS Pod Identity uses an association in the EKS API, Workload Identity Federation for GKE can grant IAM roles directly to the Kubernetes service account as a principal, with no annotation, and Microsoft Entra Workload ID on AKS uses a service account annotation plus a pod label, backed by a federated identity credential in Entra ID. Keep these bindings in per-cloud overlays; application code that uses the default cloud SDK credential chain does not change.
  6. One observability backend. Instrument workloads with OpenTelemetry and run Collectors on each cluster that ship metrics, logs, and traces to one backend, with Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and dashboards. Telemetry from every cloud lands in one place, with no dependency on CloudWatch, Cloud Monitoring, or Azure Monitor.
  7. A global traffic layer. Use external-dns with DNS-based global load balancing, or another global traffic manager, to route users to the nearest healthy cluster, with health checks per cluster and an active-active or active-passive policy per application.
  8. A data strategy per service. Stateless services need no cross-cloud data plan beyond the stores they call. For stateful services, run a portable database on Kubernetes with application-layer replication, use a managed database on each cloud with asynchronous replication between them, or keep the service on one cloud and document the lock-in. Weigh cross-cloud transfer cost and latency.
  9. Policy as code across clusters. Run OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno on every cluster with a shared policy library in Git, enforcing Pod Security Standards, resource limits, image provenance, and network policy.
  10. Regular portability drills. Deploy a service to the second cloud on a schedule and verify it works, starting with non-critical workloads. Drills expose hidden dependencies on cloud-specific features.

What tools help with cloud portability and avoiding vendor lock-in?

The main open-source tools are Terraform or OpenTofu, Argo CD or Flux, Cilium, Gateway API, External Secrets Operator or Vault, OpenTelemetry and Prometheus, Velero, and a fleet manager such as Rancher.

Category Tools What it makes portable
Infrastructure as code Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Crossplane Cluster provisioning and cloud resource definitions
GitOps Argo CD, Flux Application deployment, configuration, and drift correction
Networking and mesh Cilium (including Cluster Mesh), Calico, Istio, Linkerd Network policy, service-to-service encryption, cross-cluster connectivity
Ingress Gateway API implementations (Envoy Gateway, Cilium, Istio, NGINX Gateway Fabric) Routing definitions
Global traffic external-dns with DNS-based global load balancing Routing users between clusters on different clouds
Secrets External Secrets Operator, HashiCorp Vault Secret storage and delivery
Backup and migration Velero Moving workloads and volumes between clusters
Observability and cost OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, OpenCost Metrics, logs, traces, and Kubernetes cost allocation
Fleet and multi-cluster management Rancher, Karmada, Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management Cluster access, inventory, policy, and multi-cluster scheduling
Platforms that run workloads across clouds Control Plane Workload deployment, global routing, identity, and observability across AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes clusters you already run, and on-premises servers from one definition

GKE fleet management can also manage clusters on other clouds, but it is tied to Google Cloud. For a broader comparison, see the best Kubernetes management platforms.

Is multi-cloud a real solution to vendor lock-in?

Partly. Running on two or more clouds reduces dependence on one provider’s availability and pricing, but it removes lock-in only when each layer uses portable components. Workloads that depend on Aurora on AWS and Spanner on GCP are locked in to both providers.

Multi-cloud also adds operational cost: more credentials, networking models, billing systems, and provider quirks. Teams that adopt it without the portable stack often carry the operating complexity of two clouds and the lock-in of each.

The practical approach is selective portability. Run each workload where it fits best, keep its layers portable so it can move, and accept managed-service lock-in only with a documented exit plan. See managed services vs portability and how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

What does portability cost?

Budget for these costs when you commit to a portable stack on every cloud.

More clusters to upgrade. Each Kubernetes upgrade is tested and rolled out to every cluster, and CNI, ingress, mesh, and policy components each have their own upgrade cycle. The work grows with the number of clusters.

More components to operate. Running Cilium, a mesh, Vault, External Secrets Operator, OpenTelemetry Collectors, Prometheus, Grafana, and a policy engine on every cluster means monitoring, capacity planning, and incident response for each.

Cross-cloud egress. Providers bill data leaving their network, so cross-cloud database replication, service calls, and log shipping add recurring transfer charges. Keep chatty services and their data in one cloud and track egress spend per service.

Lowest-common-denominator features. Portable alternatives can lack the integration of managed services. A self-managed PostgreSQL cluster needs engineering effort to match a managed database’s automated backups, point-in-time recovery, and read replicas.

When managed services are worth it. A small team may be better served by a managed database despite the dependency. Document the lock-in and the migration path (most managed PostgreSQL and MySQL services support logical or binlog replication to an external target), and revisit the decision as the team grows.

Operating the clusters. The largest recurring labor cost is operating Kubernetes itself on every cloud: upgrades, node pools, autoscaler tuning, and patching. A platform that handles Day 2 operations across clouds removes much of it, which is the approach Control Plane takes.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, and Azure, VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

A workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC from one definition. Locations can be Control Plane-managed regions on AWS, GCP, and Azure, Kubernetes clusters you already run joined through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), or clusters created through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s). On Control Plane-managed locations there is no Kubernetes cluster to operate. MK8s runs worker nodes, load balancers, and storage in your AWS account or GCP project, or on servers you provide (documented providers include Generic, AWS, GCP, Hetzner, and Triton), while Control Plane operates the Kubernetes control plane.

Networking. Control Plane’s built-in global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, and every workload has a deny-by-default internal firewall with mTLS between services. Control Plane runs the service mesh for you, so there is no separate mesh to install or operate.

Identity. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. You connect each cloud account once through an IAM role or service-account grant, and workloads receive short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime, in place of the per-cluster federation setup in step 5.

Day 2 operations. Control Plane handles autoscaling, built-in observability, and security for every workload.

Tooling. The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API, so Control Plane complements the infrastructure as code tools you already run.

Availability, cost, and compliance. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Portability. Workloads on Control Plane stay standard container images, and you can export Control Plane resources to Terraform with the CLI. Your containers, Git repository, and infrastructure as code remain yours, which keeps the exit path short compared with a cloud-specific managed service.

See how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and for teams reconsidering Kubernetes itself, the best Kubernetes alternatives.

FAQ

Short answers for teams planning multi-cloud Kubernetes.

How do I run Kubernetes on EKS, GKE, and AKS with one set of tools?

Provision all three clusters from one Terraform or OpenTofu codebase. Register them with one Argo CD instance or install Flux on each, and keep one base of manifests with a Kustomize overlay per cloud for StorageClass names, load balancer annotations, and identity bindings. Use Gateway API for ingress, External Secrets Operator for secrets, one OpenTelemetry Collector configuration, one Kyverno or Gatekeeper policy library, and Rancher or Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for one access and inventory layer. With Control Plane, existing EKS, GKE, and AKS clusters join one GVC through BYOK, and one workload definition deploys to all three.

Is Kubernetes itself a form of lock-in?

No. Kubernetes is an open-source CNCF project with a consistent API across providers. The lock-in risk comes from the cloud-specific services attached to it.

Can I use managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) and still avoid lock-in?

Yes. The API server, etcd, and scheduler are largely interchangeable across EKS, GKE, and AKS. Keep the add-ons you attach portable, using the layer table above.

How do I move a Kubernetes workload from one cloud to another?

Create the target cluster from your infrastructure as code, point your GitOps controller at it with that cloud’s overlay, and move data with Velero file-system backups or database-native replication; native cloud volume snapshots do not transfer between clouds. Run the workload in both places, shift traffic gradually through the global traffic layer, then retire the old deployment.

Do I need a service mesh for multi-cloud Kubernetes?

Not always. Cilium Cluster Mesh provides cross-cluster connectivity and network policy without a full mesh. If you need mTLS and L7 traffic policy between services, Istio or Linkerd provides both.

Which multi-cloud Kubernetes cost do teams most often underestimate?

Cross-cloud egress. Replication, service calls, and log shipping between clouds add transfer charges, so design data placement to minimize cross-cloud traffic and track egress per service.

Does CSI make storage portable?

No. CSI is the interface that EBS, Persistent Disk, and Azure Disk already use, so data stays on each cloud’s disks. Use portable storage such as Rook-Ceph or Longhorn, or replicate at the application layer, and move data between clouds with Velero or database replication.

Can Control Plane replace my multi-cluster management tooling?

For running workloads, yes. Control Plane deploys, networks, secures, and observes workloads across clouds from one API and console. Control Plane-managed locations and MK8s clusters need no control plane work from your team. Clusters joined through BYOK run Control Plane workloads in the same GVC, and your team keeps operating those clusters.

What is the minimum multi-cloud setup to reduce lock-in risk?

Run primary workloads on one cloud and keep a validated environment on a second cloud where you can deploy the same workloads on demand. Keep manifests in GitOps, keep the second cloud’s infrastructure as code current, and run portability drills on a fixed schedule. Active-active can come later.

To run the same workloads across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own infrastructure without having to operate the clusters yourself, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: AssetHoard (a local first game asset manager) v0.3.1 released!
description:
Every new file type used to mean a new release. Someone asks for HEIC photos or a new engine integration, it goes on the list, and it ships whenever the next build does.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game devs, built in Rust and Tauri. Version 0.3.1 adds plugins, so file types and tool integrations can arrive without waiting for an app update.

Plugins, and the rules they run under

A plugin that reads your asset library is code running next to your files, so the defaults are cautious:

  • Sandboxed. Plugins run in a restricted sandbox rather than with the full access of the app.
  • Permissions are explicit. You approve what each plugin can access before it runs.
  • Failures are contained. A plugin that keeps failing is paused automatically instead of taking the app down with it.

There are two plugins to start with:

  • HEIC/HEIF import for photos straight off a phone or camera.
  • A Godot editor plugin. Search your AssetHoard library and copy assets into your project without leaving Godot.

Here is the Godot plugin in a real workflow, a 48 hour jam built entirely from assets already on the drive:

A public SDK and support for user-made plugins will follow once the internal API has stabilised. Freezing an API before it has been used by real plugins is how you end up supporting the wrong one forever.

Watched folders, round two

0.2.4 rebuilt how watched folders track renames and moves. 0.3.1 deals with what happens when a file really is gone.

  • One missing files screen lists broken watched folders, missing files and missing archives together.
  • Relink a whole folder in one go. Point AssetHoard at the new location and every asset under it reconnects.
  • One undo reverses the batch. A bulk relink is a single entry on the undo stack, not hundreds.

Also in 0.3.1

  • Audio export as WAV, OGG or MP3, including sounds inside zips and Unity packages. MP3 on Linux needs the LAME package.
  • Spine .skel and .atlas files (3.6 to 4.3) import as sprites, and LightWave .lwo files import as 3D models.
  • Filters adapt to the window width, can sit beside the library, and show active filters as removable chips.
  • Bundles can be dragged out to Explorer as folders.
  • Faster text search, quicker launches, faster GameMaker .yymps imports and lighter 3D previews.
  • A new open_in_app tool for the built-in MCP server.

Everything else is in the 0.3.1 release notes, and plugin setup is covered in the plugins docs. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta.

If you have added a plugin system to a desktop app, I would like to hear how you decided when the API was stable enough to open up.

title: Designing Anti-Retaliation Workflows Without Building Employee Surveillance
description:
Anonymous reporting sounds straightforward until you ask what happens after the report.

Most systems focus heavily on intake:

  • do not store IP addresses;
  • avoid unnecessary authentication;
  • separate reports from employee identities;
  • restrict case access;
  • protect communication between the reporter and investigators.

That is important.

But the harder privacy problem may begin after the report is submitted.

Suppose an employee reports misconduct involving their manager.

Two weeks later, they stop being invited to important meetings.

A month later, a critical project is reassigned.

Their next performance review drops sharply.

Soon after, a transfer is proposed.

None of those events proves retaliation.

But ignoring the pattern entirely would also be a design failure.

The interesting engineering question becomes:

How do you detect possible retaliation without turning the reporter into a permanently monitored employee?

The naive solution creates a surveillance system

The most obvious implementation would be to mark the reporter and start tracking everything that happens to them.

Something like:

protected_employee = employee_123

monitor:
- performance reviews
- meetings
- messages
- manager interactions
- project assignments
- transfers
- role changes
- termination requests

From a detection perspective, this gives you maximum visibility.

From a privacy perspective, it is terrible.

You have now created:

  • a persistent link between the report and the employee;
  • a highly sensitive internal label;
  • a larger attack surface;
  • more privileged users who may discover who reported;
  • a new surveillance capability that can outlive the original case.

The system intended to protect the reporter now becomes another system that knows who the reporter is.

That is the opposite of the original privacy goal.

Monitor events, not behavior

A better approach is to model relevant organizational events rather than continuously observing the person.

For example:

Report
 ├─ id
 ├─ status
 ├─ opened_at
 ├─ closed_at
 └─ protection_context_id

Then keep the protected identity separate:

ProtectionContext
 ├─ id
 ├─ protected_subject_reference
 ├─ active_from
 ├─ active_until
 └─ policy

Your HR systems can emit events like:

PerformanceReviewChanged
EmployeeTransferred
RoleChanged
TerminationRequested
ManagerChanged
ResponsibilityRemoved

The protection layer only needs to ask:

Did this event affect a subject currently under protection?

If yes:
    create review

If no:
    ignore

The event is not a conclusion.

It is a trigger for human review.

That distinction is critical.

A risk signal is not a verdict

One of the easiest mistakes to make is confusing correlation with causation.

Imagine this timeline:

March 10
report submitted

March 25
negative performance review

The system should not produce:

retaliation = true

At most, it should produce something like:

review_required = true

The reviewer still needs context:

  • Was the review already in progress before March 10?
  • Were there documented performance issues before the report?
  • Who authored the review?
  • Was that person involved in the original case?
  • Did the evaluation criteria change?
  • Were similar reviews given to comparable employees?

A better internal model is probably a set of signals:

temporal_proximity = true
adverse_event = true
decision_maker_conflict = true
prior_documentation_exists = false

rather than something like:

retaliation_score = 87%

The latter looks precise while hiding how subjective the underlying judgment actually is.

The system should improve reviewability, not automate guilt.

Identity separation becomes harder after the case

Anonymous intake is relatively easy to model.

Post-report protection is harder because, at some point, the system needs to know who should be protected.

A bad implementation might simply add:

reports.reporter_employee_id

Now the reporting database permanently knows who submitted the anonymous report.

That defeats much of the original separation.

A better model might keep two isolated domains.

Reporting database 

reports
- report_id
- content
- status
- investigation_metadata

Protected identity vault 

protection_contexts
- id
- encrypted_subject_reference
- active_until
- policy

The reporting system does not necessarily need the identity.

The HR event processor does not necessarily need the report contents.

Each subsystem only receives the minimum amount of context required for its job.

Conceptually:

Investigation Service
        |
        | protection_context_id
        v
Protection Service
        |
        | opaque subject reference
        v
HR Event Matcher

This does not eliminate risk.

It reduces propagation.

And in privacy-sensitive systems, reducing propagation is often the more realistic goal.

Tenant admins should not automatically see everything

This becomes especially important in B2B SaaS.

A common authorization shortcut is:

tenant_admin = full_access

That is convenient.

It is also dangerous in a whistleblowing system.

Imagine that a department director is a tenant administrator.

Now imagine that the report concerns that director.

If tenant_admin effectively means root access to all cases, identities and protection contexts, your privacy controls disappear exactly when they matter most.

Role-based access control alone is not enough.

You need contextual authorization.

Conceptually:

def can_access_case(user, case):
    if user.id in case.conflicted_users:
        return False

    if user.department_id in case.restricted_departments:
        return False

    return evaluate_case_permissions(user, case)

The important part is not the syntax.

It is the idea that:

who the user is should not be the only input to the authorization decision.

Their relationship to the case matters too.

Sensitive identity access should probably be break-glass

In many situations, nobody should routinely browse protected identities.

If access is necessary, it may deserve a break-glass workflow:

request access
      ↓
provide reason
      ↓
secondary approval
      ↓
temporary access
      ↓
mandatory audit event
      ↓
automatic expiration

The goal is to make exceptional access possible without making it normal.

This is especially relevant when support staff, security teams or internal administrators technically have enough privilege to reach sensitive data.

The database permission should not be the final authorization layer.

Audit logs should include reads, not only writes

A lot of systems only audit mutations:

case_updated
case_closed
comment_added

For highly sensitive reporting systems, reads matter too.

Useful events might include:

protected_identity_viewed
case_evidence_viewed
protected_context_accessed
report_exported

An access record could look like:

{
  "event": "protected_context_accessed",
  "actor_id": "usr_8291",
  "case_id": "case_211",
  "reason": "retaliation_review",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-06T14:32:11Z"
}

But there is an important trap here:

the audit log should not duplicate the sensitive data being protected.

Otherwise the log becomes another identity database.

Auditability is useful only if the audit layer itself follows data-minimization principles.

Protection should expire by design

A protection state should probably not be:

protected = true

forever.

A more useful model is:

protection_active_from
protection_active_until

The organization may choose a window such as 60 or 90 days depending on policy and risk.

That is a governance decision, not a universal legal rule.

From a system-design perspective, expiration matters because it prevents sensitive correlation state from remaining active indefinitely.

Extensions can still exist.

But they should be explicit.

For example:

extend protection
      ↓
reason required
      ↓
approval
      ↓
new expiration

Persistent protection flags are easy to create and easy to forget.

Expiration forces the system to revisit whether the risk context still needs to exist.

Do not copy the whole HR database

There is another architectural temptation here.

If the reporting platform needs to observe organizational events, it may seem convenient to replicate HR data into the reporting system.

Usually that is unnecessary.

You probably do not need:

  • the employee's entire performance history;
  • every manager note;
  • every compensation record;
  • every internal message;
  • every attendance event.

The HR system can emit a minimal event:

{
  "type": "EMPLOYEE_TRANSFER_REQUESTED",
  "subject": "opaque_subject_reference",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-06T14:00:00Z"
}

Then the protection service checks whether that subject has an active protection context.

If not:

discard

If yes:

create_review

This avoids turning the whistleblowing system into a shadow HRIS.

That matters both for privacy and security.

Retaliation should probably be modeled as a separate case

Suppose the original case is:

Case A
type: harassment

Later, the reporter claims retaliation.

The simplest implementation is to append:

comment: "reporter alleges retaliation"

to Case A.

But the two investigations answer different questions.

The original case asks:

Did the reported misconduct happen?

The retaliation case asks:

Did someone take adverse action because the person reported or cooperated?

Those are independent questions.

The original allegation may be unsubstantiated while retaliation still occurred.

So the domain model may be cleaner as:

Case A
type: harassment

Case B
type: suspected_retaliation
related_case_id: A

This gives you separate:

  • timelines;
  • evidence;
  • investigators;
  • conflicts of interest;
  • conclusions;
  • audit trails.

The cases remain linked without becoming indistinguishable.

Insider threat matters more than most systems assume

A whistleblowing product usually thinks about external attackers.

But some of the highest-risk actors are insiders with legitimate access.

For example:

  • tenant administrators;
  • HR administrators;
  • investigators;
  • support engineers;
  • database administrators;
  • internal developers;
  • security personnel.

That means the threat model should include questions like:

  • Who can infer the reporter's identity?
  • Who can access the protected identity vault?
  • Who can export case data?
  • Can support staff impersonate tenant users?
  • Can database operators directly query identity mappings?
  • Does emergency access create alerts?
  • Can a conflicted administrator override restrictions?

A system is not privacy-preserving simply because the public form is anonymous.

The whole access path matters.

The architecture should minimize knowledge

The design principle I keep coming back to is simple:

each component should know as little as possible.

The investigation system may need the report contents.

It may not need the employee identity.

The HR event processor may need to know that an opaque subject has an active protection context.

It does not need to know what the person reported.

The audit system needs to know that sensitive information was accessed.

It does not need to store the sensitive information itself.

The reviewer may need enough context to assess a suspicious employment event.

They do not necessarily need unrestricted access to every case and every identity.

You cannot completely eliminate sensitive relationships from this kind of system.

But you can avoid propagating them everywhere.

The paradox of anti-retaliation systems

The deeper paradox is this:

the more aggressively you try to protect someone from retaliation, the more tempting it becomes to collect information about them.

More events.

More relationships.

More metadata.

More access.

More monitoring.

Every extra piece of data may help detection.

Every extra piece of data also increases the risk of identification, leakage and abuse.

So the best design may not be the one that observes the most.

It may be the one that can detect just enough.

My current mental model is:

monitor events, not behavior

generate signals, not verdicts

separate identity, do not propagate it

limit admins contextually

audit sensitive reads

expire protection state

keep humans in the decision loop

The anonymous reporting form is probably the easy part.

The harder engineering challenge begins after someone clicks Submit.

For context, I’m the CTO and co-founder of Sigilo, where we work on privacy-first reporting and organizational feedback systems. One of the recurring product challenges in this space is translating a governance requirement like “protect the reporter from retaliation” into software without creating a new surveillance layer.

How would you model this? Would you keep a persistent technical link between identity and protection context, or only make that correlation possible through exceptional access?

title: After the AI bubble: a manifesto
description:
Computers should be tools for the people but — hidden in a malaise of fatalism — the AI bubble has made computers tools to push people around. Soon, or in some time, this will change. We have some thoughts to share with you in the meantime.

Preamble

The purpose of computers is human freedom. — Ted Nelson
  1. We are not “anti-AI.” We are against abuse, destruction, and exploitation: of people and our environment, as well as lies and manipulation that provide cover for the above.
  2. We are unsatisfied with the confusing, inaccurate term “artificial intelligence” (AI), but grimly accept it because it is widely-used.
  3. Our demands relate primarily to economic relationships, discourse and information software; we don’t see concerns we omit — such as regarding the environment and material created by AI (“slop”) — as less important, only out of focus; if you are prepared to complete the picture, contact us.
  4. We are enthusiastic about the real potential of AI and large language models (LLMs), but think that their capabilities have been overstated.
  5. We all have a horse in this race: from alternative technologies seeking customers to alternative worldviews seeking adherents.
  6. We think that the overriding character of AI today is that of a speculative bubble: at a scale for which any possible outcome will bring significant hardship — we must avoid a disaster like that which followed similar periods, particularly the 1920s and 30s.
  7. We think we can build a future that protects individual liberty and the general welfare by — among other things — using computers more humanely.
  8. Our manifesto will be stronger with your feedback and comments: please provide them.
  9. And, if you agree, please comment to sign your name.

Argument

1. Economics: an AI bubble

We are in a bubble. Generative AI does not do the things that it’s being sold as doing, and the things it can actually do aren’t the kind of things that create business returns, automate labor, or really do much more than one extension of a cloud software platform. The money isn’t there, the users aren’t there, every company seems to lose money and some companies lose so much money that it’s impossible to tell how they’ll survive. — Ed Zitron
We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future. — Anthropic (October 2026, draft S-1 filing)

The current AI bubble — perhaps best charted by Ed Zitron — is the largest in a series of tech bubbles: dot-com, crypto, with overlapping sub-bubbles like “web3” and “metaverse.” Though Open AI CEO Sam Altman has called the economic conditions around AI a bubble, many disagree, or agree that we are in a bubble but claim that this is not a problem.

Bubbles happen when excitement about a speculative investment (which can be in anything, from shares in public companies to flowers) takes on a life of its own, and investments pile in more due to momentum than the desire to build something useful.

Bubbles are neatly regressive: putting money in the pockets of those who got in early and got out early, fleecing those whose who came late to the party, with onlookers shouldering the economic fallout. Bubbles precede our most cataclysmic economic moments and the succeeding social conflicts, most obviously the roaring 20s — great depression—authoritarianism/WWII cycle.

However, many have argued that the AI bubble is a good thing, because we might get something useful out of it, such as the “dark fiber” laid down during the dot-com bubble.

There is, of course, nothing close to a guarantee that anything of the sort will happen. Datacenters, much in demand today and often cited as a useful asset that could come out of this bubble, are quite unlike fiber (which is essentially incorruptible glass buried beneath the street):

  1. Datacenters are highly specific to AI loads which may go away
  2. And wear out

Mistakes that turn out to be profitable, like dark fiber, aren’t arguments for bubbles; something either has a strong argument for it in the moment or was unjustifiable in the moment, and it paying off was merely good fortune.

Bubbles and crashes are failures of planning and capital allocation. If bubbles were actually desirable, it would be possible to find a bubble proponent who would tolerate one in an economy they control, e.g. their household or within their own company. Rather, bubbles are good only when someone else picks up the tab.

For those who think all this investment is quite sensible, i.e. that we are not in a bubble, one must ask: given that the U.S. economy would likely be in recession without AI, what are we doing this for?

Isn’t the rest of the economy — farming, transportation, healthcare, arts, etc. — the place where the actual purported benefits of AI will reach us? The gains in productivity and innovation promised by AI-proponents must be delivered to us through things. How long, therefore, should we stifle the rest of the economy while we wait to AI to pay off? And what will be left?

Bubbles hurt when they burst, but usually the sooner the burst comes the better, as bigger bubbles hurt more. Finding a way to avoid popping the bubble — such as through state intervention — stands protect those invested, while keeping the capital allocated to the wrong places.

We need to leave behind an economic regime buoyed by a series of fast-growing and capital-intensive fads, and transition to a stabler economy with broader investments and benefits.

2. Messaging: fatalism, hype, and “CEO said”

The greatest myth of technology is the myth of determinism: the belief that technology is determinate, objective, inevitable, that the nature of computers is given. […] The computer world deals with imaginary, made-up stuff that was all made up by somebody. Everything you see was designed and put there by someone. — Ted Nelson
The most important thing about a gadget isn’t what it does; it’s who it does it for and who it does it to. — Cory Doctorow

We have internalized the narrative that the way computers work is preordained, and that it is necessary that computers work the way they do currently. We can thank this narrative for the idea that AI is the next step in computing.

This puts us in a malaise of fatalism, making it easy to believe that we must accept what we are given — including LLMs and AI — or risk being left behind. We — the people — create technology and computers; we could drive it in a different direction if we wish or abolish it altogether. If people are being left behind, other people are leaving them behind, not technology.

It’s easy to see technology as something like the laws of nature — offering us gifts like solar power or antibiotics — but it also shares a great deal with fashion: a succession of trends, driven not just by utility, but significantly by imitation and novelty. Packaged technology — like computers, operating systems, applications — has much much more to do with peers and predecessors in their category and with cultural norms regarding how we work with information than it have to do with logic and physics.

Ignore — as Cory Doctrow advises in The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI — those who say “there is no alternative” (TINA). IBM said there was no alternative to the mainframe, and DEC proved overwise with the minicomputer and later Apple with the microcomputer; Microsoft said there is no alternative to Windows and Linus Torvalds proved otherwise with Linux.

AI fatalism rides along with two other ideas:

  1. AI will save the world (e.g. cure cancer).
  2. AI will destroy the world (e.g. kill us in a “Terminator-style” scenario).

These are really two sides of the same idea: that AI will, sometime in the future, attain awe-inspiring abilities and change the fate or our species. These claims are usually broached in terms familiar to most people but without practical specifics, or are otherwise nonsensical.

This serves to distract people from real questions relevant to AI today — whether and how to implement AI, how to handle datacenters, whom to complain to that you have to talk to a machine to get customer service, how to protect your data, how to respond to slop — and have them focus instead on fantasies.

This distraction gains much ground thanks to “CEO said” journalism, first christened by Chris Kottke, wherein journals will print nonsense if a CEO said it. Journalists have a moral obligation to challenge the facts and perspectives of their subjects, and especially the executives of influential and well-capitalized companies.

We should evaluate AI and any other technology on its merits, without distraction from fatalism, hype and nonsense.

3. Humanity: pretend AI personalities

You’ll have these little “Max Headroom” characters with bow ties, who you have to talk to. […] Having to deal socially with inane objects that pretend to understand you, but don’t, is much worse than a cocktail party. It’s absolutely unnecessary; it’s a council of despair. — Ted Nelson

We anthropomorphize everything, and technology companies are quick to encourage this: from the original Macintosh’s jaunty mouth, to Microsoft’s Clippy.

Large language models are so good at talking that many truly believe them to be conscious or to have personalities. LLMs have neither personhood nor personality: monitoring them to use and respond to first person pronouns is deceptive — more so, say, than Clippy because LLMs are so good at talking.

Names and personal pronouns are for intelligent beings with personalities: having people use them for LLMs puts the user in a posture of equality with the machine, which, given the growing power-imbalance between the supercorporations fielding LLMs and people, puts the machine above the human in the power relationship.

Conversely, we and our corporations and governments find it just as easy to dehumanize people: sometimes through lurid oppression, sometimes merely through bureaucratic drudgery. It is not fair to expect someone hanging onto their dignity by a thread to talk to a machine as though it has a personality (more so to require them to do) in order to proceed with whatever work, government or customer service task is required of them.

The prospectus of the LLM includes a promise to help users manage information: particularly to find the information they need, or to contextualize their work. Such solutions, however, rarely actually organize the underlying information.

While people are making some progress, such as with graph databases and markdown files, AI’s insights are typically not stored (nor is the underlying information modified) as durable links/folders/database rows, to shape information for a future date or for other people. While AI can work between silos (e.g. large information repositories like Drive and SharePoint) it creates no workable, standalone connections between them.

LLMs promote personality at the expense of durability and interoperability. AI gives users the impression that something conscious is helping them to get organized, while their (and our society’s) information’s chaos deepens.

Machines are tools: they should respond predictably to unambiguous inputs. Putting a human persona on a machine does nothing but diminish the real human.

4. Information: siren servers and the new enclosure

An economy where advertisers thrive while journalists and artists struggle, reflects the values of a society more interested in deception and manipulation than in truth and beauty .— Jaron Lanier

In Who Owns the Future?, philosopher Jaron Lanier laid out his theory of the “siren server” — that modern companies have developed a new business model, which generates a competitive advantage by having more data and thus greater insights to leverage.

This is a new form of competitiveness: it is not the same advantage that was afforded, say, to IBM by its huge network of relationships, partnerships and salespeople; or its ability to spend colossal sums on research and development.

Siren servers do not compete by innovating (at least not when they’re mature) — they compete by being big. As a result, siren servers are incentivized to get as big as possible, as quickly as possible, leading to business practices directly misaligned with user needs:

  1. Free/artificially low pricing to enroll users, who are then monetized by degrading the performance of the service and/or by new fees. (Don’t confuse this tactic for the “free trial” approach; the siren server fees are a surprise.)
  2. Barriers to leaving, such as incompatibility (e.g. enterprise information management solutions that cannot talk to each other).
  3. Invasive advertising.

Some siren server systems felt like progress at the time, but with any kind of hindsight, this is not progress. As Doctrow outlines in Enshittification, would anyone claim, for instance, that:

  1. Today’s large, closed social networks would be worse if they allowed some measure of interoperability, e.g. that one could message one’s friends there without an account (as one can with email)?
  2. People like to be followed around by advertisers?
  3. People feel good about or don’t have a bad taste in their mouth from having rushed onto free/cheap platforms in the 2010s, to find those platforms turned into cattle-pens?

It’s arguable that modern LLM companies represent the perfection of the siren server model. They aggregate incomprehensible volumes of data, in order to deliver an informational advantage to their users.

As Lanier has also observed, this results in a peculiar and new type of economic displacement: of workers (e.g. translators, writers, designers, etc.) by tools that simulate them.

Lanier points to the example of translators, who have been obviated significantly by translation AIs that used their translations as raw material. The fact of simulation is critical: AI doesn’t displace people with a new tool — unlike and regardless of the moral nature, say, of replacing horses with cars or canals with trains — today, thousands of people have been and will be displaced by simulations based on their work.

Currently, no legal protections exist, as Doctrow explains in Reverse Centaur. There is much discussion of copyright, but this relates primarily to AI firms’ illegal use of copyright material, i.e. downloading without paying for it. We face a new question: how should we treat the aggregation of people’s material to form systems which then put the same people out of the job?

Throughout human history, we have created new rights to respond to new situations: working time, copyright, patents, zoning, etc. Copyright, for instance, became relevant after the printing press made reproducing texts inexpensive. In some cases, like working hours, many unions and managers have come to acceptable settlements. (Though there is still much to discuss.)

In other cases, such changes gave way to colossal and irrevocable wealth transfers. Perhaps the most relevant example was the enclosures in Britain. For centuries, poor farmers had the right to graze cattle on the commons — land then considered inferior for farming but still useful for the people to support themselves.

As agricultural technology improved, this land became profitable and, over several centuries, landowners enclosed the commons and denied commoners the right to graze. There are still commoners and there is still common land, but this displacement was large enough to cause the exodus from the countryside to the cities which peopled the industrial revolution.

Large organizations are launching an enclosure today: they are aggregating information we thought had no value, and giving it a value. We think that we should form a new settlement (for instance Lanier’s “data as labor”) which provides both for the right of individuals and groups to scrape and study information (including “training” AI) and for the people to make something of their newly valuable data.

Beyond this, we need to wake up to the fact that anything we create can potentially be used as “training data” and therefore must never again simply create (and share) something without first asking who will use it, whether we approve of that usage, and whether therefore it requires protection.

5. AI by force, and as force

An interface is humane if it is responsive to human needs and considerate of human frailties. — Jef Raskin

All tech companies are fond of making us aware of their new features. Companies are fond also of pushing unwanted new features, such as by taking up screen space previously available for other uses, or making a feature that previously stood alone accessible only via a new one. This has reached its zenith with AI.

Appealing to the idea that software should help the user, and should act as a tool, software should not interfere, block, or interpose itself between the user and their work. (This is distinct from “doing precisely what they want, immediately” because software is duty-bound to protect a user from accidentally deleting their writing, for instance.)

Software companies can make people aware of new AI (and other) features without violating the contract set out above. Meanwhile, users should have access to simple, conventional data access features: such as searching, filtering, results lists and tables when companies can make (and have previously made) them available.

Bosses also frequently insist that employees use AI, and some job applications make AI-use a criteria (rarely for the application itself, ironically). Given the harm and uncertainty wrought by AI, bosses should afford conscientious objectors respect and possibly rights, as we do for people with their views on war, social relationships, the environment, etc.

Meanwhile — as part of a broader trend to deny users access to effective customer service (hiding phone numbers/contact information, customer help labyrinths) — companies are now making customer service available only through AI, and are scaling down their human teams. Companies have every right to deploy tools to help (some people prefer AI customer support) but not to remove avenues of communication and accountability, especially in situations where only humans can provide meaningful help.

Software should help its users, companies should help their customers and respect their employees — let us not let AI confuse straightforward questions.

Demands

Therefore, we demand an end to:

  1. The AI bubble.
  2. Fatalism, hype, and to “CEO said” journalism.
  3. Pretend software personalities, possessed by AI or otherwise.
  4. Siren servers — companies that compete only through size and data aggregation.
  5. Companies forcing AI on users, to bosses forcing AI on employees, and of AI as a barrier between people and organizations.

And, in their place, we demand:

  1. Sustainable, broad-based economic growth with broad benefits.
  2. Sound, grounded, factual discourse on AI.
  3. The choice to use conventional information retrieval interfaces.
  4. A new settlement to remunerate people for the use of their newly valuable data.
  5. The right to object to AI and to be afforded reasonable protections for doing so.

Coda: why are we here?

Untold reams of paper, not to mention U.S. Federal money, has gone to waste on the tall tales of artificial intelligence. […] People want control over their computers and their lives. So far, even the supposedly-controllable software is uncontrollable; would you trust today’s developers to create things you can understand even less? — Ted Nelson

Estimates vary, but it’s likely that knowledge workers spend around 20% of every workday just looking for information. Generally, computer users complain that:

  1. They cannot find the information they need on their computer or in the cloud.
  2. Projects get out of hand and become unmanageable, and are often abandoned.
  3. Their work, especially in collaboration with others, is hampered by the fact that different file types and information systems don’t work together.
  4. Generally, their ideas aren’t shaped like documents and spreadsheets.

How did we get here? Ted Nelson theorizes that “it all went wrong at Xerox PARC.” PARC: where in the public imagination the ideas behind modern computing like windows, the mouse pointer, text editing, etc. were developed.

At PARC, the computer — a machine capable of creating and associating information in any way — became a machine instead for undertaking minor secretarial tasks like creating and filing paper documents, rather than building ideas. People feel like they need AI because today’s software isn’t up to the task of expressing, organizing and connecting our ideas.

Users are looking for better tools to help them get organized because our information systems destroy information; companies hold out AI as the solution, when in fact it is part of the same mistake, and will make users’ problems much much worse.

Rather, we need a new approach, that:

  1. Lets users own and control their data.
  2. Puts up no barriers between information systems (folders on your drive versus database), datatypes (e.g. document versus email) and repositories (SharePoint versus Drive).
  3. Allows users to create a growing, adapting web of durable, shareable relationships between their ideas.

After the AI bubble bursts — or otherwise when we can look at computers with clarity — let us devote the energy and creativity we need to build software subtle enough to conform to the shape of human thought.

After the AI bubble: a manifesto was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Insurance Claims RAG with Go and Postgres: Versioned Retrieval in 4 Stages
description:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; keep document residency, retention, and deletion authority in the system that owns the claim record.

For an insurance claims intake service, document versioning is a data-governance problem before it is a similarity-search problem. A policy endorsement, loss notice, or adjuster note can change the answer, yet the model must still be able to show which version supplied each passage. The design below treats every retrieval result as an auditable event: a claim-scoped collection, a bounded query, a version identifier, and a source pointer travel together.

The retrieval contract for claims documents

Start by mapping the user-visible answer to a retrieval contract. Define the retrieval unit first: a signed page, a section, or a paragraph with a stable document_id and version_id. Then define metadata filters such as claim identifier, jurisdiction, document type, and effective date. Finally, write down the freshness requirement: intake triage may tolerate minutes, while a coverage decision may require an explicit re-index acknowledgement.

This is where Infrai can fit, narrowly: its public discovery endpoint describes request and response schemas with runnable examples, so wiring a vector stage does not require learning another SDK. The claims database and the specialist processor still own regulated data policy.

The contract also establishes the failure boundary. The transactional claims database remains the source of truth for retention schedules, legal holds, regional residency, and deletion requests. A vector collection is a derived index. It may contain an embedding and a short source reference, but it should not become the authoritative archive of personally identifiable information. Processor agreements and regional controls belong with the specialist storage or search provider that offers those guarantees; an AI runtime cannot manufacture a contractual residency promise. For example, when document 17 moves from version 2 to version 3, the indexer should write v3, verify the new source hash, and retire v2 in one recorded workflow; a reader inspecting an answer later must see that transition rather than an unexplained replacement.

This separation makes deletion testable. A delete event marks the source record, removes its vector entries, and leaves an audit record containing who requested the action, which version was removed, and when the collection acknowledged it. Re-index changed content deliberately. Do not silently overwrite a version and hope that a later answer can reconstruct history.

Keep it boring.

How should retrieval architecture handle insurance claims intake document versioning?

Use four stages: normalize, index, retrieve, and cite. Normalization assigns an immutable version and computes content hashes before chunking. Indexing writes only approved chunks and metadata to a collection dedicated to the claim or a tightly bounded tenant partition. Retrieval applies the claim and jurisdiction filters, requests a small top-k, and records the query plus returned identifiers. Citation then resolves those identifiers against the authoritative document store before an answer is shown.

The query must be bounded in both scope and time. A broad nearest-neighbor search across every claim is a data leak waiting to happen, even when the language model is well behaved. A filter mismatch should yield no context and a review queue, not a best-effort answer from another policy.

No context is a valid result.

Before production, measure this contract with a small labeled evaluation set. Include superseded endorsements, deleted documents, cross-jurisdiction lookalikes, and claims with no relevant passage. Track recall at the chosen k, citation coverage, and the rate of answers that cite an old version. Your mileage may vary because the right k and freshness window depend on chunk size and claim vocabulary; the evaluation set is what turns that uncertainty into an explicit operating decision.

A staged path with Go and vector collections

The critical path can remain ordinary HTTP. The self-describing discovery surface is useful here: an engineer can inspect a capability schema and runnable examples before wiring a new backend, rather than learning a bespoke SDK. Infrai's vector surface also gives a plain REST API, so the same Go client can call collection, upsert, and query operations while the claims system keeps its own residency and retention controls.

The sample is intentionally narrow. It creates a private collection, upserts one versioned chunk, and issues a filtered query. Production code should persist the request ID and source hash beside the claim audit event.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(ctx context.Context, method, endpoint, idem string, body any) ([]byte, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(body)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idem != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem) }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body); resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if v, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && v > 0 { delay = time.Duration(v) * time.Second }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, data) }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    _, _ = call(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/vector/collection/create", "claim-8842-collection-v1", map[string]any{"name": "claim-8842-vectors"})
    _, _ = call(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/vector/upsert", "claim-8842-doc-17-v3", map[string]any{
        "collection": "claim-8842-vectors",
        "items": []any{map[string]any{"id": "doc-17-v3-p2", "text": "...", "metadata": map[string]any{"claim_id": "8842", "document_id": "doc-17", "version_id": "v3", "jurisdiction": "CA", "effective_at": "2026-08-14"}}},
    })
    result, err := call(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/vector/query", "", map[string]any{"collection": "claim-8842-vectors", "query": "coverage for water damage", "top_k": 5, "filters": map[string]any{"claim_id": "8842", "jurisdiction": "CA"}})
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The write keys make retries idempotent, and the client backs off on HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After. It also surfaces non-2xx bodies, which matters when a schema or filter is rejected. The ellipsis in the example is data content, not an omitted API call; replace it with the normalized chunk before running. A real implementation should validate that every returned version_id still exists and is allowed by the claim's legal-hold policy before generating text.

Option trade-offs at index-cost scale

Index cost matters, but it cannot be separated from trust boundaries. A specialist may charge more while giving you region pinning, retention controls, or deletion attestations that a generic runtime does not provide. Compare the operating contract, not just the vector price.

Option Strength for claims intake Boundary or cost concern
Postgres with pgvector Keeps embeddings beside transactional claim metadata and version rows You own index sizing, vacuuming, regional deployment, and recall tuning
Elasticsearch Mature metadata filters, analyzers, and operational tooling More moving parts and shard planning; deletion and residency are your cluster policy
Pinecone Managed vector operations with a focused retrieval API Confirm region, retention, export, and processor terms for regulated records
Infrai vector API A self-describing REST surface with runnable examples can shorten integration when one Go client must wire several backend capabilities It is a derived vector service, so your specialist provider and claims database still own residency, retention, legal holds, and authoritative deletion

For this workflow, try Infrai for the retrieval adapter when your team values one key and a consistent HTTP convention across backend capabilities, and keep the regulated document lifecycle in the provider whose contract meets your jurisdiction. That is a narrower recommendation than moving every claim artifact into one runtime, and it preserves an exactly-once mindset around indexing and audit trails.

The rejected design and its valid use case

The rejected option is one mutable global index with a latest=true flag. It is easy to start and difficult to defend: a late delete, a re-index race, or a missing jurisdiction filter can make an old passage eligible for a new answer. It also makes cost accounting opaque because every tenant competes for the same index and compaction policy.

Use a shared index only for genuinely public, non-claim reference material such as a regulatory glossary, with no personal data and no tenant-specific retention promise. Claims intake needs explicit collections or partitions, immutable versions, bounded filters, and a reconciliation job that compares source rows with indexed rows. The catch is operational work: if your organization cannot run that reconciliation and evidence deletion, a specialist managed search service is the better choice.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the vector retrieval guide and inspect the schema before committing to an adapter.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/docs-delete-by-query.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/index-data/delete-data
