title: The Life of a Django Request
description:
A guided tour of everything that happens between someone clicking a link and your view function running. No traps, no gotchas, just how it actually works.

Most articles about Django are about what goes wrong. This one isn't. This is a tour.

Every time someone loads a page in your Django app, a small, elegant machine springs into motion. It unwraps the request, threads it through a stack of layers, finds the right view, runs your code, and packages the answer back up, usually in well under a tenth of a second.

Most of us write views for years without ever watching that machine run. We know our view function gets called with a request object, and we know we return a response, and the space between is a comfortable fog.

Let's clear the fog. We're going to follow a single request from the instant it leaves a browser to the instant the response arrives back, and at each stop I'll show you what Django is actually doing and why.

By the end, request and response won't be magic. They'll be things you understand from the inside. That understanding is quietly one of the most useful things you can have as a Django developer, because once you can see the machine, you know exactly where to reach when something needs explaining, debugging, or extending.

Here's the whole journey at a glance, and then we'll walk it step by step:

Browser → Nginx → Gunicorn (WSGI) → Django handler
      → Middleware (in) → URL resolver → Your view (ORM + templates)
      → Middleware (out) → Gunicorn → Nginx → Browser

Stop 1: The Browser and the Web Server

It starts with a browser making an HTTP request (GET /articles/42/) and sending it across the internet to your server. The first thing it hits isn't Django at all. It's a web server, typically Nginx, sitting at the front door.

Nginx handles the things Django shouldn't be bothered with:

  • Serving static files (CSS, images) directly
  • Terminating SSL
  • Load-balancing across multiple app processes

For anything dynamic (anything that needs your code), Nginx hands the request off to an application server like Gunicorn or uWSGI.

Think of Nginx as the receptionist who deals with routine visitors themselves and only forwards the real business inward.

So already there are two programs involved before Django wakes up. This is worth knowing, because when people say "Django is slow to serve static files" or debug a deployment, the answer usually lives right here in the handoff between the web server and the app server.

Stop 2: WSGI, the Universal Handshake

Gunicorn now has the request, but Gunicorn and Django are separate projects written by different people. How do they talk? Through a contract called WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface), and understanding this contract demystifies a huge amount.

WSGI is dead simple. The server calls your application as a plain function with two arguments:

  • environ: a dictionary holding everything about the request (the path, headers, method, all of it)
  • start_response: a callback for setting the status and headers

Your application does its work and returns the response body as bytes.

That's the entire contract. And it's why you can run Django under Gunicorn or uWSGI or others interchangeably. They all speak WSGI, so any of them can talk to any WSGI framework.

Django's end of this handshake lives in a file you've seen and probably never opened: wsgi.py. That file exposes a WSGIHandler, the object Gunicorn calls. This is the true front door of Django itself.

(There's a newer async version of this contract called ASGI, in asgi.py, which is what makes websockets and async views possible. Same idea, built for concurrency. But the classic synchronous path is WSGI, and that's the one we're walking.)

Stop 3: Django Wakes Up and Builds the Request Object

Now Django's WSGIHandler takes over, and the first meaningful thing it does is fire a signal: request_started. This is genuinely your earliest possible hook into the lifecycle. Code can subscribe to that signal to run the moment any request begins, before anything else happens.

Then Django takes that raw environ dictionary and wraps it into the object you know and love: the HttpRequest. This is the request that gets passed to every view you've ever written: request.method, request.path, request.GET, request.user. It's not magic; it's a friendly Python object built from the raw WSGI environment.

Here's a lovely detail most people never learn: parts of the request are lazy. request.body, request.POST, and request.FILES don't actually read the incoming data from the network socket until you access them.

Django creates the request object instantly without reading the (potentially huge) body, and only pulls it in when your code asks. It's an elegant efficiency: why read a 10MB upload into memory if this particular view never looks at it?

(One consequence: once you've read request.body, you generally can't read it again. The stream's been consumed.)

Stop 4: The Middleware Onion (Going In)

Now the request begins its journey inward through the middleware stack, and the onion is the perfect mental image. The request travels from the outside layer toward the center, and later the response travels back out through the same layers in reverse.

Middleware is just a list in your settings.py, and Django processes it top to bottom on the way in. Each layer is a chance to inspect, modify, or even stop the request before it reaches your view. Walk the default stack and you'll recognize old friends, each doing one job:

Middleware What it does on the way in
SecurityMiddleware Enforces HTTPS and security-related rules
SessionMiddleware Loads the user's session from the session store and attaches it
CommonMiddleware Handles URL normalization and a few housekeeping rules
CsrfViewMiddleware Checks the CSRF token on form submissions
AuthenticationMiddleware Gives you request.user, by reading the session and looking up who's logged in

That last one explains something you've used a thousand times: request.user isn't conjured from nowhere. A specific middleware put it there, on the way in, before your view ran. (And it's lazy too: request.user is only actually fetched from the database the first time you touch it.)

The power of the onion is that any layer can short-circuit the whole thing. If CsrfViewMiddleware sees a bad token, it returns a 403 right there. Your view never runs, and the response turns around and heads back out.

Middleware is where cross-cutting concerns (security, sessions, auth) live so your views don't have to repeat them.

Stop 5: The URL Resolver Finds Your View

The request has made it through middleware. Now Django needs to answer: which view handles /articles/42/? That's the job of the URL resolver (the URL dispatcher), driven by your urls.py.

Django takes the request path and tests it against your URL patterns, in order, top to bottom, until one matches. When path("articles/<int:article_id>/", views.article_detail) matches, two things come out of it:

  • The view function to call (article_detail)
  • The captured arguments from the URL (article_id=42, already converted to an int by the <int:> converter)

A great under-the-hood detail: the resolver is cached. Django builds the URL-pattern structure once and keeps it in memory rather than rebuilding it on every request. That's an important efficiency, since every single request needs it.

This is also the quiet reason that changing your urls.py requires a server restart in production: the resolved URL configuration is cached at startup, so new patterns aren't picked up until the process reloads. If you've ever wondered why a URL change "didn't take" until you restarted, now you know exactly why.

Stop 6: Your View Runs (the Part You Already Know)

Here we are at the center of the onion: your code. Django calls your view with the request object and the captured URL arguments:

def article_detail(request, article_id):
    article = Article.objects.get(id=article_id)   # ORM → SQL → database
    return render(request, "article.html", {"article": article})

This is the part you write every day, so I'll just point out the two systems it usually reaches for:

  • The ORM. Article.objects.get(...) doesn't talk to the database directly. It builds a description of a query that the ORM translates into SQL, sends to the database, and turns the result rows back into Python Article objects. (Lazy, as ever: the query runs when the data is actually needed.)
  • The template engine. render(...) takes your template and the context dictionary, and the template engine produces the final HTML string, which gets wrapped in an HttpResponse object.

One detail worth carrying with you, especially for class-based views: Django creates a new view instance for every request. That's deliberate. It keeps requests isolated from each other.

(It's also why a mutable class attribute on a view is shared across all requests while instance attributes aren't: a direct consequence of this one-instance-per-request design.)

Your view's job ends the moment it returns a response object. Now that response begins its journey back out.

Stop 7: Back Out Through the Middleware (in Reverse)

The response now travels back out through the same middleware stack, but in reverse order, bottom to top. This symmetry is the elegant heart of the onion: each middleware that got a look at the request on the way in gets a look at the response on the way out.

And they use it. On the way out:

  • SessionMiddleware saves any changes you made to the session back to the session store.
  • SecurityMiddleware and others add security headers to the outgoing response (things like X-Content-Type-Options).
  • Other middleware can compress the body, set cookies, or add their own headers.

So the response that leaves is richer than the one your view returned. Middleware decorated it on the way out with sessions, headers, and cookies.

The same layers, in mirror order: request going in, response coming out. That mirror is the whole design.

Stop 8: The Response Goes Home

The finished HttpResponse (status code, headers, and body) is handed back to the WSGI server (Gunicorn), which converts it into raw HTTP bytes and passes it to Nginx, which sends it across the internet to the browser, which renders the page. The machine goes quiet, waiting for the next request.

The whole round trip happened in a fraction of a second:

  1. Browser to Nginx to Gunicorn to Django's handler
  2. In through middleware
  3. Resolve the URL
  4. Run the view, query the database, render the template
  5. Back out through middleware
  6. And home again

And now you can see every stop.

Why Knowing This Makes You Better at Django

Here's the payoff, and it's real. Almost every Django concept that feels like "magic" is actually just one specific stop on this tour, and once you can place it, it stops being mysterious:

The question Where it lives
Where does request.user come from? AuthenticationMiddleware, on the way in (Stop 4)
Why do my security headers appear even though my view didn't add them? Middleware, on the way out (Stop 7)
Why did my URL change not work until I restarted? The cached URL resolver (Stop 5)
Where should I put code that runs on every request? Middleware, or the request_started signal (Stops 3–4)
Why is a class attribute on my view shared between users? One view instance per request (Stop 6)
How can I run Django under Gunicorn or uWSGI? They both speak WSGI (Stop 2)

None of these need memorizing once you hold the map. They all fall out of understanding the flow. That's the difference between using a framework and understanding it, and it's the difference between guessing where a problem lives and knowing.

Django's request/response cycle is, honestly, a beautiful piece of design. A raw network request enters, gets progressively wrapped and enriched into a friendly Python object, passes through orderly layers that each do one job, reaches your code at the calm center, and the answer flows back out through the same layers in mirror image.

It's an onion, and now you've seen every ring of it. The next time you write def my_view(request):, you'll know exactly what that request went through to reach you, and exactly where it's going next.

The 30-Second Takeaway

  • A request hits a web server (Nginx) first. It serves static files and forwards dynamic requests to an app server (Gunicorn/uWSGI).
  • Gunicorn and Django talk through WSGI, a tiny contract (environ dict in, response bytes out), which is why any WSGI server can run any WSGI framework. Django's entry point is wsgi.py (async apps use asgi.py).
  • Django fires the request_started signal, then wraps the raw environ into the HttpRequest you know, with body/POST/FILES read lazily, only when accessed.
  • The request travels inward through middleware (top→bottom): SecurityMiddleware, SessionMiddleware, AuthenticationMiddleware (this is what sets request.user), etc. Any layer can short-circuit and return early.
  • The URL resolver matches the path against urls.py (top→bottom) and extracts view + arguments. It's cached, which is why URL changes need a restart.
  • Your view runs (a new instance per request for CBVs), uses the ORM and template engine, and returns an HttpResponse.
  • The response travels back out through middleware in reverse (bottom→top), saving the session and adding security headers, then back through WSGI → Nginx → browser.
  • Nearly every "magic" Django behavior is just one stop on this tour. Knowing the map turns mysteries into locations.

Your Turn

Enjoyed the tour? The best way to make it stick is to open your own project's settings.py, read your MIDDLEWARE list top to bottom, and trace one real URL from urls.py to its view. You'll never see def my_view(request): the same way again.

Which stop on the tour surprised you most? Tell me in the comments 👇

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

title: I asked 3 LLMs to triage bug bounty exploits. So I built a contract that runs them instead
description:
A bug bounty asks the hunter to go first. You hand over the bug, then a human triager decides whether it counts and how much it is worth. The protocol can patch it, call it "known" and pay nothing. And now a growing share of the reports in that queue are AI-written, confident and wrong.

I wanted to see how bad the second problem is, so I measured it. Then I built a bounty where nobody triages at all: the contract runs the exploit and pays the first real break.

Repo: https://github.com/edycutjong/sealed · Live: https://sealed.edycu.dev · Demo (1:34): https://youtu.be/sEMg3q7gG5k

The measurement: can a model be talked into paying?

I built a 52-item corpus against five unmodified OpenZeppelin Ethernaut levels (Fallback, Telephone, Delegation, Force, King): real exploits, near-misses, no-ops, wrong-snapshot runs, malformed input, abuse input, and 15 submissions written by three different LLM families, each with the "hunter's" own explanation attached.

Then I gave every item to three models acting as triagers. Each got the level source, the bounty goal and the submission, and had to answer VERDICT: PAY or VERDICT: REFUSE.

Of the 21 non-breaking submissions:

Triager Fakes it would pay (of 21) Real breaks it would pay (of 15)
muse-wonder-1.0 1 12
nemotron-3-ultra 3 12
qwen3.8-omni-flash 3 11
executing verifier 0 5 of 5 on the demo bounty

Read it with the limits I put in the repo: one run per model, no code execution allowed, and only 5 of the 21 fakes came with a written claim. Every fake a model paid was one of those 5. So this is not "LLMs are useless at triage". It is narrower and more useful: a convincing explanation is enough to move a model to PAY, and it also refuses real breaks. Both failure modes cost a bounty money or reputation.

The verifier has neither failure mode, because it never reads the explanation. It runs the transactions.

The design: commit, verify in a TEE, deliver, get paid

Sealed is a NEAR contract that holds the bounty pool on an account with zero access keys (deployed from global contract code), so nobody, including me, can move the pool by hand. At funding it commits three hashes: the chain snapshot, the invariants, and the verifier WASM.

  1. The hunter stores the exploit as an encrypted secret in NEAR OutLayer, then commits H(exploit ‖ hunter ‖ salt) with a bond. The exploit stays sealed.
  2. The contract calls OutLayer's request_execution, pinned to the verifier's hash. A TEE worker decrypts the exploit, replays it in revm on the committed snapshot, and asks the level's own validateInstance whether it broke.
  3. The verdict comes back through a yield/resume callback. The first valid break per invariant is awarded into escrow. Everything else is refused on chain with a reason, and a hunter-caused failure slashes the bond.
  4. The hunter delivers the exploit sealed to the protocol's key. The contract checks it hashes to what the worker attested, and only then pays.

The protocol still decides what counts as a break, but up front, before any claim, and in public.

The verifier: no Rust-side opinion

The core of the verifier is short on purpose. It runs every exploit transaction from the player, then calls the level's own validator. There is no predicate I wrote that could be argued with:

/// Run every exploit tx from the player, then call the level's own `validateInstance` from the validator.
pub fn execute(snap: &Snapshot, exploit_bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<(bool, u64, Option<String>), String> {
    // ...load the committed snapshot into revm...
    for (to, data, value) in txs {
        let left = EXPLOIT_GAS_BUDGET - gas;
        match evm.transact_commit(tx(player, kind, data, value, left)) {
            // Revert / halt / out-of-gas are normal EVM outcomes.
            Ok(r) => gas = gas.saturating_add(r.tx_gas_used()).min(EXPLOIT_GAS_BUDGET),
            // Invalid tx (e.g. value above the player's balance): the tx simply does not happen.
            Err(e) => trace(|| format!("tx {kind:?} -> invalid {e:?}")),
        }
    }
    let r = evm.transact(tx(validator, TxKind::Call(factory),
                            validate_calldata(instance, player), U256::ZERO, VALIDATE_GAS_LIMIT))?;
    let broken = match r.result {
        ExecutionResult::Success { output, .. } => {
            let o = output.data();
            o.len() == 32 && o[31] == 1 && o[..31].iter().all(|b| *b == 0)
        }
        _ => false,
    };
    Ok((broken, gas, None))
}

It compiles to wasm32-wasip1, about 1.5 MB, and the build is byte-reproducible on the pinned host, so the hash the contract commits is the hash anyone can rebuild. The heaviest real exploit used 0.37% of OutLayer's 2e9 instruction limit; the heaviest fake, 23.98%.

The callback: refusals are first-class

Most of the contract is about saying no correctly. A verdict that says "broken" still has to match the commit, the invariant and the snapshot, or it is refused and the bond is slashed:

let reason: Option<String> = if !broken {
    Some(err.map(|e| e.to_string()).unwrap_or_else(|| "no invariant broken".into()))
} else if h_exploit != c.commit_hash {
    Some("commit mismatch".into())
} else if v_inv != c.invariant_id {
    Some("wrong invariant".into())
} else if h_snapshot != want_snap.as_str() {
    Some("snapshot mismatch".into())
} else if !h_enc_ok {
    Some("malformed h_enc".into())
} else {
    None
};

Six refusal kinds landed on testnet (pool pull, invariant busy, duplicate, fake, delivery mismatch, expired award), each with a transaction you can look up. Twenty near-workspaces sandbox tests cover the invariants: conservation (pool + escrow + paid = funded − withdrawn after every call), one payout per invariant, one verdict in flight, a withdraw guard so the protocol cannot pull reserved funds, and the delivery hash check.

The numbers, and how to check them without trusting me

On NEAR testnet the demo bounty paid 5 of 5 real exploits and 0 of 21 submitted fakes. Request to verdict was p50 7.27 s, p95 10.85 s over 29 runs, read from OutLayer events.

You do not need a NEAR account or a key to check any of that:

git clone https://github.com/edycutjong/sealed && cd sealed
make replay       # re-runs every published commit offline under wasmtime = its on-chain verdict
make verify-demo  # reads the chain: pinned hash, worker key, verdict, PAID; FAILs unless the bounty has 0 keys
make corpus       # all 52 corpus items vs golden verdicts

make replay needs only python3 and wasmtime.

What it does not do (yet)

  • Testnet only. The mainnet leg is scripted and has not run.
  • Attestation is partial. make verify checks that OutLayer's scoped worker key answered a request pinned to the verifier hash. It does not check the TDX quote, so it does not prove the worker ran exactly those bytes; make replay re-runs them locally instead.
  • RPC trust. Verification believes the archival node it queries; an RPC error is reported as RECORDED, never as a pass.
  • Griefing. A fresh account can keep one invariant busy for the cost of gas plus the OutLayer fee.
  • No outside users yet. Every measured run is my own hunter agent plus the fakes corpus.

That last one is the real gap. If you run bounties or hunt them, clone it, run make replay, and tell me where it breaks. I'd also like to know: would you put a pool behind a contract that pays without asking you first, and what would you need to see?

Built at NEAR HACKATHON 2026 with NEAR OutLayer. Repo: https://github.com/edycutjong/sealed

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: Why Stateless AI Fails at SRE (And How Contextual Memory Fixes It)
description:
During a P1 production outage, every minute of downtime costs thousands of dollars. Standard AI assistants lack organizational context, providing generic textbook advice or hallucinating destructive CLI commands.

To solve this, I built NerveCenter, an intelligent SRE agent that replaces generic AI with historically grounded runbooks.

NerveCenter uses Streamlit, Groq (gpt-oss-120b), and Vectorize Hindsight as a dynamic memory layer. When a "Redis OOM Error" alert fires, NerveCenter queries the vector database for similar past incidents. It retrieves Incident 892, outputs the exact redis-cli FLUSHALL ASYNC command used to fix it, and injects the post-mortem notes directly into the context. If flushing the cache previously caused a latency spike, the agent actively warns the engineer before executing the command.

By grounding the LLM in real execution logs, we eliminate hallucinations and prevent repeated mistakes.

Check out the Hindsight GitHub or learn about Vectorize agent memory to see how this works. You can also read the Hindsight docs.

title: Why Sign Remote Commands in the Browser? Fleetd Authorization and Trust Boundaries
description:
Once a machine is connected to a dashboard, running commands from the browser is an obvious next step. Checking a disk, restarting a service or opening a terminal makes managing servers and routers easier. It also gives the dashboard the ability to change those machines. A monitoring outage and a compromised command interface have very different consequences.

The previous article covered outbound connections, device approval and identity. This article follows the next decision: if an agent already trusts its server, why verify a browser signature before running a command? The details below describe Fleetd v0.3.0. Signing adds an independent check, but its assumptions include the code served to the browser and what happens after an interactive terminal opens.

A dashboard session is not unlimited authority

In a conventional design, the administrator logs in, the server authorizes an operation, and the agent executes the server's message. Execution authority is concentrated at the server.

Fleetd adds a local question: did a key trusted by this machine authorize this operation? The browser constructs and signs a request, the server forwards it, and the agent checks the signature against its own configuration. Login and connection authentication remain necessary; they answer different questions.

Confirm targets and command → Browser signs the request
→ Server forwards it → Agent checks authorization → Execution

A message arriving through an authenticated connection does not automatically qualify for execution.

Sign the whole operation

Signing only the word uptime leaves unanswered which machine may run it, when, and whether the same request can be submitted again. Fleetd signs an envelope containing these fields:

Field Purpose
v Protocol version
id Identify this authorization and detect repeated requests
kind Command execution or terminal opening
targets Authorized machine fingerprints
argv or action Program and arguments, or a locally configured action
issued_at, expires_at Acceptance window
timeout Runtime timeout, subject to the agent's limit

The current command form wraps its input as ['sh', '-c', input]. Entering uptime signs a request containing those arguments. Pipes and && work because the interface explicitly invokes a shell.

The browser serializes the request into JSON bytes and signs them with Ed25519. The agent verifies those exact bytes before decoding the JSON. Changing uptime to reboot, or adding another target, invalidates the existing signature. If several machines were included originally, each may legitimately execute the request: target binding constrains scope rather than requiring a single target.

The agent evaluates the authorization

Each agent stores a trusted_signers list. A public key included with a request must already be trusted locally. Otherwise anyone could generate a key and authorize their own commands.

Beyond the signature, the agent checks the request type, its own fingerprint in the target list, timestamps and local permissions. Unknown JSON fields are rejected to avoid inconsistent interpretations of the request.

The browser creates requests valid for five minutes. The agent allows two minutes of clock skew and rejects declared validity intervals longer than ten minutes. Five minutes describes the acceptance window, not how long a command may run. Runtime timeout is separate. The skew allowance also means acceptance does not stop at an exact five-minute boundary. Both ends still need reasonably correct clocks.

Together these checks ask whether this trusted authorization applies to this machine now.

Replay protection is not exactly-once execution

An unchanged, correctly signed request can still be sent repeatedly. Fleetd gives each request an ID generated from 16 random bytes. After authorization succeeds, the agent records the ID and rejects another use of it.

The record is persisted in seen.json in the state directory, which defaults to /var/lib/fleetd. With that state retained, an ordinary process restart does not make still-valid requests reusable. If persistence fails, execution does not proceed.

This is not an exactly-once guarantee for business effects. The ID is recorded before the concurrency check and process launch. A request can therefore consume its ID without starting because all execution slots are occupied. Conversely, a command may already have changed the machine before a disconnect prevents the dashboard from receiving its result.

Clicking Run again creates a new ID and a new authorization. The agent cannot infer whether you are replacing a failed attempt or repeating a completed operation. For upgrades, configuration changes and database migrations, inspect the real state and design for idempotency where possible. State loss or disk rollback also differs from an ordinary process restart; persistent replay records do not magically survive either.

Local permission still applies

Permission What the agent accepts
monitor Monitoring; no commands or terminals
allowlist Trusted, signed requests for locally configured actions
full Trusted, signed arbitrary commands and terminal requests

A newly enrolled monitoring-only machine can stay on monitor. For a small set of maintenance actions, an allowlist can narrow authority. For example, on a systemd machine with nginx installed:

permission: allowlist
allowlist:
  nginx-status: [systemctl, is-active, nginx]

This is only a permission configuration fragment; connection settings and trusted public keys are still required. A signed request carries action: nginx-status, while the agent obtains the actual executable and arguments from its own configuration. The sender cannot append arbitrary arguments, and a request cannot contain both action and argv.

The v0.3.0 command form sends shell commands and has no preset-action selector. Typing nginx-status into it will not invoke this action on an allowlist-only machine. The protocol and UI do not yet offer the same level of support.

Under the current deployment model the agent runs as root, so full commands have corresponding authority. A signature cannot determine whether a command is mistaken or destructive. Nor is local configuration immutable: an authorized root command can modify it. Local policy limits unauthorized requests, not the power of an already authorized root process.

Browser keys have a lifecycle

WebCrypto generates the Ed25519 key pair with a non-extractable private key, and IndexedDB stores the pair. The normal registration flow sends the public key to the server, not the private signing key.

Switching computers or clearing browser site data can therefore remove the ability to sign requests that existing agents recognize, even when login still works. A new browser needs a new key, and the agents must trust its public key. Registering it on the server does not automatically update existing installations.

Revocation also has to reach the agents. Deleting a public key from the dashboard does not revoke it on already configured machines. Remove it from their trusted_signers lists and restart the agents using the appropriate service manager.

The release-signing key is separate. Command signing authorizes an operation; release signing authenticates an agent update package. A later article will cover that update lifecycle.

Two important trust boundaries

The server also distributes the frontend

Non-extractable means normal WebCrypto APIs cannot export the private key material. It does not prevent malicious same-origin code from invoking the key to sign.

Fleetd serves its management UI from the server. A compromised server may distribute modified JavaScript during a later visit. That page could display one command and sign another, or otherwise misuse an existing key. A confirmation dialog supplied by the same page cannot independently prove the page is trustworthy.

The agent can reject modified requests without valid signatures, but trusted frontend code remains an assumption. Distributing a signing tool separately could reduce this dependency. The design document mentions a CLI signer; v0.3.0 does not implement it.

Only opening a terminal is signed

Opening a terminal uses a signed kind: shell request and requires local full permission. Subsequent keystrokes use the existing session without individual browser signatures. A compromised server could inject input into an already-open terminal.

Open interactive sessions when needed and close them afterwards. A clearly scoped one-shot command is often easier to review than an ongoing interactive session. The initial signature does not protect every later input in the same way.

Signing also does not hide commands or output. Encryption between agent and server protects the network path, but the server is an endpoint. This is not browser-to-agent confidentiality that excludes the server.

Look at rejection paths

Successful output is the obvious demo. Authorization also needs clear failure cases. Existing Fleetd tests cover modified payloads, untrusted keys, wrong targets, expired or future requests, insufficient permissions and duplicate IDs after replay state is reloaded. These tests constrain individual rules; they are not a complete security audit and do not automatically test malicious frontend delivery, terminal input or every deployment environment.

For a self-hosted operator, the useful result is an explainable chain: which keys are trusted, which machines were authorized, when a request is acceptable, what local policy permits and how duplicates are handled. The preset-action UI, independent signing and terminal protection remain concrete areas to improve.

Next comes a deployment question: how does the same Go agent run on both ordinary Linux servers and OpenWrt routers?

  • Fleetd repository
  • Commands and terminals
  • Browser signing, v0.3.0
  • Agent authorization and replay protection
  • Authorization tests

title: 5 Ways to Send Email Daily in Node.js: Third-Party Scheduling
description:
Fintech reservation expiry is a recovery problem before it is a timer problem. For a fixed hold window, the least complex design is a daily or frequent third-party trigger that hands work to a durable worker; the worker finds reservations past their deadline, marks each one idempotently, and sends the report email separately. Keep the mail send out of the scheduler request.

Keep it boring.

Recovery is the product.

For this scheduler-to-mail seam, Infrai fits teams that want one plain REST API and one credential for the trigger, queue, and email boundary. It is an option inside the architecture, not a replacement for the reservation database or a workflow engine.

Choose this shape Pick it when Recovery trade-off
Managed cron -> public Node.js endpoint -> worker queue Expiry work is short and the endpoint is already operated Fewer moving parts, but your endpoint and queue still need ownership
Managed cron -> queue -> Node.js worker -> email provider You need bounded requests, retries, and a visible backlog More operational pieces, with a cleaner retry boundary
Node.js process + BullMQ Redis is already a platform dependency Good queue control; you operate Redis and the scheduler
Inngest or Temporal The process is a multi-step workflow with durable state Strong orchestration; more concepts than one expiry job needs

These are five practical ways to decide where recovery belongs. The recommendation is conditional: for a reservation system where a missed run must be found and replayed, use the queue-backed shape. A cron callback should enqueue a bounded unit of work, not hold an HTTP request open while it scans a ledger.

What should recover when the expiry run is missed?

Start with the invariant. A reservation is eligible when expiresAt <= now and its state is still held. The expiry operation is idempotent: applying it twice produces the same final state and never releases a reservation that has already been paid, cancelled, or renewed. The report is a consequence of the resulting state, not the source of truth.

That distinction changes the diagram in words: clock fires, queue records intent, worker reads authoritative state, database transition wins, email summarizes committed results. If the clock is late, the next worker run scans by deadline and catches up. If the worker dies after the database transition, an idempotency key prevents the retry from applying it twice. If email fails, the financial state remains correct and the email can be retried.

There are sharp boundaries. A cron task has a 900-second execution limit, so a large expiry scan belongs behind the trigger. Delayed messages top out at 7 days, message bodies at 256 KB, and retention at 30 days. Standard queues are at-least-once; consumer idempotency is mandatory. A paused cron does not backfill missed triggers. Those facts should shape the recovery policy, not appear as footnotes after deployment.

Five ways to place the boundary

  1. Inline Node.js cron. A process calls the database and sends mail in one scheduled function. It is readable and fine for a small internal report, but a restart, long query, or mail timeout couples unrelated failure modes. Use it only when the run is comfortably below the timeout and replay is explicit.

  2. Cron to a public Node.js endpoint. A managed scheduler sends an HTTP request, and the endpoint starts the work. This is a useful first step, but the endpoint must be publicly reachable; a private network URL cannot receive a push. Return quickly after enqueueing. Do not turn the callback into a hidden worker.

  3. Cron to queue to worker. This is the default for stale reservations. The cron trigger emits a small job such as expire-reservations:2026-10-25, and the worker processes pages. The job key is stable, the state transition is conditional, and each retry re-reads current state.

  4. BullMQ with Node.js. BullMQ gives a Node-first queue model and is a sensible fit when Redis is already managed by the team. Its boundary is familiar to JavaScript engineers. Redis becomes part of the availability and recovery story, though, and the team owns its retention, monitoring, and failover decisions.

  5. Inngest or Temporal. Inngest is attractive for event-driven functions and retries. Temporal is the stronger choice when the expiry process grows into a long-lived workflow with timers, compensations, and multiple durable steps. Neither is necessary merely to run a bounded daily report. Choosing a workflow engine for one timer can make the operational surface larger than the business rule.

SendGrid and AWS SES solve a different half of the problem: email delivery. Resend is another focused mail API. They do not remove the need to decide how a missed expiry run is detected, replayed, and made idempotent. A dedicated mail provider is the better boundary when deliverability controls, templates, domain tooling, or provider-specific email events are the main concern.

How does one key connect scheduling and email in Node.js?

The useful seam is the handoff, not a vendor catalog. A single REST API can put the scheduler and mailer behind the same Authorization: Bearer key and the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base URL. That means the worker does not need a second credential injected just to turn a completed expiry run into a report. It also means one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface. That cost is real.

The alternative pairing, such as Inngest or a system cron plus Resend, normally means two signups, two credential sets, and glue code for the scheduler-to-mail handoff, error mapping, and operational correlation. It may still be the better choice when a specialist's workflow or deliverability controls matter more than a unified boundary.

Here is the handoff shape in TypeScript. The scheduled job is the first capability; its result feeds the email capability. Keep the concrete request schemas in the live discovery documentation for the selected capability, and keep the application contract narrow: the scheduler invokes your public Node.js handler, while the handler owns the reservation query and report payload. That separation is deliberate: the expiry decision stays in the system of record, while the report is a recoverable side effect that can be retried without changing money movement.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function sendEmail(body: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/email/batch/send`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": `reservation-expiry-${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryAfter * 1000));
    return call(path, body);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`email batch failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

async function publishReport(report: { subject: string; html: string }) {
  return sendEmail({
    subject: report.subject,
    html: report.html,
  });
}

export async function finishExpiryRun(report: { subject: string; html: string }) {
  return publishReport(report);
}

The snippet intentionally leaves recipient and scheduling fields to the live request schema; inventing them in a financial workflow is worse than making the boundary explicit. In production, replace the recursive retry with bounded exponential backoff, honor Retry-After, and persist the idempotency key with the run. The same key is safe for the email write only when the provider's idempotency behavior and request schema are confirmed. A standard queue still requires the worker to tolerate duplicate deliveries.

What does the worker actually guarantee?

Measure recovery, not just successful invocations. Emit a run identifier, scheduled time, scan watermark, eligible count, transitioned count, duplicate count, mail status, and final outcome. Keep the detailed result in your own store: cron history output retains only the first 4 KB. Alert on an old watermark and a growing queue age, not only on a missing HTTP 200.

For the database transition, use a conditional update keyed by reservation ID and expected state. The report should be built from committed transitions. A retry then becomes boring: read the same reservation, see that it is no longer held, record a duplicate or skip, and continue. That is the operational recovery property the timer alone cannot provide.

Limits and the decision

Use the queue-backed architecture when the expiry scan can outlive one request, when duplicate delivery is acceptable only with idempotency, or when operators need a backlog to inspect. A plain cron endpoint is enough for a small, bounded report with a tested replay command. BullMQ is compelling with Redis already in the platform. Inngest or Temporal earns its weight once the job becomes a workflow rather than a single state transition.

Infrai is worth trying for the queue-and-email boundary when one plain REST API and one credential reduce integration work across the two capabilities. It is a poor fit for DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, private push targets, replay beyond 30 days, or nonstandard cron extensions. In those cases, Temporal, Airflow, or a direct specialist may fit the requirement better. If this boundary matches your system, start with the cron capability discovery.

Further reading

  • https://docs.sendgrid.com/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.temporal.io/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid
  • https://resend.com/docs

title: Ubuntu 26.04 Ships sudo-rs: How to Audit Your Scripts and sudoers Before the Upgrade Breaks Production
description:
Nếu bạn đang chạy server Ubuntu và dự định nâng cấp lên 26.04 LTS, có một thay đổi rất dễ bị bỏ qua: lệnh sudo mặc định giờ là sudo-rs, bản viết lại bằng Rust, chứ không còn là sudo truyền thống (bản của Todd Miller, sudo.ws) nữa. Phần lớn thời gian bạn sẽ không thấy khác biệt gì. Nhưng nếu bạn có script deploy, Ansible playbook, file sudoers tự viết hoặc CI pipeline phụ thuộc vào vài flag và option ít dùng, thì bản nâng cấp có thể làm hỏng chúng một cách âm thầm. Tuần này trên HN có thảo luận khá sôi nổi về chủ đề này. Mình sẽ chia sẻ cách audit hệ thống trước khi nâng cấp, theo đúng quy trình team mình đang dùng.

sudo-rs khác sudo truyền thống ở đâu?

sudo-rs được thiết kế để thay thế trực tiếp, nhưng chủ động không hỗ trợ toàn bộ tính năng của sudo gốc. Lý do khá hợp lý: sudo gốc có hơn 30 năm lịch sử, hàng trăm option trong sudoers, và mỗi tính năng ít dùng đều là thêm bề mặt tấn công. Một số khác biệt bạn nên biết:

  • Không có plugin system và không hỗ trợ sudoers lưu trên LDAP.
  • Nhiều Defaults trong sudoers không được hỗ trợ, ví dụ các option liên quan đến gửi mail (mail_badpass, mailto), insults, và một số option về log/IO.
  • Luôn dùng pseudo-terminal (pty), trong khi sudo gốc cho phép tắt qua use_pty.
  • Một số flag và cách xử lý biến môi trường có chi tiết khác nhau, đặc biệt là với -E / --preserve-env và env_keep.

Vấn đề nằm ở chỗ: khi sudo-rs gặp directive nó không hiểu trong sudoers, tùy loại directive mà nó có thể báo lỗi parse hoặc bỏ qua. Cả hai trường hợp đều nguy hiểm. Báo lỗi thì có thể khóa luôn quyền root của bạn, còn bỏ qua thì policy bạn tưởng đang áp dụng thực ra không còn tác dụng.

Luôn kiểm tra thực tế trên máy của bạn:

# Đang dùng bản sudo nào?
sudo --version | head -1
readlink -f "$(command -v sudo)"

# Xem các implementation có sẵn
update-alternatives --display sudo 2>/dev/null
ls -l /usr/bin/sudo* /usr/lib/cargo/bin/sudo 2>/dev/null

Trên Ubuntu từ 25.10 trở đi, sudo gốc vẫn được cài kèm dưới tên sudo.ws, và bạn có thể chuyển lại bằng update-alternatives --config sudo. Đây là đường lui, nhưng đừng xem nó là giải pháp lâu dài.

Quy trình audit trước khi nâng cấp

Đây là flow team mình áp dụng cho mỗi nhóm server:

flowchart TD
    A[Inventory: sudoers + scripts + playbooks] --> B[Scan option và flag không hỗ trợ]
    B --> C{Có vấn đề?}
    C -- Không --> D[Test trên container ubuntu:26.04]
    C -- Có --> E[Sửa config / script]
    E --> D
    D --> F{Pass?}
    F -- Có --> G[Rollout canary 1-2 server]
    F -- Không --> E
    G --> H[Rollout toàn bộ]

Bước quan trọng nhất là bước đầu tiên: bạn cần biết chỗ nào đang gọi sudo. Ngoài /etc/sudoers và /etc/sudoers.d/, hãy tìm cả trong repo infra, systemd unit, cron job và Dockerfile.

Script tự động scan sudoers

Đoạn Python dưới đây đọc toàn bộ sudoers và đánh dấu các directive có rủi ro. Danh sách RISKY_DEFAULTS chỉ là điểm khởi đầu. Hãy đối chiếu với tài liệu của bản sudo-rs bạn đang chạy (man sudoers trên chính máy 26.04), vì danh sách option được hỗ trợ thay đổi theo từng release.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# audit_sudoers.py - chạy với: sudo python3 audit_sudoers.py
import re
from pathlib import Path

RISKY_DEFAULTS = {
    "mail_badpass", "mail_always", "mail_no_user", "mailto", "mailerpath",
    "insults", "log_input", "log_output", "iolog_dir", "use_pty",
    "lecture", "lecture_file", "requiretty", "syslog", "logfile",
}
RISKY_PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"^\s*#?@?includedir\b"), "includedir: kiểm tra cú pháp được hỗ trợ"),
    (re.compile(r"\bNOEXEC\b"), "tag NOEXEC: hành vi có thể khác"),
    (re.compile(r"\bLDAP\b", re.I), "LDAP: sudo-rs không hỗ trợ"),
]

def scan(path: Path):
    issues = []
    for no, line in enumerate(path.read_text().splitlines(), 1):
        s = line.strip()
        if s.startswith("Defaults"):
            opts = re.split(r"[\s,]+", s.split(None, 1)[-1])
            for opt in opts:
                name = opt.lstrip("!").split("=")[0].split("+")[0]
                if name in RISKY_DEFAULTS:
                    issues.append((no, f"Defaults {name}"))
        for pat, msg in RISKY_PATTERNS:
            if pat.search(s):
                issues.append((no, msg))
    return issues

files = [Path("/etc/sudoers"), *sorted(Path("/etc/sudoers.d").glob("*"))]
for f in files:
    if f.is_file():
        for no, msg in scan(f):
            print(f"{f}:{no}: {msg}")

Kết quả có dạng /etc/sudoers.d/90-deploy:3: Defaults log_output. Mỗi dòng là một điểm bạn cần quyết định: bỏ đi, thay bằng cơ chế khác (ví dụ chuyển audit log sang auditd thay vì log_output), hoặc giữ lại và chấp nhận dùng sudo.ws cho máy đó.

Với script shell, một lệnh grep đơn giản đã bắt được phần lớn trường hợp:

# Tìm các cách gọi sudo có flag "nhạy cảm" trong repo infra
grep -rnE 'sudo\s+(-[a-zA-Z]*[EAHbS]|--preserve-env|--askpass|-u\s+#)' \
  --include='*.sh' --include='*.yml' --include='*.yaml' \
  --include='Dockerfile*' --include='*.service' .

# Script nào đọc output của sudo -l? (format có thể khác)
grep -rn 'sudo -l' --include='*.sh' --include='*.py' .

Đặc biệt chú ý đến sudo -l. Mình đã thấy nhiều script parse output của lệnh này để kiểm tra quyền, và chỉ cần format output lệch một chút là logic sai ngay.

Test thật trong container trước khi chạm vào server

Scan tĩnh chỉ tìm được những gì bạn đã biết. Cách chắc chắn nhất là chạy chính script của bạn trên Ubuntu 26.04 trong container, với chính file sudoers của bạn:

cat > Dockerfile.sudotest <<'EOF'
FROM ubuntu:26.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y sudo python3 \
 && useradd -m deploy
COPY sudoers.d/ /etc/sudoers.d/
COPY scripts/ /opt/scripts/
RUN chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/*
USER deploy
EOF

docker build -f Dockerfile.sudotest -t sudotest .

# 1. sudoers có parse được không?
docker run --rm --user root sudotest visudo -c

# 2. Chạy script deploy thật
docker run --rm sudotest bash -x /opt/scripts/deploy.sh

visudo -c là bước bắt buộc. Nếu nó fail trong container, nghĩa là sau khi nâng cấp server bạn sẽ không dùng được sudo nữa. Khi đó chỉ còn cách vào bằng console hoặc recovery mode, và với VPS ở xa thì đó là một buổi tối rất tệ.

Nên đưa bước này vào CI để mọi thay đổi sudoers đều được test trên cả hai implementation:

flowchart LR
    PR[Pull Request sửa sudoers] --> CI[CI job]
    CI --> T1[ubuntu:24.04 + sudo gốc]
    CI --> T2[ubuntu:26.04 + sudo-rs]
    T1 --> M{Cả hai pass?}
    T2 --> M
    M -- Có --> Merge[Merge]
    M -- Không --> Fix[Sửa lại]

Trong giai đoạn chuyển tiếp, khi fleet của bạn có cả 24.04 lẫn 26.04, test song song như vậy giúp bạn không phải đoán.

Những bẫy mình đã gặp

Một vài bài học thực tế:

  1. Đừng sửa sudoers trực tiếp trên server đang chạy. Luôn dùng visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/xxx và luôn mở sẵn một session root khác trước khi thử.
  2. Cloud-init và golden image. Nếu bạn build AMI hoặc image bằng Packer, sudoers được tạo trong lúc build. Hãy kiểm tra template đó, không chỉ server đang chạy.
  3. Biến môi trường. Script dựa vào sudo -E để giữ HTTP_PROXY hoặc PATH nên được viết lại theo kiểu tường minh: sudo env HTTP_PROXY="$HTTP_PROXY" cmd. Viết như vậy rõ ràng hơn và không phụ thuộc vào implementation.
  4. Đừng vội update-alternatives về sudo.ws cho cả fleet. Làm vậy thì vấn đề vẫn nằm đó, chỉ bị dời sang lần nâng cấp sau.

Kết luận

Việc Ubuntu chuyển sang sudo-rs là một bước đúng về mặt bảo mật, nhờ memory safety và codebase gọn hơn. Cái giá phải trả là bạn cần dọn dẹp những config đã tích tụ qua nhiều năm. Checklist hành động:

  • Chạy sudo --version và update-alternatives --display sudo để biết bạn đang dùng gì.
  • Scan /etc/sudoers* bằng script ở trên và đối chiếu với man sudoers trên máy 26.04.
  • grep repo infra để tìm sudo -E, sudo -l và các flag ít dùng.
  • Build container ubuntu:26.04, chạy visudo -c và chạy script deploy thật.
  • Đưa test sudoers lên CI cho cả 24.04 và 26.04.
  • Rollout theo canary, luôn có sẵn session root dự phòng.
  • Coi sudo.ws chỉ là đường lui tạm thời, không phải đích đến.

Chỉ mất khoảng nửa ngày để audit, nhưng có thể giúp bạn tránh được một sự cố mất quyền root trên production. Làm ngay bây giờ, trước khi do-release-upgrade tự nhắc bạn.

title: Control AI crawlers and assistants separately in Vercel Firewall
description:
You can now log or block requests from AI crawlers and AI assistants separately with the AI Bots managed ruleset in Vercel Firewall.

  • AI crawlers: bots that collect content for indexing and model training

  • AI assistants: bots that fetch pages in response to user actions or search queries

For example, you can block AI crawlers while allowing AI assistants to retrieve your content to answer users’ questions. Vercel updates the rules as new bots are added.

To configure these controls, open your project’s Security > Firewall > Rules. Under Bot Management, enable AI Bots and select the gear icon beside it. Set an action for AI crawlers and AI assistants, then review and publish your changes.

You can also modify these rule settings using the Vercel CLI:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 30azXU4HVTfrsO9MbBOCLv

title: Designing the Network Between Clouds: A Planning Outline for Multi-Cloud Estates
description:
Most multi-cloud architecture diagrams draw each cloud as a tidy box. Inside the boxes there are VPCs, subnets, managed services, and careful labels. Between the boxes there is usually a single line, sometimes labelled just "VPN" or "internet".

That line is where a surprising amount of production pain lives.

As soon as a workload in one cloud genuinely depends on data or services in another — a reporting job reading from a database that stayed behind, an application calling an AI endpoint hosted elsewhere, a failover that suddenly reroutes traffic across providers — the lines between the boxes stop being decoration. They become a network that somebody has to design, secure, document, and debug at 2 a.m.

This is a planning outline for treating inter-cloud connectivity as a designed layer in its own right, before the estate grows enough that retrofitting it becomes expensive.

1. Inventory the flows before choosing any technology

The most common mistake is starting with connection products. Start with flows instead.

For each cross-cloud dependency, write down:

  • Source and destination — which account, VPC/VNet, and region on each side
  • What it carries — application traffic, replication, backups, admin access, inference calls
  • How sensitive it is — does it cross a trust boundary? Does it carry regulated data?
  • What breaks if it stops — a degraded feature, or a full outage?
  • Who owns it — a named team, not "the cloud team" in general

Most estates discover flows nobody remembered creating: a one-off tunnel from a migration two years ago, a peering set up for a demo that quietly became load-bearing. The inventory is unglamorous work, but every later decision — routing, security policy, cost — depends on it being complete.

2. Plan address space and DNS as if there will be a third cloud

Overlapping private address space is the multi-cloud problem that bites earliest and gets discussed least. Two clouds adopted independently often arrive with the same RFC 1918 ranges, because both teams picked 10.0.0.0/16 as the obvious default. The collision only surfaces when a workload in one cloud genuinely needs to reach a service in the other — at which point the fixes are all unpleasant: NAT at the boundary, proxy layers, or renumbering something already running in production.

A few habits prevent most of it:

  • Allocate private ranges centrally, per cloud, per region, per environment — and record the allocations somewhere engineers actually check before creating a new VPC or VNet.
  • Reserve space for future clouds and regions even if there is no current plan for them. Reserving address space costs nothing; renumbering costs weekends.
  • Agree on one DNS resolution convention early. Each cloud resolves names differently, conditional forwarding rules pile up, and an internal service that resolves fine in one environment silently fails in another. Private zones, forwarding rules, and naming conventions should be designed once and applied consistently across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle environments rather than invented per project.

3. Decide deliberately where private paths earn their place

Not every cross-cloud flow needs private connectivity. Public internet routing with TLS and strong authentication is fine for plenty of low-sensitivity, latency-tolerant traffic — and it is simple, cheap, and quick to set up.

Private paths earn their place where one or more of these is true:

  • The traffic carries sensitive or regulated data and the organisation wants it off the public internet entirely.
  • The flow is latency- or jitter-sensitive, such as synchronous replication or real-time inference calls.
  • Predictability matters: internet paths change, and troubleshooting "it was fast yesterday" across two providers and an unknown middle is miserable.
  • An auditor is going to ask, in writing, how traffic between environments is protected — and "the public internet, but encrypted" is not the answer the business wants to give.

Whichever mix an estate ends up with, the decision should be recorded per flow, with the reason. Undocumented exceptions have a way of becoming permanent.

4. Document routing intent, not just the primary path

A link diagram shows the happy path. Operations live on the unhappy ones.

For each important cross-cloud flow, document the intended path for failover as well as for normal operation. Asymmetric routing is a recurring cause of baffling failures: after a failover, return traffic takes a different path than the request, stateful inspection on the new path has no session for it, and packets get dropped in a way that looks — from the application side — like random flakiness.

Writing down "traffic from A to B should return via X, and here is the firewall/NAT behaviour on that path" before the failover happens turns a multi-hour debugging session into a checklist lookup.

5. Treat it as one layer, with one owner

The pattern behind most of the problems above is the same: inter-cloud connections built team by team and project by project, each one reasonable in isolation, adding up to a tangle nobody fully owns or can draw accurately.

The alternative is to treat the network between clouds as its own designed layer — planned address space, consistent DNS, deliberate private paths, documented routing intent, and a single place where those decisions live. That is the layer providers in this space work in: CloudVerg, for example, covers private cloud and multi-cloud networking for US businesses across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle, with platforms such as VergMesh and VergRail for the connectivity side of the estate and zero-trust security and SOC 2 readiness work alongside it: https://cloudverg.com

Whether that layer is built in-house or with outside help, the planning questions are the same.

A short checklist

Before the next cloud, region, or major workload lands:

  • [ ] Every cross-cloud flow inventoried, with an owner and a sensitivity rating
  • [ ] Private address ranges allocated centrally, with space reserved for growth
  • [ ] One DNS naming and resolution convention, applied in every cloud
  • [ ] Per-flow decision on private vs public paths, with the reason recorded
  • [ ] Failover paths documented, including return-path and stateful-inspection behaviour
  • [ ] One team accountable for the inter-cloud layer as a whole

The boxes in the diagram will keep multiplying. The lines between them deserve the same engineering attention as what is inside them — ideally before, not after, the first cross-cloud incident makes the case the hard way.

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.
