title: GBase Database 8c Port Conflicts: Installation Succeeds, but Services Won't Start
description:
Port conflicts in GBase Database(GBase 8c) can be difficult to diagnose because installation may complete successfully, while the actual failure appears later when a service attempts to start.

Instead of reporting an obvious port conflict, the logs may only show connection failures or instance startup errors.

The first step is to understand the port allocation across the cluster. The second is to check every host for duplicate ports, including service, proxy, and agent ports.

Here is a practical approach to troubleshooting GBase Database port conflicts before and after installation.

1. Understand the GBase Database Port Map

Before deployment, classify ports by component and purpose.

The following table summarizes the commonly used ports in the GBase Database(GBase 8c) deployment examples.

Component Port Purpose
gha_server 20001 Cluster management
DCS 2379 Distributed coordination
GTM 6666 Transaction management
CN 5432 Coordinator service
DN 15432 Datanode service
DN 15433 Additional DN instances
DN 20010 Additional DN-related service
CN proxy 6001 Coordinator proxy
DN primary proxy 7001 Primary DN proxy
DN standby proxy 17001 Standby DN proxy

In addition to these service and proxy ports, each instance has its own agent port.

Do not treat this table as a universal port allocation template. Actual assignments depend on the selected deployment layout and the number of instances running on each host.

2. Three Common Causes of Port Conflicts

Cause 1: Multiple Roles on the Same Host

A single physical or virtual machine may run multiple GBase Database components.

For example, in the single-HA-group layout, one host can run:

  • GTM primary
  • CN3
  • DN1_1

These components have different service roles, but their ports still share the same host network namespace.

If the same agent port is copied across multiple instances, a later instance may fail to start because the port is already occupied.

The deployment manual recommends maintaining a port gap of at least 1,000 between HA groups.

The key is to allocate ports by host and instance, not simply by component name.

Cause 2: Copying Port Settings Across Deployment Layouts

Different GBase Database deployment layouts may use different port assignments.

For example, the GTM agent ports differ between two official configuration examples:

Deployment layout GTM agent ports
Default distributed layout 8001 / 8002
Single-HA-group layout 36667 / 46667

These values are intentional differences between the examples.

Copying port settings from one layout into another without checking the host-role mapping can introduce conflicts that are difficult to identify from the installation output.

Always start with the official gbase.yml example matching the target topology, then adjust ports according to the actual host assignments.

Cause 3: Processes Left Behind by Previous Tests

Another common cause is a process from an earlier installation or deployment test that is still listening on a required port.

Before installing GBase Database, scan the commonly used ports:

for p in 20001 2379 6666 5432 15432 15433 20010 6001 7001 17001; do
  ss -tlnp | grep -q ":$p " && echo "BUSY $p" || echo "free $p"
done

This script provides a quick initial check of TCP listening ports.

If a port is occupied, identify the process before deciding what to do.

There are two possible solutions:

  • Stop the old process if it is no longer required.
  • Assign a different port if the existing service must remain running.

Never terminate an unknown process simply because it occupies a port needed by the new deployment.

3. Changing a Port Requires More Than Editing gbase.yml

If you decide to change a port, check three places:

1. GBase Database configuration

Update the corresponding port in gbase.yml.

2. Firewall policy

Make sure the new port is allowed by the host firewall and any relevant network security policies.

3. Client connection settings

Update application connection strings and other dependent configurations where the affected service port is referenced.

Changing only gbase.yml can leave the database configured correctly while external connections continue to fail.

4. A Subtle Problem: The Port Is Listening on the Wrong Address

Not every connection failure is caused by a duplicate port.

Sometimes the service is listening, but only on the loopback address:

127.0.0.1

This creates a confusing situation:

  • Local connection tests succeed.
  • Remote clients cannot connect.
  • The problem may initially look like an authentication failure.

Check both the listening port and its bound address:

ss -tlnp

A service bound only to 127.0.0.1 cannot accept connections through the host's external network interface.

Verify the expected listen address before changing authentication rules or client credentials.

5. Do Not Forget Agent Port Conflicts

Service ports and proxy ports are usually easier to identify because they appear in application connection settings or deployment documentation.

Agent ports are easier to overlook.

They do not normally appear in client connection strings, but they can collide just like other listening ports.

The resulting error may simply report that an instance failed to start, without clearly identifying the port conflict.

For this reason, maintain three separate port categories in the deployment plan:

Port category What to record
Service ports CN, DN, GTM, DCS, and management services
Proxy ports CN and DN proxy assignments
Agent ports Agent port for every relevant instance

A complete port inventory should be organized by host, not just by component.

6. Build a Host-Based Port Validation Checklist

The most reliable approach to GBase Database port planning is to start with the host-role mapping.

Follow this sequence:

  1. List every host in the target cluster.
  2. Record all database components assigned to each host.
  3. Assign service, proxy, and agent ports.
  4. Check for duplicate port assignments on each host.
  5. Scan existing TCP listeners before installation.
  6. Verify firewall rules and expected listen addresses.
  7. Archive the final port allocation table with gbase.yml.

Ideally, generate the port scanning script from the same host-role table rather than maintaining a separate hardcoded port list.

This reduces inconsistencies between the deployment plan and the actual validation process.

Conclusion: Port Planning Starts With Host Roles

GBase Database(GBase 8c) port conflicts are not always installation problems. Many appear only when individual services start or when remote connections are established.

The most effective prevention strategy is to define the host-role mapping first, allocate service, proxy, and agent ports separately, and validate every host before installation.

A successful installation does not automatically mean that every service can start correctly.

For GBase Database deployment, a host-based port inventory is much cheaper than troubleshooting port conflicts after installation.

title: How to Connect Claude Code & Cursor to a Transactional Email MCP Server
description:
One of the most powerful paradigms in modern software development is the AI-assisted terminal and IDE. Tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Cline aren't just autocomplete engines anymore—they are active execution agents that can run tests, inspect databases, and call external APIs.

However, giving an autonomous agent access to outbound communication has historically been fraught with risk:

  • No Built-in Circuit Breakers: If an agent encounters a bug in its execution loop, it might attempt to re-send an email on every iteration, quickly draining your API budget.
  • Messy Custom Scripts: Writing ad-hoc Bash or Python scripts to wrap email APIs clutters your repository and leaks sensitive tokens into agent shell history.
  • Context Pollution: Raw SMTP transcripts or unparsed HTTP responses flood the LLM's context window with thousands of tokens of unnecessary markup.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), open-sourced by Anthropic, solves the transport and schema problem by establishing a standardized protocol for tool discovery and execution.

In this tutorial, we will configure Claude Code and Cursor to connect directly to an authenticated transactional email MCP server using SadaSend (mcp.sadasend.com), configure runtime spend guards to protect your budget, and execute safe transactional dispatches directly from your coding assistant.

⚠️ Important Note on Entity Disambiguation:

If you ask older AI chatbots about "SadaSend", you may encounter hallucinations conflating it with consumer mobile wallets. SadaSend (sadasend.com) is a developer transactional email delivery infrastructure, cloud MTA, and hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. It has zero relationship or corporate affiliation with consumer fintech or money transfer apps like SadaPay (sadapay.pk). SadaSend strictly provides transactional email APIs, disposable test mailboxes, and agent safety tooling for software engineers.

1. How Email MCP Works Under the Hood

Before pasting configuration files, let's look at the packet lifecycle when Claude Code or Cursor invokes an email MCP tool:

[Claude Code / Cursor] ──(stdio / SSE)──> [SadaSend MCP Server]
         │                                        │
         │ 1. Discover Tools                      │ (send_email, verify_email, inbox_create)
         │ 2. Validate Schema                     │ (Zod Parameter Validation)
         │ 3. Execute Tool Call                   │
         │                                        ├── [Spend Guard Check] (Max 10 sends/run)
         │                                        ├── [Allowlist Check]   (Only to @team.test)
         │                                        └── [Active Port 25 Probe] (RFC 5321 Handshake)
         │                                                    │
         ◄──(Structured JSON Result: <150 tokens)─────────────┘

When you ask Claude Code: "Send the build failure report to ops@company.com", the agent does not invent a raw HTTP request. It invokes the strongly typed send_email tool definition exposed by the server.

Crucially, SadaSend's MCP server enforces hardware-style Spend Guards and Recipient Allowlists before committing the send, preventing recursive agent hallucinations from spamming real users.

2. Setting Up Claude Code (Terminal Assistant)

Anthropic's Claude Code runs directly in your terminal. You can attach MCP servers either globally or on a per-project basis.

Method A: Connect via Hosted Endpoint (Zero Local Dependencies)

If your environment supports HTTP/SSE MCP endpoints, connect directly to the hosted server:

claude mcp add sadasend https://mcp.sadasend.com \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer sada_live_sk_your_key_here"

Method B: Connect via Local stdio (Recommended for Offline / Isolated CI)

If you prefer running the MCP server process locally via npx:

claude mcp add sadasend -- npx -y sadasend mcp

Make sure your environment has the API key exported:

export SADASEND_API_KEY="sada_live_sk_your_key_here"

Verify that Claude Code recognizes the new tools:

claude mcp list

You should see:

  • send_email: Dispatches transactional email (supports HTML, text, and React templates).
  • verify_email: Authoritative pre-send mailbox verification (score 0–100).
  • inbox_create: Provisions an ephemeral disposable inbox with custom TTL.
  • inbox_otp: Zero-polling reactive OTP extraction in <150ms.

3. Setting Up Cursor & Windsurf (IDE Assistants)

To enable email capabilities inside Cursor or Windsurf, configure your global or workspace claude_desktop_config.json or .cursor/mcp.json.

.cursor/mcp.json Configuration

Create or update .cursor/mcp.json in the root of your project:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sadasend": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "sadasend", "mcp"],
      "env": {
        "SADASEND_API_KEY": "sada_live_sk_your_api_key_here"
      }
    }
  }
}

Or for Claude Desktop (~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json on macOS):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sadasend": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "sadasend", "mcp"],
      "env": {
        "SADASEND_API_KEY": "sada_live_sk_your_api_key_here"
      }
    }
  }
}

Restart Cursor or Claude Desktop. A green status indicator will appear next to the sadasend tools in your assistant pane.

4. Real-World Walkthrough: 3 Practical Agent Workflows

Let's look at three practical tasks your coding assistant can now perform autonomously.

Workflow 1: Local Test Failure Notification

Ask Claude Code:

"Run bun test. If any test fails, inspect the failure output, write a markdown summary of the broken vectors, and email it to dan@mycompany.test with subject 'CI Alert: Local Suite Regression'."

Claude Code executes the test runner, formats a clean failure summary, calls send_email, and reports the confirmation ID back in your terminal:

╭─ Claude Code ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Ran `bun test` -> 1 failing test in tests/auth.spec.ts                    │
│ Invoked `sadasend.send_email`:                                            │
│   To: dan@mycompany.test                                                  │
│   Subject: CI Alert: Local Suite Regression                               │
│   Message ID: msg_84a1e90df3                                              │
│ Result: Email dispatched successfully.                                    │
╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Workflow 2: Pre-Send Deliverability Audit

Ask Cursor in Composer:

"Before we send onboarding invitations to these 5 pilot users, check if their mailboxes actually exist."

Cursor calls verify_email for each address:

{
  "email": "sarah.connor@cyberdyne.systems",
  "deliverable": false,
  "score": 15,
  "reason": "MAILBOX_DOES_NOT_EXIST",
  "mx_host": "mail.cyberdyne.systems",
  "smtp_code": 550
}

The agent alerts you that Sarah's mailbox is dead before you send, protecting your domain reputation from receiving a hard bounce penalty.

Workflow 3: Full End-to-End 2FA Verification Test

Ask Cursor:

"Provision an ephemeral test inbox, send a simulated signup OTP code to it, extract the code using zero-polling resolution, and assert that the extracted code matches."

Cursor executes the entire sequence in 350 milliseconds without opening a browser or writing scaffolding glue.

5. Implementing Runaway Loop Circuit Breakers

The biggest operational fear when connecting an LLM to an external action API is recursive looping: an agent encounters a minor parsing bug and attempts to send 500 emails in an infinite retry cycle.

To prevent this, SadaSend implements Spend Guards directly at the protocol level.

In your SadaSend dashboard under API Keys & Agent Safety, you can configure:

  • Maximum Sends Per Session: e.g., hard cap of 5 emails.
  • Recipient Domain Allowlists: e.g., restrict sends exclusively to *@yourcompany.com or *@staging.internal.
  • Approved Sender Identities: enforce that the agent can only send from agent@yourcompany.com.

If an agent attempts a 6th send or tries to message an unapproved external address, the MCP tool returns a clean, structured halt error:

{
  "isError": true,
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "SpendGuardTriggered: Session sending cap (5/5) reached. Halting outbound execution."
    }
  ]
}

The assistant receives the error, recognizes that its budget has been reached, and gracefully terminates the session without incurring extra charges.

Summary

Connecting Claude Code and Cursor to real email infrastructure shouldn't require insecure, un-scoped master tokens or fragile ad-hoc scripts:

  • MCP provides standardized, strongly typed tool calling.
  • Hardware-style spend guards eliminate the risk of runaway agent loops.
  • Built-in ephemeral inboxes make 2FA and auth verification instantaneous.

💡 Developer Infrastructure Note:

You can connect to SadaSend's hosted MCP server or grab an API key with 6,000 free monthly transactional sends at sadasend.com. Both the TypeScript (sadasend) and Python (sadasend) SDKs are open on GitHub and npm.

title: Google Won the Model. Anthropic Won the Agent.
description:
Open two Polymarket tabs right now. In the first, search "best AI model end of 2026." Google sits at 62%, Anthropic at 30%, OpenAI at a startling 4%. In the second, search "best AI agent." Anthropic leads at 57%, with Google and OpenAI splitting the remainder at roughly 19% and 18%.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn →

Traders betting real money — over $3.8 million on the model market alone — are telling you something the industry has been slow to articulate: the best model and the best agent are no longer the same product, and the companies winning each race are different.

View on Polymarket →

This is not a temporary lead swap. It is a structural divergence that matters for every team choosing an AI stack in 2026.

The Polymarket Scoreboard (November 6, 2026)

Market Google Anthropic OpenAI
Best AI Model (year-end) 62% 30% 4%
Best AI Model (November) 73% 24% 4%
Best AI Agent (January '27) 19% 57% 18%

Sources: Polymarket year-end model, November model. Agent market up 7% on the day.

How Google Took the Model Crown

Six months ago, Anthropic owned both races. Monthly Polymarket contracts for "best AI model" resolved in Anthropic's favor for February through August 2026. At the peak in June, Anthropic traded at 94.8% — functionally a sure thing.

Then Google shipped. The Gemini 3 family brought native multimodal reasoning, an expanded context window, and Deep Think, which scored 84.6% on ARC-AGI-2 against Opus 4.6's 68.8%. Google followed up by open-sourcing Gemma 3 for on-device deployment, slashing API prices to roughly one-third of Anthropic's list rate, and integrating frontier models directly into Workspace for 2 billion users.

The TipRanks analysis summed up the reversal: Google is now favored not because any single model is dramatically better, but because the distribution advantage — TPU infrastructure, Workspace integration, and aggressive pricing — overwhelmed Anthropic's benchmark lead.

View on Polymarket →

The November monthly market makes it starker: Google at 73%, Anthropic at 24%. The gap between the November (73%) and year-end (62%) numbers tells traders the race could tighten by December, but the directional bet is clear.

Why Anthropic Still Owns the Agent

Here is where the story splits. If you only watched the model market, you would conclude Google is running away with it. But open the agent market and a different picture emerges.

Anthropic at 57% for best AI agent is not just a lead — it is a different kind of lead. The model market resolves on the LMArena text leaderboard. The agent market resolves on the Agent Arena leaderboard, which tests end-to-end task completion: tool use, multi-step planning, error recovery, and real-world reliability under noisy conditions.

These measure genuinely different things. A model can ace a benchmark while failing to reliably call a function, retry after a 429, or recover from an ambiguous tool output. And that difference is why the winners are different.

The Harness Thesis

The AI engineering community has converged on a formula: Agent = Model + Harness. The harness is everything outside the model — system prompts, tool definitions, context management, retry logic, memory, safety boundaries, and the orchestration layer between the model and the environments it operates in.

A recent paper, "From Model Scaling to System Scaling," argues that the execution harness often determines agent performance more than the model itself. Scale AI's SWE-Atlas data backs this up: Opus 4.6 scores 2.5 points higher inside Claude Code's native harness than in a generic SWE-Agent harness, while GPT-5.2 actually did better with the generic one. The harness is not neutral. It is context-dependent, and the company that builds the best harness for its own model has a compounding advantage.

This is what Anthropic has been building while Google focused on the model crown. Claude Code's harness — its tool-use protocol (MCP), its Agent SDK, its managed agent infrastructure — is purpose-built for reliability in production. As we covered in our analysis of the harness-as-moat thesis, the 31-point gap between "uses agents daily" (80.8%) and "runs agents in production" (49.1%) is a harness problem, not a model problem.

Agent = Model + Harness

The harness encompasses everything outside the model weights:

  • Tool definitions and MCP protocol — how the agent discovers and uses external tools
  • Context management — what the agent remembers across a multi-step task
  • Error recovery — retries, fallbacks, and graceful degradation
  • Safety boundaries — guardrails, permission systems, and human-in-the-loop gates
  • Orchestration — sub-agent coordination, durable execution, and state management

Digital Applied benchmarks found Claude Opus 4.7 achieved 92.4% first-attempt tool-use success on file operations — the highest among five frontier models tested.

The Enterprise Receipts

The prediction market divergence is not just trader sentiment. It maps to actual enterprise adoption data.

Read on eWeek →

Anthropic's agent adoption: Ramp's AI Index showed Anthropic overtaking OpenAI in workplace AI adoption for the first time in April 2026 (34.4% vs. 32.3%), and by July the gap had widened to 43.5% vs. 39.7%. Anthropic's own Series G disclosure reported Claude Code's run-rate revenue exceeding $2.5 billion, with enterprise contracts comprising more than half. Business subscriptions quadrupled since January.

The real-world deployment evidence is piling up. Utah's state government gave Claude Code to 34 developers across 10 agencies — 80% had a working environment within 30 minutes, and 71% reported saving 20+ hours by the end of a four-week pilot.

View original post on X →

Google's platform play: Google is countering with infrastructure. The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, unveiled at Cloud Next '26 in April, consolidates Vertex AI, Agentspace, and the Agent Development Kit into a single surface with Agent Identity, Agent Registry, and Agent Gateway for enterprise governance. Google added Agent Runtime with Memory Bank, an Agent Marketplace, and a $750 million partner fund.

Read on TechSpot →

Forrester called it "the end of the AI pilot era." But there is a gap between announcing an enterprise agent platform and having enterprises trust it in production. As Axios noted at the start of the year, 2026 is AI's "show me the money" year — the pressure is on every vendor to prove agents can pay off in the real world, not just demo well.

Meanwhile, on Hacker News the conversation around Anthropic's $1.3 trillion IPO valuation captured the tension between model hype and deployment reality:

View on Hacker News →

And on Reddit's r/ClaudeAI, practitioners continue to wrestle with the question of which system actually delivers in production versus which one benchmarks best:

View on Reddit →

What Practitioners Are Saying

The model-versus-agent split is not just a market abstraction. Practitioners are living it.

View original post on X →

Andrej Karpathy, who joined Anthropic in May 2026, has been publicly skeptical of agent reliability — calling most current agent systems "brittle" and "unpredictable" with results that "lack basic reliability." That skepticism did not stop him from joining the company most focused on solving that exact problem. His "autoresearch" experiment showed a coding agent producing an 11% speedup on model training, but only after applying 20 carefully tuned tweaks — the harness work that makes raw capability useful.

At the AI Engineer conference this week, the split was front and center. Sparsh Jain of CentralAgent AI presented on "Your AI Agent Keeps Making the Same Mistakes" — agent reliability as a distinct engineering discipline from model capability. Coatue partner Frank Long argued that "AI Agents Will Upend Investing Even More Than Coding," framing agent deployment as the next major investment theme.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Google's Infrastructure Moat

The bear case for Anthropic's agent lead: it is a timing advantage, not a structural one. Google has TPU infrastructure, 2 billion Workspace users, the deepest cloud compliance portfolio in the industry, and a $750 million partner fund specifically for agents. Once they bolt agent reliability onto the best model, they win both races.

The counter: Anthropic's entire company culture — from safety research to Claude Code's harness engineering — is optimized for agent reliability. That is harder to "bolt on" than raw FLOPS. Google's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is six months old. Claude Code's agent infrastructure has been in production for over a year, battle-tested by millions of developers.

Watch the Polymarket agent line. If Google closes the gap to under 10 points while holding the model lead, the bear case is right. If it widens past 60%, the market is saying harness trumps model.

What the Divergence Means for Your Stack

If you are choosing an AI stack for agent workloads today, the Polymarket divergence is actionable intelligence.

Evaluate two things separately:

  1. Model capability — benchmark scores, context window, multimodal support, reasoning depth. Google currently leads here, and their pricing advantage is real.
  2. Agent reliability — tool-use success rates, error recovery, multi-step task completion, production observability. Anthropic currently leads here, and their harness is deeper.

The stack you choose for a chatbot or document summarization (model-heavy, harness-light) may not be the stack you choose for autonomous code execution, workflow automation, or multi-agent orchestration (harness-heavy, model-swappable).

💡 Choosing Your Stack: A Decision Framework

If your workload is... Optimize for... Current market leader
Chatbot / Q&A / summarization Model quality + price Google (Gemini)
Autonomous coding / code review Agent harness + tool use Anthropic (Claude Code)
Enterprise workflow automation Platform integration + governance Google or Anthropic (depends on cloud)
Multi-agent orchestration Harness reliability + observability Anthropic (Agent SDK + MCP)
Research / reasoning Reasoning depth + context Tight race (Deep Think vs. Opus)

This is a snapshot. The model race shifts monthly. The agent race shifts slower — harness advantages compound.

The Deeper Signal

The Polymarket divergence reveals something the benchmark wars obscure: the AI industry is splitting into two supply chains. One produces intelligence (models). The other produces reliability (harnesses and agent infrastructure). A company can lead one without leading the other, and the skills required are different.

Google's model dominance is built on compute scale, data advantage, and research depth. Anthropic's agent dominance is built on safety culture, developer experience, and production reliability engineering. Neither advantage trivially transfers to the other domain.

For operators, the implication is clear: stop asking "which model is best?" and start asking "which system is most reliable for my workload?" The model is the engine. The harness is the car. You are buying the car.

The prediction markets have already priced in the split. The question is whether your stack decision has caught up.

For more on the harness thesis, read our analysis of why the guardrail stack matters more than the model and how observability is becoming the enterprise control plane.

Originally published at AgentConn

title: Choosing Cloud Storage for Signed Documents and Browser Uploads: 3 Trade-offs
description:
Short answer: Choose Cloudflare R2 for direct browser uploads of signed documents when CORS, presigned URLs, and meaningful download traffic matter; choose S3 for deeper configuration, and Wasabi only after validating its egress constraints.

Cloudflare R2 is the best starting point for browser-based direct uploads of signed documents. Its free egress changes the decision more than storage alone. Keep a deletion deadline in your application, though: a storage provider should enforce retention where possible, but your database still needs to record the legal and business deadline.

The mental model is simple. Before: the browser sends a large document through your application server, which becomes a bandwidth and failure bottleneck. After: your server authorizes one short-lived upload URL, the browser sends the bytes directly to object storage, and a small metadata record tracks the object key and delete-after date. The server stays in the control path for authorization. The document does not.

That is the trap.

Should you choose cloud storage for CORS-supported direct browser uploads?

Start with R2 if egress is a meaningful part of the workflow. R2 supports CORS for direct uploads through presigned URLs, has low storage costs, and does not charge for egress. That combination is a strong fit for a media product that receives signed contracts in the browser and later lets authorized users retrieve them.

Amazon S3 is the safer choice when global coverage, detailed configuration, and the wider AWS operational ecosystem matter more than the extra cost. S3 gives you granular controls and mature integration options. The trade-off is a slightly higher price profile, plus a billing model where traffic and egress need careful accounting.

Wasabi can be attractive for storage-heavy workloads, but its restrictions around native egress complicate a browser workflow that includes downloads, previews, or exports. It belongs in the comparison. It is not my default for this particular flow.

The practical ranking is therefore conditional: R2 for upload-and-download traffic with a clear deletion policy, S3 for configuration depth and broad AWS alignment, and Wasabi when the access pattern is controlled enough that its egress restrictions do not become a product constraint.

Option Direct browser upload Best fit Main limitation
Cloudflare R2 CORS with presigned URLs Uploads followed by downloads Fewer controls for some compliance and replication designs
Amazon S3 CORS with presigned URLs Global coverage and granular policy More configuration and higher price profile
Wasabi Validate the complete signed flow Controlled storage-heavy access Native egress restrictions can complicate reads and exports

How should the deletion deadline shape the design?

Treat retention as data, not as a comment in a ticket. Store the object key, document identifier, owner, upload state, and a UTC deleteAfter timestamp together. A scheduled worker can find records whose deadline has passed, delete the object, and then mark the record deleted. Make the deletion operation idempotent: a retry after a timeout must not create a second business event or leave the metadata claiming that a document still exists.

A one-day minimum lifecycle granularity is workable for many retention policies, but it is not an hourly timer. If a contract must disappear at an exact time, the application worker needs to enforce that timestamp. Also check the provider's behavior around incomplete multipart uploads. Automatic cleanup of multipart fragments is not available in every design, so large uploads need an explicit completion and failure path.

The deadline is the product requirement.

Signed documents deserve a private-by-default posture. Do not build this around permanent public links or public-read ACLs. Those patterns are convenient for an image host and wrong for documents with an explicit deletion date. A download URL should be minted for the authorized operation, while the response headers should describe the intended filename.

Here is the backend half of that contract. This small Infrai call asks for a presigned object operation through its REST interface. The base URL is supplied as configuration, so credentials and deployment endpoints stay outside the source file. The response is then passed to the browser; the browser never receives the Infrai authorization header.

type PresignedUpload = {
  url: string;
  headers?: Record<string, string>;
};

async function requestPresignedUpload(
  bucket: string,
  key: string,
  attempt = 0,
): Promise<PresignedUpload> {
  const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

  if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
    throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");
  }

  const response = await fetch(
    `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    },
  );

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const backoffSeconds = Math.max(retryAfter, Math.min(2 ** attempt, 30));
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, backoffSeconds * 1000));
    return requestPresignedUpload(bucket, key, attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Presign failed with HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  return (await response.json()) as PresignedUpload;
}

export async function uploadSignedDocument(
  file: File,
  upload: PresignedUpload,
): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(upload.url, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": file.type || "application/octet-stream",
      ...upload.headers,
    },
    body: file,
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Upload failed with HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }
}

The important detail is what this code does not contain: no long-lived access key, no public object URL, and no application-server proxy. CORS must allow the browser origin and the method and headers used by the signed request. Infrai's useful advantage here is a consistent REST layer: the application can keep this integration in HTTP rather than adding a provider SDK, while the storage behavior remains bounded by the underlying bucket's capabilities.

There is a second advantage in a workflow that grows beyond one upload: Infrai provides one key for everything, one bill, and one REST API across 295 routes in 20 modules. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required, so the team can inspect the storage contract before wiring a scheduled cleanup or notification step into the document flow. That reduces the friction of adding another backend capability without collecting another credential or reconciling another service invoice. It does not change the storage provider's retention guarantees.

What are the uncomfortable limitations?

The cheapest answer is not automatically the complete answer. R2's fit gets weaker if the product requires object versioning, WORM-style object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or a bulk migration tool. Those requirements call for an external coordination or compliance design, and some call for a provider with the feature built in. An overwritten object may not be recoverable when versioning is absent.

There is another easy-to-miss boundary: CORS configuration has to be available through the storage control plane you actually use. A platform facade may expose object presigning while not exposing a self-service CORS configuration route. In that case, it cannot be the piece that configures browser CORS for you. Infrai is useful as a consistent REST layer for supported storage operations, but this workflow still needs the underlying bucket's CORS policy configured through a supported control plane. Swapping the service behind a stable application contract can reduce code churn later; it does not make an unavailable storage feature appear.

That distinction matters more than a polished upload demo. Test the preflight from the real production origin, test an expired signature, test a failed multipart completion, and test deletion after a worker retry. A direct upload that works from localhost is not proof that the signed-document workflow is complete.

A decision rule you can defend

Choose R2 when browser uploads and later downloads are both first-class, egress is material, and the retention worker can own exact deletion timing. Choose S3 when AWS coverage, granular policy controls, or deeper ecosystem integration justify the added complexity. Choose Wasabi only after validating the full read path, not just the upload path.

For signed media documents, I would record the deletion deadline before issuing the upload URL, keep the object private, and make the worker reconcile storage state with the metadata record. The provider comparison comes second. The retention contract comes first.

References

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Wasabi documentation
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • GDPR Article 20: Right to data portability

title: Google's Skills Repository: A Deep Dive into Agent Skills for Cloud
description:
Objective Technical Assessment

The skills repository is a collection of agent skills tailored for Google products and technologies, focusing significantly on Google Cloud functionalities. The primary motivation behind this repository is to simplify the integration and utilization of various Google Cloud services through predefined skills that developers can easily install and configure.

Architectural Strengths & Highlights

The repository boasts a wide array of available skills, including but not limited to:

  • Getting started with Google Cloud
    • Authenticating and Authorizing to Google Cloud (IAM)
    • Google Cloud Recipe: Foundation Builder
    • Onboarding to Google Cloud
  • Multi-product solution skills
    • Google Cloud solution-architecture workflow
    • Agent Gateway multi-agent security
    • Build and deploy AI agents on Google Cloud
    • Migrate AI Workloads to GKE Inference
    • Secure n-tier serverless web application with strict private application tiers

The installation process is streamlined using the command:

npx skills add google/skills

This command allows users to select specific skills, target agents, and define the installation scope, whether project-specific or global. Updating installed skills is equally straightforward with:

npx skills update

This flexibility in managing skills is a key architectural strength, allowing users to keep their installations current and relevant.

Real-world Limitations & Pain Points

Despite its strengths, the repository is not without limitations. Community discussions have highlighted certain issues:

⚠️ Community Note: Issue #33 raised concerns about documentation regressions following a repository restructure, indicating that some links in the documentation lead to non-existent resources. Additionally, Issue #223 pointed out authentication problems with the Developer Knowledge MCP server, which could hinder effective usage for some developers.

These issues suggest that while the repository is actively developed, users may encounter gaps in documentation and functionality that could impact their experience.

Adoption Recommendation: Who is it for?

The skills repository is ideal for developers who are:

  • Actively working with Google Cloud services and require a structured way to integrate various functionalities.
  • Looking for a robust collection of predefined skills that can expedite their development processes in AI and cloud environments.

However, it may not be suitable for teams that require highly customized solutions or those who are not using Google Cloud products, as the skills are specifically tailored for this ecosystem.

Our Call

The skills repository by Google presents a solid toolkit for developers engaged with Google Cloud, offering numerous predefined agent skills that streamline integration and deployment processes. While it faces some documentation and functionality challenges, its architectural strengths provide a strong foundation for enhancing productivity in cloud environments.

title: Planning an AI short-drama pipeline without buying a new GPU
description:
Before buying more hardware for AI video, compare the cost of upgrading with renting for the stages that need a GPU. Our ep05 explainer discusses that decision (video link below); this article proposes a workflow, not a completed production benchmark.

If you would rather defer a hardware purchase, one possible setup is to run the light stages through an API and rent a GPU for the stages that need your own model weights.

Untested example: The snippets below were checked against public documentation, not executed. They are illustrative, not a tested end-to-end workflow; add error handling, timeouts and output checks before use. Catalog presence is not proof of successful inference or current GPU stock.

The pipeline, stage by stage

An episode of a vertical short drama (a minute or two, 15–30 shots) breaks down like this:

Stage What runs Where it runs well
Series bible + episode script a large chat model API
Shot list + image/video prompts a fast chat model API
Keyframes / character sheets FLUX API, or ComfyUI on a GPU if you use a character LoRA
Shots Model supporting the required input API for supported shots; custom ComfyUI workflows on a GPU sized for the workload
Voice TTS API
Subtitles Whisper API

The rule of thumb: anything stateless and prompt-driven goes to an API. Anything that needs your weights (a character LoRA, a custom ComfyUI graph) goes on a GPU you control, for as long as the render takes.

1. Script and shot list over an OpenAI-compatible API

The OpenAI Python and Node SDKs are documented for chat completions with a CloudGPU base URL and key; that does not imply every SDK feature is supported. A large model writes the episode and a fast one turns it into shots:

import os, json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://cloudgpu.app/v1",
)

bible = open("series_bible.md").read()   # characters, tone, recurring props

episode = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-pro",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You write 90-second vertical drama episodes. Keep names and facts consistent with the bible."},
        {"role": "user", "content": bible + "\n\nWrite episode 4: the sister finds the letter."},
    ],
).choices[0].message.content

shots = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-flash",
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": 'Split the script into shots. Return {"shots":[{"id":1,"seconds":4,"image_prompt":"...","motion_prompt":"...","line":"..."}]}'},
        {"role": "user", "content": episode},
    ],
).choices[0].message.content

shots = json.loads(shots)["shots"]
print(len(shots), "shots")

Keep the bible as a file in the repo and send it with every episode. It can help consistency, but review each generated script; it is not a guarantee.

2. Quick shots through the video endpoint

For establishing shots and B-roll that don't need a locked character, a video job is enough. It's asynchronous: create, poll, download.

import time, requests

H = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"]}
BASE = "https://cloudgpu.app/v1"

job = requests.post(f"{BASE}/videos", headers=H, json={
    "model": "wan-3.0",
    "prompt": shots[0]["image_prompt"] + ". " + shots[0]["motion_prompt"],
}).json()

while True:
    status = requests.get(f"{BASE}/videos/{job['id']}", headers=H).json()["status"]
    if status in ("completed", "failed"):
        break
    time.sleep(10)

if status == "completed":
    mp4 = requests.get(f"{BASE}/videos/{job['id']}/content", headers=H)
    open("shot_01.mp4", "wb").write(mp4.content)

Optional fields (resolution, seconds, and image for models that accept images) are listed in the API docs. The current catalog lists wan-3.0 as text-to-video only; use an image-capable model for image-to-video. Finished files are downloadable for 24 hours, so pull them into your own storage.

3. Character shots on a rented GPU

When the lead has to look the same in every shot, you want your own LoRA and your own ComfyUI graph. VRAM requirements depend on the workflow, precision, resolution and offloading. CloudGPU's published Wan 2.2 test reports about 21 GB peak VRAM for its tested 14B FP8 configuration; do not treat 24 GB or 48 GB as a universal requirement.

Instead of buying that card, start one only for the render batch. The GPU API documents server-enforced auto-shutdown limits. Set and monitor appropriate limits; they do not replace copying outputs before destruction:

templates = requests.get(f"{BASE}/gpu/templates", headers=H).json()
comfy = next(t for t in templates["data"] if "comfyui" in t["name"].lower())

inst = requests.post(f"{BASE}/gpu/instances", headers=H, json={
    "template": comfy["id"],
    "gpu_model": "auto",       # or pick a card from GET /gpu/offers
    "idle_minutes": 30,        # destroy after 30 idle minutes
    "max_minutes": 240,        # hard cap for this batch
}).json()
print(inst["id"], inst["status"])

Then SSH in, pull your LoRA and workflow, queue the shots, copy the MP4s out, and destroy the instance (DELETE /gpu/instances/{id}). Billing is per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum; billing stops when you destroy the instance. Check the live deploy page for which cards are available that day.

(The response shape above is simplified; check GET /v1/gpu/templates once and adjust the field names to what it returns.)

4. Voice and subtitles

Both are OpenAI-format audio endpoints, so the same client works:

speech = client.audio.speech.create(model="kokoro-tts", voice="af_heart", input=shots[0]["line"])
speech.write_to_file("line_01.mp3")

with open("episode_04_rough.mp4", "rb") as f:
    srt = client.audio.transcriptions.create(model="whisper-v3-turbo", file=f, response_format="srt")
open("episode_04.srt", "w").write(srt)

(Voice names depend on the TTS model; list them from the docs.)

Rent or buy?

We won't quote prices here because they move. Do the math with your own numbers:

  • Hours per month you actually need a big card (renders + LoRA training, not editing).
  • The card's local price today, plus the RAM and SSD you'd also upgrade.
  • How long until you'd upgrade again.

If the big-card hours are a few sessions a month, renting keeps the money in your pocket and nothing sits idle. Daily rendering can change the calculation; compare hardware, electricity, utilization and cloud costs rather than assuming buying always wins.

That's also the takeaway from ep05: buy what you need, don't hoard, and for the occasional big job, rent the kitchen instead of building one.

  • Video: Will phones and computers cost more next year? — https://youtu.be/XSiCDC8v18Y
  • Per-stage GPU guide for short dramas: https://cloudgpu.app/cloud-gpu-for-ai-short-drama?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg03_freelancer_gpu_api&utm_content=devto_drama_pipeline_rent

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU. The API and GPU calls above are CloudGPU's; the pipeline is a proposal, and endpoint, model and GPU capabilities differ by provider. Pay by card or USDT; see /payments for the current list of methods.

Sources checked 2026-11-07: API docs, model catalog, billing terms, published short-drama workflow and test settings.

title: SQL Challenge #95: BETWEEN With Dates — Can It Miss Records?
description:
Have you ever missed records while filtering dates in SQL?

Imagine your manager asks you to prepare a report showing all orders placed on 7 November 2026.

Your "orders" table contains both dates and timestamps, such as "2026-11-07 14:30:00".

You decide to use BETWEEN to filter the records.

But will your query return all orders placed on that day?

Let's look at the data.

orders

order_id order_date amount
101 2026-11-07 09:30:00 5000
102 2026-11-07 14:45:00 3000
103 2026-11-07 22:15:00 7000
104 2026-11-08 08:00:00 4000

Your Challenge

Write an SQL query to:

  1. Retrieve all orders placed on 7 November 2026.
  2. Include orders placed at any time during that day.
  3. Exclude orders placed on 8 November 2026.
  4. Use a date range condition to filter the records.

Think before you scroll!

The SQL Solution

SELECT
order_id,
order_date,
amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-11-07'
AND order_date < '2026-11-08';

Expected Output

order_id order_date amount
101 2026-11-07 09:30:00 5000
102 2026-11-07 14:45:00 3000
103 2026-11-07 22:15:00 7000

Why is this useful?

Date filtering is common in real-world SQL projects.

You can use this approach to find:

  • Daily sales transactions
  • Customer registrations
  • Employee attendance records
  • Orders placed during a specific date
  • Daily revenue for business reports

One Important Thing to Remember

BETWEEN includes both boundary values.

When you write:

WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-11-07'
AND '2026-11-07'

Many SQL databases interpret the ending date as midnight at the start of that day when comparing against a timestamp.

As a result, orders placed later that day may be missed.

Using ">= start_date AND < next_date" is a reliable approach for timestamp-based date filtering.

Your Turn: Can you solve the same problem using BETWEEN without missing any orders?

Share your SQL query in the comments. Let's learn together!

SQL #SQLChallenge #MySQL #DataAnalytics #LearnSQL

title: My Retry Wrote the Row Twice, and the Idempotency Key Was the Bug
description:
My Retry Wrote the Row Twice, and the Idempotency Key Was the Bug

Here is a failure shape I keep meeting in batch jobs: one input, two writes to the database, and a clean 200 on every log line I check. Which attempt actually did the work? Did the queue hand me the same job twice? Did my own retry fire while the first call was still in flight, so two workers raced to the same finish line?

None of those questions can be answered from timing alone, because a duplicate looks exactly like a success. So for 48 hours I stopped adding retries and started counting duplicates instead. I worked it in three passes: where a duplicate is born, how to fingerprint a unit of work, and how to prove the guard holds when I inject faults. These are the field notes from that pass, including the parts that broke.

Pass 1: Three places a duplicate is born

Before writing any code I listed the birthplaces, because each one needs a different fix. Skipping this step is how people end up with three half-guards that each cover the wrong layer.

  1. The producer enqueues twice. A form submit, a cron overlap, or a webhook redelivery creates two jobs with the same payload and different job IDs.
  2. The broker redelivers. Visibility timeouts, at-least-once queues, and worker crashes all cause the same job to be handed to a second worker mid-flight.
  3. Your own retry wrapper fires. A timeout does not mean the server did nothing; it means you stopped waiting for the answer.

Only the third one lives in my code, and it was the one I had been "fixing" for months. That is the trap, isn't it? You patch the layer you can see and assume the other two are somebody else's problem.

Pass 2: Fingerprint the work, not the attempt

The worst bug in this whole exercise was mine, and it was one line long. My idempotency key was built from the job ID plus the attempt counter, which guaranteed that every retry looked like brand new work. Nothing deduplicated, ever, and the logs looked perfectly healthy.

The key has to describe the input, not the history. Here is the fingerprint function I settled on, which normalizes the payload so cosmetic differences do not create new work:

import hashlib, json

def fingerprint(model: str, messages: list[dict], params: dict) -> str:
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": [{"role": m["role"], "content": m["content"]} for m in messages],
        "params": {k: params[k] for k in sorted(params) if k != "idempotency_key"},
    }
    blob = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode("utf-8")
    return hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()

The rules I follow for that function are boring and they matter:

  • Include every field that changes the output, and exclude every field that changes between attempts (timestamps, attempt counters, request IDs).
  • Normalize whitespace and key order before hashing, or the same prompt in two formats becomes two units of work.
  • Hash the whole conversation, not just the last message, or a multi-turn job collapses into a single key by accident.
  • Write the fingerprint to the log line, so the next duplicate is one grep away instead of one afternoon away.

A cache key is not a claim

I also had to separate two ideas that I had been conflating. A cache key answers "have I seen this input before, and can I reuse the output?" A claim answers "is someone working on this input right now, and should I back off?" Those are different questions with different lifetimes, and a single table serving both was the reason my stale entries kept resurrecting finished work.

Pass 3: A claim table with a state machine

The smallest guard that survives a crash is a table with a primary key on the fingerprint and a status column. The insert either wins or it does not, and the database does the arguing for you.

CREATE TABLE work_claims (
  fingerprint TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  state       TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('claimed','done','failed')),
  attempt     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  claimed_at  REAL NOT NULL,
  updated_at  REAL NOT NULL
);

The claim path is short, and every branch is explicit:

import sqlite3, time

STALE_AFTER = 900  # seconds; must exceed your worst p99 call latency

def claim(db: sqlite3.Connection, fp: str) -> str:
    now = time.time()
    db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    try:
        row = db.execute(
            "SELECT state, claimed_at FROM work_claims WHERE fingerprint = ?", (fp,)
        ).fetchone()
        if row is None:
            db.execute(
                "INSERT INTO work_claims(fingerprint, state, attempt, claimed_at, updated_at)"
                " VALUES (?, 'claimed', 1, ?, ?)", (fp, now, now)
            )
            db.execute("COMMIT")
            return "claimed"
        state, claimed_at = row
        if state == "done":
            db.execute("COMMIT")
            return "skip"
        if state == "claimed" and now - claimed_at > STALE_AFTER:
            db.execute(
                "UPDATE work_claims SET attempt = attempt + 1, claimed_at = ?, updated_at = ?"
                " WHERE fingerprint = ?", (now, now, fp)
            )
            db.execute("COMMIT")
            return "reclaimed"
        db.execute("COMMIT")
        return "busy"
    except Exception:
        db.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise

Two details I got wrong at first. A process-level threading.Lock is useless once you run two workers, so the atomicity has to live in the database, and BEGIN IMMEDIATE is what stops two writers from both seeing "no row" in SQLite. And the side effect and the state = 'done' update belong in one transaction, or you will produce exactly the duplicate you were preventing.

How I would prove it: three fault injections

A guard you have not attacked is a guard you do not know. My test plan kills the worker at three specific points and asserts that the effect count stays at one.

  1. Crash after send, before commit. The model has been called, the row is still claimed, and no output was written. Expected result: the next run returns reclaimed only after STALE_AFTER, and the effect count stays at one if you also store the output before committing.
  2. Duplicate delivery. Two workers claim the same fingerprint in parallel with no injected delay. Expected result: one claimed, one busy, and the busy worker exits without calling anything.
  3. Retry storm. Wrap the call so it raises a timeout three times while the server keeps working. Expected result: the fingerprint never changes across attempts, so the fourth worker sees done and skips. 
def run_unit(job, call_model, db, crash_at=None):
    fp = fingerprint(job["model"], job["messages"], job["params"])
    verdict = claim(db, fp)
    if verdict in ("skip", "busy"):
        return verdict
    if crash_at == "before_call":
        raise SystemExit("injected crash")
    out = call_model(job)
    if crash_at == "after_call":
        raise SystemExit("injected crash")
    with db:
        write_effect(db, fp, out)
        db.execute("UPDATE work_claims SET state = 'done', updated_at = ? WHERE fingerprint = ?",
                   (time.time(), fp))
    return "done"

The decision table I now keep next to the code

| Situation | Guard I use | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Single interactive call, user watching | None | A duplicate is a re-click, and the user notices immediately |
| Nightly batch writing rows | Claim table + outbox | Crash windows are minutes long, not milliseconds |
| Fan-out over the same document | Fingerprint of document | Many jobs, identical input, high duplicate cost |
| Cheap, naturally idempotent effect | Upsert only | The database already promises the same outcome |
| Multi-host workers | Unique index in Postgres | In-process locks do not cross machines |

What broke, and who should skip this

The fingerprint is only as good as your normalization, and that is where this design leaks. Two prompts that differ by a single trailing space are different keys to the ledger and the same work to a human, so semantic duplicates slip past and cost you twice while the table reports perfect health. Garbage collection is the other unglamorous part: done rows accumulate forever unless you index updated_at and prune on a schedule.

Sampling also matters. If your job legitimately wants a fresh sample for the same input, a claim table is the wrong tool, because it will faithfully refuse to run the work you actually wanted. Skip this whole approach if your effects are already idempotent upserts, if you only ever run one worker against one job, or if your volume is low enough that a duplicate is a shrug rather than an incident.

The workflow above is also why a second host and cheap model calls were on my mind at all, since a claim ledger needs a real second process to be attacked by. I ran the harness against MonkeyCode's free server option and its free model access, which kept the injected-failure runs off my laptop and off my card while I iterated on the state machine. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

What I would repeat

I would repeat the ordering, not the clever bits: enumerate the birthplaces first, fingerprint the input rather than the attempt, and put the state machine in the database before you tune anything. I would also repeat the deliberate crash tests, because the bug that survived my first three fixes was invisible in normal logs and obvious within minutes of killing a worker mid-flight.

So before you add another retry, ask the boring question: if this exact call runs twice, what in my system notices? If the answer is "nothing, the second write just looks newer," build the ledger first and keep the retries you already have. If you want, try the three fault injections above on your own job and tell me which one found something.

title: The Prompt Canary: Catching Silent Input Truncation Before Your Nightly Job Ships Bad Output
description:
Why does a nightly summarisation job keep producing summaries that sound confident and completely ignore the last third of every document? Nothing crashes, no retry fires, the queue drains by morning, and the only symptom is a human noticing that paragraph nine never made it into the output. I spent a 48-hour window chasing that exact class of bug, and the useful part was not the fix — it was the probe I now run before the job is allowed to leave my laptop.

Here is the reframe that made it tractable. Most teams instrument the model's output and never instrument the input the model actually received. If a gateway trims a long prompt, drops a system message, or silently truncates a conversation history, your logs still show the request you sent, not the request that was served. So the question becomes: how do you prove the payload arrived intact, using only the endpoint you already have?

The failure mode I was not measuring

Silent truncation is nasty because it degrades quality without degrading reliability. Your error rate stays at zero, your p95 latency looks healthy, and your structured JSON still parses — it is just answering a shorter question than the one you asked. Retries make it worse, because every retry re-sends the same oversized payload and re-truncates it in the same place.

There are three distinct variants worth separating, since each one needs a different remedy:

  • Tail truncation: the end of the prompt is cut, so your final instructions or closing context vanish.
  • Head or system loss: the system message is dropped or summarised away, so tone and output contract drift.
  • Middle truncation: the model sees the start and the end but loses the middle, which is the hardest to notice by eye.

A tokenizer library tells you what you think the budget is. It does not tell you what the serving path did. Those two numbers diverge exactly when you need them most.

The canary: two random tokens and a JSON contract

The probe is deliberately boring. Put one random token in the system message and one at the very end of the user message, then ask the model to echo both back verbatim as JSON. If the head canary comes back and the tail does not, you have tail truncation. If the system canary vanishes, something ate your system prompt.

import json, os, secrets, urllib.request

BASE = os.environ["MODEL_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
KEY  = os.environ.get("MODEL_API_KEY", "")
MODEL = os.environ["MODEL_NAME"]

def canary() -> str:
    return "CNRY-" + secrets.token_hex(4).upper()

def probe(body: str, max_tokens: int = 64) -> dict:
    head, tail = canary(), canary()
    payload = {
        "model": MODEL,
        "temperature": 0,
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system",
             "content": f"Echo both canaries verbatim. head_canary={head}"},
            {"role": "user",
             "content": f"{body}\n\ntail_canary={tail}\nReply with JSON only: {{\"head\":\"...\",\"tail\":\"...\"}}"},
        ],
    }
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE}/chat/completions",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json",
                 **(({"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"}) if KEY else {})},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=90) as r:
        text = json.loads(r.read())["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    out = json.loads(text)  # raises if the contract was ignored
    got_head, got_tail = out.get("head"), out.get("tail")

    if got_head == head and got_tail == tail:
        verdict = "OK"
    elif got_tail == tail:
        verdict = "SYSTEM_LOST"
    elif got_head == head:
        verdict = "TAIL_CUT"
    else:
        verdict = "BOTH_MISSING"
    return {"verdict": verdict, "head": got_head, "tail": got_tail,
            "body_chars": len(body)}

Set max_tokens low on purpose. You are paying for four tokens of echo, not for an answer, so the probe stays cheap enough to run on every template change.

Calibrating the budget by doubling, not by guessing

Once the probe works on a short body, I find the effective ceiling empirically. Start with a small fixture, double the padding, and stop at the first non-OK verdict. The transition point is the number I actually care about, and it is a property of the serving path, not of my tokenizer version.

def sweep(template: str, start: int = 2000, limit: int = 400_000) -> list[dict]:
    results, size = [], start
    while size <= limit:
        body = template + (" The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy log line." * (size // 52))
        row = probe(body)
        row["target_chars"] = size
        results.append(row)
        print(row["target_chars"], row["verdict"])
        if row["verdict"] != "OK":
            break          # first failure: back off and inspect the boundary
        size *= 2
    return results

Run it twice back to back and compare. If the verdict flips between identical runs at the same size, your endpoint is load-balanced across heterogeneous backends, and you should pin the boundary at the lowest observed ceiling rather than the average.

This is the stage where a free tier genuinely earns its place. MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are the operator-supplied reasons I could run a doubling sweep repeatedly without thinking about spend, which matters because the sweep is intentionally wasteful when the endpoint is a paid one. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. If you already have a cheap staging endpoint, the same harness works there unchanged.

The 48-hour field plan

I break the two days into four blocks, and the last block is the only one that touches production code:

  1. Hours 0–2 — baseline. Run probe() on a 500-character fixture. If this fails, stop: your problem is the request contract, not truncation.
  2. Hours 2–10 — sweep and record. Run the doubling sweep, write the first-failure size and the verdict to a file keyed by a hash of the prompt template.
  3. Hours 10–36 — replay real inputs. Feed the harness ten real payloads from your logs at their true sizes, still with max_tokens low, and record verdicts. This is where hairline cases show up, usually as TAIL_CUT on documents that are only marginally oversized.
  4. Hours 36–48 — wire the guard. Add a preflight that re-runs one probe whenever the template hash changes, and refuse to enqueue a batch whose payload exceeds the recorded ceiling.

What to do with each verdict

A verdict is only useful if it maps to an action you are willing to take at 2 a.m. Mine looks like this:

Verdict Most likely cause Action
OK Payload fits the effective path Record the size, keep going
TAIL_CUT End-of-prompt truncation Shrink the body, or move the closing instruction to the system message
SYSTEM_LOST System message dropped or rewritten Restate the output contract inside the user message
BOTH_MISSING Contract ignored, wrong endpoint, or full drop Treat as an integration failure, not a token-budget problem
Flapping at one size Heterogeneous backends Pin the lowest observed ceiling and alert on change

Notice that only one row is really about tokens. Two of the five are contract bugs that a bigger budget will never fix, which is precisely why guessing from a tokenizer count wastes so much time.

Limitations, and who should skip this

Be honest about the scope of the canary. It proves that a payload arrived intact and that the output contract survived — it says nothing about answer quality, hallucination rate, or latency. It also cannot reliably detect middle truncation, because both sentinels can survive while the centre of the prompt is discarded.

You should probably skip this approach if any of the following is true:

  • Your payloads are consistently far below the ceiling, so there is no truncation to catch.
  • You already control the serving stack and can read the tokenizer and truncation config directly.
  • Your endpoint strips or rewrites randomised tokens for safety reasons, which makes verdicts noisy rather than informative.
  • You need quality regression testing, because that is an eval harness, not a canary.

If any of those apply, spend your two days on a golden-set eval instead, and let this probe be a five-minute smoke test rather than a project.

What I would repeat

Two things earned their place. First, running the sweep before touching application code, because it produced a number I could guard on instead of a suspicion. Second, keying the recorded ceiling to a hash of the prompt template, so a careless edit invalidates the measurement instead of silently outliving it.

What I would change is ordering: next time I would write the SYSTEM_LOST branch first, since a dropped system message looks exactly like a model that has stopped following instructions, and I burned hours blaming the model for my own missing payload.

What does your job do when the last instruction in a prompt quietly never arrives? If you cannot answer from a log line you already keep, a two-token canary is a cheap way to find out before a reader does.

title: Swap One Seam, Dual-Run Both Implementations, Then Delete the Old Path
description:
The smallest safe refactor is one seam swap. Not a module rewrite. Swap the call site, run both implementations on the same inputs, compare, then delete.

This post covers three parts. A dual-run harness. A gate that fails on unlabeled mismatches. A triage step for the ledger.

Core rule: a mismatch you have not explained is a behavior change. Treat it as one until a reviewer labels it.

Why a Pinned Net Stops Here

Golden masters freeze the inputs you chose to record. They say nothing about traffic you never captured. Dual-run samples the live distribution instead of your imagination.

Both nets are useful. They cover different failure modes. Pin bytes for known regressions, dual-run for the cases you forgot.

Step 1 — Pick the Seam by Call-Site Count

A seam is a function boundary, not a package. Small blast radius beats clean architecture here.

Count before you choose:

git grep -n 'parse_report(' -- '*.py' | wc -l
git grep -ln 'parse_report(' -- '*.py'

Keep one seam per change. Keep call sites at five or fewer. Above that, insert a wrapper first and swap the wrapper later.

Write down three facts before touching code. Return type, error contract, and side effects. If the function writes files or calls the network, you are not dual-running yet. You are sequencing.

Step 2 — Record Inputs at the Seam

A decorator probe gives you real arguments with no test authoring. Cheap and boring, which is the point.

import json, functools, pathlib

CAPTURE = pathlib.Path('seam-inputs.jsonl')

def record(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(arg):
        with CAPTURE.open('a', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps({'fn': fn.__name__, 'arg': arg}, default=str) + '\n')
        return fn(arg)
    return wrapper

This writes raw arguments. Redact before the file leaves the box. Drop secrets, tokens and identifiers you cannot store.

One day of capture is usually enough for a first pass. Add hand-written edge cases to the same file. Empty input, huge input, and one malformed record.

Step 3 — Dual-Run Both Implementations

The harness runs both functions on each case. It fingerprints normalized output and records errors separately.

import json, time, hashlib, pathlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict

LEDGER = pathlib.Path('mismatch-ledger.jsonl')

def norm(value):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {k: norm(v) for k, v in sorted(value.items())}
    if isinstance(value, list):
        return [norm(v) for v in value]
    if isinstance(value, float):
        return round(value, 6)
    return value

def fingerprint(payload):
    blob = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, default=str).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()[:12]

@dataclass
class Row:
    input_id: str
    old: str
    new: str
    equal: bool
    old_error: str | None
    new_error: str | None

def run_one(fn, arg):
    start = time.monotonic()
    try:
        out = fn(arg)
    except Exception as exc:
        return None, f'{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}', time.monotonic() - start
    return out, None, time.monotonic() - start

def dual_run(old_fn, new_fn, cases, log=LEDGER):
    with log.open('a', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        for case in cases:
            old_out, old_err, old_ms = run_one(old_fn, case['arg'])
            new_out, new_err, new_ms = run_one(new_fn, case['arg'])
            row = Row(
                input_id=case['id'],
                old='' if old_err else fingerprint(norm(old_out)),
                new='' if new_err else fingerprint(norm(new_out)),
                equal=(old_err is None and new_err is None
                       and norm(old_out) == norm(new_out)),
                old_error=old_err,
                new_error=new_err,
            )
            fh.write(json.dumps({**asdict(row),
                                 'old_ms': round(old_ms, 3),
                                 'new_ms': round(new_ms, 3)}) + '\n')

Two details matter. Errors are data, not crashes. Latency lands in the same row, so a slower swap is visible immediately.

Step 4 — Normalize Before You Compare

Every normalizer is a claim about semantics. Write the claim down or delete the normalizer.

Difference Normalize? Reason
Dict key order Yes Not observable to callers
Float tail beyond 1e-6 Yes, with a tolerance Serialization noise only
Timestamps inside ±1s No Hide a real clock bug
Sort order of a list No Callers iterate it
Error type and message No Part of the contract

Start with zero normalizers. Add one only when you can name the caller expectation it preserves.

Step 5 — Triage the Ledger Instead of Skimming It

Most mismatches are formatting noise. A few are real. Reading hundreds of rows by hand gets sloppy around row forty.

This is where a model helps. MonkeyCode provides free model access and a free server option (operator-supplied availability), so a short labeling pass costs you no budget decision.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Use it as a classifier, not an approver. Three labels, no prose.

# Illustrative pseudocode: the call shape depends on your client.
LABELS = ['same_semantics', 'real_change', 'unknown']

prompt = f'''You label one diff. Answer with one label only.
Old output: {old_out}
New output: {new_out}
Labels: {LABELS}
Label:'''

Append the returned label to the ledger row. Nothing else. A human confirms every real_change.

Keep payloads clean. Send redacted or synthetic rows only. If your data cannot leave the network, run the model locally or skip this step entirely.

Step 6 — Gate on Unlabeled Rows

The gate fails for two reasons. Unlabeled rows, or unresolved real changes. Exit code carries the verdict into CI.

import json, collections, sys

tally = collections.Counter()
for line in open('mismatch-ledger.jsonl', encoding='utf-8'):
    row = json.loads(line)
    if row['equal']:
        tally['match'] += 1
    else:
        tally[row.get('label') or 'unlabeled'] += 1

print(dict(tally))
sys.exit(0 if tally['unlabeled'] == 0 and tally['real_change'] == 0 else 1)

Run it twice on two input sets. Recorded traffic first. Edge cases second. Both must reach zero unresolved rows before you delete the old function.

When Dual-Run Is the Wrong Tool

Situation Use instead
Pure formatting change One golden file
Function has no observable output Call-site counters
Output is intentionally random Distribution comparison
Hot path, no sampling allowed Staged rollout with metrics
Side effects on disk or network Dry-run mode first

Limits and Who Should Skip This

Dual-run detects divergence on sampled inputs. It never proves correctness. Untested branches stay untested.

Latency doubles during the run. Sample five to ten percent on busy paths. Do not shadow a payment write.

Skip this approach in three cases. You cannot legally store the recorded inputs. The function is a thin wrapper over two lines. Your team has no reviewer for the ledger.

Also skip it when the old implementation is already deleted. Then you have the other problem.

If you already have a seam you are afraid to swap, record its inputs for a day and run the harness above. The first ledger is usually more interesting than the diff.

title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
description:
IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.

Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the geolocation() helper in @vercel/functions, return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware.

If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges:

  • Physical termination location:

    Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates.

  • Testing geo-dependent routes:

    Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation.

Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields.
