title: How to obfuscate a Minecraft plugin (free, step by step)
description:
Assume your premium plugin will be decompiled the day it goes on sale. Anyone can open the jar in a decompiler and read your code like the source, including the license check you spent an evening on.

Obfuscation won't make that impossible. It turns readable code into a puzzle, so copying your logic or patching out a check takes far more work. The catch: a careless obfuscation pass is the fastest way to ship a plugin that doesn't load. Paper and Spigot find your main class by name and call your event handlers by reflection. Rename the wrong thing and the server throws ClassNotFoundException at startup.

This guide shows two ways to do it safely: the quick way, with a free hosted obfuscator that writes the keep rules for you, and the by-hand way with ProGuard. Then a checklist to test the jar before you sell it.

What obfuscation does, and what it doesn't

It does: rename your classes, methods and fields to a, b, c, encrypt string constants, and scramble control flow. A decompiler still produces Java, but it reads like noise.

It doesn't: stop someone determined, or stop a buyer from sharing the jar. It raises the cost of reading and patching your code. For sharing you need a license key per buyer (more at the end). The two work best together: obfuscation hides the check, and the license makes a shared jar useless.

The quick way: free hosted obfuscation

I build SunLicense, a licensing service for plugin and app sellers. Its free plan includes 3 obfuscation runs a month, which covers a release or two. It runs ProGuard, yGuard and Skidfuscator on its servers, and it reads your jar to find what must keep its name, so you don't write keep rules.

Step 1: Create a free account

Sign up with Google, GitHub, Discord or email. No credit card.

Step 2: Developers → Obfuscation → Java

Open Obfuscation under Developers in the sidebar and pick Java. (The same page handles JavaScript, Python and Lua for FiveM, if you sell those too.)

Step 3: Pick Maximum or ProGuard

Engine What it does Pick it when
Maximum (recommended) ProGuard renames, then Skidfuscator adds control flow and string encryption You want the strongest protection and will test the result
ProGuard Renames classes, methods and fields You want the safe standard, or Maximum broke something
yGuard Renames only You need the most compatible option
Skidfuscator Control flow and strings, keeps names You want flow and string protection without renaming

Start with Maximum. If your plugin leans heavily on reflection (NMS, Gson models, a command framework) and something misbehaves in testing, run the same jar again with ProGuard.

Step 4: Upload the built jar

Build the jar you actually ship (with Shadow, ./gradlew shadowJar) and drop it in. A .jar or a .zip of several jars, up to 100 MB, Java up to 25.

SunLicense reads the jar and keeps the names that must survive: the main class in plugin.yml, paper-plugin.yml or bungee.yml, velocity-plugin.json, Fabric and Forge entry points and mixins, META-INF/services, @EventHandler and @Subscribe methods, enums and serialisable types.

One detail that saves a lot of pain: if you sell on BuiltByBit or Voxel Shop with a download placeholder (a string like %%__SUNLICENSE__%% the store replaces with the buyer's key), string encryption would hide that string from the store. Classes that hold a placeholder are never string-encrypted, so key injection keeps working.

Optional: Advanced options has a Keep unrenamed list for extra packages or classes (for example com.example.api.**), and lets you add library jars you compile against if the report mentions missing classes.

Step 5: Run, then download three files

Choose Obfuscate and watch the live log. It runs as a background task, so you can close the page and come back; results are kept for 7 days and stay on the History tab. You get:

  1. The obfuscated jar: the one you upload to your store.
  2. The mapping file: keep it for every release. When a buyer sends a stack trace full of a.b.c, ProGuard's retrace tool turns it back into your real names.
  3. A short report on the run, including any warnings.

Releasing often? The same run works from a release script with the CLI:

sunlicense obfuscate build/libs/MyPlugin-1.0-all.jar --profile release -o dist/

The by-hand way: ProGuard

If you'd rather run it yourself, ProGuard is the safe choice. What you must keep:

Keep Why
The main: class in plugin.yml (and paper-plugin.yml, bungee.yml, velocity-plugin.json) The server loads it by exact name
@EventHandler methods Found by annotation; shrinking removes "unused" methods
ConfigurationSerializable classes Saved configs store the class name
Enum values() / valueOf() Used when reading config values back
Anything loaded by reflection The name is a string in your code

A starting config for a shaded jar:

-injars  build/libs/MyPlugin-1.0-all.jar
-outjars build/obf/MyPlugin-1.0.jar
-libraryjars <java.home>/jmods/java.base.jmod(!**.jar;!module-info.class)
-libraryjars libs/paper-api.jar

# Plugins are loaded by reflection: don't shrink or optimise
-dontshrink
-dontoptimize
-keepattributes *Annotation*,Signature,InnerClasses,EnclosingMethod,SourceFile,LineNumberTable

-keep public class com.example.myplugin.MyPlugin { *; }
-keepclassmembers class * { @org.bukkit.event.EventHandler <methods>; }
-keep class * implements org.bukkit.configuration.serialization.ConfigurationSerializable { *; }
-keepclassmembers enum * {
    public static **[] values();
    public static ** valueOf(java.lang.String);
}

-printmapping build/obf/mapping.txt
-dontwarn

Add a -keep line for every package you reach by reflection. For more strength, run Skidfuscator after ProGuard: turn on string encryption first, test, then control flow, and test again. Exclude the class holding any store placeholder from string encryption.

Test the jar before you sell it

Never upload an obfuscated jar you haven't started. Five minutes:

  • Start a clean Paper server with only your plugin. No errors in the console.
  • Run every command, including tab completion.
  • Trigger your main events (join, break a block, open your GUI).
  • Restart the server: config and saved data load back.
  • Test on every server version listed on your store page.
  • Open the jar in a decompiler yourself and check it reads like noise.

If something fails, the error names the class. Keep that package unrenamed, or step down from Maximum to ProGuard, and run again.

Obfuscation is half the job

An obfuscated jar that anyone can run is still a jar anyone can share. The other half is one license key per buyer, checked on startup: a shared key then shows up on too many servers, and a leaked jar names its buyer. I wrote that up separately: How to add license keys to a Minecraft plugin in 10 minutes.

Licensing and obfuscation are both on SunLicense's free plan, with no cut of your sales. See how it works for Minecraft plugins.

This article was written with the help of an AI assistant and reviewed by me before publishing.

title: Node.js Message Queue Setup — Create and Publish Background Tasks for 3,000 Subscribers
description:
Short answer: Use Node.js to create a message queue, publish a background task, and let workers fan a shipment update out to subscribers; Infrai is a reasonable fit when one key and one REST surface matter more than replayable history.

A marketplace shipment update has two different jobs: accept the event quickly, then fan it out without making the checkout or seller dashboard wait. I would put a queue at that boundary. The producer publishes one well-formed job; workers consume it, deliver the update to subscribers, and acknowledge only after the work is complete.

The trade-off is latency versus operational cost. A managed queue keeps the handoff small and observable, while a specialist event platform buys richer replay and fanout semantics at the price of another system to operate. For a solo team, that boundary matters more than choosing the fanciest broker.

Then test the failure path.

What should the queue own?

The queue should own durable delivery of a shipment-update task, not the business workflow around it. A message can contain a shipment ID, an event ID, and the subscriber slice to process. Keep the message under 256 KB, use a stable queue name such as shipment-updates-prod, and make the consumer idempotent: standard queues are at-least-once.

That last point is easy to skip when the happy path works. It is also where duplicate email, duplicate push notifications, or repeated seller callbacks begin. Store the event ID with the side effect, or make the downstream operation accept an idempotency key. A retry should be boring.

Infrai belongs at this boundary when the marketplace already wants several backend capabilities behind one REST API. The same bearer key can cover the queue handoff, and one bill is easier to reconcile than a collection of service credentials. That is an operating advantage, not a reason to pretend the queue has event-log semantics.

Here is the smallest producer boundary. It creates the queue once, then publishes a task through the same REST base URL and bearer key. The retry policy handles 429 responses and uses an idempotency key so a transport retry does not intentionally create a second task.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const queue = "shipment-updates-prod";
const eventId = "shipment_evt_20261024_0007";

async function request(route: "create" | "publish", body: unknown, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const endpoint = route === "create"
    ? "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/create"
    : "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish";
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`Queue request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const waitSeconds = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter
      : 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitSeconds * 1000));
  }
  throw new Error("Queue request exhausted its retries");
}

await request("create", { queue }, `queue-create-${queue}`);
await request("publish", {
  queue,
  message: {
    event_id: eventId,
    shipment_id: "shp_1842",
    subscriber_ids: ["sub_17", "sub_42"],
    kind: "shipment_status_changed",
  },
}, `shipment-event-${eventId}`);

The create call belongs in deployment or provisioning, not in every request path. In production, treat an already-existing queue as a successful desired state, then alert on any other create error. Publishing is the hot path.

How should Node.js setup create and publish a message queue?

For 3,000 subscribers, I would publish one task that identifies the shipment event and lets workers partition the subscriber work, or publish a bounded batch when the message remains comfortably below the body limit. The queue is a handoff, not a topic with unlimited replay. Delayed messages can be scheduled for at most 7 days, retention tops out at 30 days, and acknowledging removes a message. There is no Kafka-style replay or multiple-consumer-group history.

That boundary also clarifies the provider choice. AWS SQS is a strong fit when visibility-timeout controls, mature worker integrations, and a large cloud operating model matter; its visibility timeout must be sized around the longest processing attempt. RabbitMQ is better when routing patterns, explicit exchanges, and low-latency broker control are central. Kafka is the better choice when an event log, replay, and several independent consumer groups are first-class requirements. None of those differences is cosmetic.

Inngest and Trigger.dev suit teams that want application-oriented background workflows with developer-facing retries. Temporal is the stronger choice for durable, long-running orchestration, especially when the process has several dependent steps. BullMQ is attractive when the team wants a Node.js-native queue backed by Redis and is willing to own that infrastructure. Those are real alternatives, but they solve a wider or more application-specific problem than this two-route producer boundary.

Option Best fit Boundary to accept
Infrai One REST handoff and shared backend credentials No replayable log or consumer groups
SQS AWS-native queue operations Visibility settings and cloud coupling
RabbitMQ Explicit routing and broker control More broker operations to own
Kafka Replay and independent consumer groups A larger event-streaming system
BullMQ Node.js workers with Redis Redis becomes part of the stack

This is a boundary decision, not a popularity contest.

Infrai fits the narrower case where the marketplace wants queue creation and publishing behind one REST surface already used for other backend capabilities. One key and one bill remove a set of service-specific credentials and invoice reconciliation from the handoff. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples across ten languages also reduce the cost of checking the contract before wiring a worker.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the shipment-update queue when a single producer-to-worker handoff and one shared backend credential are more valuable than replayable event history. Choose Kafka for replay and consumer groups, RabbitMQ for broker-level routing, or SQS when AWS-native operations are the decisive constraint.

Is a queue enough for the whole workflow?

No. It is not a DAG engine, it has no join primitive for fanout aggregation, and it has no native debounce or throttle. If a shipment update needs a scheduled trigger, use the cron trigger to enqueue work and let a worker perform the long task; a cron execution is limited to 900 seconds. Cron also requires a public http_url, and missed triggers are not backfilled after a pause.

For this application I would keep the operational checklist short: use a stable queue naming convention, include an event ID in every message, enforce consumer idempotency, keep delays and retention inside their limits, send poison messages to a dead-letter path, and measure the worker's actual processing time before setting its visibility window. One provider is one trust boundary, one billing relationship, and one outage surface. That cost belongs in the decision.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the background job queue guide.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation
  • AWS SQS visibility timeout
  • RabbitMQ tutorials
  • Apache Kafka documentation

title: Detecting and Patching Log4j (Log4Shell): A Practical Playbook
description:
Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) is more than four years old, and it is still the reference point for every "how did this get in?" conversation. If you are building a detection playbook today, Log4j is the right template — not because it is current, but because it shows exactly how a logging library becomes a remote code execution vector.

The mechanism in one paragraph

Log4j's message substitution feature let a logged string trigger a JNDI lookup. An attacker who could get an application to log a crafted string — a username, a user-agent, a header — could make the JVM connect to an attacker-controlled LDAP or RMI server and load a payload. No authentication, no user interaction beyond the request.

The lesson generalises: any component that parses structured input and then acts on it is a potential execution surface. Logging frameworks are just the most common example.

Detection: find it before you patch it

Manual auditing does not scale. You need automated Software Composition Analysis (SCA) that reads your build files and produces a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM).

  • Scan pom.xml, build.gradle, and runtime libraries for log4j-core versions between 2.0-beta9 and 2.14.1.
  • Treat transitive dependencies as first-class findings — Log4j is rarely a direct dependency in modern frameworks.
  • Complement SCA with network monitoring: outbound LDAP/RMI connections from application servers that do not normally make them are a strong signal.

Short-term mitigation

When you cannot upgrade immediately:

  • Set log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true on affected JVMs. Be aware that bypasses were documented for some versions, so this is a speed bump, not a fix.
  • Add WAF rules that inspect headers and request bodies for ${jndi:ldap://...} patterns. Attackers can obfuscate these, so treat the rule as a deterrent, not a guarantee.
  • Block outbound connections from application hosts to the internet at the firewall where possible.

Patching

For Maven:

<!-- Before -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>log4j-core</artifactId>
    <version>2.10.0</version>
</dependency>

<!-- After -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>log4j-core</artifactId>
    <version>2.17.1</version>
</dependency>

If Log4j is bundled inside a larger framework, prefer upgrading the framework to a version that ships the patched library. If that is not possible, use dependency exclusions to force the safe version across all modules.

After the patch

  • Regression-test logging specifically. A major version jump can change log output or break custom appenders.
  • Never pass raw user input directly into a logger call. Sanitise or encode before the value reaches the logging statement.
  • Run the logging service account with minimal permissions, and segment your log aggregation platform from production assets.
  • Integrate SCA into CI so a future CVE fails the build instead of reaching production.

The pattern to remember

The Log4j story is not really about Log4j. It is about a trusted, ubiquitous component that interpreted input it should have treated as data. The controls that matter — dependency inventory, least privilege, network egress filtering, and CI gates — are the same ones that protect you against the next one.

This is an expanded technical note based on our Log4j detection and patching guide. The original is here: https://hsecurities.in/blog/detect-patch-log4j-vulnerability

title: Google Cloud ACE Exam Guide 2026: Sections, Renewal, Study Plan
description:
The Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer (ACE) exam tests whether you can set up, deploy, run and secure workloads on Google Cloud. Here is the 2026 format, the four exam guide sections and their weights, the product-name changes to watch for, your renewal options, and a study plan based on the weights.

The exam at a glance

  • Length: two hours
  • Format: 50–60 multiple choice and multiple select questions
  • Fee: $125, plus tax where applicable
  • Languages: English, Japanese, Spanish and Portuguese
  • Delivery: online-proctored from a remote location, or onsite-proctored at a testing centre
  • Prerequisites: none. Google recommends 6 or more months of hands-on experience with Google Cloud
  • Age: you must be at least 18 to take a Google Cloud certification exam
  • Validity: three years from the date you certify

Google reports only pass or fail and does not publish a passing score. You see a provisional result on screen as soon as you submit. Google then confirms it, which can take 7 to 10 days. If you do not pass, the score report under Exam History in the Candidate Portal breaks your result down by section.

Retakes: you can make up to four attempts in a two-year period. After a first fail you wait 14 days, after a second fail 60 days, and after a third fail 365 days. You pay for every attempt.

Who the exam is for

Google describes an Associate Cloud Engineer as someone who deploys and secures applications, services and infrastructure, monitors the operations of multiple projects, and maintains enterprise solutions to meet target performance metrics. The role performs common platform tasks, supported by AI tooling, using Google-managed or self-managed services. In short, it is a hands-on, day-to-day operations role rather than a design or architecture role.

The four official sections

Section Weight
Setting up a cloud solution environment ~20%
Planning and implementing a cloud solution ~30%
Ensuring the successful operation of a cloud solution ~30%
Configuring access and security ~20%

The two middle sections make up about 60% of the exam. In brief, the exam guide describes each section like this:

  • Setting up a cloud solution environment: the resource hierarchy, organization policies, IAM roles in a project, users and groups in Cloud Identity, enabling APIs, Google Cloud Observability, quotas, Workforce Identity Federation, and billing accounts, budgets, alerts and billing exports.
  • Planning and implementing a cloud solution: choosing between Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and Agent Runtime; launching VMs, Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk, autoscaled managed instance groups and Spot VMs; GKE Autopilot, regional and private clusters; data and storage products; VPCs, firewall rules, Cloud NGFW policies and load balancers; and Infrastructure as Code tools such as Terraform, Config Connector and Helm.
  • Ensuring the successful operation of a cloud solution: snapshots and images, GKE node pools and Pod autoscaling, Cloud Run versions and traffic splitting, Cloud Storage lifecycle rules, database backup and restore, CMEK, subnets, static IPs, Cloud DNS and Cloud NAT, and Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging, audit logs and log routing.
  • Configuring access and security: IAM policies and inheritance, role types and custom roles, service accounts with minimum permissions, service account impersonation, short-lived credentials, service accounts with GKE, and Workload Identity Federation.

A note on product names

Google’s certification page says the exam was updated to reflect recent branding changes, and it points you to the exam guide for the product names used on the exam. Google gives no date for this update. The current guide uses names such as:

  • Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI Agent Engine
  • Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Workbench, formerly Vertex AI Workbench

The guide also lists AI-assisted tools: Gemini CLI, Google Antigravity, Gemini Cloud Assist and Application Design Center. If your course or notes are older, check each product name against the current exam guide so the names on the exam do not catch you out.

Renewal options

The certification is valid for three years. You can renew by exam from 180 days before it expires. Outside that window you cannot sit the same exam while you are still certified. Google offers three ways to renew:

Option Details Adds
Standard exam The full two-hour exam, $125 plus tax 3 years
Renewal exam One hour, 20 multiple choice and multiple select questions, $75 plus tax, in English or Japanese 3 years
Google Skills Designated courses or skill badges, completed in the last year of your certification 1 year

The shorter renewal exam has its own exam guide. It leaves out the first section, Setting up a cloud solution environment, and weights the other three at about 40%, 40% and 20%. To take it, your certification must be active and you must be within the renewal eligibility period.

A study plan by weight

This is our suggestion, not Google’s. It splits your time in line with the exam guide weights. If you have about 40 hours, that works out roughly as:

  • 12 hours: Planning and implementing a cloud solution
  • 12 hours: Ensuring the successful operation of a cloud solution
  • 8 hours: Setting up a cloud solution environment
  • 8 hours: Configuring access and security

If you are preparing for the renewal exam, our suggestion is to drop the first section and use the renewal weights instead. With about 20 hours, that is 8 hours each on planning and implementing and on operations, and 4 hours on access and security.

A few habits we suggest for each block:

  1. Work in a real project. The objectives are practical. Create VMs, managed instance groups, a GKE cluster and a Cloud Run service yourself, then change and delete them.
  2. Learn the choices, not just the steps. Many objectives ask you to choose the right compute, storage or networking option. For each product, note when you would pick it over the others.
  3. Practise IAM until it is routine. Grant roles at different levels of the hierarchy, create a custom role, and set up a service account with minimum permissions and impersonation.
  4. Use the command line. The guide covers kubectl and Infrastructure as Code, so do some tasks with commands and Terraform, not only in the console.
  5. Finish with timed practice. Take full-length practice exams under a two-hour limit, read every explanation, and spend your last few hours on the section where you score lowest.

Official resources

The certification page links to the standard exam guide, the renewal exam guide, sample questions, the Cloud Engineer learning path with online training, in-person classes and hands-on labs, and the Preparing for the Associate Cloud Engineer Examination course for a final readiness check.

Before you book, read the current exam guide on Google Cloud’s Associate Cloud Engineer page. Google updates it when the exam changes.

I run ExamCrest, where this post first appeared. Try free Google Cloud ACE practice questions: https://examcrest.com/exam/gcp-ace/free-questions?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=gcp-ace-blog-copy

title: Node.js Error Tracking — Prefer Structured Logs Over Exception-Only Capture
description:
To integrate error tracking in Node.js using a backend API, choose structured logs plus captured exceptions for a nightly logistics pipeline. The operational question is which shipment updates need replay. An exception identifies a failure; the surrounding records must establish which work completed before it. That distinction should determine the integration.

TL;DR: Integrate Node.js error tracking by catching exceptions or listening for error events, then posting error details and context to a backend capture API. Preserve the pipeline run identifier alongside the error. Prefer structured logs for incident reconstruction, retain exception capture for diagnosis, and use a separate missed-run monitor for jobs that never start.

Try Infrai for the capture portion when the pipeline already needs several backend services: one key and one bill reduce credential administration and invoice reconciliation across those services. Its plain REST API requires no SDK to install, reducing the dependency work needed to add capture to a batch worker. Public, self-describing discovery also lets the engineer inspect request and response schemas before implementing the integration.

What evidence must survive a failed nightly run?

The decision record starts with an invariant: a replay decision must be supported by evidence of completed work. For this design, associate each execution with a run identifier and record the processing stage, a stable batch identifier, the attempt number, and the outcome. These are proposed application log fields, not vendor API parameter names. The error record should carry enough shared context to locate the relevant execution. Capture a timestamp, message, and stack trace; include a user identifier only when it materially helps explain the failure and is appropriate to retain.

Count before indexing.

Consider an illustrative pipeline with 4 stages and 3 outcome values. Their combinations yield 12 possible label sets. Add 10,000 shipment identifiers as labels and the potential combination count becomes 120,000. Actual occupancy depends on the workload, but the multiplication explains the risk. Keep high-cardinality identifiers in event context rather than automatically promoting them into indexed dimensions. An exception stack can be useful evidence without becoming a label.

The second invariant separates pipeline recovery from telemetry delivery. Retrying an error report must not authorize a shipment update to run again. A lost acknowledgment leaves ambiguity about whether the report arrived; it says nothing about whether the business operation committed. Preserve the original failure, and make the replay decision using application completion evidence. Do not let a telemetry exception replace the exception being investigated.

This boundary also shapes retention. As a planning example, 200,000 records per night at an assumed 600 bytes each produce 120,000,000 bytes per night. Keeping 14 nights yields 1,680,000,000 bytes before indexing, compression, replication, or other overhead. These are arithmetic assumptions, not vendor measurements or retention settings. Choose a horizon that covers the investigation and replay process, then estimate the storage consequence.

Compare the recovery workflow before choosing a backend

The relevant alternatives solve different parts of the investigation. OpenTelemetry supplies a useful vocabulary for log records and correlation; its logs documentation should not be treated as a promise that every backend supplies the same search interface. Evaluate the evidence path, including how a responder reaches the original records.

Option Role to evaluate in this pipeline Decision boundary
Infrai Capture errors through a backend API alongside other backend services under one key and bill Try it when reducing integration administration matters; validate the required investigation workflow before adoption
Sentry Specialist exception investigation Prefer this evaluation path when source-map-assisted debugging or session replay drives the decision; still require evidence of completed pipeline work
Grafana Loki Structured-log investigation Evaluate when searching pipeline records is the central task; decide separately how exceptions and missed runs enter the response process
Elastic Observability Search-centered investigation across retained records Evaluate when the search workflow determines the architecture; include schema, indexing, and retention decisions in the review
Healthchecks Detection of a scheduled job that fails to check in Use for the missed-run boundary; a missing check-in cannot explain which shipment update failed

These are evaluation choices, not benchmark rankings. No comparative latency, availability, or savings measurements support a numerical winner here. For this decision, the useful test is concrete: can a responder identify a run, distinguish its attempts, locate the error, and determine the replay boundary? A demonstration that only displays an exception message does not establish that result.

The trade-off is diagnostic scope. Infrai is not a replacement for a specialist when source-map resolution, crash symbolication, session replay, distributed span-tree investigation, or integrated notifications is a mandatory acceptance criterion. Prefer a specialist whose documentation and trial demonstrate the requirement; evaluate Sentry first for interactive exception debugging. For this architecture, capture, searchable execution evidence, and missed-run detection are separate responsibilities.

How should you integrate error tracking using a backend API?

At the Node.js boundary, a try-catch block or error event listener supplies the exception. The backend request is an explicit POST carrying error details, such as the message and stack trace, with relevant timestamps and identifiers. The transport must check status codes and preserve the response body on a failed request so the actual rejection reason reaches the operator.

Schema comes first.

Infrai provides a unified API spanning 295 routes across 20 modules. For a worker that uses several backend services, this breadth allows the same REST API conventions to carry beyond error capture. The interface is SDK-free: plain HTTP is sufficient, so capture need not introduce another client library into the pipeline.

Use this runnable contract-inspection step before building the capture payload. It performs a read, requires no API key, and avoids guessing field names from prose. The curl retry option enables bounded retries and respects Retry-After when supplied; without that header, curl uses increasing retry delays for retryable responses, including HTTP 429. The maximum retry time bounds the retry period.

curl --request GET \
  --url 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery' \
  --header 'Accept: application/json' \
  --fail-with-body \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 60

Locate the error-capture capability in the returned discovery document and use its declared path and request schema. This read establishes the contract; it does not capture an exception. The capture request belongs in the application's failure path after that schema has been checked. Infrai documents runnable examples in 10 languages, so the implementation can follow the declared example rather than treating this article's proposed log context as a request schema.

For authenticated capture, read the credential from the INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable and send it as an Authorization bearer token. Use an explicit POST method. Follow the platform's Idempotency-Key convention for a retried write, with a stable key for the same captured event; consult the capability's idempotency declaration rather than assuming that every operation shares the same semantics. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise back off exponentially within a bounded retry budget. A tight loop adds traffic precisely when delivery is constrained.

The event identity and the incident grouping identity serve different purposes. A retry of one captured event should retain its identity, while a later occurrence remains a distinct event even if its message matches. Separately, a retried business operation needs its own application idempotency design. Conflating these identities can make the diagnostic record misleading even when every request succeeds.

Retain enough evidence to authorize a replay

Sampling is a decision about what an investigator may later be unable to prove. As a proposed policy, retain all stage outcomes and failure records, then consider sampling repetitive progress messages. Sampling those progress messages reduces volume at the cost of intermediate detail. Sampling completion evidence can make it impossible to distinguish completed work from work whose record was discarded.

That is consequential.

Suppose an illustrative run has 1,000 progress records and one final outcome record. Keeping every tenth progress record leaves 100 progress records; retaining the final outcome separately preserves the explicit completion claim. This is a policy example, not a measured workload or a backend sampling feature. It still requires testing against the failure modes of the application: an outcome logged before the business commit is weaker evidence than an outcome tied to the commit boundary.

The reconstruction procedure should therefore start with the run and its attempts, locate the last supported completion point, and inspect the associated exception context. Correlation identifiers help connect records, but an identifier alone does not establish causality or provide a distributed trace view. Require evidence for each inference used to authorize replay.

Retention has an equally practical boundary. Do not approve an investigation design merely because the initial capture request works. Establish how long the required evidence must remain available, who can retrieve it, and how deletion obligations will be met before sending sensitive identifiers. The arithmetic above estimates volume; it does not establish those operational controls.

Rejected decision: exception capture as the entire record

Exception-only capture is rejected for this logistics pipeline because the job is to reconstruct a run and choose a safe replay boundary. A stack trace explains where execution failed, but it does not enumerate earlier successful shipment updates. Structured execution records supply that missing evidence at a deliberate storage and indexing cost.

The rejected design has a valid use case. For a small task whose completion can be established independently, exception capture may provide enough diagnostic context without a detailed progress stream. Likewise, a team focused on rich interactive exception debugging should evaluate Sentry first, while a team whose main requirement is structured-log search should compare Loki and Elastic against its actual investigation queries. Choose the evidence workflow before choosing the ingestion API.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Sentry Node.js documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/guides/node/
  • Grafana Loki documentation: https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/
  • Elastic Observability documentation: https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/observability/current/index.html
  • Healthchecks documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • curl retry behavior: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--retry

If the shared-credential capture boundary fits your pipeline, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Introduce GreyShip
description:
I have been building Greyship, a serverless platform made only for Go. It is open source (AGPL-3.0) and runs on a server you own. Today I am releasing it publicly.

The problem

I wanted what serverless promises (push code, get a URL, pay nothing while idle) without wrapping my handlers, writing a Dockerfile, or renting capacity I do not use. The platforms that come close either run your app like an always-on server or ask you to change how you write it.

What Greyship does

You bring a normal Go project: a go.mod and one or more main packages. You run:

grey deploy

Greyship reads your code (it never runs it) and finds every main package. One that starts an HTTP server becomes a web service with an HTTPS URL. The rest become workers. A release command, such as a migration, runs before the new version starts.

This is a real run:

$ grey deploy
Created project you/testapi

  testapi  web  .  starts a server in main.go:13 (http.ListenAndServe)

Building here with go1.27.3 for linux/amd64
Uploaded 1 binaries (2.4 MB)

Deployment 5e7c26de-6e97-422e-8ac1-4a70528e3d19 queued:
  │ using the 1 binaries built on your machine
  │ checked testapi: Go 1.27.3, linux/amd64 (5.6 MB)
  │ starting testapi on your-server
  │ live

✓ Live
  testapi  https://testapi-testapi.greyshipapp.tech

How it behaves

  • Scale to zero. A web service with no requests pauses after 30 seconds. Its memory stays where it is, but it uses no CPU. The next request resumes it, which is usually much faster than a cold start.
  • Safe switchover. The new version starts and must pass its health check before it gets traffic. If anything fails, the live version keeps serving.
  • Rollbacks. Go back to any earlier deployment without a rebuild.
  • Sandboxes. Every app runs in its own gVisor sandbox with its own network, so apps cannot reach each other, the host or Greyship's internals.
  • Build where you like. Compile on your laptop and only changed binaries are uploaded, or let the server build inside a sandbox so you do not need Go installed.
  • Deploy your way. The CLI, the dashboard and GitHub push-to-deploy all use the same API.

Run it yourself

On a fresh Ubuntu or Debian server with 4 GB of RAM, as root:

curl -fsSL https://greyship.tech/install | sudo sh

It installs Docker, gVisor, Postgres, an S3-compatible store and the Greyship services, then prints the address of your dashboard and asks you to create the owner account. No domain is needed to start. The owner adds everyone else and can limit how much memory, CPU and how many builds each user may use.

On your laptop:

curl -fsSL https://greyship.tech/cli/install | sh
grey server https://your-greyship-address
grey login

What to know

Greyship runs on a single server, so how many apps you can run depends on the size of that server. Idle apps hold no CPU, which helps a small machine go a long way. There is no high availability yet, so keep backups of anything that matters. The installer includes backup, restore and upgrade commands.

Links

  • Code: https://github.com/greylabss/greyship
  • Docs: https://docs.greyship.tech
  • Install guide: https://docs.greyship.tech/self-hosting

If you write Go, I would like to hear what breaks. Open an issue or tell me on X: https://x.com/shellhaki

  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: Do not use Apigee hybrid v1.17.2 due to a potential regression in apigee-connect-agent (see known issue 578314600). Use v1.17.3 instead.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
568860869 Fixed an issue in the RegularExpressionProtection policy where patterns starting and ending with .* whose middle section contained regular expression syntax were matched as literal text instead of regular expressions.
560272924 Apigee hybrid now supports continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Fixed an issue where Model Armor policies did not honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: when set, Model Armor callouts now bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic, while streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
549779897 Apigee analytics now reports the Model Armor template, verdict, and matched filters for each request on both the prompt and model-response directions.
546141116 The SemanticCacheLookup policy now reports the cache key and cache name to analytics in the ai_semantic_cache_key and ai_semantic_cache_name fields.

524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
502231886 Fixed an issue where the SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies failed to extract content using default source templates when the <Source> element was omitted and <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> was set to false.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.

If you use the Cloud Profiler Java agent, take one of the following actions:

  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

title: Base64 is not encryption: what it is, when to use it, and the Unicode gotcha
description:
Every few months I see Base64 described as "encoding for security." It isn't. Here's what it actually does.

What Base64 is

Base64 turns arbitrary bytes into text made only of safe characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, +, /, plus = padding). That makes it possible to put binary data in places that only accept text: JSON, URLs, HTML, email.

Common uses:

  • Data URIs: data:image/png;base64,...
  • HTTP Basic auth headers
  • Parts of JWTs
  • Embedding small files in JSON APIs

What it is not

It's not encryption. There's no key and no secret. Anyone can decode it instantly:

atob("c2VjcmV0LXBhc3N3b3Jk"); // "secret-password"

If you see credentials "protected" with Base64, they're not protected.

It makes data bigger

Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, so output is about 33% larger. That's fine for small icons and tokens, but a bad idea for large files.

The Unicode gotcha

btoa only handles characters in the Latin-1 range:

btoa("héllo");  // works
btoa("नमस्ते");   // InvalidCharacterError
btoa("😀");      // InvalidCharacterError

The fix is to convert text to UTF-8 bytes first:

function toBase64(str) {
  const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode(str);
  let binary = "";
  bytes.forEach(b => (binary += String.fromCharCode(b)));
  return btoa(binary);
}

function fromBase64(b64) {
  const binary = atob(b64);
  const bytes = Uint8Array.from(binary, c => c.charCodeAt(0));
  return new TextDecoder().decode(bytes);
}

fromBase64(toBase64("नमस्ते 😀")); // "नमस्ते 😀"

Base64URL: the URL-safe variant

Standard Base64 uses + and /, which have special meaning in URLs. Base64URL swaps them for - and _ and usually drops the = padding. JWTs use this variant, so decoding one with plain atob can fail until you convert the characters back.

const toStandard = s => s.replace(/-/g, "+").replace(/_/g, "/");

Quick rules

  • Use it to move binary data through text-only channels
  • Don't use it to hide anything
  • Avoid it for large files
  • Always go through UTF-8 for non-English text

For quick checks while debugging, I use a Base64 encoder/decoder from the free tools on Erapse, a site I run. For anything sensitive, decode locally instead.

What's the strangest place you've found Base64 in the wild?

title: Kubernetes: limpiar datos de email en CI sin perder señales
description:
Un pipeline de CI puede terminar en verde y dejar un problema invisible: buzones de prueba, secretos temporales y mensajes de verificación que siguen existiendo mucho después de que acaba el job.

En equipos que ejecutan pruebas de registro, OAuth o recuperación de contraseña dentro de Kubernetes, el fallo suele aparecer días después. El clúster parece sano, pero los datos de email se acumulan, los artefactos pierden contexto y nadie sabe qué ejecución creó cada recurso.

La solución no es borrar todo al final sin mirar. Es dar a cada ejecución una identidad, separar la evidencia mínima de los datos sensibles y hacer la limpieza idempotente.

El síntoma: el pipeline termina, pero el buzón queda vivo

Imaginemos un job que crea un namespace efímero, levanta la aplicación y solicita un generador de cuentas de correo temporal para validar un enlace de activación. La prueba pasa. El runner se cierra. Sin embargo, pueden quedar tres cosas:

  • Un buzón asociado a la ejecución.
  • Un secreto de Kubernetes con una dirección o token de acceso.
  • Un log que dice “email recibido”, pero no indica qué mensaje ni qué versión lo generó.

Cuando llega un fallo intermitente, el equipo reintenta y crea otro conjunto de recursos. Despues de varias horas, la limpieza manual se convierte en parte del incidente.

Qué debe identificar cada ejecución

El primer cambio es usar un run_id que viaje por todo el flujo. No debe depender solo del nombre del branch, porque dos ejecuciones del mismo branch pueden ocurrir al mismo tiempo.

Un identificador útil aparece en:

  1. La etiqueta del namespace o del recurso temporal.
  2. El asunto o encabezado técnico del mensaje de prueba.
  3. El nombre del artefacto de CI.
  4. Los logs de la aplicación y del consumidor.

Por ejemplo:

metadata:
  labels:
    ci.run_id: "run-20261107-0522-a81f"
    ci.owner: "checkout-tests"
    data.class: "synthetic-email"

La etiqueta data.class ayuda a distinguir datos sintéticos de cualquier dato que no debe tocar un proceso automático. Parece pequeño, pero hace la limpieza mucho mas segura.

Separar evidencia de datos temporales

Un error común es guardar el contenido completo del email como artefacto porque “puede servir para depurar”. En realidad, el HTML suele contener tokens, nombres y enlaces que ya no hacen falta cuando la prueba termina.

Conviene conservar una evidencia compacta, por ejemplo:

{
  "run_id": "run-20261107-0522-a81f",
  "message_id": "msg-7b2c",
  "event": "verification_received",
  "latency_ms": 1840,
  "result": "passed"
}

El cuerpo del mensaje puede eliminarse o redacted en el origen, según la capacidad del sistema de email. Para diagnosticar una demora, message_id, estado y latencia suelen ser mas útiles que guardar todo el contenido.

También ayuda registrar el momento de expiración. Si el buzón debe vivir diez minutos, esa regla debe estar en los metadatos y no solo en la memoria del desarrollador. Un expires_at explícito permite que un reconciliador actúe aunque el runner se corte.

Un patrón sencillo para Kubernetes

Hay dos caminos razonables, y pueden convivir:

Limpieza al terminar el job. El pipeline intenta borrar el namespace, el secreto y el buzón. Es rapido y barato, pero no cubre un runner cancelado, un timeout o un nodo perdido.

Reconciliación periódica. Un proceso busca recursos con data.class=synthetic-email, compara expires_at con la hora actual y elimina los vencidos. Es la red de seguridad que evita depender de un único finally.

El reconciliador debe ser conservador. Primero comprueba que el recurso pertenece al entorno de pruebas, luego confirma que está vencido y finalmente elimina por run_id. Si una ejecución todavía está activa, no debe asumir que su buzón está huérfano solo por ser antiguo.

Para mantener la operación trazable, cada decisión puede producir un evento pequeño: kept, expired, deleted o skipped_active. Esos eventos son mas faciles de buscar que un log narrativo largo. Para trabajos programados, un contrato de salida con estado, motivo y run_id también evita que un agente o un job aguas abajo interprete un borrado incompleto como éxito; este contrato de salida para el job es un buen patrón aplicable.

Limpieza segura y observable

Antes de activar el borrado automático, haría estas comprobaciones:

  • Modo de observación: durante un día, el reconciliador solo informa qué eliminaría.
  • Permiso limitado: la cuenta de servicio solo puede leer y borrar recursos con las etiquetas esperadas.
  • Idempotencia: borrar un buzón ya eliminado debe producir un estado conocido, no una alerta falsa.
  • Retención de evidencia: conserva el resumen de la ejecución por un periodo corto y definido.
  • Métrica de residuos: mide recursos vencidos, edad máxima y tiempo de limpieza.
  • Alerta útil: avisa cuando el volumen o la edad superan un umbral, no por cada recurso individual.

La telemetria debe responder tres preguntas: qué ejecución creó el dato, por que todavía existe y qué acción tomó el sistema. Si no puede responderlas, hay automatización, pero no hay control operacional.

Un caso especialmente delicado es el fallo parcial. La prueba puede pasar, pero la limpieza del buzón fallar. El resultado del job debería separar test_status de cleanup_status; de ese modo, el equipo sabe que la funcionalidad está bien y que queda una tarea de higiene pendiente.

Checklist para SRE

Antes de considerar terminado el diseño, revisa:

  • ¿Cada recurso de email tiene run_id, propietario y expiración?
  • ¿La evidencia excluye tokens y cuerpos innecesarios?
  • ¿Existe un reconciliador para jobs cancelados o nodos perdidos?
  • ¿El borrado está restringido a datos sintéticos?
  • ¿Se puede explicar cada decisión en los logs?
  • ¿Hay una métrica de recursos vencidos y otra de tiempo de limpieza?
  • ¿El proceso esta probado con ejecuciones simultáneas?

No hace falta empezar con un operador complejo. Un job pequeño, etiquetas consistentes y una política clara ya reducen mucho el riesgo. Incluso una búsqueda rápida de “tem email” en documentación interna debería llevar a la misma definición de datos sintéticos, no a una colección de scripts distintos.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Debo borrar el mensaje antes de guardar evidencia?

Guarda primero un resumen sin secretos y elimina el cuerpo tan pronto como termine la aserción necesaria. Si una investigación necesita más detalle, usa una retención explícita y con acceso limitado.

¿Qué pasa si el pipeline se cancela?

El reconciliador debe detectar el expires_at vencido. No dependas únicamente de un paso final del runner, porque ese paso no siempre se ejecuta.

¿Cuándo conviene usar un namespace por ejecución?

Cuando las pruebas cambian configuración o despliegan varios componentes. Para una prueba pequeña puede bastar con etiquetas y nombres únicos, siempre que la limpieza pueda aislar exactamente sus recursos.

La idea central es simple: los datos de email de CI son recursos operativos, no basura anónima. Si tienen identidad, expiración y evidencia mínima, Kubernetes puede ayudar a limpiarlos sin borrar las señales que un equipo SRE necesita para entender el siguiente incidente.

title: Turning polled battery readings into charge sessions, and flagging the ones you only half saw
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of ScooterLog, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working on my behalf from the app's source code. ScooterLog is an independent app, not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Ola Electric.

ScooterLog shows every charge in a timeline: start and end percent, how long it took, when it reached 100%. No system hands us that list. The scooter's cloud reports a current state, the server polls it every few minutes, and a "charge" is something we have to reconstruct from a row of samples.

The reconstruction is about 40 lines of Python and SQLite. The interesting part is less the state machine than being honest about what the samples can't tell you.

The input

Each poll produces a reading, stored once:

CREATE TABLE history(
    user_id TEXT, vehicle_id TEXT, source_ms INTEGER,
    battery_soc REAL, charging_state TEXT, odometer REAL,
    -- ...
    PRIMARY KEY(user_id, vehicle_id, source_ms));

source_ms is the timestamp the upstream attached to the reading, not the time we fetched it. That choice does a lot of work, because a poll can return the same reading again:

cur = c.execute('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO history(...) VALUES (...)', (...))
new = cur.rowcount > 0
if new:
    _update_charging(c, user_id, vehicle_id, point)

A repeat insert changes nothing, so the session logic only runs on genuinely new information. Downstream, alarm checks hang off the same return value, so a reading can't trigger them twice.

The state machine has no explicit state

There are two ingredients: is this reading charging, and is there an open session row (end_ms IS NULL)? That gives three actions, and the fourth combination does nothing:

charging = state in ('SLOW_CHARGING', 'FAST_CHARGING')

if charging and not openrow:      # open: record start time, %, odometer
    ...
elif charging and openrow:        # extend: update end %, keep it open
    ...
elif not charging and openrow:    # close: record end time, %, odometer
    ...

The "state" is just the database. A server restart in the middle of a charge loses nothing, since the next reading finds the open row and carries on.

Two details are easy to get wrong. A charge that moves from slow to fast is one session, not two, because both states count as charging. The test pins this down:

pts = [
    {'source_ms': 1, 'battery_soc': 20, 'charging_state': 'NOT_CHARGING'},
    {'source_ms': 2, 'battery_soc': 22, 'charging_state': 'SLOW_CHARGING'},
    {'source_ms': 3, 'battery_soc': 55, 'charging_state': 'FAST_CHARGING'},
    {'source_ms': 4, 'battery_soc': 80, 'charging_state': 'NOT_CHARGING'},
]
# -> exactly one session: start 22% at t=2, end 80% at t=4

And end_soc is written on every extend as well as on close, so a session in progress always shows its latest percent.

The real problem: you weren't watching

Say you read 40% and charging, then the server is down for three hours, then you read 100% and not charging. The naive result is a three-hour session. The truth might be a 90-minute charge and 90 minutes sitting at full. Nothing in the data distinguishes them.

You can't recover what you didn't sample, but you can refuse to present a guess as a measurement. So every update checks the gap to the previous reading:

CHARGE_GAP_MS = 40 * 60 * 1000

prevrow = c.execute(
    'SELECT source_ms FROM history WHERE user_id=? AND vehicle_id=? AND source_ms<?'
    ' ORDER BY source_ms DESC LIMIT 1', (user_id, vehicle_id, ms)).fetchone()
gap = prevrow is not None and (ms - prevrow[0]) > CHARGE_GAP_MS

The threshold sits above the slowest normal polling interval, which is 30 minutes for a sleeping vehicle. Ordinary quiet doesn't trip it. A real outage does.

The flag is applied at all three transitions, and each means something different:

A gap before... What it means
opening The charge may have started during the gap, so the start time and start % are late
extending Readings are missing from the middle, so the curve isn't fully known
closing The unplug may have happened any time in the gap, so the duration may be too long

And it is sticky, so one gap marks the session for good:

UPDATE charging SET end_soc=?, state=?, partial=COALESCE(partial,0) | ?
WHERE user_id=? AND vehicle_id=? AND start_ms=?

COALESCE handles older rows from before the column existed. The bitwise OR means a later clean reading can't wash the flag away.

Deriving the numbers at read time

Sessions store only what was observed. Everything else is computed when asked for, so a better formula applies to old sessions too.

When it reached 100% comes from the history rather than from the session, since a scooter often stays plugged in long after it is full:

f = c.execute('SELECT MIN(source_ms) FROM history WHERE user_id=? AND vehicle_id=?'
              ' AND source_ms>=? AND source_ms<=? AND battery_soc>=99.5',
              (user_id, vehicle_id, start, end or now)).fetchone()

The 99.5 tolerates a reading just under 100.

Charge speed stops the clock at full, not at unplug. Otherwise, leaving it plugged in overnight would make a good charger look slow. Very short sessions get no speed at all:

stop = full_ms or end_ms
if stop and start_soc is not None and stop - start_ms >= 10 * 60000:
    top = 100.0 if full_ms else end_soc
    if top is not None and top > start_soc:
        rate_pct_h = round((top - start_soc) / ((stop - start_ms) / 3600000.0), 1)

The limits I'd rather state

  • Timing is only as fine as the polling. The end of a session is the first reading that says "not charging", not the moment of unplugging, so durations can run long by up to one poll interval.
  • partial is a flag, not a fix. It tells the reader not to trust the duration. It doesn't repair it, and the session stays in the list.
  • A short top-up can be missed. A very short top-up that begins and ends between two polls never appears. Nothing in the data says it happened.
  • The app only knows what the scooter reports, and readings can lag a few minutes.

The pattern, for any polled device

  1. Key readings on the source's own timestamp and run logic only on new rows.
  2. Keep the session state in the table, so a restart costs nothing.
  3. Choose a gap threshold just above your slowest normal sample interval.
  4. Flag uncertain records instead of dropping them or quietly trusting them.
  5. Store observations, derive numbers on read.

ScooterLog is on Google Play. ScooterLog is an independent app, not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Ola Electric. It reads what the scooter reports and does not control it.

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: What to Look for in a React Marketplace Starter Kit
description:
Building a two-sided marketplace means solving more than just the frontend. Buyers need a way to request services, providers need onboarding, and administrators need a way to manage the workflow.

If you are evaluating a starter kit for a marketplace MVP, here are five practical questions to ask:

1. Can you actually edit the source code?

A starter kit should give developers room to change the business model, UI, validation, and data flows. Check the framework versions and project structure before purchasing.

2. Where does the backend run?

For an edge-native application, confirm how API routes are implemented, where data lives, and how deployment is configured. A Cloudflare Workers API with a D1 schema is one possible foundation.

3. What marketplace workflows are already represented?

Look for concrete flows such as buyer quote requests, provider registration, provider approval, and lead assignment. A demo landing page alone is not a marketplace backend.

4. What is not included?

This matters as much as the feature list. Ask whether payments, automatic matching, dashboards, and production operations are built or still require development. Budget time accordingly.

5. Is there enough documentation to customize and deploy?

A README and a clear schema can save time, but developers should still review security, authentication, database migrations, testing, and production readiness for their own use case.

An example I'm offering

Through Launch & Grow Hub, I offer the Edge-Native Full-Stack React 19 Starter Kit ($149), an editable source-code starting point for developers. It includes a React 19 / TypeScript / Vite frontend, Cloudflare Workers API, Cloudflare D1 schema, buyer quote requests, provider registration and approval, exclusive lead assignment logic, protected admin API endpoints, and setup documentation.

It is not a turnkey SaaS. Integrated payments, automated matching, paid credits, and a visual admin dashboard are not included; implementation and customization are the buyer's responsibility.

I am also open to conversations with developer educators and creators about an affiliate referral opportunity. If your audience builds React or marketplace applications, you can learn about joining here: https://payhip.com/auth/register/af6ad44f573f3ed

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: RAG Pipeline Utils v3.8.1
description:
A security release. Upgrade now if you use RetrievalGuard access control, plugin signature verification, the development server (DevServer) or @devilsdev/rag-mcp-server, and re-ingest FileVectorStore indexes whose documents set acl or requiredRole at the top level. One change in access control can hide documents that were visible before.

npm install @devilsdev/rag-pipeline-utils@^3.8.1
# and, if you use the MCP server:
npx @devilsdev/rag-mcp-server@3.8.1 ./docs

Security

Four advisories are fixed in this release. Each one lists the affected
versions and workarounds for anyone who can't upgrade yet.

  • Access control (RetrievalGuard with enforceACL, and the built-in MemoryRetriever, FileVectorStore and BM25Search): a document restricted to a role could be passed to users without that role, depending on where the restriction was set on the document and how the user's permissions were passed in. GHSA-8393-cmg7-9rv3
  • Plugin signatures (PluginSignatureVerifier with requireContentDigest: true): a crafted plugin manifest could pass verification for code its signer never approved. GHSA-w693-22gp-m69r
  • The development server (DevServer): in some setups it could be reached from the network, or by other web pages open in your browser, which could then run queries on your LLM provider's credits. GHSA-6h47-g8cw-366q
  • The MCP server (@devilsdev/rag-mcp-server): a crafted HTML file in an indexed folder could stall indexing for minutes. GHSA-j2vr-gm7f-3r37

After upgrading

  • Re-ingest FileVectorStore indexes whose documents set acl or requiredRole at the top level (not in metadata). Index files written by earlier versions don't contain that field, so upgrading alone doesn't restrict those documents. Documents with the restriction in metadata, and the in-memory stores (MemoryRetriever, BM25Search), need no action beyond upgrading.

Changed

  • RetrievalGuard now requires every restriction a document sets. A document can set requiredRole or acl at its top level, in metadata and on doc; access now requires meeting each one that is set (any one role of a list is enough for that list). This can hide documents that were visible before.

The full list is in the CHANGELOG.

Originally published on the rag-pipeline-utils blog.

title: I made three AI seats argue over the spec before any code. Here's what 10 runs showed.
description:
Most of the bad code I've gotten from coding agents wasn't badly written. It was the right code for the wrong plan. The agent misread the task, assumed something about the repo that wasn't true, and then executed that assumption very well.

So I built a tool that spends its effort before the code. It's called Open Council. Three seats argue over a PRD until they all sign off on the same document:

  • Lead PM writes the brief and the PRD.
  • Chief Engineer checks every claim against the real code. Every objection has to cite a file:line.
  • Chief Architect rules on deadlocks and reviews the agreed document. It runs with no tools, so it judges the text, not the repo.

When all three sign off, I approve the PRD with a token. Only then does the Engineer implement it, in an isolated clone. The harness runs the project's gates (its real test commands) and opens a PR only if they pass. Anything else ends as BLOCKED or STALLED, never DONE.

Last week I had ten councils run on version 0.2.1 to see how this holds up. Here's what happened, including the parts that didn't work.

The setup

All ten ran in solo mode, which means every seat is Claude Code (Lead PM on Sonnet, Chief Engineer on Opus, Chief Architect on Sonnet with tools off). They used the quick profile, with at most 4 rounds. The targets were local copies of two small repos: a toy slugify library I keep for testing, and Open Council itself. Local copies have no GitHub remote, so no run could open a PR. That last step ends BLOCKED by design.

# Task Outcome Rounds Minutes
1 slugify: empty string + accents signed off, gate passed 4 6.6
2 gates --json signed off, gate passed 4 6.8
3 gate recipes for Python, Go, Rust signed off, gate passed 3 7.3
4 slugify: maxLength STALLED 4 6.2
5 slugify: empty + accents (repeat) signed off, gate passed 3 4.2
6 gates --json (repeat) STALLED 4 7.2
7 slugify: ß ø æ œ đ ł þ signed off, gate failed, BLOCKED 2 3.4
8 slugify: maxLength (repeat) signed off, gate passed 4 6.3
9 gate recipes (repeat) signed off, gate passed 4 9.2
10 slugify: empty + accents (repeat) signed off, gate passed 2 3.1

8 of 10 signed off. 7 of those 8 passed their gate. The median time to a sign-off or a stall was 6.5 minutes.

The catch nobody asked for

Six of the runs were on the slugify repo. In all six, the Chief Engineer's first objection had nothing to do with the task.

The repo's package.json had "test": "node --test test/". On Node 22 that argument is read as a module path, not a folder, so npm test ran 0 of the 2 existing tests. It had been quietly broken since before I started. No task mentioned it.

In run 1 the Engineer reproduced it, tried two working alternatives, and made fixing the test script the first commit of the plan. Its reasoning was simple: you can't claim the new tests pass if the runner doesn't run tests.

This is the thing I wanted from the design. A single agent asked to "handle empty strings in slugify" would most likely write the fix and the tests and report that they pass. A seat whose only job is to check claims against the repo found that the claim couldn't be checked at all.

What went wrong

Two runs stalled, and the same way. In both, the Engineer had no objections left. Then the Architect raised one more concern. In run 4 it asked for a README line the task never mentioned. The revision that answered it introduced a new problem: one of the new assertions would fail on a correct implementation. The Engineer objected in the last round, the budget ran out, and nothing reached me for approval. The harness wrote the last draft and the open objections to a file and stopped.

A stall is the system working, because nothing wrong got built. But two stalls with the same shape tell me the Architect's late concerns cost more than they're worth. I already made one change for this: a concern that could have been raised in an earlier round is waived on a resubmission. These two runs show it isn't enough yet.

One run was blocked by its own plan. In run 7 the council agreed on a plan and named its own test command, node --test test/slug.test.js. But the project config runs npm test, which was still broken in that repo, and the Architect had ruled that fixing package.json was out of scope. So execution ran the configured gate, it failed, and the run ended BLOCKED. Nothing was pushed. The code itself passed the plan's own 7 tests when I checked afterwards.

The harness did the right thing by not calling it done. The real bug is that a PRD can name a gate the project doesn't run, and nothing flags that before execution. That's an open issue now.

Solo mode isn't the real test. Every seat in these runs was the same model family. The point of separate seats is that they don't share blind spots, and the council is designed to put Claude, Gemini and Grok in different seats. I haven't run that mixed setup enough to say whether it catches more. Ten runs on two small repos, with three tasks repeated, is a smoke test, not a rate.

What I took from it

  1. Review the plan, not just the diff. The most useful objection in these runs was about the repo's state, not the task. It only came up because a seat was told to check claims against the code before anyone wrote any.
  2. Make "done" something the harness checks, not something the agent says. Run 7 had passing code and still ended BLOCKED, because the gate the project actually runs failed. I'd rather read a BLOCKED than find out later.
  3. Publish the failures. The stalls taught me more than the sign-offs, and they're the part I'd want to see before trusting a tool like this.

Trying it

You need Node 18 or later, macOS or Linux, and Claude Code. In a git repo:

npm install -g open-council-cli
council init --solo
council doctor
council backlog add "your task here" --priority 1
SESSION=$(council open my-task --item 001)
council deliberate "$SESSION"

When it signs off, it prints the PRD's path and the exact council approve command. That step is yours to run. Then council handoff "$SESSION" and council run "$SESSION" implement it and open the PR.

The code, and full replays of these runs with every objection, are at https://github.com/goshtasb/OpenCouncil. It's MIT licensed. If you run a council and it stalls or ships something wrong, that's the report I'd most like to read.

This article was written with the help of AI, and the ten runs were driven by an AI agent on my behalf. I checked the numbers against the run logs before publishing.

title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
description: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly.
