title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: So sánh TCO 5 Năm: Microsoft Office 2024 Vĩnh Viễn vs Microsoft 365 Doanh Nghiệp
description:
So sánh TCO 5 Năm: Microsoft Office 2024 Vĩnh Viễn vs Microsoft 365 Doanh Nghiệp

Doanh nghiệp thường đứng trước bài toán hóc búa khi chuẩn bị trang bị bộ ứng dụng văn phòng: Nên mua bản quyền Office 2024 vĩnh viễn (One-time purchase) hay đăng ký Microsoft 365 hàng tháng/hàng năm (Subscription)?

Dưới đây là mô hình phân tích Tổng Chi Phí Sở Hữu (TCO - Total Cost of Ownership) trong chu kỳ 5 năm.

1. Bản Chất Kiến Trúc Khác Biệt

  • Microsoft Office 2024 (Home & Business): Cấp phép vĩnh viễn cho 1 thiết bị PC hoặc Mac. Bộ cài cố định gồm Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook. Không tự động nâng cấp tính năng mới và không kèm dung lượng lưu trữ đám mây OneDrive doanh nghiệp.
  • Microsoft 365 (Business Basic / Standard): Thuê bao trả theo người dùng (User). Mỗi người dùng có thể cài đặt trên tối đa 5 máy tính, 5 máy tính bảng và 5 điện thoại. Tích hợp sẵn 1 TB OneDrive bảo mật cao, Exchange Mail theo tên miền công ty và Microsoft Teams.

2. Bảng Phân Tích Bài Toán Chi Phí TCO 5 Năm (Quy mô 20 nhân sự)

Hạng mục so sánh Office 2024 Vĩnh Viễn (H&B) Microsoft 365 Business Standard
Hình thức hạch toán CapEx (Chi phí đầu tư tài sản một lần) OpEx (Chi phí vận hành định kỳ)
Chi phí năm 1 (20 license) ~ 110.000.000 VNĐ ~ 55.000.000 VNĐ
Chi phí lũy kế 5 năm ~ 110.000.000 VNĐ (0 đồng từ năm 2-5) ~ 275.000.000 VNĐ (Tăng theo từng năm)
Dung lượng đám mây & Email Phải mua thêm dịch vụ mail ngoài (~15tr/năm) Đã bao gồm trọn gói 20TB Cloud + Mail doanh nghiệp
Độ linh hoạt nhân sự License gắn liền với máy tính Cấp phát / thu hồi tài khoản linh hoạt khi nhân sự nghỉ việc

3. Doanh Nghiệp Của Bạn Nên Chọn Gói Nào?

  • Chọn Office 2024 Vĩnh Viễn: Phù hợp với các công ty có cấu trúc nhân sự ổn định, máy tính để bàn cố định, kế toán/hành chính chỉ cần xử lý bảng tính offline và muốn dứt điểm ngân sách một lần.
  • Chọn Microsoft 365: Phù hợp với doanh nghiệp cần bảo mật dữ liệu lưu trữ đám mây, nhân viên làm việc kết hợp (Hybrid Working) và muốn có email doanh nghiệp tên miền riêng chuyên nghiệp.

Để cập nhật báo giá chính ngạch kèm hóa đơn VAT điện tử, truy cập bản quyền Microsoft chính hãng có hóa đơn VAT.

Xem thêm chi tiết tại cổng thông tin vietlicense.org.

Bản quyền nội dung thuộc về VietLicense - Đơn vị tư vấn giải pháp bản quyền phần mềm doanh nghiệp uy tín.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

title: Don't rebuild the link: a test that a scanned UPI QR reaches the next app byte for byte
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code.

Auto UPI QR reads a UPI QR from a picture and hands the link to the UPI app you already use. The whole job is to be a clean pipe: what the QR says goes in, the same thing comes out.

The tempting code is the opposite of a pipe. You have just parsed the link, you have the fields, so you build a fresh one:

// Looks tidy. Changes the link.
val rebuilt = Uri.Builder()
    .scheme("upi").authority("pay")
    .appendQueryParameter("pa", qr.payeeVpa)
    .appendQueryParameter("pn", qr.payeeName)
    .appendQueryParameter("am", qr.amount)
    .build()

This post is about why that is wrong, and the small Robolectric test that keeps it from coming back.

What a round trip does to a UPI link

Take a merchant-style link. The values here are made up:

upi://pay?pa=shop@okaxis&pn=A+B%26C&mc=5411&tr=ORD%2F17&sign=MEUCIQDx+/ab==

Decode and re-encode it through Uri and several things move:

  • @ becomes %40. appendQueryParameter encodes everything outside a small safe set, so pa=shop@okaxis becomes pa=shop%40okaxis.
  • + becomes a space, then %20. getQueryParameter treats + as a space when decoding. In a name that may be harmless. In a Base64 signature, + is data.
  • Duplicate keys collapse. getQueryParameter returns the first value, so a second pa= silently disappears.
  • Unknown parameters vanish. Rebuild from the fields you know about and you drop orgid, mode, sign and whatever else the issuer put there.
  • Order changes to whatever order your code happens to append.

The last two matter most. A signed QR's signature was computed over something. I don't know exactly which bytes each verifier checks, and neither does your app. The only safe assumption is that all of them count.

Keep the string, read from a copy

The fix is structural. The class holds the original text as its identity, and parsed fields are read-only views over it:

data class UpiQr(val raw: String) {
    private val uri: Uri = Uri.parse(raw)

    val payeeVpa: String? get() = param("pa")
    val payeeName: String? get() = param("pn")

    val viewUri: Uri get() = uri

    private fun param(name: String): String? =
        try { uri.getQueryParameter(name)?.trim() } catch (e: Exception) { null }
}

Uri.parse doesn't normalise. It wraps the string and decodes lazily when you ask for a part, and toString() gives back what went in. So the decoded values can drive the screen ("you are paying this name") while the hand-off uses the untouched original:

fun payIntent(qr: UpiQr, app: UpiApp): Intent =
    Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, qr.viewUri).setPackage(app.packageName)

There is no setter and no builder anywhere on that path, so there is nothing for a later "small cleanup" to hook into. No extras are added either, because the link is the entire message.

The one exception, and why it exists

One normalisation does happen. Some stickers encode UPI://PAY in capitals, and Android matches intent-filter schemes case-sensitively, so that link would open nothing. So the prefix is matched case-insensitively and rewritten, and trailing whitespace is trimmed:

private val PREFIX = Regex("^\\s*upi://pay", RegexOption.IGNORE_CASE)

fun parse(text: String?): UpiQr? {
    if (text == null) return null
    val m = PREFIX.find(text) ?: return null
    val normalised = "upi://pay" + text.substring(m.range.last + 1).trimEnd()
    val qr = UpiQr(normalised)
    return if (qr.payeeVpa.isNullOrBlank()) null else qr
}

Everything after the prefix is copied by substring. It never passes through a parser on the way to the output. That's the property worth protecting: the exception is written so it cannot reach the query string.

The test

The assertion is one line. The value is in the sample list, where each entry is a shape that round-tripping would damage:

@RunWith(RobolectricTestRunner::class)
@Config(sdk = [34])
class PayRouterIntentTest {
    private val app = PayRouter.UpiApp("com.example.upi", "Example", null)

    private val samples = listOf(
        // percent-escapes, '+' and '/' inside a signature
        "upi://pay?ver=01&mode=19&pa=shop@okaxis&pn=A%20SHOP&tr=X1&cu=INR&mc=5211&sign=MEUCIQDx+/ab==",
        // '+' and an encoded '&' in a name, an empty amount
        "upi://pay?pn=A+B%26C&pa=a.b-c_d@okhdfcbank&am=&cu=INR",
        // duplicate key, non-ASCII escapes, empty values
        "upi://pay?pa=x@ybl&pa=y@ybl&tn=caf%C3%A9%20%E2%82%B9&orgid=000000&mid=&msid=",
        // encoded slashes and a whole URL inside a value
        "upi://pay?pa=m@sbi&pn=Shop&am=2400.00&tr=ORD%2F2026%2F17&url=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.in%2Fo%3Fid%3D1",
    )

    @Test fun `pay intent carries the decoded string byte for byte`() {
        for (s in samples) {
            val i = PayRouter.payIntent(UpiQr.parse(s)!!, app)
            assertEquals(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, i.action)
            assertEquals(s, i.dataString)
            assertEquals(app.packageName, i.`package`)
            assertNull("no extras may be added", i.extras)
        }
    }
}

Three things make this a useful test rather than a tautology:

  1. It uses Robolectric, not a mocked Uri. The behaviour under test belongs to the framework classes. A mock would only confirm what the mock was told, so the test needs a real Uri and a real Intent.
  2. It asserts on dataString, the exact text the receiving app will see. Comparing Uri objects or decoded fields would pass even after the encoding changed.
  3. The samples are ugly on purpose. A tidy pa=a@b&pn=Name survives almost any implementation. Only odd order, empty values, duplicates and + catch a rewrite.

This is trimmed from the real test, with the sample values changed. The same check runs on the other routes into the hand-off: the system chooser (unwrap EXTRA_INTENT and compare), a link found inside a longer shared message, and the upper-case scheme case, which asserts that only the prefix and the trailing whitespace changed.

What the test doesn't promise

It proves the link leaves this app unchanged. It says nothing about what happens next. The receiving UPI app and the banks behind it can still refuse a payment for their own reasons, and no amount of string care changes that. Keeping the pipe clean only rules this app out as the cause, which is most of what you want when something fails after the PIN screen.

If you hand any signed or third-party link to another app

  • Keep the original string as the source of truth, and treat parsed fields as display values.
  • Never route the output through a builder, even "just to add one parameter".
  • Write any normalisation so it touches a known prefix and cannot reach the rest.
  • Test against the string the receiver will read, with samples chosen to break a round trip.

Auto UPI QR is on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.autoupiqr. It reads UPI QR codes from images and hands the link to your own UPI app. It is not a bank and never sees your PIN. The code and test here are from the current source, and I don't claim which Play build contains them. Always check the payee name before entering your UPI PIN.

title: Baton: Who Keeps the Promise When the Shift Ends?
description:
“Shift’s over. Who keeps the promise to call the customer back?”

That question is where Baton started.

I come from support and solutions engineering, and I’m teaching myself to code. When I think about a handover, I think about the customer waiting for a call, the vendor still investigating, and the incoming colleague trying to work out what they have actually agreed to do.

A conversation can contain all the facts and still leave responsibility unclear. “Seen” is an acknowledgement. A name in a summary is a suggestion. Neither tells me whether someone has accepted the callback at its latest promised time.

For WeMakeDevs’ “Flip the Switch” hackathon, I built Baton around that gap. The demo cases are fictional; the operational question is the one I wanted to explore.

Transparency note: I set the goals and made the key calls, such as when a claim counts as stale. AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) wrote most of the code and the first draft of this post, and reviewed each other’s work. The rules, tests and eval numbers below can be reproduced from the repository.

LLM proposes, code enforces, humans own the promise.

Baton has three participants. @baton, running through Claude Code, drafts a versioned handover ticket from the conversation. @checker, running through Codex, reviews it against the conversation, shared procedures, and ledger replies. @ledger is a custom Node.js agent with no LLM.

The ledger records explicit claims. An incoming owner enters a command such as:

@ledger claim SR-1077 v1

It uses the sender name supplied by Switch rather than accepting a name written inside the command. Putting someone in the ticket’s owner field does not create a claim.

The distinction matters when a promise changes. In the English rehearsal, SR-1077 initially had a callback at 16:00. The incoming shift claimed it. The customer then moved the callback to 15:30.

Once ledger accepted the updated ticket, the earlier claim became stale. The same owner had to claim again against v2. A change to another case, or to what the team was waiting for, would not invalidate that claim if its promise time stayed unchanged.

Ledger also rejects new claims against older tickets, prevents a second person from claiming an already held case, and flags promises without valid claims when they are less than 30 minutes away. That urgency check happens when someone requests status.

Switch provided the place where these participants could work together.

The room holds the conversation. Room instructions describe roles, ticket formatting, and ownership rules. Room documents hold the SOP, escalation matrix, and current handover ticket. Baton updates that ticket document after ledger accepts the version; checker can read it without editing Baton's documents.

The Discord bridge connects the staff channel to the Switch room. Through Switch’s custom agent protocol, my non-LLM ledger receives room events over WebSocket and sends replies and operations over HTTP.

I also used !invite-agent @checker to bring the reviewer into an ongoing handover. Once tagged, checker could read the existing history and documents without someone repeating the brief. That was a useful test: could a reviewer join late and still identify what had changed?

Building this taught me several things that were less obvious than the architecture.

The first was how easily formatting can become a business decision.

An independent Codex review found that the original parser stopped at a blank line. Imagine a new ticket containing two cases, separated by an empty line. The parser could accept only the first case.

That was dangerous because an accepted replacement ticket must contain every open case. Omitted cases become closed. A harmless-looking blank line could therefore close the second case accidentally.

The revised specification explicitly skips blank lines and requires every other line inside the block to be valid. Malformed blocks apply nothing. For me, this connected a parser detail directly to the support workflow: stopping early could make unfinished work disappear.

The second lesson came from disagreement between the AI tools.

The instruction review initially recommended reflecting ownership changes in a new ticket version. A follow-up review withdrew that recommendation: ledger already stores ownership, and publishing another version just because someone claimed a case would create unnecessary R2 rejections for subsequent claims against the previous version.

That exchange helped clarify the boundary. Ticket versions describe the handover facts; ledger records who has accepted them. The SOP also needed to respect that distinction, otherwise checker could keep asking for unnecessary versions.

I learned to look for the consequence of a proposed instruction. “Keep everything updated” sounds reasonable until it causes another person’s valid next action to fail.

The third lesson was that a rehearsal has its own timing problems.

The English transcript contains a checker mention blocked by an addressing policy. Baton noticed and passed the reminder along. Later, checker produced a reminder saying claims still needed doing, even though the claim commands had already appeared.

Both moments remain in the transcript. They show why an 18/18 checkpoint score needs context.

The clock needs context too. Ledger supports a fake time for demonstrations, but that setting does not control the LLM agents’ clocks. For a live manual demo, the promises need to be in the future in UTC+7. The setup instructions also call for a fresh room and fresh ledger for another take, so previous rehearsal context does not become part of the next handover.

The recorded results from 6 November 2026 give me evidence for some parts of Baton.

The deterministic ledger evaluation passed 18/18 scenarios, with 92 checks. It supplied known-correct ticket blocks and exercised parsed commands against expected behavior. Thirteen scenarios tested violations covered by the ownership rules, and two tested clean handovers without false alarms.

The mutation checks made that result more meaningful. Changing the urgency boundary from < 30 to <= 30 caused S12 to fail. Disabling stale-version rejection, changed-time handling, or duplicate-owner protection failed the corresponding scenarios. Removing the explicit-ownership rule failed eight scenarios.

A separate English rehearsal passed 18/18 checkpoints using a real Switch room, Claude Code, Codex, and ledger, with two staff roles simulated by API agents. It demonstrated the callback change, renewed ownership, rejection of an old-version claim, completed handover, and a follow-up answer using 15:30.

Those results have clear limits. Three ledger scenarios pass precisely because ledger behaves as specified while missing risks outside its rules: a changed contact channel, closure mentioned only in chat, and an owner lacking permission to perform the action. Checker’s detection rate for those risks has not been systematically measured. Neither has Baton's extraction accuracy across the scenario set.

There are implementation limits too. Human-only claiming is currently an instruction-level restriction; ledger does not reject agent claimants, and the automated rehearsal relies on that. State lives in a local JSON file. There is no automatic reconnect or scheduled reminder loop, and promises across different days need manual review.

I have not measured customer outcomes.

What I have built is a small workflow where drafting, checking, and accepting responsibility are separate actions. Teaching myself to code through Baton meant learning to make those boundaries explicit—and finding the places where my own design blurred them.

The question I want Baton to answer is simple: who accepted this promise, at this time?

Explore the repository: https://github.com/neweraXX/baton

title: Metro/Metro 3D: We made a modular system that could support complexity in small spaces

title: Python Data Structures Explained: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Python data structures are the built-in containers that hold groups of values in your program: lists for ordered, changeable collections; tuples for ordered, fixed collections; sets for unique values with no duplicates; and dictionaries for labelled values stored as key and value pairs. Choosing the right container makes your code shorter, faster and easier to read, because each structure is designed for a different job. This guide explains all four in plain words, with small examples you can type and run, and a simple rule for picking the right one every time.

Why Containers Matter at All

A single variable holds a single value, like one name or one price. Real programs juggle many values at once: all the students in a class, the items in a cart, the words in a sentence. Saving each one in its own variable would be like carrying groceries home one item per trip. Data structures are the bags and boxes: they carry many values together, each with its own shape and rules.

The official Python tutorial has a full chapter simply called Data Structures in the Python Tutorial, covering lists in depth, the del statement, tuples and sequences, sets, dictionaries and looping techniques. This guide follows the same ground in simpler words, so you can read the official chapter afterwards without fear.

Lists: Ordered and Changeable 

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]
fruits.append("orange")
fruits[0] = "green apple"
print(fruits)       # ['green apple', 'banana', 'mango', 'orange']
print(fruits[1])    # banana

A list keeps values in order, written inside square brackets, and you can change it after creating it: add, remove, replace or sort items freely. Positions are counted from zero, so the first item is index 0, a rule that surprises every beginner exactly once. Lists are the workhorse of Python: shopping carts, to-do items, search results and rows from a database all live naturally in lists. When order matters and the collection will grow or shrink, reach for a list first. Our detailed guide to Python list methods covers append, insert, remove, pop, sort and the rest with examples.

Tuples: Ordered but Fixed 

point = (10, 20)
city = ("Delhi", 28.6, 77.2)
print(city[0])      # Delhi
# city[0] = "Jaipur"   # Error: tuples cannot be changed

A tuple looks like a list written with round brackets, but once created it cannot be changed. That fixed nature is a feature, not a flaw. Tuples suit values that belong together and should stay together: coordinates, an RGB colour, a day-month-year date, or a database record returned as one row. Because a tuple cannot be edited by accident, it also works as a dictionary key, which a list cannot. A tuple with one item needs a trailing comma, like (5,), otherwise Python sees plain brackets around a number, a tiny trap worth knowing before it bites you.

The official Python Tutorial page "5. Data Structures" on docs.python.org, opening with "More on Lists" and the list methods append, extend, insert, remove and pop.

Sets: Unique Values, No Duplicates 

tags = {"python", "coding", "python", "tutorial"}
print(tags)         # {'python', 'coding', 'tutorial'} - duplicate gone
print("python" in tags)   # True, and very fast
tags.add("beginners")

A set stores unique values only, written with curly brackets. Add the same value ten times and it is stored once, quietly, without an error. Sets do not promise a useful order, so you cannot ask for the third item; that is the trade you make. In return, checking whether a value exists in a set is extremely fast, and set maths is elegant: union joins two sets, intersection keeps common values, and difference shows what is in one but not the other. Sets shine for removing duplicates, checking membership, and comparing groups, like students enrolled in either of two courses. Think of a set as a guest list with a strict door: every name appears once, no matter how many times it was written down.

Dictionaries: Labelled Values with Keys 

student = {"name": "Asha", "age": 21, "course": "Python"}
print(student["name"])        # Asha
student["marks"] = 88         # add a new pair
student["age"] = 22           # update a value

A dictionary stores pairs: a key that labels, and a value that belongs to it. Instead of remembering that age is "the second item", you simply ask for student["age"]. Dictionaries model real things beautifully: a student, a product, a user profile, or the settings of an app. Keys must be unique and unchangeable types like strings or numbers; values can be anything, including lists and other dictionaries. Our side-by-side guide to Python list vs dictionary shows exactly when indexed access beats labelled access, with the same data written both ways.

Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries Side by Side

Structure Written as Ordered? Changeable? Duplicates? Best for
List [1, 2, 3] Yes Yes Allowed Collections that grow and change
Tuple (1, 2, 3) Yes No Allowed Fixed groups that belong together
Set {1, 2, 3} No useful order Yes Removed automatically Unique values and fast membership checks
Dictionary {"a": 1} By insertion Yes Keys unique, values may repeat Labelled data about one thing

The official Python documentation on built-in types is the complete reference for these containers, including every method and edge case, once the basics here feel comfortable.

A Simple Rule for Choosing

Ask three quick questions. Do the values need labels, like name and age? Choose a dictionary. Must duplicates disappear, or is fast "is it in there?" checking the main job? Choose a set. Should the group stay exactly as created, like coordinates? Choose a tuple. For everything else, the everyday growing, shrinking, ordered collection, choose a list. Most beginner programs live happily on lists and dictionaries alone for months, and there is no prize for using all four in every file, however tempting it feels.

Looping Through Each Structure

All four containers work with a plain for loop, but what the loop hands you differs, and that difference is worth seeing once, clearly. Looping a list or tuple gives you each value in order. Looping a set gives you each unique value, in no promised order. Looping a dictionary gives you its keys, and the common pattern student.items() gives you key and value together, which reads almost like English.

for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, "=", value)
# name = Asha
# age = 22
# course = Python

Beginners often write loops that count positions by hand, like range(len(fruits)), when Python happily gives the items directly. If you ever need both the position and the value, enumerate() provides them cleanly. Simple loops over the container itself are shorter, clearer and harder to break, which is why experienced Python programmers reach for them first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the four main data structures in Python?

Lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries. Lists are ordered and changeable, tuples are ordered and fixed, sets hold unique values, and dictionaries store key and value pairs.

When should I use a tuple instead of a list?

Use a tuple when the group should never change after creation, such as coordinates, colours or a fixed record. Use a list when you plan to add, remove or edit items.

Can a dictionary have a list as a value?

Yes. Dictionary values can be any type, including lists, tuples, sets and other dictionaries. Only the keys must be unchangeable types such as strings, numbers or tuples.

How do I remove duplicates from a list?

Convert it to a set and back: unique = list(set(my_list)). This removes duplicates, but the order may change, so sort the result if order matters for your program.

Are Python data structures the same as DSA data structures?

They overlap but are not identical. These four are Python's built-in containers for daily coding. DSA as a subject also covers structures you build or study, like stacks, queues, trees and graphs, often using these built-ins as parts.

Conclusion

Lists carry, tuples protect, sets clean, and dictionaries label. Learn those four personalities and Python code becomes much easier to plan before you write it. Start with lists and dictionaries, add sets when duplicates annoy you, and use tuples when a group must stay fixed. The right container is a small decision that quietly makes everything after it simpler.

title: GBase Database 8c: Comparing Configuration Complexity Across Three Deployment Layouts
description:
Choosing a GBase Database(GBase 8c) deployment layout is not just an infrastructure decision. It also determines how much configuration work, port planning, and review effort the deployment will require.

This is not a performance comparison. The focus here is configuration complexity across three common GBase Database deployment layouts: minimal single node, single HA group, and default distributed.

Four dimensions make the differences easier to quantify: host count, component instances, port allocation, and configuration review effort.

1. Compare the Three GBase Database Deployment Layouts

The following table summarizes their configuration differences.

Dimension Minimal single node Single HA group Default distributed
Hosts 1 3 3
Component instances 5 11 12
DN groups 1 1 2
DN instances 1 3 6
Main ports 5 8 10+
Requires az Yes Yes No
Requires proxy_port Yes Yes No

The numbers represent the three configuration examples, not universal requirements for every possible deployment.

The differences become clearer when each dimension is examined separately.

2. Component Count: More Instances Mean More Configuration to Verify

The minimal single-node layout has five component instances on one host.

The single-HA-group layout expands to eleven instances distributed across three hosts.

The default distributed layout contains twelve instances, including six datanode instances across two DN groups.

As component count increases, engineers have more configuration sections to verify:

  • Instance definitions
  • Host assignments
  • Service ports
  • Agent ports
  • Directory settings
  • Primary and standby relationships

This does not necessarily mean every additional instance introduces the same amount of work. However, more instances increase the number of relationships that must be checked across the configuration.

For GBase Database deployment planning, instance count is a useful starting point for estimating configuration review effort.

3. Port Allocation: The Main Source of Configuration Complexity

Port planning becomes increasingly important as more components share the same hosts.

The minimal layout uses five main ports.

The single-HA-group layout requires additional port assignments, including proxy ports.

The default distributed layout introduces more DN instances and additional port ranges, resulting in ten or more main port assignments in the example.

Port count affects two things:

  1. The amount of work required to build and maintain the port inventory.
  2. The number of potential conflicts that must be checked on each host.

A port allocation table should therefore be organized by host and component rather than maintained as a flat list.

For GBase Database(GBase 8c), service, proxy, and agent ports should all be included in the deployment review.

4. Configuration Fields: Similar Structures Do Not Mean Identical Requirements

One easily overlooked difference is the presence of az and proxy_port.

The minimal single-node and single-HA-group examples include these fields, while the default distributed example does not.

This means the default distributed configuration is not simply a larger version of the single-HA-group configuration.

It is not a strict superset of the other layouts.

Copying an existing gbase.yml file and deleting fields that appear unnecessary can leave behind inappropriate settings or remove fields required by the target topology.

The safer approach is to select the official configuration example that matches the intended deployment layout, then modify host addresses, directories, and other deployment-specific values.

5. Configuration Review Effort: Different Layouts Need Different Decisions

The three GBase Database layouts also require different levels of review.

Minimal single node

This is the simplest configuration and is suitable for functional validation. A focused review by one engineer may take approximately 30 minutes, depending on the environment.

Single HA group

This layout introduces multi-host coordination, replica placement, and port planning. A network engineer should participate to confirm ports and subnets.

Default distributed

This layout adds multiple DN groups and data-distribution decisions. Reviewers must confirm primary placement, replica relationships, and the distribution-key design.

The important point is that configuration review effort does not increase in direct proportion to YAML line count.

A configuration with fewer fields can still require more architectural judgment.

6. Why Configuration Complexity Is Not Linear

The default distributed layout has the most component instances, but its example does not include az and proxy_port.

This creates an important distinction:

  • Component count measures how many instances need to be configured.
  • Port count measures how many assignments need to be validated.
  • Field count measures the amount of configuration text.
  • Review effort measures the decisions engineers must make.

These dimensions are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A longer YAML file does not automatically mean a more difficult deployment. The real complexity comes from topology, port allocation, replica placement, and data-distribution requirements.

This is why estimating GBase Database deployment effort by counting configuration lines is unreliable.

7. Which GBase Database Layout Should You Start With?

Each layout serves a different deployment objective.

Deployment objective Suggested starting layout
Functional validation Minimal single node
Initial production HA deployment Single HA group
Multi-group data distribution Default distributed

The minimal layout provides the lowest configuration cost for functional validation.

The single-HA-group layout introduces high availability and is a practical starting point for production-oriented deployments.

If the architecture requires data distribution across multiple DN groups, start with the default distributed example rather than converting a simpler configuration later.

The decision should follow the target architecture, not the number of fields in the YAML file.

Conclusion: Configuration Decisions Matter More Than YAML Length

GBase Database(GBase 8c) uses a consistent deployment command set across these three layouts, but their configuration requirements are not interchangeable.

The real differences are in component instances, port allocation, topology-specific fields, and the decisions required during review.

A practical rule is:

  • Use the minimal layout for functional validation.
  • Use the single-HA-group layout when planning an initial HA deployment.
  • Use the default distributed layout when multiple DN groups are part of the target architecture.

Choose the topology first, start from its corresponding official example, and estimate the deployment effort based on decisions that must be verified—not simply the number of YAML lines.

When estimating GBase Database deployment complexity, do you count configuration fields, component instances, or the decisions engineers need to make?

title: How to Build a Queue-Based Daily Scheduled Email Node.js Example — Shipment Delivery
description:
How to Fan Out Shipment Updates Reliably — Queue Retries and Live Delivery

Use a queue-based Node.js worker for a daily scheduled email report, then hand each accepted shipment update to a live-delivery channel with the same idempotency key. That boundary keeps a temporary subscriber disconnect from deleting durable work.

Before: cron -> generate report -> notify everyone -> one timeout hides several failures.

After: cron -> queue -> idempotent worker -> acknowledgement -> live publish.

The daily report is the durable unit. The realtime message is a delivery attempt. Those are different jobs.

What should the scheduler own?

A scheduler should start work, not perform all of it. A daily report can cover many shipment updates, so the trigger should enqueue a small job and return. The worker consumes that job, generates the report, and publishes the notification. A cron task has a 900-second execution limit; a queue worker is the right place for work that might outlive that window.

For a public cron trigger, expose an HTTPS endpoint that publishes the job. Keep the payload below the queue’s 256 KB message limit. The worker carries a stable key because standard delivery is at-least-once. A retry can happen. Plan for it. Infrai fits this early boundary when one REST API and one key for the queue and live delivery matter more than operating two specialist services; its public discovery surface also documents runnable examples.

One useful identity is shipment-report:2026-10-25. It makes a duplicate visible in logs and gives the report generator a deterministic fence.

Can a queue-based daily scheduled email use one Node.js worker?

Yes, if it acknowledges the durable job only after the work it owns has completed. The worker generates the daily report, publishes the notification, and then acknowledges. A failed attempt should be retried with backoff or moved to a dead-letter queue. Do not acknowledge first and hope the next system succeeds.

Here is the smallest handoff example. It uses the same INFRAI_API_KEY and base URL for queue and realtime publish calls. The identifiers are application-owned, so a repeated delivery can be recognized by the receiver.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

async function post(url: string, body: unknown, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: "Bearer " + apiKey,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(url + " failed (" + response.status + "): " + detail);
  }

  return response.json() as Promise<Record<string, unknown>>;
}

async function publishShipmentUpdate() {
  const shipmentId = "shp_4821";
  const eventId = "shipment-delivered:" + shipmentId + ":2026-10-25";
  const update = {
    event_id: eventId,
    shipment_id: shipmentId,
    status: "delivered",
    report_date: "2026-10-25",
  };

  await post(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
    { queue: "shipment-report", message: update },
    eventId,
  );

  await post(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish",
    {
      channel: "shipment:" + shipmentId,
      event: "status.updated",
      data: update,
    },
    eventId,
  );
}

publishShipmentUpdate().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

The same key and URL remove a real integration seam: the queue that retains the notification and the socket that attempts delivery use one credential boundary. If the subscriber is offline, the queue message remains durable work. The realtime publish can be retried with the same event ID rather than producing a second business event.

That is also the honest trade-off. One provider means one credential and one bill to reconcile across these backend calls, but it creates one vendor dependency and one outage surface.

Where do retries stop?

A retry policy needs three decisions: what is transient, what is permanent, and when to stop. A 429 should back off and honor Retry-After; a validation error should go to the dead-letter queue without an endless loop. Delayed messages are limited to 7 days, retention to 30 days, and acknowledgement removes a message.

Standard queues deliver at least once. Make report generation idempotent with the report date and merchant identity. Make notification handling idempotent with event_id. If the worker crashes after publishing but before acknowledgement, redelivery must become a no-op.

A compact worker policy looks like this:

type Delivery = {
  event_id: string;
  shipment_id: string;
  status: string;
  report_date: string;
};

async function handle(delivery: Delivery) {
  if (await hasApplied(delivery.event_id)) {
    await acknowledge(delivery);
    return;
  }

  try {
    await persistShipmentStatus(delivery);
    await markApplied(delivery.event_id);
    await acknowledge(delivery);
  } catch (error: unknown) {
    if (isPermanent(error)) {
      await moveToDeadLetter(delivery, error);
      await acknowledge(delivery);
      return;
    }

    await retryWithBackoff(delivery, error);
  }
}

The helper functions are application boundaries: persistShipmentStatus owns the database transaction, and markApplied must share a unique constraint with event_id. Queue configuration does not replace that constraint.

How does this compare with other queue choices?

RabbitMQ is a strong fit when you want explicit acknowledgements, routing controls, and a broker your team already operates. Its consumer acknowledgement model maps cleanly to the worker rule above. The operational cost is that you own more broker configuration and deployment.

Amazon SQS is a strong fit for an AWS-centered system that wants a managed queue and a familiar dead-letter pattern. Its visibility-timeout model makes processing duration a first-class setting. It does not, by itself, solve the live subscriber boundary; you still connect it to a realtime provider.

BullMQ is a practical Node.js choice when Redis is already part of the platform and the team wants job-oriented APIs close to the application. Delayed jobs can feel natural there. The trade-off is another infrastructure dependency, plus glue between Redis-backed job state and a separate live delivery service.

Inngest is a good fit when the team wants application-defined background functions and managed retries. Temporal suits durable, long-running workflow orchestration, especially when joins and stateful steps are central. Trigger.dev is aimed at TypeScript background tasks and developer-friendly execution. Those products address different boundaries; none should be dismissed just because this example is a queue-first design.

Option Integration shape Best fit Boundary
RabbitMQ Broker client and acknowledgements Teams operating a routing-focused broker More broker operations
Amazon SQS Managed queue API and visibility timeout AWS-centered systems Realtime delivery still needs a second service
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Redis is already foundational Redis and live delivery need glue
Inngest Application-defined background functions Managed retries around app code Less direct broker control
Temporal Workflow SDK and durable orchestration Long workflows, joins, and state More workflow machinery than this job needs

The single-API approach fits a team optimizing for integration friction: one discovery surface, one key, and runnable examples across the capability surface. The live manifest exposes 295 routes across 20 modules. For this workflow, queue and realtime publish calls use the same authentication and base URL. That is the concrete advantage: one credential boundary replaces separate queue and realtime signup work, while the REST surface avoids an SDK install.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the queue-to-notification portion when reducing credential sprawl and first-result setup matters more than owning separate broker and realtime failure domains. The supporting benefit is a consistent idempotency convention, including the Idempotency-Key header, so the retry contract is visible at the integration boundary. Choose RabbitMQ, SQS, or BullMQ when your organization already has strong operational ownership of a specialist or needs its deeper routing and replay model.

The boundary matters. There is no queue-wide replay model like Kafka consumer groups, no native debounce or throttle, and FIFO deduplication lasts only 5 minutes. There is also no DAG or workflow join primitive. For a daily shipment report with a worker and an at-least-once queue, those limits can be acceptable. For long-running workflows with joins, replay, and orchestration, a specialist wins.

What should you verify before shipping?

First, fire the public cron trigger and inspect the job identity. Confirm that a second trigger for the same report date does not create a second business result. Then stop the worker after live publish but before acknowledgement. Redelivery should be harmless.

Next, test a disconnected subscriber. The queue should retain the work while the realtime delivery attempt fails or waits for the consumer policy. Finally, test a malformed payload and verify that it reaches the dead-letter path instead of consuming every retry. Keep the output small enough for the queue limit, and keep the cron request short enough to enqueue rather than process the report inline.

The Pusher-plus-SQS version would require two signups, two credential sets, and glue code to correlate an SQS message with a Pusher event. That can be the right architecture when independent vendors are a requirement. It is also the integration work the shared boundary removes.

If the queue-to-live-delivery boundary fits your system, start with the daily report queue guidance and verify the request schema in discovery before wiring production jobs.

References

  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • BullMQ guide
  • Pusher Channels events
  • Infrai scheduling discovery

title: Your CRM Remembers What Happened. We Wanted It to Remember Why.
description:
A sales representative offers a 20% discount. The customer doesn't like and two weeks later, another representative joins the conversation and offers an even better deal.

Problem is nobody remembers that the customer had already explained what was actually bothering them.

The problem wasn't the price. It was the integration they were waiting for.

This is a fairly common situation in sales. It's also an interesting problem to solve with AI, but can it?


https://in.pinterest.com/pin/509469776581405594/

We started building RevenueOS around a simple idea: what if a sales assistant could remember everything a company had heard from a customer, connect conversations across different people and more importantly, use that history to make better decisions?

Not just remember what happened. Remember why it happened.

The problem with giving AI a conversation history

Most AI applications I've worked with have some way of providing context to a model. You can pass the previous messages, retrieve relevant documents, or query a vector database before generating an answer.

That works reasonably well when the information is relatively self-contained.

But customer relationships aren't.

Consider a customer called Halcyon Logistics.

During the first meeting, their CFO mentions that the subscription is expensive and asks for a 15% discount. Their CTO, meanwhile, has a completely different concern: they need SAP integration and want the implementation completed within 30 days.

The sales representative promises to send the integration documentation by Friday.

Two weeks later, another representative speaks to the same customer. This time, the customer says that even a 20% discount isn't convincing enough. The CTO again asks about automated SAP synchronisation.

Now imagine asking an AI assistant:

"Why isn't Halcyon Logistics closing? What should I do next?"

If the assistant only sees the latest conversation, it might recommend another discount.

If it has access to the complete history, it can connect the dots:

The CFO initially raised a pricing concern.
A 20% discount was subsequently rejected.
The CTO's integration concern appeared in multiple conversations.
The implementation timeline remains important.
The integration documentation promised during the first meeting is still outstanding.

The recommendation changes entirely.

Instead of offering another discount, the assistant should recommend resolving the technical concerns and fulfilling the outstanding commitment.

This is the distinction we wanted to explore.

Introducing RevenueOS

We built RevenueOS as a sales intelligence and deal negotiation workspace for B2B sales teams.

The idea is to give every customer a persistent memory that grows with every interaction.

Different representatives can log meetings, calls, emails and uploaded documents. RevenueOS analyses the information, connects it with previous interactions and makes the accumulated context available to anyone working on that account.

The application has a few important parts:

  • Revenue Memory: Maintains long-term customer context.
  • Deal Negotiator: Uses historical conversations to recommend negotiation strategies.
  • Commitment Tracker: Remembers promises made by both the sales team and the customer.
  • Memory Explorer: Provides a visual way to explore what the system remembers.
  • Negotiation Playbook: Learns from previous won and lost deals.
  • Ask RevenueOS: Allows representatives to ask questions about individual customers or the entire sales pipeline.

But the interesting part isn't the number of features. It's how the memory layer connects them.

Why I chose Hindsight

We didn't want to build another chatbot that simply stores previous messages and appends them to the next prompt.

We wanted something that could retain information, retrieve relevant memories later, and consolidate observations over time.

That's what led me to Hindsight, an open-source memory system for AI agents, developed by Vectorize.

*Hindsight provides three operations that became central to RevenueOS:
*

  • Retain: Store information as long-term memory.
  • Recall: Retrieve relevant memories when needed.
  • Reflect: Generate answers using accumulated knowledge.

There's also an important distinction between remembering individual facts and developing a broader understanding from repeated interactions.

For example, one conversation might contain a pricing objection. Another might contain a rejected discount. Over time, the system can develop a more useful observation: discounts aren't resolving this customer's actual blocker.

You can explore the Hindsight documentation to understand its memory architecture in more detail.

We particularly liked the idea that memory should be more than a storage mechanism. It should help an AI system build a progressively better understanding of the information it encounters.

The architecture: structured data and conversational memory

One decision we made early was not to use Hindsight as a replacement for the application's database.

RevenueOS has two different kinds of information.

The first is structured business data:

  • Customers
  • Deals
  • Stakeholders
  • Offers
  • Objections
  • Commitments
  • Sales representatives

The second is contextual information:

  1. What a stakeholder said during a meeting.
  2. Why a particular offer was rejected.
  3. How a customer's position changed over time.
  4. Which technical requirements keep appearing.
  5. What the sales team promised.

I use PostgreSQL for the structured CRM information and Hindsight for long-term conversational memory.

The architecture looks roughly like this:

                Sales Interactions
                       |
                       v
              Interaction Analysis
                       |
             +---------+---------+
             |                   |
             v                   v
       PostgreSQL             Hindsight
       Structured             Customer
       CRM data               Memory
             |                   |
             +---------+---------+
                       |
                       v
                Deal Negotiator
                       |
             +---------+---------+
             |                   |
             v                   v
       Customer Memory      Shared Playbook
             |                   |
             +---------+---------+
                       |
                       v
               Cited Recommendation

We don't need a memory system to calculate the total value of an open pipeline. That's structured data.

But we do need it to understand why a particular deal has been stuck for three weeks.

One memory bank per customer

This was another important architectural decision.

Instead of putting every customer's conversations into one shared memory bank, RevenueOS creates a separate Hindsight bank for each customer.

The implementation is deliberately simple:

customerBank(customerId: string) {
  return `${config.hindsight.bankPrefix}-customer-${customerId}`;
}

Every interaction associated with that customer goes into the same bank, regardless of which representative logged it.

This gives us two things.

First, representatives can share knowledge about an account without manually forwarding meeting notes to each other.

Second, customer memories remain isolated. A negotiation with one company shouldn't accidentally influence an answer about another company's confidential conversations.

There is also a separate memory bank for the negotiation playbook. I'll come back to that because it introduced an interesting problem of its own.

The interesting part: recalling before remembering

One of my favourite implementation decisions in RevenueOS happens when a new interaction is logged.

A naive implementation would take the latest conversation, extract some facts and store them.

But that misses an important opportunity.

Before processing new information, I first retrieve what Hindsight already knows about that customer.

The new conversation is then analysed against the existing memories.

The workflow looks like this:

const bank = memory.customerBank(customer.id);


await memory.ensureCustomerBank(
  customer.id,
  customer.name
);


// Retrieve existing context first.
const prior = await memory.recall(
  bank,
  text,
  { maxTokens: 2500 }
);


// Analyse the new interaction against
// the information already remembered.
const analysis = await llmJson({
  schema: AnalysisSchema,
  system: analysisInstructions,
  user: buildAnalysisContext({
    interaction: text,
    previousMemories: prior
  })
});

This is important because the system isn't analysing the latest conversation in isolation.

It can identify:

  • Facts that have already been mentioned.
  • New requirements.
  • Changes in customer preferences.
  • Contradictory statements.
  • Repeated objections.
  • Commitments that remain unfulfilled.

For example, a customer initially asks for a 15% discount and later says that even 20% isn't enough.

Those two statements mean something different when considered together than when read independently.

I also wanted to preserve the distinction between what the customer promised and what our own sales representative promised.

A customer saying they'll arrange a technical review is not the same as a salesperson promising to send integration documentation.

That distinction matters when determining what is blocking a deal.

The extraction pipeline uses structured schemas to validate the information before it is persisted. This is particularly useful because the system needs more than a paragraph summarising the meeting. It needs identifiable stakeholders, objections, offers, commitments and relationships with previous memories.

A negotiator that can explain its recommendations

Once customer memories start accumulating, the next question becomes:

How do we actually use them?

We didn't want the Deal Negotiator to simply retrieve the top few memories and ask an LLM to generate a generic sales strategy.

A negotiation decision usually depends on multiple dimensions.

For example:

  • Pricing history.
  • Technical requirements.
  • Implementation concerns.
  • Previous objections.
  • Unfulfilled promises.

So we implemented multi-angle recall.

The negotiator retrieves account memories using multiple queries, merges the results, removes duplicates and ranks the relevant information.

It also retrieves relevant lessons from the shared negotiation playbook.

A simplified version of the retrieval logic looks like this:

const results = await Promise.all(
  queries.map((query) =>
    memory.recall(
      bank,
      `${customer.name}: ${query}`,
      { maxTokens: 1500 }
    )
  )
);


const merged = new Map<string, MemoryHit>();


results.flat().forEach((hit) => {
  const previous = merged.get(hit.id);


  if (!previous ||
      (hit.score ?? 0) > (previous.score ?? 0)) {
    merged.set(hit.id, hit);
  }
});

The important detail is that these aren't five unrelated chatbot conversations.

They are different retrieval angles over the same customer's accumulated memory.

The negotiator then combines:

  1. Customer-specific memories.
  2. Existing CRM commitments.
  3. Anonymised lessons from other closed deals.

The output is a negotiation brief containing the actual blocker, a verdict, recommended strategy, risks, stakeholder-specific actions and supporting evidence.

I also wanted recommendations to be explainable.

Every recommendation should reference the memories or commitments that influenced it.

RevenueOS uses references such as M1 for account memories, C1 for CRM commitments and P1 for playbook lessons.

This makes it possible to trace a recommendation back to the information that produced it rather than treating the model's answer as unquestionable.

Teaching the system from previous deals

This is where RevenueOS becomes more interesting than a system that only remembers individual customers.

Imagine one customer closes a deal because the sales team offers a phased implementation plan.

Another customer is negotiating with us and has similar implementation concerns.

Could the system use the previous experience to make a better recommendation?

We wanted it to.

Whenever a deal is marked as won or lost, RevenueOS records the full outcome in that customer's private memory bank.

It also creates an anonymised lesson in a separate shared playbook bank.

There is a reason for keeping these memories separate.

The system should learn that a particular negotiation tactic worked without exposing the identity or confidential details of the original customer.

For example:

Original deal information:

A specific customer accepted a multi-year contract after the sales team proposed a phased implementation.

Generalised lesson:

Customers concerned about implementation complexity may respond better to phased implementation plans than additional discounts.

The anonymisation process uses an LLM to generalise the lesson, followed by a deterministic sanitisation step.

The latter removes identifiable names, domains, exact amounts and dates that might remain in the generated text.

This is an important distinction: We don't want to share customer conversations across accounts. We want to share the lessons learned from them.

Over time, the playbook can consolidate observations about which tactics tend to work against particular blockers.

You can read more about the broader concept of agent memory and how AI systems learn from past interactions.

Making memory visible

One thing we didn't want was for Hindsight to become an invisible dependency hidden behind an API call.

If persistent memory is the central idea of the application, users should be able to inspect it.

That's why we added Memory Explorer.

It provides two ways to explore customer memory:

A traditional memory list with retrieval information.
An interactive knowledge map built using React Flow.

The knowledge map places the customer at the centre and organises related information into categories such as stakeholders, conversations, negotiations, objections, commitments and deal history.

Users can explore individual memories, see their sources and follow relationships between them.

We find this particularly useful because a memory without provenance is difficult to trust.

If RevenueOS tells me that a customer repeatedly raised an integration concern, we should be able to inspect the conversations that support that conclusion.

The goal isn't just to show that the AI remembers something. It's to make that memory inspectable.

What We've learned building RevenueOS

There were a few things we found particularly interesting while working through this architecture.

1. More context doesn't automatically mean better answers

Passing every previous conversation to an LLM isn't a reliable memory strategy.

It increases the amount of information the model has to process without guaranteeing that the relevant information will be available or interpreted correctly.

Retrieval needs to be intentional. The right memories matter more than the number of memories.

2. Memory and structured state solve different problems

We wouldn't use conversational memory to replace a relational database.

A commitment needs an owner, recipient, due date and completion status. Those are structured business properties.

But understanding why that commitment was made requires conversational context.

Both representations are useful, and they should work together.

3. Customer isolation should be an architectural decision

We didn't want privacy to depend entirely on instructions in an LLM prompt.

Separate customer memory banks provide a stronger boundary for retrieval.

The system also needs to keep shared, anonymised learning separate from private customer history.

4. Recommendations need evidence

An AI-generated negotiation strategy can sound convincing even when it is wrong.

Connecting recommendations to specific memories makes it easier to inspect the reasoning and challenge incorrect conclusions.

We consider this an important requirement for any AI system that influences business decisions.

5. A promise is more valuable when the system remembers whether it was kept

Remembering that someone promised to send a document is useful.

Remembering that the document was eventually sent is equally important.

Otherwise, the system keeps treating resolved issues as outstanding blockers.

The memory needs to evolve with the relationship.

The bigger idea

RevenueOS started with a fairly simple question:

What if a sales representative never had to ask another colleague what happened during the previous meeting?

But the problem turned out to be more interesting than that.

A useful sales assistant shouldn't merely retrieve an old conversation. It should understand how the customer's position has changed, connect information from different people, identify unresolved commitments and use previous deal outcomes to inform future decisions.

That's what we wanted to explore with Hindsight.

I'm still particularly interested in where persistent memory takes AI applications beyond sales. The same underlying problem exists anywhere decisions depend on information accumulated over time.

A system that remembers conversations is useful. A system that understands how those conversations connect is much more interesting.

title: Treat Every Email Bounce as a Routing Decision
description:
A bounce report can look like a technical afterthought: a row of rejected addresses, provider messages, and percentages reviewed after the campaign ends.

That view is too passive. A bounce is a routing decision for the next send. It tells the system whether an address should leave the queue, pause temporarily, or return only after someone fixes the underlying problem.

Teams protect their sending reputation when bounce handling changes future behavior automatically.

Separate permanent failures from temporary ones

Not every rejection means the same thing.

A permanent bounce usually indicates that the address or domain cannot receive the message: the mailbox does not exist, the domain has no valid route, or the recipient address is malformed. Repeatedly sending to it wastes volume and signals poor list maintenance.

A temporary bounce can mean the mailbox is full, the receiving server is unavailable, the message is too large, or the provider has deferred the traffic. Some temporary problems justify a later retry. Others become permanent when they continue.

Store the provider response and the category used by the sending system. Do not reduce every failure to one “bounced” label.

Change the recipient state immediately

When a permanent bounce arrives, suppress that address before another stage of the sequence becomes due. The first rejection should affect scheduled follow-ups, future campaigns, and any retry worker using the same contact record.

Temporary bounces need a defined retry policy. Set the number of attempts, spacing, and the condition that stops retrying. A queue should not keep trying forever simply because the error was initially marked temporary.

The recipient state should be shared across campaigns. If one campaign learns that an address does not exist, a different campaign should not rediscover the same fact tomorrow.

Fix the source, not only the row

One bad address is a contact problem. A cluster of similar failures is often a source problem.

Group bounces by import, form, partner, event, or other acquisition source. Look for patterns:

  • the same misspelled domain appears repeatedly;
  • a required email field accepted incomplete values;
  • an old export contains addresses that have not been used for years;
  • a partner list has a much higher permanent-bounce rate;
  • one segment receives a message larger than its servers accept.

Correct the collection or import process that created the records. Deleting individual rows without fixing the source allows the same problem to return.

Validate before the queue is built

Pre-send checks cannot guarantee delivery, but they can remove obvious failures before the domain spends reputation on them.

Normalize whitespace and casing, reject malformed addresses, check that the domain can receive mail, and apply the suppression and unsubscribe lists. Remove duplicates before the contacts become separate queue items.

Keep validation honest. An address that looks valid may still be abandoned, protected by a strict provider, or unable to receive this message. Describe validation as risk reduction, not proof that the mailbox is active.

Watch the first batch before expanding

A small initial batch gives the team time to observe bounce quality before committing the whole list.

Inspect the actual rejection reasons, not only the overall rate. A few permanent failures from one imported segment may justify stopping that source. A wave of temporary deferrals from one provider may justify reducing the pace. A message-size rejection may require changing the email itself.

Write the stop rule before launch. For example: pause the import when permanent bounces exceed the team’s threshold, or slow the campaign when one provider begins deferring traffic.

The exact threshold depends on the domain history, audience, and message type. What matters is that evidence can change the schedule.

Keep transactional and campaign traffic connected

Marketing and product email may share a domain, provider, or suppression system. They should not maintain separate memories of an invalid address.

If a product notification permanently bounces, a campaign should not continue sending to the same mailbox. If a campaign reveals a domain-wide routing problem, the product team should know before an important receipt or security message is attempted.

At the same time, preserve the difference between message types. A campaign can pause while the team investigates; a password reset needs a clear product response when delivery cannot happen.

Review bounce handling as a workflow

Test more than the provider callback. Confirm the full state change:

  1. a test rejection reaches the application;
  2. the event is stored once even if delivered more than once;
  3. the contact receives the correct bounce category;
  4. scheduled follow-ups are cancelled when required;
  5. new campaigns exclude the suppressed address;
  6. the activity log explains why the recipient was skipped.

This test catches the gap where the dashboard records a bounce but the next queue ignores it.

SendHustle filters malformed, suppressed, unsubscribed, and already-contacted recipients before sending. It supports paced campaigns, automations, transactional email, and reply-aware sequence stopping from a verified domain.

A bounce should not become a number that someone reads next week. It should become a decision the sending system applies before the next message leaves.

Explore SendHustle at https://sendhustle.com/.
