title: Treat a crawler skill's output as a versioned interface
description:
A saved crawler workflow is easier to reuse when the next person can trust its output shape. Finding the same button again is only part of the job. Downstream code still needs stable field names, clear missing values, and a way to distinguish a complete collection from an interrupted one.

Here is a small contract I would put around a reusable extraction skill. It is an application-side design example, not a BrowserAct API, a generated Skill Forge artifact, or a claim that a real website passed these checks. This article comes from the BrowserAct team.

Write the consumer's assumptions first

Start with the code or person receiving the result. Which fields identify a row? Which values may be absent? What does the caller do when pagination stops early?

For a directory collection, a consumer might require a source-specific record ID and a source URL. A contact email could remain null when it was not visible. The workflow should not invent a value simply because an export column exists.

Decide those rules before saving the skill. Otherwise a changed extraction path can return plausible JSON that quietly breaks an importer.

Separate shape from coverage

Consider this fictional response:

{
  "schema_version": "records.v1",
  "stop_reason": "row_limit",
  "rows": [
    {
      "record_id": "demo-17",
      "source_url": "https://example.com/records/demo-17",
      "email": null
    }
  ]
}

The response can be structurally valid while covering only part of the requested data. A row limit is an intentional stop, not proof that the directory ended. A blocked page is another reason to return a partial collection with an explicit status.

Use a separate coverage check when you have an authoritative expected set. Without that set, report what was observed and how traversal ended. Do not infer completeness from the absence of an exception.

Put a small validator at the boundary

The following Python example checks a deliberately narrow contract. It does not fetch a website, validate that a URL belongs to the requested source, or prove that row values are true.

def validate_result(result):
    if not isinstance(result, dict):
        raise ValueError("result must be an object")
    if result.get("schema_version") != "records.v1":
        raise ValueError("unsupported schema version")
    if result.get("stop_reason") not in {
        "exhausted", "row_limit", "blocked"
    }:
        raise ValueError("unknown stop reason")
    rows = result.get("rows")
    if not isinstance(rows, list):
        raise ValueError("rows must be a list")
    seen = set()
    for index, row in enumerate(rows):
        if not isinstance(row, dict):
            raise ValueError(f"row {index} must be an object")
        for field in ("record_id", "source_url"):
            value = row.get(field)
            if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
                raise ValueError(f"row {index}: missing {field}")
        key = row["record_id"].strip()
        if key in seen:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate record_id: {key}")
        seen.add(key)
    return result

Here, IDs are unique within this one result. A cross-source collection would need a key that includes the source identity. Do not copy this deduplication rule into a different dataset without checking what makes a record unique.

The validator permits additional fields so optional additions do not automatically break this consumer. It also permits an empty list. Whether an empty collection is an acceptable business result belongs in the coverage and acceptance rules, not in a guessed minimum row count.

Test the contract without pretending to test the crawler

Before connecting it to an importer, try synthetic fixtures: a valid response, a partial blocked response, an empty response, a duplicate ID, a missing source URL, an unsupported version, and a non-list rows value.

The last four should be rejected by this validator. The first three should pass shape validation, with their different business meanings preserved. Passing these fixtures establishes the behavior of this local check. It says nothing about browser access, pagination correctness, or extraction accuracy on a live portal.

Then test the actual saved skill separately, with authorized access and new inputs. Inspect source evidence as well as the returned structure. Keep those results distinct from the synthetic checks.

Version meaning changes, not only field names

A change from a local record ID to a global identifier may keep the same JSON type while changing the meaning. Changing a date from local time to UTC can do the same thing. Treat those changes as contract decisions.

Record the skill revision and contract version with each run. When introducing a breaking change, retain a representative old result and exercise the migration before replacing the importer. A version label is useful only when consumers actually check it.

For missing optional values, document whether null means not observed, unavailable, or not applicable. If your business needs those distinctions, add a separate status field rather than overloading null with several incompatible meanings.

Our Skill Forge workflow guide discusses turning exploration into something reusable. An output contract gives the next caller a concrete boundary to review, even when the website path changes.

Which breaks your downstream pipeline more often: changed fields, duplicate records, or an incomplete collection that looked successful?

title: Node.js Webhook Retries: Delayed Queues and Replaceable Recovery Boundaries
description:
If a weekly media digest webhook fails, retry the delivery outside the request handler. Put the task in a delayed queue, record the attempt and payload identity, and make the worker’s acknowledgement decision explicit. The application should own that small contract. The queue provider should be replaceable behind it.

Short answer: use a delayed queue with exponential backoff, stable task IDs, and explicit ACK/NACK handling; choose the provider whose recovery boundary matches your operations, then hide it behind a small Node.js adapter.

That shape gives you operational recovery without tying the digest code to one queue API. A failed delivery can be retried with backoff, moved to a dead-letter path after a policy limit, and inspected with enough history to answer a very practical question: what happened to this customer’s digest?

Good retries are boring.

For this particular workflow, Infrai is a candidate when a plain REST queue lets several backend services share one integration boundary. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, with request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so an adapter can be checked before the worker is deployed. It also uses one key and one bill across backend services, which removes a concrete piece of operational bookkeeping when the digest service grows beyond one queue. That does not make it the right choice for a workflow engine; it makes the queue boundary easier to inspect and move.

What changes when the queue is replaceable?

Before the boundary, the webhook handler knows too much: provider-specific delay fields, acknowledgement rules, and retry counters leak into business code. After the boundary, the digest service knows only that it is publishing a task and that a worker returns ack or nack.

Think of the flow as a sentence:

digest created -> task delayed -> worker delivers -> ack, or nack with a later retry

The queue owns waiting. The worker owns delivery semantics. Your application owns identity, attempt history, and the decision to retry.

This matters for a media product because a weekly digest is time-sensitive but not usually a reason to build a workflow engine. A retry two minutes later can be useful. A duplicate email or webhook can be expensive in trust, so the receiver still needs an idempotency key. Standard queues are at-least-once; a successful response must not be treated as proof that the task was delivered exactly once.

I initially treated a retry counter as enough. It is not. The counter tells you how many times the worker tried. It does not tell you which payload was sent, which endpoint responded, or why the next attempt is scheduled. Keep those fields together in structured logs, and keep the provider message ID as a correlation field rather than as your business identity.

How do you handle webhook task retries after failure?

Use a small policy object and keep the provider adapter at the edge. This example is deliberately provider-neutral: publish, ack, and nack are the only operations the worker needs. The local adapter can map them to BullMQ, SQS, or a REST queue without changing digest logic.

type DeliveryTask = {
  taskId: string;
  customerId: string;
  webhookUrl: string;
  payload: string;
  attempt: number;
};

type QueueAdapter = {
  publish(task: DeliveryTask, delayMs: number): Promise<void>;
  ack(task: DeliveryTask): Promise<void>;
  nack(task: DeliveryTask, delayMs: number): Promise<void>;
};

const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;
const BASE_DELAY_MS = 30_000;

function retryDelay(attempt: number): number {
  return Math.min(BASE_DELAY_MS * 2 ** Math.max(attempt - 1, 0), 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
}

async function deliverWebhook(task: DeliveryTask): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(task.webhookUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "content-type": "application/json",
      "idempotency-key": task.taskId,
    },
    body: task.payload,
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`webhook returned ${response.status}`);
  }
}

export async function handleTask(
  task: DeliveryTask,
  queue: QueueAdapter,
): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await deliverWebhook(task);
    console.info(JSON.stringify({ event: "webhook_delivered", taskId: task.taskId, attempt: task.attempt }));
    await queue.ack(task);
  } catch (error) {
    const nextAttempt = task.attempt + 1;
    console.error(JSON.stringify({
      event: "webhook_failed",
      taskId: task.taskId,
      customerId: task.customerId,
      attempt: task.attempt,
      payload: task.payload,
      error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error),
    }));

    if (nextAttempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
      await queue.nack({ ...task, attempt: nextAttempt }, 0);
      return;
    }

    await queue.nack({ ...task, attempt: nextAttempt }, retryDelay(nextAttempt));
  }
}

The adapter can map the ACK/NACK operations to a REST queue. The route names are stable, while the request schema should come from the provider's discovery document rather than from a hand-written guess. This small health check is a complete, authenticated HTTP call that a Node.js adapter can run before enabling a queue integration:

export async function checkQueueContract(): Promise<void> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`queue contract lookup failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }
}

Do not copy this discovery check into every delivery attempt. Cache the contract at deployment time, then keep the runtime adapter limited to the documented queue operations.

The important detail is the identity. taskId stays stable across attempts, so the receiver can discard a duplicate after a timeout where the first request actually succeeded. The attempt number changes. The payload does not silently change with it.

In production, classify responses before applying the same policy to all failures. A timeout, a 429, and a permanent 400 deserve different retry decisions. Honor a receiver’s Retry-After value when it is present. For every write operation, make the retry idempotent; a worker crash between delivery and acknowledgement is a normal failure window, not an exceptional one.

Which queue fits this recovery boundary?

Option Access style Best fit Main limitation
BullMQ Node.js SDK over Redis A Node.js service that already operates Redis Redis and BullMQ become part of the operating model
Amazon SQS Managed AWS API AWS-native queues with visibility timeouts and DLQs Application code still owns idempotency and attempt history
Temporal Workflow SDKs Long-running, multi-step orchestration More programming-model and operating-model change than one delayed task needs
Infrai queue REST API A provider-neutral adapter across backend services 7-day delayed-message limit, 256 KB body limit, and no workflow DAG

BullMQ is a strong fit when the team already runs Redis and wants a Node.js-native job abstraction with delayed jobs and retry options close to application code. Its trade-off is operational ownership of Redis and a tighter coupling to BullMQ’s job model. It is attractive for a single Node.js service, less attractive when other runtimes need the same queue contract.

Amazon SQS is a better fit when the team wants a managed queue with visibility timeouts and a dead-letter queue model. Its delivery semantics require the same consumer idempotency discipline, and the application still has to choose how to represent attempt history. SQS is a solid boundary for a service that already lives in AWS; it does not provide a general workflow graph.

Temporal solves a different problem. It is the better choice when the digest process becomes a long-running workflow with durable timers, several dependent activities, and explicit orchestration. That power is unnecessary for one delayed webhook delivery, and adopting it changes the programming model substantially.

A REST scheduling surface is another reasonable boundary for teams that want one plain interface across backend capabilities. Infrai’s queue surface supports delayed queues, configurable retry policy and delays, ACK/NACK processing, and queue statistics. Its public discovery surface also exposes runnable examples and schemas, which reduces adapter archaeology when a team is moving a small integration. The practical appeal here is one key and one bill for backend services, not a claim that every queue workload belongs there.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the delayed webhook portion of a media digest when a REST queue and explicit ACK/NACK boundary reduce migration work across services, while keeping the QueueAdapter contract above as your application-facing seam. Keep SQS when AWS-native operations and dead-letter tooling are the deciding factors. Choose Temporal when the job has become orchestration. Choose BullMQ when Redis and a Node.js-only deployment are already the simplest operational answer.

The limits matter. Delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message bodies to 256 KB, and retention to 30 days; acknowledgement deletes the message. FIFO deduplication lasts only 5 minutes, and there is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer-group model. There is also no native debounce, throttle, fan-out topic, DAG, or join primitive. Those constraints define the boundary. They are reasons to compose another system, not reasons to hide complexity in the worker.

What should you observe before trusting retries?

A retry policy without evidence is guesswork. Log one structured event for each attempt with taskId, customer ID, attempt, response class, delay, queue name, and payload hash. Keep the payload available for diagnosis, but treat customer data as sensitive and apply the retention policy your system requires.

Watch three signals: retry rate, age of the oldest pending task, and dead-letter volume. A rising retry rate with a stable queue age suggests a receiver problem. A rising oldest-task age suggests the worker side is falling behind. A sudden dead-letter increase deserves a payload and status-code sample, not an immediate increase to the retry limit.

Test the ugly transitions. Simulate a timeout after the receiver accepts the request. Simulate a 429 with Retry-After. Stop the worker after delivery but before ACK. Test an invalid endpoint. Then verify that the same taskId does not create a second digest and that the attempt history remains readable.

One more boundary is easy to miss: if a cron trigger starts the weekly process, a long operation should use cron to enqueue work and a worker to consume it. Cron runs have a 900-second upper limit, and missed triggers during a pause are not replayed. A queue is the recovery mechanism for the task, not a promise that every calendar event will be reconstructed later.

Two objections worth answering

“Why not retry directly in the HTTP handler?” Because the handler has a request lifetime and the weekly digest does not. Direct retries hold resources, make timeouts harder to reason about, and blur the point at which the system has accepted the task. Enqueue once, return, and let the worker own the delay.

“Does a queue make webhook delivery reliable?” No. It makes recovery explicit and observable. The receiver can still be down, the endpoint can still reject the payload, and a worker can still crash. Reliability comes from the combination of stable task identity, bounded backoff, idempotent consumption, ACK/NACK semantics, and evidence that lets an operator recover the remaining work.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the queue capability documentation. Keep the adapter small. Migration is much easier when the business code never learns which queue is underneath it.

References

  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ retrying failing jobs
  • Temporal documentation
  • Infrai queue.publish capability discovery

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs

title: Paletas accesibles: calcular contraste WCAG desde colores HEX con JavaScript
description:
Paletas accesibles: calcular contraste WCAG desde colores HEX con JavaScript

Una combinación de colores puede ser atractiva y, al mismo tiempo, difícil de leer. Si diseñamos una app que crea paletas, la vista previa debería ayudarnos a evaluar el contraste, no solo la armonía cromática.

El problema y el alcance del ejemplo

La ficha de Color Palette Hub: Paletas resume su función así: «Crea paletas cromáticas, combina tonos y edita imágenes en una sola app.» Color Palette Hub reúne herramientas de selección cromática y espacios de color. Este tutorial se concentra en la luminancia relativa sRGB y el contraste como una comprobación mínima de accesibilidad. No es una descripción de su algoritmo interno.

Cómo reproducir la idea

Abre la consola de cualquier navegador moderno o utiliza Node.js. Copia el código sin dependencias.

function luminance(hex) {
  const raw = hex.replace(/^#/, '');
  if (!/^[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$/.test(raw)) throw new Error('HEX de 6 dígitos');
  const rgb = [0, 2, 4].map(i => parseInt(raw.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255);
  const linear = rgb.map(v => v <= 0.04045 ? v / 12.92 : ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);
  return 0.2126 * linear[0] + 0.7152 * linear[1] + 0.0722 * linear[2];
}
function contrast(foreground, background) {
  const a = luminance(foreground), b = luminance(background);
  return (Math.max(a, b) + 0.05) / (Math.min(a, b) + 0.05);
}
console.log('Negro/blanco:', contrast('#000000', '#FFFFFF').toFixed(2));
console.log('Gris/blanco:', contrast('#777777', '#FFFFFF').toFixed(2));

Qué demuestra el código

La función transforma canales sRGB a luz lineal antes de calcular luminancia. El resultado del cociente va de 1:1 a 21:1. Para texto normal, el criterio WCAG AA suele exigir al menos 4.5:1, con excepciones y requisitos distintos según el tipo de contenido.

Pruebas recomendadas

Primero verifica que negro sobre blanco produce 21.00. Cambia el color de texto entre #777777 y #333333 para observar cómo varía el contraste. Después prueba una de tus propias paletas.

Límites que conviene reconocer

La comprobación cubre colores sRGB opacos y no evalúa fondos complejos, gradientes, transparencias, tipo de letra ni todo el conjunto de WCAG. Tampoco reemplaza pruebas con usuarios ni la validación de controles e iconos.

Qué aprendemos

Una paleta útil debe considerar el contexto de uso del color. El contraste medido es una señal objetiva, no una garantía absoluta de buena experiencia.

Contexto y enlaces del autor

El tema se relaciona con las funciones declaradas públicamente de Color Palette Hub: Paletas, una aplicación Android de AppInitDev. El código anterior es un ejemplo independiente: no se ha inspeccionado el repositorio privado ni se afirma que sea la implementación interna de la app. La referencia aparece al final para ofrecer contexto, no como requisito para completar el tutorial.

  • Google Play: Color Palette Hub: Paletas
  • Página de la aplicación: https://color-premium.appinitdev.com/
  • Sitio del desarrollador: AppInitDev

W3C: Understanding Contrast (Minimum)

title: A 402 Front Door Is Not an Upstream
description:
This content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record. Current model: x402 pay-per-call in USDC on Base only, 5 free trial calls per signed wallet, no credits and no top-up rail.

A 402 Front Door Is Not an Upstream

2026-11-07 · operational notes

Our catalog count dropped by three overnight. No deploy, no error spike, no report. Three
third-party listings had active=0, and every obvious explanation was wrong: no
deregister request in the gateway log, no rows in delivery_outcomes, no open
reports. The rows were removed by our own daily sweep — correctly, as it turned out, but for a
reason nobody could have read afterwards, including the sellers.

Two things in that sentence are worth keeping.

1. The challenge is our answer, not the seller's

While tracing the removal, the probe data looked self-contradictory. The same rows carried:

status:      payment_required
http_code:   402
latency_ms:  14
error:       null
upstream:    unreachable
upstream_error: URLError

Read quickly, that says “the service is fine, the tool is confused”. It is not confused. Those
are two different measurements of two different machines.

field who produced it what it proves
status / http_code / latency our edge, on our own hostname our gateway can emit a challenge
upstream / upstream_error a request to the seller's own URL, using the method its description declares the seller answers — or does not

A 402 in 14ms is our quote. It is generated before anything is forwarded, so it stays 402
whether the endpoint behind it is healthy, slow, or gone. If your only health signal is “does the
listing answer 402”, you are measuring your own uptime and calling it the seller's.

The upstream probe is the honest one, and it was unambiguous: roughly 400 attempts over
several days, about 60 that got an answer, the rest connection-level failures. The listing was
not a victim of a bad probe. It was flaky enough that a buyer following it would mostly have
paid into a timeout.

2. “Didn't ask in time” is not “dead”

Everything above only works if the probe keeps those two apart. A connection error, a DNS
deadline, an HTTP 404, and a declared method the endpoint refuses are four different claims, and
only some of them justify removal. Our probe already separates them into
unreachable, route_missing, server_error and
declared_method_refused — and the last one is deliberately excluded from the delist
rule, because “the description says GET but the endpoint only speaks POST” is a metadata bug, not
a dead service. When a probe collapses those into one boolean, a typo in a description becomes a
removal.

3. A removal nobody can read is indistinguishable from a deletion

The interesting part was not the delist. It was that, from the seller's side, the listing had
simply stopped existing. There is exactly one surface where a submitter can read the state of
their own row — a signed call that returns it along with a free-text note — and that note was
empty. The row said active: false and nothing else.

So we changed the sweep to write the reason into that note when it removes something, and to
never overwrite a note that already exists: a rejection reason belongs to review, not to an
uptime sweep. The sweep also stops pretending in its own documentation that it only touches
first-party routes — it judges one field, and that field is not filtered by who owns the row.

A marketplace that can remove a listing with one UPDATE should be able to
say, in the same statement, why — and to whom.

What we deliberately did not build is automatic resurrection. Re-activating on the
next successful probe would bypass the review gate that every new listing goes through, and it
cannot distinguish “removed by the uptime sweep” from “removed by a human for a reason”. The
path back is republishing, which is also the path that gets a human to look at it again.

The measured end state

Same day, after the fix and a review pass over the pending queue: 1,842 → 1,851 live
listings (3 removed, 12 approved, 3 rejected as duplicates, 10 held because their host could not
be measured), 1,932 discovery resources, and all four counting surfaces — the API catalog, the
MCP tool list, the well-known manifest, and the page counters — agreeing at 1,851. The three
removed rows now carry a note that names the rule and points at the way back.

minia2a is an x402 marketplace: pay-per-call APIs in USDC on Base, called by agents with
no accounts and no subscriptions. The numbers above come from our own catalog and probe tables,
taken the day this was written.

Originally published at minia2a.uk.

title: Game Tenant Object Storage for Low-Volume Image Uploads — Retention Boundaries
description:
Short answer: for a game that stores a small number of private tenant snapshots, choose the provider that makes deletion explicit and recovery testable. R2 and Backblaze B2 are sensible cost-conscious candidates, while S3 is a useful baseline when its surrounding controls already match your platform. A plain REST option such as Infrai fits a team that wants private bucket operations behind one API key, but it is the wrong choice for public image hosting, immutable records, or browser-direct uploads that require self-service CORS configuration.

The expensive mistake is usually not the object count. It is an unclear lifecycle. A tenant leaves, an operator deletes the wrong snapshot, or a retry creates two records with the same logical name. In a multiplayer game, those failures are visible during an incident, when nobody wants to discover that retention was a paragraph in a ticket rather than a rule in code.

What must be true before storage is cheap

Start with the data contract, not a provider comparison. Each object should have a tenant identifier, a snapshot identifier, a creation timestamp, and a state such as candidate, selected, or deleted. Keep the object key private and derive it from stable identifiers, for example tenants/{tenant_id}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/manifest.json. The manifest can point to image files without turning object metadata into a search system.

For this scenario, I would make five checks non-negotiable:

  • A tenant can list only its own snapshots through the application boundary.
  • A restore names one selected snapshot, rather than relying on the newest object returned by a list call.
  • Retention deletes only snapshots older than the policy and outside the selected set.
  • A failed delete can be retried without changing the decision.
  • The team can prove that a restore works before shortening retention.

That last check matters more than a small difference in unit cost. A backup that has never been restored is an assumption with a key.

Deletion is policy.

Which object storage solutions fit low-volume image uploads?

Use the same fixture against every candidate. I would create three tenants, five snapshots per tenant, one selected snapshot, one snapshot exactly on the retention boundary, and one deliberately duplicated logical name with a distinct snapshot id. Record the provider, region, object key, operation result, and elapsed time for the test run. Do not call that a benchmark; it is a pass/fail acceptance test.

The decision rule is simple: reject a candidate if it cannot keep private objects, identify a selected snapshot deterministically, or delete only the objects that the policy marks. Among the candidates that pass, prefer the one whose integration leaves the least policy logic in an operator's head. Run the fixture again after a restore and after a retry.

Here is a small policy oracle. It does not pretend to be a storage SDK, so it is useful even before the provider adapter exists. The delete set is the expected result that each adapter must match exactly.

import json
import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def list_infrai_buckets() -> object:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/list",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
                payload = response.read().decode("utf-8")
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai returned HTTP {response.status}: {payload}")
                return json.loads(payload)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai returned HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
        except URLError as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai request failed: {error.reason}") from error
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Snapshot:
    tenant_id: str
    snapshot_id: str
    created_at: datetime
    selected: bool = False


def deletion_set(
    snapshots: list[Snapshot],
    now: datetime,
    retention_days: int,
) -> set[tuple[str, str]]:
    cutoff = now - timedelta(days=retention_days)
    return {
        (item.tenant_id, item.snapshot_id)
        for item in snapshots
        if item.created_at < cutoff and not item.selected
    }


def run_fixture() -> None:
    now = datetime(2026, 10, 24, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    snapshots = [
        Snapshot("alpha", "a-old", now - timedelta(days=31)),
        Snapshot("alpha", "a-selected", now - timedelta(days=45), True),
        Snapshot("alpha", "a-edge", now - timedelta(days=30)),
        Snapshot("beta", "b-old", now - timedelta(days=31)),
        Snapshot("beta", "b-duplicate-name-id", now - timedelta(days=31)),
    ]

    expected = deletion_set(snapshots, now, retention_days=30)
    actual = {("alpha", "a-old"), ("beta", "b-old"), ("beta", "b-duplicate-name-id")}
    assert actual == expected, (actual, expected)
    assert ("alpha", "a-selected") not in actual
    print("PASS: retention fixture matches the deletion policy")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(list_infrai_buckets())
    run_fixture()

The boundary is intentional: this fixture uses a strict older-than comparison. If your policy says an object exactly 30 days old is eligible, change the operator and the test name together. Do not leave that decision implicit. Also, make the delete operation idempotent at the application layer. A standard queue is at-least-once, and a retry after a timeout must not restore or delete the wrong snapshot.

Comparing the candidates by their boundary cases

R2 and Backblaze B2 deserve the first trial for low-volume image and backup data because the stated requirement is modest data volume with future room to grow, rather than a large platform of specialized storage features. Test their private-object behavior and lifecycle semantics with the fixture. The winner is the one that passes your deletion and restore contract with fewer adapter-specific exceptions.

Option Integration shape Best fit for this test Boundary to verify
Cloudflare R2 Provider storage API Low-volume private images and snapshots Retention and restore behavior
Backblaze B2 Provider storage API Small data requirements with room to grow Private access and deletion semantics
Amazon S3 Broad storage platform Existing AWS identity and audit conventions The controls your platform already requires
Infrai Plain REST API A small backend avoiding an SDK dependency No public ACL, versioning, object lock, or self-service CORS route

This table is a starting hypothesis, not a ranking. The fixture decides the result.

Amazon S3 is the broad baseline. It is the sensible comparison when the game already depends on AWS identity, audit, or storage conventions, or when the team expects to use a wider AWS data platform later. That surrounding fit can outweigh a simpler initial configuration. It also makes S3 a useful control in the experiment: if a candidate only looks attractive because the test omitted a required control, the baseline exposes that gap.

Infrai is a different integration shape. It exposes storage through a REST API, so a backend can make HTTP requests without installing an SDK or managing a client-library version. The storage surface includes bucket listing and creation, private object operations, presigning, lifecycle configuration, and multipart operations. That is useful for a small backend that already wants one consistent request boundary. The public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples, which lowers the cost of checking an integration before wiring it into a game service.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for private, application-mediated tenant snapshots when the main friction is integrating a small backend with a REST surface, then run the retention fixture and a real restore drill before committing. It is a strong fit for that narrow workflow because the no-SDK boundary keeps the adapter small. It is not the fit for a public image host: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url is always null.

The caveats change the decision. There is no object versioning or object lock, so accidental overwrites are not recoverable through storage-native history and finance-grade immutability needs an external design. There is no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent mutation needs coordination in a database or queue. Browser-direct uploads also need care because there is no independently exposed CORS-setting route, even though the bucket model has a cors_rules field. Cross-region automatic replication and cross-cloud bulk migration are absent as well.

Lifecycle rules have sharp edges: the shortest expiration is one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. Those are manageable for a modest, private snapshot service, but they are not details to discover after launch.

Roll out deletion as a reversible decision

Ship the policy in observation mode first. The worker computes the expected deletion set, records the tenant and snapshot ids, and performs no delete. Compare that set with an operator review and with the restore index in your database. Then enable deletion for one test tenant, run a restore, and repeat the same fixture after a retry.

Keep the database as the authority for selected; object listing is not a substitute for that state. Use signed or presigned delivery for private reads, and never send the storage service's authorization header to a returned presigned URL. For browser uploads, verify the CORS contract against the chosen provider before promising a direct-upload flow.

The final choice should be boring in the best sense: a provider passes the private-object, retention, deletion, and restore checks; its limitations are written beside the policy; and a new engineer can explain why a selected snapshot survives cleanup. R2 or B2 may be the pragmatic result for this low-volume workload, S3 may win on existing platform fit, and Infrai may win when one REST boundary matters most. The experiment decides the boundary, not a generic cheapest label.

If the private-snapshot boundary fits your system, the storage documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc is the appropriate place to inspect the available API surface before implementing an adapter.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage documentation: https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: A kanban board in React with native drag and drop (and a fallback that works on phones)
description:
I recently built Tandem, a CRM dashboard template with Next.js 16 and Tailwind CSS 4. The centerpiece is a kanban pipeline: deals move from Lead to Won. I wanted it without a drag-and-drop library, and I wanted it to work for people who can't drag. Here is the whole approach.

1. State: one array, stage is just a field

Columns don't own their cards. There is one list of deals, and a column is a filter:

const [deals, setDeals] = useState(initialDeals);

function move(id: string, stage: StageId) {
  setDeals((list) => list.map((d) => (d.id === id ? { ...d, stage } : d)));
}

// in render
stages.map((s) => {
  const list = visible.filter((d) => d.stage === s.id);
  // ...
});

Moving a card is a single map. Totals per column, the weighted forecast and filters all fall out of the same array for free.

2. Native HTML drag and drop

The browser already has drag and drop. You need three handlers.

On the card:

<article
  draggable
  onDragStart={(e) => {
    e.dataTransfer.setData("text/plain", deal.id);
    e.dataTransfer.effectAllowed = "move";
  }}
>

On the column:

<section
  onDragOver={(e) => {
    e.preventDefault(); // without this, drop never fires
    setOver(stage.id);
  }}
  onDragLeave={() => setOver((o) => (o === stage.id ? null : o))}
  onDrop={(e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    move(e.dataTransfer.getData("text/plain"), stage.id);
    setOver(null);
  }}
  className={over === stage.id ? "border-brand bg-brand-soft/50" : ""}
>

The over state only exists to highlight the column you're about to drop into. That small detail makes the board feel much more solid.

3. The part most boards skip: a non-drag way to move cards

Native drag and drop doesn't work with touch on most mobile browsers, and it never works with a keyboard. Instead of fighting that, every card has a plain <select>:

<label className="sr-only" htmlFor={`move-${deal.id}`}>
  Move {deal.company} to stage
</label>
<select id={`move-${deal.id}`} value={deal.stage} onChange={(e) => move(deal.id, e.target.value as StageId)}>
  {stages.map((s) => <option key={s.id} value={s.id}>{s.label}</option>)}
</select>

It calls the same move function. On a phone, it opens the native picker, which is honestly nicer than dragging a card across a horizontally scrolling board.

4. A bug I didn't expect: sr-only broke the mobile layout

On a 390px screen the whole page suddenly scrolled sideways, even though the board sat in an overflow-x-auto container.

The cause: Tailwind's sr-only is position: absolute. With no positioned ancestor, those hidden labels were positioned relative to the page, not the scroll container, so they escaped the overflow clip and stretched the document to 1500px.

The fix was one word, relative on the scroll container:

<div className="relative -mx-4 overflow-x-auto px-4">

If a page scrolls horizontally on mobile and you can't see why, look for absolutely positioned elements without a relative parent.

I built Tandem with AI assistance, then reviewed and tested everything myself.

Try it

  • Live demo: crm.bontemplates.com. Drag a few deals around.
  • The template: pipeline, contacts, contact timeline, tasks, settings and auth pages, light and dark mode: crm.bontemplates.com/product
  • Free starter in the same design system: Pulse Lite on GitHub

Questions about the board? Ask in the comments.

title: I built an MCP server for glucose data that refuses to lie
description:
Ask an AI assistant for a glucose reading through most integrations and you'll get a number back. 132 mg/dL.

Great. From when?

Thirty seconds ago? Two hours ago, before the phone lost signal? Is "the last 7 days" actually seven days of data, or the twelve hours the API happened to return? When a language model gets a bare number, it does the natural thing: it treats the number as current and complete, and it sounds confident about it.

For most data that's an annoyance. For continuous glucose monitor (CGM) data, it's the whole problem.

So I built librelink-mcp-rs: a local Model Context Protocol server, in Rust, that reads FreeStyle Libre data from a LibreLinkUp follower account. Its one design rule is that every answer says how fresh, how complete, and how trustworthy it is. It's MIT licensed and at 1.0 now.

johnohhh1 / librelink-mcp-rs

Privacy-conscious Rust MCP server for LibreLinkUp sharing data, with eight compatible tools and honest data freshness.

librelink-mcp-rs

Give your AI assistant honest, private access to FreeStyle Libre glucose data.

A local Model Context Protocol server, written in Rust, that reads a LibreLinkUp follower account and answers with readings that say exactly how fresh, how complete, and how trustworthy they are.

Important

Unofficial and not affiliated with Abbott. It describes data; it does not diagnose or give treatment advice. Use a LibreLinkUp follower account, and enter credentials only in the local setup prompt, never in a chat.

Why this one

  • It never pretends. A stale reading is labeled stale, not served as live. A 12-hour graph is never passed off as a 7-day summary. A gap stays a gap, with a cause attached.
  • It gets the math right. Time in range is weighted by time, not by sample count, and GMI appears only when the consensus 14-day, 70%-coverage bar is met. On the validated setup, 14-day…
View on GitHub

Here are the five problems that shaped it, and how each one ended up enforced by a test rather than by good intentions.

Problem 1: the timestamps don't have timezones

LibreLinkUp is an unofficial, reverse-engineered API. Every reading comes with two clock strings, and neither has an offset:

"Timestamp":        "11/5/2026 9:54:32 PM",
"FactoryTimestamp": "11/6/2026 2:54:32 AM"

The community consensus is that Timestamp is the sharer's phone wall clock and FactoryTimestamp is UTC. But "community consensus" isn't something I wanted to hard-code silently, because if it's wrong, every freshness calculation is wrong.

So the server only infers UTC when the two clocks are consistent with that story. The gap between them has to look like a real timezone offset, and the factory time can't be in the future:

fn infer_factory_utc(
    display: NaiveDateTime,
    factory: NaiveDateTime,
    now: DateTime<Utc>,
) -> Option<DateTime<Utc>> {
    let gap_seconds = display.signed_duration_since(factory).num_seconds();
    // Real timezone offsets are quarter-hour aligned and within this range.
    // This is a consistency check, not a timezone assertion from the API.
    if gap_seconds % (15 * 60) != 0 || gap_seconds.abs() > 14 * 60 * 60 {
        return None;
    }
    let observed = DateTime::<Utc>::from_naive_utc_and_offset(factory, Utc);
    (observed <= now).then_some(observed)
}

When it passes, the reply says so: time_basis: "factory_utc_inferred". When it doesn't, freshness is unknown, never a guess. I checked the inference against a live account (a −300 minute gap, matching the phone's Eastern time) and against public captures from a UTC+2 summer account, so it holds across two timezones and both DST states.

The rule that falls out of this: fetching a reading never makes it current. Retrieval time and observation time are separate fields, and a cached response keeps its original retrieval time so it can't look fresher than it is.

Problem 2: a careless client can lock the account

The first version used an existing Rust crate for the API. Reading its source, I found it would log in again and retry after any failed request, including a 429 Too Many Requests.

Think about what that means when an agent fires four tool calls in a row while the API is throttling: eight requests and a stream of fresh logins. That's exactly the pattern that gets an account locked. And this account is a caregiver's window into someone's glucose.

I replaced the crate with a small owned client (eight endpoints, reqwest plus rustls) behind a DataSource trait. It logs in only when there's no valid session, or once after a 401. Nothing else triggers a login. The core guarantee is a test that counts logins against a mock server:

#[tokio::test]
async fn throttling_never_triggers_a_login() {
    let server = MockServer::start().await;
    mount_session(&server, in_one_hour()).await;
    mount(&server, "GET", GRAPH_PATH, ResponseTemplate::new(429)).await;
    let client = client(&server);

    for _ in 0..2 {
        assert_eq!(client.read().await.unwrap_err().code, "rate_limited");
    }
    assert_eq!(logins(&server).await, 1);
}

Every failure test in the suite asserts the login count, not just the error code.

Some errors can't be fixed by retrying at all, so retrying them only costs requests. Those latch until restart:

pub(crate) fn latches_until_restart(error: &FetchError) -> bool {
    matches!(
        error.code,
        "authentication_failed"
            | "client_version_rejected"
            | "request_rejected"
            | "patient_selection_changed"
    )
}

The background collector exits with status 78 on a latched error, and the shipped systemd unit sets RestartPreventExitStatus=78. So a wrong password produces one failed login, not one every five minutes until Abbott locks the account.

Problem 3: "the last 7 days" from a 12-hour API

The LibreLinkUp graph covers about twelve hours. Ask the naive version for weekly stats and you get twelve hours of numbers wearing a "7 days" label.

Two fixes.

First, coverage is always reported. Every summary carries its first and last observation, span, cadence, and gaps. If the data doesn't reach the edges of the requested window, the reply says period_status: "partial". Every interior gap gets a cause:

Cause Meaning
no_data_from_api The collector polled during the gap, and the API had nothing
no_data_in_export The device's own exported history has nothing there (a sensor change, say)
before_collection Before collection started; the cause is unknown, and the label says so
collector_not_running Nobody was watching

That third one came from a live test. The first version called a gap in the backfilled history collector_not_running, which sounds authoritative but was simply wrong: the collector hadn't started yet, so it couldn't know why that data was missing.

Second, real history. An opt-in collect command polls once a minute (a 60-second floor enforced in code, plus jitter) into a local SQLite database. import-csv backfills older history from a LibreView export, offline. While the collector runs, serve answers every tool from the database:

  LibreLinkUp API ──collect (60 s)──▶ ┌──────────────┐
  LibreView CSV  ───import-csv──────▶ │ local SQLite │──read-only──▶ serve ◀──stdio──▶ MCP client
                                      └──────────────┘                ▲
  LibreLinkUp API ·········· live fallback when no collector ·········┘

Only one process ever talks to Abbott. I verified that by running serve under strace: across every tool call, zero AF_INET connections. Every reply carries data_source: "local_store" or "live_api", so the model knows which world it's in.

Problem 4: counting samples quietly skews the statistics

With the collector running, the database mixes two densities: graph points every five minutes, and current readings every minute. Compute "percent of readings in range" over that, and the most recent hour, the one with minute-by-minute data, outweighs everything else.

The fix is to weight by time, not by count. Each reading stands for the time until the next one, capped at 15 minutes so a gap is never bridged:

let cap = Duration::minutes(MAX_SAMPLE_MINUTES);
(0..timed.len())
    .map(|index| {
        let (at, sample) = timed[index];
        let until = timed.get(index + 1).map_or(to, |(next, _)| *next);
        (sample, (until - at).min(cap).num_seconds())
    })

The test that guards it builds twelve hours of in-range readings every 15 minutes, plus one hour of minute-by-minute high readings. By sample count, "high" is over half the data. By time, it's 1/13. Only the second number describes reality.

From there the server reports the five international consensus ranges by time, plus a time-weighted mean, SD and CV. GMI (an estimate of A1C) is gated the way the consensus paper recommends: a window of at least 14 days with at least 70% coverage, or you get null and a reason (window_too_short, coverage_too_low).

The acceptance test I'm proudest of: after importing a real 14-day LibreView export, I compared the server's figures with the AGP report LibreView itself generated from the same data. Every range band agreed within 1 percentage point, the mean within 1 mg/dL, CV within 0.1, and coverage within half a point. The vendor's own report was the test oracle.

Problem 5: privacy you can actually test

"We take privacy seriously" isn't a property. These are:

  • Credentials live only in the OS credential store (Keychain, Credential Manager, Secret Service). No MCP tool accepts a password; there's a test that configure_credentials rejects a password argument without echoing it.
  • The patient is stored as a salted SHA-256 pseudonym, with a random salt per database. A test plants a recognizable patient ID and byte-searches the database, including the WAL and shared-memory sidecar files, to prove it never lands on disk. The sidecars are where a leak would actually hide.
  • CSV import reads only the timestamp, record type, and glucose columns. Insulin, carbs, notes, and the name line at the top of the export never make it into storage or logs. A fixture fills those columns with marker strings, and the test asserts none of them appear anywhere.
  • Errors use fixed messages and public codes. A test harness plants markers in fake credentials and fake server responses, drives every error path, and asserts no marker reaches stdout or stderr. A panic prints a fixed message with no payload unless you opt in.

How it was tested

A few habits did most of the work:

  • Synthetic data only, in the repo. No real readings in fixtures, issues, or history. Real data only touched the live checks on my own machine, and those were recorded as "what was checked", never as values.
  • Mutation checks for the important tests. For every key test, deliberately break the code it guards, confirm the test fails, and restore. That caught tests that passed for the wrong reason more than once.
  • A live check before every release. Each version was smoke-tested against a real account before tagging, and that caught real bugs: a gap mislabeled on backfilled data, and a serve that would have quietly migrated the database out from under a running older collector.
  • Boring CI, on purpose. Linux, macOS and Windows, the minimum supported Rust (1.89), and cargo-deny for advisories and licenses. A Windows-only test failure turned out to be the test reading the clock twice; the fix was to capture the time once per fixture.

That's 149 tests over about 10,000 lines of Rust.

The elephant in the room

This uses an unofficial API. Abbott's newer LibreLinkUp app encrypts its responses, and the older plain-JSON endpoints this project uses could be shut off.

The project will not try to circumvent that encryption. It will detect a changed API and say so (api_changed), and because history lives in your local database, everything you've already collected or imported keeps working if the live API ever goes away.

Try it

Release binaries are on the releases page for Linux, macOS and Windows, along with a Claude Desktop bundle. Or:

cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/johnohhh1/librelink-mcp-rs --tag v1.0.0
librelink-mcp-rs setup    # local prompt; the password never touches the MCP client
librelink-mcp-rs check

It's validated on one US follower account with a FreeStyle Libre 3. If you're in another region or on another sensor, the compatibility guide shows how to test it and report the result without sharing a single reading. That's the most useful contribution right now.

This software describes data; it doesn't diagnose or give treatment advice. Thanks to Amandeep Khurana, whose original LibreLink MCP server defined the eight tools this one implements.

title: Your Minecraft plugin leaked. Here's how to find who leaked it and stop the copies
description:
You search your plugin's name and there it is: your premium jar, free to download on a leak forum. It happens to almost every plugin that sells well, and it tends to happen the week of a big release or sale.

Here's what to do in the first hour, in order, and how to set things up so the next leak takes five minutes instead of a weekend.

1. Don't run the leaked file

Leak sites are a common way to spread malware: "cracked" jars often carry a backdoor that was added after the leak. Download the file only to inspect it, in a throwaway folder or a VM. Never put it on a server, not even a test one.

2. Find out whose copy it is

This only works if every buyer got a unique copy. If they did, you have three ways to find the buyer.

Look for the key in the jar. If you sell on BuiltByBit with an External license key placeholder, or on Voxel Shop or SpigotMC with their buyer placeholders, the store wrote something unique into each download. A jar is just a zip file:

mkdir leak && cd leak && unzip -q ../leaked.jar
grep -r "%%__" .                                   # a placeholder nobody replaced?
grep -rlE "[A-Z0-9]{4}-[A-Z0-9]{4}-[A-Z0-9]{4}" .  # files that contain a key
strings path/to/Match.class | grep -E "[A-Z0-9]{4}-"

If the placeholder was replaced, you'll find the buyer's key or user ID in a class file or in config.yml. If the class is hard to read, open it in a decompiler (Recaf, JD-GUI) and look at its constants.

Look for a watermark. If your downloads carry a mark (a line in the manifest, an archive comment, an ID compiled into a class), read it back the same way.

Ask your license server. Search for the key you found. It points to the license, and the license to the buyer. Its activations tell you more: a key on twelve servers in four countries is a shared key, not a stolen account.

A careful leaker may have swapped the key for another, or cut the check out entirely. Then the watermark and your license server's logs (which key started showing up on new servers when the leak appeared) are your best leads.

If every buyer got the same jar, you can't trace this leak. Skip to step 5, and make sure the next version is traceable.

3. Stop the leaked copies

Revoke the buyer's key. If your plugin checks its license on startup and re-checks every few hours, every copy of that jar stops at its next check, on every server that downloaded it. Your other buyers notice nothing.

Two things make this work:

  • Re-check while running. A startup-only check stops new installs, but servers that were already running keep going until they restart. A re-check every few hours reaches them.
  • Don't punish a network outage. Only stop on a clear "revoked" or "suspended" answer, never on a timeout. That keeps you on the right side of BuiltByBit's DRM rules, and keeps paying customers safe when your license server has a bad day.

If your plugin has no license check yet, this is the step you can't do today. How to add license keys to a Minecraft plugin in 10 minutes fixes that for the next version.

4. Deal with the buyer

Look at their history before you assume the worst. Sometimes their account was compromised, or a staff member they trusted shared it. Then:

  • Refund or chargeback? If they charged back, revoke and move on. Stores don't always tell your license server about refunds (BuiltByBit's placeholder doesn't), so check.
  • Report them to the marketplace with your evidence: the key, the leak URL, the date.
  • Give a second chance if it was an accident: issue a new key and ask them to keep it private.

5. Get the post taken down

Most leak sites are hosted somewhere that responds to copyright notices. Send a DMCA takedown to the site, or to its host if the site ignores you, with:

  • a link to your original listing,
  • the exact leak URL,
  • a statement that you own the copyright and didn't authorise the copy.

BuiltByBit has its own DMCA form for copies uploaded there. Expect reposts, and don't spend your week chasing every mirror: revoking the key in step 3 already made those copies useless for anyone who restarts.

6. Make the next leak traceable

If this leak was hard to trace, fix it for the next version:

  1. One key per buyer, written into each download by your store's placeholder.
  2. A server limit per key, so a shared key gets refused on the third server.
  3. A startup check with a re-check every few hours, that keeps running when your license server can't be reached.
  4. Alerts for shared keys: one key on many servers, or in two countries an hour apart.
  5. Obfuscation and a sealed core, so the check is hard to cut out of the leaked jar. See How to obfuscate a Minecraft plugin.

How I handle this with SunLicense

I build SunLicense, so here's the same process in it:

  • Each BuiltByBit download gets the buyer's key through the placeholder. The license is named after their BuiltByBit user ID, so the key in a leaked jar points straight at the buyer.
  • Obfuscated jars stay traceable: classes that hold a download placeholder are never string-encrypted, so the key is still readable in step 2.
  • Sentinel flags keys being shared (too many servers, impossible travel, a revoked key still in use, a key posted in your Discord) and offers one-click fixes you can undo.
  • Revoke from the dashboard, the CLI or Discord. The free Paper template re-checks every few hours and keeps running when SunLicense can't be reached.
  • On Standard, downloads from SunLicense carry a watermark, Whose copy is this? names the customer when you upload a leaked file, and the web patrol looks for copies offered online.

The free plan covers 3 products and 100 licenses, with no cut of your sales. See how it works for Minecraft plugins before your next release, so the next leak takes five minutes.

This article was written with the help of an AI assistant and reviewed by me before publishing.

title: Claude Code forgets everything when you close it. Here's how I made it remember (and share it with Claude.ai)
description:
Every morning I opened Claude Code and did the same thing: explained my project again. What we changed yesterday. Why we picked that approach. What was still broken.

Then I'd switch to Claude.ai on my phone, or hand a task to Codex, and do it all over again.

The worst part wasn't repeating myself. It was the AI forgetting why we made a decision, and quietly undoing a fix from two days ago.

So I built a small open-source tool to fix it for myself: CogniCore. This post shows how it works and how to set it up in a couple of minutes.

What actually gets lost between sessions

When a Claude Code session ends, the useful parts are gone:

the goal you were working toward
decisions, and the reason behind each one
open tasks you left for later
exact values: ticket IDs, versions, file paths, ports

A CLAUDE.md file helps, but you have to remember to update it, it keeps growing, and Claude.ai or ChatGPT can't read a file on your laptop.

The idea: a handoff, saved automatically

CogniCore uses Claude Code's hooks. After each turn it saves a short, structured handoff:

text
Goal: Make the deploy pipeline survive restarts
State: PR #193 merged, downtime 27 min -> 6 s
Decisions:

  • Uploads run in a background process (why: a turn never waits on the network) Open tasks:
  • Publish the next release to PyPI Values: fix/deploy-permissions, port 8765

When the next session starts, it injects a short brief (about 450 tokens) instead of the whole history. If the agent needs more, it asks for a specific section.

Two design choices I'm happy with:

Rule-based extraction by default. It only calls an LLM to compress a session when it's over 3,000 tokens, so most saves cost zero model calls and memory is ready in about a second.
Newest revision wins. Uploads run in the background, and an older upload can never overwrite newer work.
Setup (about 2 minutes)
bash
pipx install "cognicore-env[mcp]"
cognicore install # sets up Claude Code and Codex

Restart Claude Code. That's it for local memory. Nothing leaves your machine.

Want the same memory in Claude.ai, ChatGPT or Cursor? Turn on sync:

bash
cognicore login

Then add the CogniCore connector in Claude.ai. Only the short handoff is synced, never your transcripts or file contents.

The test that convinced me

In Claude Code, I asked it to remember a code word: BLUE-HERON-4417.

The next day, in a separate Claude.ai chat, I asked: "What did I just do in Claude Code?"

It told me what I'd worked on, and gave me the code word back.

How it compares

I benchmarked it against claude-mem 15.7.0, the most popular memory plugin, on the same tasks. Both finished every follow-up correctly. CogniCore used 53K-60K new tokens vs 147K-216K, and memory was ready in about 1 second vs 70-130 seconds.

It's my own benchmark, so be skeptical: the script (scripts/bench_realworld.py) is in the repo and I'd genuinely like to hear if you get different numbers.

What's still not great
On Claude.ai, memory only updates when Claude decides to call the tool. There are no hooks on the web.
The saved summaries are sometimes noisy. I'm improving the extraction every week.
Try it

It's free and open source (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/cognicore-dev/cognicore-env

CogniCore — Memory that follows you between AI apps

CogniCore gives Claude, ChatGPT and coding agents like Claude Code and Codex a shared memory, so every new chat picks up where the last one stopped.

cognicoree.tech

Carries your Claude Code work into Codex and back, so a new session resumes the same goal, decisions and open tasks. Hooks save each session from its…

claudepluginhub.com

mcp.market

How do you keep context when you switch between AI tools? A notes file, copy-paste, or just re-explaining? I'd love to hear what works for you.

I built CogniCore largely with Claude Code, and used AI help to draft parts of this post.

title: Secure File Downloads Using Presigned URLs in Node.js Cloud Storage: Replaceable Access
description:
Short answer: put the authorization decision in your application, put the bytes in private object storage, and treat the presigned URL as a short-lived delivery artifact. For an e-commerce export or a large product video, that boundary keeps the app from proxying the file while leaving the storage provider replaceable. The important choice is access control versus delivery simplicity; a download link that is easy to serve is still a bad design if it quietly turns a private bucket into a public origin.

What must remain true after a provider change?

Start with invariants, not an SDK. The order service must authenticate the requester and authorize the object before it asks storage for a URL. The bucket and objects remain private. The URL has an expiration chosen for the actual download experience, and the browser receives the returned URL without the storage-service Authorization header. Finally, application code stores an object identifier such as exports/order-1842/receipt.pdf, not a provider-specific public URL.

That last rule is the migration hinge. A signed URL is temporary, so it belongs in a response or redirect, never in a durable order record. If a customer retries tomorrow, the application checks access again and creates another link. Existing links still live until their expiry, which is why expiry is a security parameter rather than a cosmetic timeout.

Keep it private.

For teams that want a provider-neutral REST boundary, Infrai is a plausible presign adapter here: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, so the integration can be inspected before the application depends on it. Its ten-language runnable examples are useful when the export service has a Node.js edge but other internal tools do not.

No public URL is part of this design.

For a large media export, I would begin with a few minutes and validate the observed download path, then increase it only when the file size and customer network conditions justify that choice. There is no universally safe duration. A link that expires before a slow customer finishes is a support problem; one that lasts all afternoon is a larger exposure window.

Option Access boundary Delivery path Migration concern Good fit
Amazon S3 presigned URL IAM-controlled signing and private objects Object store serves bytes directly AWS signing and object conventions must stay behind an adapter Teams standardized on S3
Cloudflare R2 presigned URL S3-compatible signed access to private objects Object store or Cloudflare edge serves bytes directly R2 account and endpoint details remain provider-specific A Cloudflare-centered delivery design
Azure Blob SAS Delegated, time-limited SAS permissions Blob service serves bytes directly SAS construction and Azure naming need an adapter Azure-native identity and storage
Google Cloud Storage signed URL Signed request to a private object Cloud Storage serves bytes directly Its portability story is separate from an S3 abstraction Google Cloud Storage workloads
A REST storage adapter Application issues one provider-neutral operation Provider URL serves bytes directly The contract must preserve expiry and private-object assumptions A reversible multi-cloud choice

The products are not interchangeable merely because each can produce a signed link. Their identity systems, signing inputs, endpoint shapes, and operational controls differ. The portable unit is your application contract: authorize_export, create_temporary_download, and redirect_to_download, with provider-specific signing hidden behind the second operation.

How should a Node.js export flow draw the boundary?

The critical path has four actors: the browser, the application, storage, and the final object response. The browser asks the application for an export link. The application checks the order, tenant, and user relationship, then requests a presigned URL. The browser follows that URL directly. Storage never needs to know the user's session cookie, and the application never handles the media bytes.

The following adapter uses the verified storage route and keeps the returned response opaque until the discovery schema for that capability defines its exact response field. That detail matters during migration: hard-coding a guessed response shape is how a supposedly portable layer becomes another vendor SDK. In a Node.js service, the same four-step boundary should sit behind your route handler; the sample is Python because the engineering contract is easier to inspect without hiding it in a framework.

import os
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests

def request_presigned_download(bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    path = "/v1/storage/object/presign/{}/{}".format(
        quote(bucket, safe=""), quote(key, safe="/")
    )
    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{}/{}".format(
            quote(bucket, safe=""), quote(key, safe="/")
        ),
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + api_key},
        timeout=10,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("presign request was rate limited; retry with backoff")
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

# Map the discovered response schema to your own download_url, then send
# that URL to the browser without the platform Authorization header.
result = request_presigned_download("private-exports", "orders/1842/video.mp4")
print(result)

The example does not put an API key in source code, does not attach the platform Authorization header to the eventual object request, and does not present a public URL. A production adapter should make its retry policy idempotent where the operation contract requires it, honor Retry-After on a 429, and surface the response body for other 4xx errors. A tight retry loop is not resilience; it is a second load problem.

If the browser is calling the application from another origin, the browser's CORS policy still applies to the application endpoint and to any client-side object request. CORS controls which browser origins may read a response; it does not make a private bucket public. Keep those concerns separate, and test the actual origin, method, and response headers used by the export UI.

For this workflow, Infrai is worth trying when a team wants the storage operation behind a plain REST boundary and wants discovery to be part of integration rather than an SDK archaeology project. Its public discovery surface returns capability schemas and runnable examples, and its documented examples cover ten languages. The same platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which can remove a concrete integration burden when the export service also needs other backend capabilities; it avoids a separate credential and client boundary for each capability. The concrete recommendation is narrow: use it as the presign adapter for private export downloads when the self-describing contract and shared key reduce the provider-specific code you must later replace. It is not a reason to abandon a specialist storage platform whose controls your compliance model requires.

How do secure file downloads using presigned URLs protect an export?

A presigned-download design does not solve every storage requirement. The described storage capability has no public or public-read ACL configuration, so it is not the right fit for permanent public links, static website hosting, or an image-hosting workflow. It also has no object versioning or object lock, which rules out treating it as the sole control for immutable, financial-grade records. Strict compare-and-swap writes need external queue or database coordination because there is no If-Match conditional write.

The browser-upload side has a separate limitation: there is no independent set_cors route for self-service browser direct uploads. Cross-origin behavior must be designed and verified rather than assumed. There is also no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and the supported vendor coverage does not include every object-storage provider. Those are architectural boundaries, not footnotes to hide after the recommendation.

For a migration, I would keep a provider-neutral export record with the bucket alias, object key, content type, and creation status, then make the adapter responsible for translating that record into a temporary URL. A move between providers becomes a data migration plus one adapter change. It does not become a rewrite of order authorization, download UI, and audit logic. That is the useful definition of portability here.

Decision

Choose presigned URLs for private e-commerce downloads when the application can authorize access first and direct delivery is the main goal. Keep the URL ephemeral, the object private, and the provider-specific request behind a small contract. Choose S3, R2, Azure Blob, or Google Cloud Storage when its identity, replication, compliance, or delivery ecosystem is the real requirement; choose a REST storage adapter when reducing migration work matters more than adopting one provider's full feature surface.

If this boundary fits your system, the team that wants a self-describing REST presign adapter and one key across related backend capabilities should try Infrai first; a specialist remains the better choice when immutable records, replication, or public delivery are requirements. Start with the storage documentation and verify the capability schema before binding your adapter to request or response fields.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob Storage user delegation SAS
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs

title: GHSA-PJFF-C2WC-F6JM: CVE-2026-48769: Arbitrary File Write and Remote Code Execution via Trusted Image Hash in Canonical LXD…
description:
CVE-2026-48769: Arbitrary File Write and Remote Code Execution via Trusted Image Hash in Canonical LXD and Linux Containers Incus

Vulnerability ID: GHSA-PJFF-C2WC-F6JM
CVSS Score: 9.9
Published: 2026-11-06

A critical path traversal vulnerability caused by improper input validation (CWE-20) exists in the direct image download handler of Canonical LXD and Linux Containers Incus. When an authenticated user requests an image import using the URL source type, the daemon reads the image fingerprint from an untrusted HTTP response header (Incus-Image-Hash or LXD-Image-Hash) without validating that it conforms to a SHA-256 format. This unvalidated string is concatenated directly into a filesystem path via filepath.Join prior to file creation and cryptographic verification, allowing directory traversal sequences to write arbitrary files on the host filesystem as root.

TL;DR

Canonical LXD and Linux Containers Incus fail to validate the Incus-Image-Hash and LXD-Image-Hash HTTP headers during URL-based image imports. Attackers with low-privilege API access can supply path traversal sequences in this header to write arbitrary files as root on the host filesystem (such as /etc/cron.d/), resulting in full host remote code execution.

⚠️ Exploit Status: POC

Technical Details

  • CVE ID: CVE-2026-48769 (GHSA-pjff-c2wc-f6jm / GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x)
  • Weakness Class: CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation / Path Traversal)
  • CVSS v3.1 Score: 9.9 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)
  • Attack Vector: Network / Authenticated API (POST /1.0/images with source.type=url)
  • Impact: Arbitrary Host File Write and Remote Code Execution as root
  • Exploit Status: Public Proof-of-Concept (PoC) Available
  • EPSS Score: 0.78% (56.21st Percentile)
  • CISA KEV Status: Not Listed

Affected Systems

  • Canonical LXD
  • Linux Containers Incus
  • Incus: < 7.2.0 (Fixed in: 7.2.0)
  • LXD: >= 4.0.0, < 4.0.11 (Fixed in: 4.0.11)
  • LXD: >= 5.0.0, < 5.0.7 (Fixed in: 5.0.7)
  • LXD: >= 5.1.0, < 5.21.5 (Fixed in: 5.21.5)
  • LXD: >= 6.0.0, < 6.9.0 (Fixed in: 6.9.0)

Exploit Details

  • GitHub Advisory (Incus): Official upstream advisory containing the complete Python Proof-of-Concept exploit script demonstrating host cron RCE.
  • GitHub Advisory (Canonical LXD): Canonical LXD security advisory detailing the vulnerability and exploit mechanism.

Mitigation Strategies

  • Upgrade Linux Containers Incus and Canonical LXD packages to the patched release versions across all container hosts.
  • Restrict access to the Incus and LXD local Unix domain sockets and remote HTTPS APIs (port 8443) to trusted host administrators only.
  • Enforce strict outbound egress firewall policies on container hosts to prevent the Incus/LXD daemon from connecting to untrusted HTTP/HTTPS endpoints.
  • Monitor host filesystem integrity in critical directories such as /etc/cron.d/, /etc/systemd/system/, and /root/.ssh/ for unauthorized file creation.

Remediation Steps:

  1. Identify all hosts running Incus (< 7.2.0) or Canonical LXD (< 4.0.11, < 5.0.7, < 5.21.5, < 6.9.0).
  2. For Incus installations, update the incus package to version 7.2.0 or later via the distribution package manager.
  3. For Canonical LXD installations managed via Snap or system packages, refresh or upgrade to 4.0.11, 5.0.7, 5.21.5, or 6.9.0 depending on the active channel.
  4. Verify the running daemon version using 'incus version' or 'lxc version' and restart the service if required.
  5. Review /etc/cron.d/ and system logs on previously exposed multi-tenant hosts for any indicators of transient file creation or unauthorized image import attempts.

References

  • Canonical LXD Security Advisory (GHSA-pjff-c2wc-f6jm)
  • Incus Security Advisory (GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x)
  • Incus 7.2 Release Announcement
  • National Vulnerability Database (NVD) Record for CVE-2026-48769
  • CVE.org Authoritative Record for CVE-2026-48769
  • Linux Containers Forum Release Announcement: Incus 7.2
  • Canonical LXD GitHub Repository
